item.title: Traditional gumbo, kettle-boiled bagels, Chelsea buns: What do ‘endangered dishes’ tell us about the world today?
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 4.70
Globalization, overtourism, climate crisis, and social change can all contribute to the loss of beloved cultural practices—including what we eat. But what does this mean for cultural and food heritage? And how can travelers help preserve the flavors that make our experiences so much richer?

item.title: On a yoga mat, this Irish writer rediscovers the language of her motherland
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 4.05
The Irish language—Gaeilge—is experiencing a cultural revival in Ireland. Éalú Aran is one of a wave of retreats and courses that teach the language in an informal setting outside the classroom, keeping it alive for generations to come. “Up onto the toes. Na méara coise, as they’re called. The ‘fingers of your feet’.” Weaving between Irish and English phrasing, Áine Seoighe is directing a yoga and breathwork session. We’re on Inis Oírr, the smallest of the Aran Islands off Ireland’s western coast. This is a Gaeltacht region, where Irish, or Gaeilge, is the dominant language. We’re a few hours into an Éalú Aran day retreat, a bilingual wellness program run by native islander Seoighe since 2023. Through activities such as meditation, nature walks, basket-making and sea swimming, participants are gently immersed in the language. It’s one of many Irish-language-focused events cropping up all over the country, propelled by a resurgence of interest in the vernacular. Now a mandatory subject in the Irish education system, Gaeilge is Ireland’s first official language, followed by English. It seems more people are embracing this aspect of Irish identity that was historically marginalized under British colonial rule. However, despite enjoying it in school, I rarely had cause to use it in my hometown, Dublin, afterwards. But when I recently returned to Ireland after living overseas, I realized attitudes to the language had shifted. Peers are doing re-immersion courses, Irish-speaking cafés have opened, and I’ve started to hear more families speaking ‘as Gaeilge’, a colloquial turn of phrase that means ‘in Irish’. A short ferry ride from Doolin village brings us to the island, with the Cliffs of Moher looming in our rearview as we sail west. On the approach, Inis Oírr’s waymarks emerge: The rusting MV Plassy shipwreck, striped Fardurris Point Lighthouse, O’Brien’s Castle. By the pier, horse-drawn carriages and bicycle rental shops await visitors—the few cars on the island belong to its population of roughly 340 residents. Meeting us by the harbor, Seoighe launches into a welcome ‘as Gaeilge’ before guiding us on a walk around the island’s wind-whipped perimeter. Limestone forms Inis Oírr’s foundations, ground down into white-sand beaches along the shore. Generations of islanders spread seaweed across the land to render it tillable. Miles of dry stone walls crisscross the island’s 2.3-square-mile (5.9 square kilometer) expanse. “The language is such an important part of the island, of the community, of our past and present. Doing anything here on the island has to incorporate the language.” - Áine Seoighe, Éalú Aran retreats An ancient Celtic language, Irish was gradually excluded from legal proceedings, classrooms and state affairs when Ireland was under British rule. Clandestine educators (known as ‘hedge schools’) and rural communities quietly kept the language alive, but it was threatened with extinction by the Great Famine of the 1840s, when Irish-speaking rural areas were plagued by high death rates and mass emigration. When the Irish Free State was founded in the 1920s—giving independence to 26 of Ireland’s 32 counties—its status was restored. English nevertheless remains more widely spoken, but 40 percent of the Republic of Ireland’s population reported that they could speak Irish in the latest census, recorded in 2022. Gaeltacht regions are pivotal to the language’s survival. Seoighe, now 36, was raised speaking Irish at home on Inis Oírr. “When I was growing up, island life was still quite slow,” she tells me. “Irish was very much the only language really spoken in the community.” Though still fluently spoken on Inis Oírr, its use on the island has waned somewhat in recent decades for a number of reasons, including societal changes, social media and TV, Seoighe admits. Bringing Gaeilge into Éalú Aran retreats, which vary in length from a day to a week, was instinctual. “The language is such an important part of the island, of the community, of our past and present,” she says. “Doing anything here on the island has to incorporate the language.” Fionnuala Ní Uallacháin, multimedia officer for Scéal.ie, which catalogues Irish-language events around the country, confirms there has been a surge in their number and variety, from “ciorcal comhrá” (conversation circles) and park runs to stained glass workshops and hillwalking meet-ups. Language courses are “increasing in popularity exponentially,” she says. High-profile Irish artists such as Kneecap, the Belfast group that lyricize in Irish, are partially to credit for the resurgence, and widely seen as a “cool band doing new things with Irish,” Ní Uallacháin tells me. A fresh wave of Irish-language podcasts, such as How to Gael and Beo Ar Éigean, and content creators (among them, Cúán de Búrca and Mollie Guidera) is also driving renewed interest. This grassroots revival is something Declan O’Connor, who teaches surfing through Irish and English at Tonn Nua Surf School in County Mayo on Ireland’s west coast, has observed. “There’s definitely been a resurgence. I’ve noticed it with the surf school, but also I’ve noticed it outside at festivals and in random meetings with people.” This year, he started hosting bilingual surf and yoga retreats on the Mullet Peninsula in the northwest of the county, in collaboration with Irish-language surf group Surfála. “The informal setting, it just loosens [people] up and gives them the opportunity to give it a try,” he says. On the yoga mat, the vocabulary I studied in classrooms of my childhood resurfaces. I’m surprised by how much I remember. A recent study by Irish language course provider Gaelchultúr found nearly 70 per cent of adults want to improve their grasp of the language while almost half of those aged under 25 reported using Irish when socializing. Its research also showed that close to half of people under 44 would send their child to a Gaelscoil, where subjects are taught through Irish—a 20 percent increase on a similar 2015 study. Older generations feel a “wistfulness” for the language, Fionnuala observes. “You see a lot of people going back to [learn] Irish when they retire,” she says. Éalú Aran retreats are open to Irish-language novices, as well as experienced speakers. Attendees have visited from wider Europe, North America and Australia. My British partner finds he can follow along without any basis in the language. Participants are “surprised at how much communication isn’t vocal,” says Seoighe. During one of our hikes, Seoighe forages sea beet, an ancient plant often called ‘wild spinach’, for us to taste and points out currachs stacked on the sand, the traditional Irish boats that once were the only way to access the island. Alternating between Irish and English as we go, she translates Gaelic turns of phrase without interrupting the conversation’s flow. Eventually, we reach a ‘garraí’, a walled plot overlooking a freshwater lake, Loch Mór. Inside is a yurt, the setting for our yoga class. “I’ll go in and out of Gaeilge, but you’ll follow that, I’m sure,” Seoighe tells us, as we begin. The tent is open to the elements. Currachs move across the lake, while a sleepy calf is feeding in the adjoining garraí. “Learning a language keeps the mind active, curious and engaged,” she says. “So for me, wellness and language-learning are a very natural combination: We are looking after the body, the mind and our connection to our culture and the world around us.” For Seoighe, movement facilitates learning. “When we move, we are focused mainly on the movement, not the words. We hear the language repeatedly and naturally, and over time the sounds and words begin to become familiar.” This is certainly my experience. On the yoga mat, the vocabulary I studied in classrooms of my childhood resurfaces. I’m surprised by how much I remember. “Dún na súile … weʻll close the eyes here,” Seoighe says, encouraging us to think of the “gaineamh agus an fheamainn, the sand and seaweed that made the land” as we stretch out on the “talamh” (ground). Lunchtime arrives. A picnic of cheddar cheese, homemade bread and potato salad has been prepared by the island’s Teach an Tae café. It’s been spitting rain all morning, but suddenly the sky brightens and the water glitters; we enjoy lunch on the rocks overlooking the lake. Later, on the island’s main beach, Seoighe fires up the sauna, and we join locals and holidaymakers in the icy water. By the shore, the words snámh (swim) and fuar (cold) come back to me. My time on Inis Oírr has proven I haven’t fully lost my Irish, but I’ll have to put in some work to find it again. It’s a beautiful language to rediscover and we owe so much to its custodians, like Seoighe, who are safeguarding it for future generations. “Keeping the language living is about much more than preserving words,” she says. “It is about preserving a different way of seeing and understanding the world.” ** The writer was a guest of Éalú Aran. Retreats are priced from EUR€95 ($110/AUD$155) per person. Transport and accommodation were arranged by the writer. **** Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. item.title: Are hikes, homestays and conservation-first tourism an alternative to Cancún’s heady nightlife and sprawling hotels?
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 3.42
In the 1960s, the Mexican government backed mass-market tourism with its development of Cancún, but a 2026 directive by President Scheinbaum now puts the focus on regenerative tourism. What does that mean for the region? The Yucatán Peninsula is a dichotomy. You only need to look out of the airplane window as you start your descent into Cancún to see the contrasts. One moment, you’re looking at a 12-mile-long (20-kilometer) spit of sand lined with huge hotel resorts. The next, as the plane drops further, an impenetrable carpet of dark-green jungle rolls out as far as the eye can see. Cancún’s Hotel Zone sprung up in the 1970s and since then, has cultivated its reputation for all-inclusive resorts, high-energy nightlife and out-of-the-box holiday experiences. Overdevelopment has placed a strain on natural resources; the demand for fresh water is draining the region’s ancient cenote (sinkhole) network, while sudden demand for workers is creating overcrowded, unplanned inland neighborhoods. But you don’t have to go far to find pockets of low-impact, community tourism. And this year, for the first time ever, the Mexican government has recognized the importance of the latter. In March 2026, Mexico’s National Fund for Tourism Promotion (Fonatur) and the government signed an agreement to encourage its tourism industry—which represents nearly 10 percent of the country’s GDP—to serve as a tool for social justice, allowing local communities to become active participants in a region’s economic growth. While the Mexican government’s focus was on resorts like Cancún several decades ago, President Claudia Sheinbaum’s current vision is different. They want to support destinations where local communities are the protagonists, ensuring the conservation of natural resources under the stewardship of people who have lived there for generations. The government has named three community tourism projects—Pueblos Mancomunados in Oaxaca, and Maya Ka’an and Camino del Mayab in the Yucatán Peninsula—to receive support during 2026. For the latter, the investment will fund better water and wastewater management, trail maintenance, project equipment, public space maintenance and signage. With the Maya Ka’an and Camino del Mayab within 180 miles of Cancún, it appears to show a change of focus. “Maya communities are not treated as attractions or objects of observation. Instead, they’re recognized as active participants, storytellers and custodians of their own culture and territory.” - Fernando Sarvide, local guide This summer, I hiked the Camino del Mayab in Yucatán with local guides José Luis Bé and Fernando Sarvide. The Camino is a 68-mile (110-kilometer) trail through the jungle just south of Mérida, in the northwest of the Yucatán Peninsula, which connects 14 Mayan communities. The terrain on this route, which opened in 2020, is flat and undemanding, but the high temperatures add challenge to the distances, which average around 14 miles (23 kilometers) per day. My hike began with a short opening ceremony in which our guide Fernando reminded the group that we were guests in the jungle, walking through a place that had existed long before us. The three-mile (five-kilometer) walk from X‘Matkuil to Molas, two of the communities on the Camino, runs along the disused railway that once transported henequen (sisal) from haciendas to the coast for export. In Molas, we learnt more about the Mayan way of life, the history of the haciendas, and the surrounding jungle from community members, before finding refuge in the home of Doña Norma for lunch; we enjoyed traditional pibil chicken and refried beans alongside jugfuls of ice-cold horchata (white rice with milk or water, sweetened with cinnamon and sugar). I soon learnt that mornings start early in these communities, with most activity is done and dusted by lunch. Afternoons are set aside for cooling off with a dip in a cenote or taking a siesta in a hammock in the shade. Camino del Mayab was founded by EcoGuerreros, an initiative that promotes community development, environmental conservation and sustainable tourism. One of the project’s greatest achievements is creating opportunities for local people to earn a living within their communities, instead of having to relocate to Yucatán cities such as Mérida or Cancún for work. Doña Norma is a case in point. She had no way of earning money in her community before but now, she loves cooking lunch for trekkers, welcoming them in her home as part of the Camino del Mayab ‘package’. “It opens the door to new experiences for everyone,” she told me. “Visitors learn about our culture, and we learn from them as we share stories, traditions and perspectives. These meaningful connections go far beyond a shared meal.” Chatting to José Luis, who grew up in the Tzacalá community, he said he believed the Camino has had a positive impact. “It’s helped diversify the local economy while strengthening our cultural identity. It’s encouraged us to value and preserve the traditions, knowledge and heritage that make our community unique.” Thanks to the Camino del Mayab and EcoGuerreros, the community now has a library in a previously disused building. As well as distributing books and keeping local stories alive, it’s also a place where young people can get help applying for university, and other life and work opportunities. For Fernando, a guide from Mérida and former teacher of Mexican history, the hike has changed the relationship between visitors and local people. “Maya communities are not treated as attractions or objects of observation,” he told me. “Instead, they’re recognized as active participants, storytellers and custodians of their own culture and territory.” During the afternoons, we bathed in cenotes, the sinkholes scattered about the Yucatán Peninsula. Now a welcome respite from the merciless heat for hikers and locals, they were once believed to be doorways to the Mayan underworld and are still seen as sacred spaces by many. The hike had been an enriching experience. I had gone hoping to learn more about Mayan culture and met many passionate locals keen to share their way of life with me; particularly memorable was learning to play pok da pok, an ancient Mayan ball sport still played in seven Latin American countries, and sees players hitting the ball with only hips, knees and elbows with the aim of getting it through a hoop suspended from the ceiling. “Those of us who live here have fallen back in love with it, thanks to our visitors. Seeing someone’s eyes light up in wonder… that’s the most powerful thing I’ve experienced.” - Manuel Enrique Galindo Triay, guide and biologist It was the more recent history of the haciendas and henequen dictatorships that struck home the most. Haciendas in Yucatán operated as dictatorships until the 1980s, taking land from Indigenous communities and small farmers. José Luis told me part of the Camino’s mission is to change the mindset in the communities: “You work hard, you accept your lot and you have no power.” I’d met old men who’d worked in the hacienda regime as young boys, while the grand buildings, many of which now lie in ruins, are an ever-present reminder of the injustices of the past and of how life once was in those communities. I was heartened to know that 80 percent of what I’d paid to hike the Camino del Mayab would go directly to local people. Mariana Ramos, commercial coordinator for Camino del Mayab, was optimistic about the impact of government support: “It will help improve infrastructure and signage,” she told me, “and fund safe places where visitors can obtain information, eat, shower and stay overnight, supporting the expansion of our self-guided hiking experiences.” The other initiative in the Yucatán Peninsula to receive support from the government is Maya Ka’an, a large sustainable tourism project that encompasses the Sian Ka’an Biosphere Reserve 16 miles (25 kilometers) south of Tulum, created in 2012 to protect the area’s tropical jungle, wetlands, mangroves, freshwater canals and coastal marine environments while prioritizing community leadership in tourism. Like Camino del Mayab, Maya Ka’an focuses on nature-based and cultural experiences and it’s hoped that government support will help improve infrastructure as well as visibility. Román Caamal Coh, general manager of Community Tours Sian Ka’an (CTSK), led by a 100 percent Maya cooperative and one of the projects within Maya Ka’an, explained why he thinks it was chosen by the government. “It’s a low-impact model, managed by communities and community-based enterprises, and it’s one of the most mature and representative examples in Mexico of conservation led by the communities that live there.” Maya Ka’an’s jungle walks, kayaking, birdwatching, cooking and handicraft workshops are a far cry from the pools, beach bars and snorkeling boats that line the Mexican Caribbean coast. And its accommodation offering—intentionally limited to eco-lodges, rustic cabins or guesthouses—contrasts with the large chain hotels that lie behind gated perimeters along Highway 307 from Cancún to Tulum. I met the team behind Community Tours Sian Ka’an to see how the initiative has been transforming the lives of locals. For its treasurer Lucía Pacheco May, her work has enabled her to pay for her children’s education. “I’m happy, because I never had the chance to study,” she told me. “Where I’m from, there’s only a primary school.” Boat captain Ricardo Caamal Aban, who takes visitors on the project’s Ancient Canal tour through Mayan lagoons and mangrove channels, told me: “I’m proudly Maya… I’m passionate about being in contact with nature and sharing what I know with the people who visit us.” It’s a similar story for guide and biologist Manuel Enrique Galindo Triay: “Those of us who live here have fallen back in love with it, thanks to our visitors,” he said. “Seeing someone’s eyes light up in wonder… that’s the most powerful thing I’ve experienced.” For the Camino del Mayab and Maya Ka’an, recognition by the national government as a worthy alternative to the mass tourism and private investment of Tulum and Cancún has been a significant gamechanger. As CTSK’s Román told me, “”The Maya Ka’an tourism model translates into dignified employment, less migration to the cities, and a community that values its own culture and natural resources.” ** The writer traveled with her family and self-funded this trip including their time with Community Tours Sian Ka’an. Her own spot on the Camino del Mayab was hosted by environmental conservation organization, EcoGuerreros. **** Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. item.title: This Indigenous-led tour in BC is part of a Canada-wide initiative to put First Nations tourism in the spotlight
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 3.12
Seven in 10 Canadians say they’d enjoy learning about Indigenous cultures on their travels, but many don’t know how or where to find a tour. Indigenous-owned Talaysay Tours and B Corp tour operator Intrepid Travel are hoping to fix that. “We are on the unceded territories of the Squamish and Lil’wat people,” says Talaysay Campo, whose name translates to ‘ocean breeze’, ‘wind blowing on the water’ or ‘whispering winds’. “There’s one thing I want to share, and that’s that the land is absolutely everything.” We’re just outside Whistler Village in British Columbia about to embark on a forest trail walk to Lost Lake (Sḵwiḵ), a critical stopping point for Indigenous communities to gather resources and fish when traveling between the coast and the interior. Today we’re on a preview of Campo’s new ‘We Are The Land’ tour. “The reason we chose this name for the tour is something my Aunty Talaysay would tell me when I was a little girl: ‘We are the land’. It means that we are the caretakers of the land,” she says. Campo is co-owner of Talaysay Tours, an Indigenous, women-owned tourism company offering Indigenous-led experiences across British Columbia. Founded by her mother Candace Campo, in 2002, the company is rooted in the traditions and knowledge of both the Shíshálh (Sechelt) and Sḵwx̱wú7mesh (Squamish) Nations, of which the women are members. Walking beneath a canopy of towering old-growth Western Hemlock trees, Campo points out the Devil’s club, a woody shrub used by her ancestors for pain relief. “It’s important to have Indigenous tourism so our local guests and out-of-town guests can build a stronger relationship with the land,” says Campo as we pause by a babbling brook, where glimmers of sunlight dance on the slow-moving creek. “There’s so much going on with logging, global warming—one thing I’ve realized is that if (people) don’t have a relationship with the land, how are they going to take care of it or know how to take care of it?” It’s a question that sits at the heart of a growing conversation about what responsible travel in Canada should look like. As part of this conversation, Talaysay Tours has partnered with B Corp tour operator Intrepid Travel on this new ‘We Are The Land’ experience. It’s aim is to help bring place-based learning, cultural ecology, stewardship and storytelling to Intrepid’s 10-day Grand Canadian Rockies itinerary beginning in 2027. “For us, it’s at the cornerstone of everything that has to do with responsible tourism. We think it’s also just an amazing experience for our customers to really understand the real Canada, and the only way to do that is to partner with an Indigenous-led company.” - Christian Wolters, Intrepid Travel Canada President The Talasay partnership is part of a broader initiative by Intrepid to include more Indigenous tourism across its Canadian itineraries, with the goal to have an Indigenous-led experience on 75 percent of Canada tours by the end of this year, and one on every Canadian itinerary by the end of 2031. According to new research from non-profit foundation Angus Reid, commissioned by Intrepid Travel in July this year and surveying a group of 1,507 Canadians, 57 percent say they are interested in participating in an Indigenous-led tourism experience within Canada, yet fewer than one in five have ever done so. Part of the problem may be visibility. Among Canadians who have never participated in an Indigenous-led experience, 42 percent say they have not encountered one while planning a trip, while another 30 percent say they don’t know where to find one. According to the survey, seven in 10 Canadians would enjoy learning about Indigenous cultures, while more than four in 10 would be more likely to choose a Canadian trip that includes an Indigenous-led tourism experience. The appetite is certainly there. For Intrepid Travel Canada President Christian Wolters, who has joined us on the walking trail, making these experiences easier to access is more than a business opportunity. “For us, it’s at the cornerstone of everything that has to do with responsible tourism,” he tells me, after stopping to taste a few reddish salmonberries, native to the Pacific Northwest. “We think it’s also just an amazing experience for our customers to really understand the real Canada, and the only way to do that is to partner with an Indigenous-led company.” Intrepid is also working closely with the Indigenous Tourism Association of Canada (ITAC) and has committed over USD$350,000 over five years to support the growth and promotion of Indigenous tourism in Canada. This includes adding Indigenous experiences to existing tours, as well as developing new, bespoke experiences alongside Indigenous tourism operators. “Partnerships like this create tangible opportunities and ensure communities gain direct economic and cultural benefits, while supporting our vision of Canada becoming a world leader in Indigenous tourism by 2030,” said Keith Henry, chief executive officer and president of ITAC in a press release. Coming up in 2027, a Huron-Wendat experience in Wendake, Quebec, will be added to Intrepid’s Eastern Canada by Rail itinerary, which will include a guided visit to the Huron-Wendat longhouse at the Huron Traditional Site. This addition will see Intrepid reach its goal of an Indigenous-led experience on 75 percent of their Canada itineraries—a significant milestone on the road to integrating Indigenous-led experiences across every Canada trip. “When it comes to Indigenous tourism in Canada, we only take up five percent of tourism and that’s such a small percentage,” says Campo, as we stand before the lovely Lost Lake with its mountainous backdrop. “So this partnership with Intrepid and other Indigenous companies throughout Turtle Island—these are the partners I wanna work with.” As she distributes traditional ‘hush’ tea made with soothing raspberry leaf, refreshing mint sweet licorice root and vibrant rose hips, we talk of the importance of stories. “When it comes to a lot of Indigenous history and our government, they try to write our story for us,” she says. “We’re redirecting that chapter so we can write and share our stories ourselves.” The writer was hosted by Intrepid Travel **** Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. We are powered by, but editorially independent of, Intrepid Travel, the world’s largest travel B Corp, who help ensure Adventure.com maintains high standards of sustainability in our work and activities. You can visit our sustainability page or read our Contributor Impact Guidelines for more information. Journalist and wanderluster Charmaine Noronha is a travel writer with a penchant for adventure, culture and chocolate. She started her career as a reporter with The Toronto Star before becoming the EIC of Vervegirl Magazine for five years then reported on Canadian news for The Associated Press for 11 years. Most recently, she was a Lifestyle reporter/editor at HuffPost Canada.

item.title: 10 undertouristed destinations where your travel spending will actually make a difference
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 2.89
Sometime, what’s hot is what’s ‘not hot’. That’s the thinking behind Intrepid’s annual Not Hot List, which highlights 10 places around the world that are undervisited, want tourism, have a great reason to visit in 2027, and have the facilities to welcome more travelers. item.title: These 6 Gear Trends Took the Long Trails By Storm in 2026
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 5.46
(Photo: Zoe Gates) On long trails, gear and clothing trends can seem as fad-driven as they were in high school. Caps are out, bucket hats are in. Heavy boots are so 2005. And if you aren’t dressed in a hooded, collared shirt with donuts all over it, are you even a thru-hiker? Show up to the trailhead with the wrong setup, and just like when you were a teenager, you might feel like you risk being laughed all the way back to town for a resupply. Not that every trend exists across every trail, of course. Trail culture—and the gear that contributes to it—varies from place to place. For example, “Ultralight felt very ‘in’ out west in a way that it didn’t out east,” says thru-hiker Madelyn Dukart, who has trekked long trails across the country. When something is hot in the thru-hiker community, it’s only a matter of time before it trickles down to the rest of the backpacking world. And while some gear crazes only stay in vogue for a season or two, plenty of fresh gear and apparel becomes popular thanks to its practicality or innovation. Here are the trends that took the long trails by storm this past season. To say the ultralight material Alpha Direct swept the thru-hiking community off their feet may be an understatement. “Just a year or two ago [thru-hikers] were all about microgrid hoodies, but they definitely have moved on to Alphas,” notes Mary Pillsbury, owner of 2 Foot Adventures outdoor stores located along the PCT in Julian and Kennedy Meadows. It makes sense: Alpha Direct is lighter, more compact, breathes better, and still insulates well when layered under a windproof jacket. Hoodies made from the material have been popular for a few seasons, but this year’s hikers aren’t stopping there: pants, hats, socks, even gloves have been hot ticket items this year for their gram-consciousness and versatility. Head to any trail town and there’s one thing you’re practically guaranteed to find in every hiker box: a quarter-full IsoPro fuel canister or three. After all, no one wants to leave town with one day of fuel left in their canister then have to carry it empty to the next resupply. Enter fuel transfer devices. These pocket-sized wonders allow hikers to combine fuel from multiple partially empty containers into one. They aren’t new this year, but they were formerly built of hefty metal materials. But a 2.4-gram plastic version is becoming ubiquitous: “Almost every hiker carries a fuel transfer device thanks to Alpenglow Gear. They are so light and inexpensive; 3D printing is changing the market,” says Pillsbury. “This is the first year I’ve heard thru-hikers talk about microplastics,” says Pillsbury. Where Smartwater bottles were once the go-to, more hikers have made the swap this year to using reusable CNOC or M!Go bottles, she’s noticed. Smart, since studies have shown that reusing single-use plastic bottles results in ingesting more microplastics. Plus, reusable bottles are designed to last for years and are only marginally heavier. “Most people that get involved in outdoor recreation begin with their love for nature, and it can feel dissonant to preach respecting nature while relying on single-use plastics for such a crucial piece of gear. Seeing multiple brands with thru-hiker-friendly water bottles seems to alleviate some of that dissonance,” Dukart says. Long gone are the days of huffing and puffing into your inflatable sleeping pad every night thanks to the rise of ultralight pad pumps. In fact, the gadgets have gotten so small and light––thanks in part to the rise of 3D-printed gear and the cottage industry––that there’s little reason not to pack one. After all, there’s an option to suit every hiker, from the stupendously light Alpenblow that you plug into a power bank to the battery-powered Flextail Zero Pump. Wander into any thru-hiker camp this season, and you’re unlikely to see many people inflating their pad the old fashioned way. While Durston has enjoyed a loyal cult following for several years now, this past thru-hiking season brought an explosion in popularity. “It feels like you can hardly walk through a campsite without seeing an X-Mid,” says Amber Rae Hedman, a thru-hiker who completed the PCT in 2022 and 2025, among other trails. It makes sense: The unique offset design of the trekking pole tent offers a more spacious layout and for staggering low weight. Plus, while they were once difficult to get as limited batches were often released months apart, more regular production has allowed hundreds—if not thousands—more hikers to become instant die-hard fans. A more surprising piece of gear that’s made an appearance on long trails in the last year are standalone cameras. Be they digital, film, or disposable, more thru-hikers are ditching the photo capabilities of their phones for a dedicated image-capture experience. “Documenting the journey has become such a big part of the thru-hiking experience,” Hedman says. To do so, many modern hikers are turning away from their smartphones. Is it worth the weight? That’s a personal choice. But compact cameras take measurably better photos than phones (and without draining your battery).

item.title: “Bison Belong on This Landscape”: Judge Blocks Federal Order to Remove 1,000 Animals in Montana
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 5.04
Bison grazing on American Prairie (Photo: Courtesy American Prairie) Nearly 1,000 bison that faced removal from federal land in Montana will be able to continue grazing for now after a judge blocked a Bureau of Land Management order seeking to kick the animals out. The lawsuit stems from an order by the BLM this May that sought to remove the bison from public portions of American Prairie. The nonprofit preserve covers more than 600,000 acres of private land and public grazing leases on Montana’s shortgrass prairie, all of it open to the public, and features camping, wildlife-watching, and hiking. The BLM granted the permits for the animals to graze in the first place in 2005. Its new order is rooted in a reinterpretation of the Taylor Grazing Act, which allows the department to issue livestock permits for public grazing. The rewrite seeks to re-categorize the definition of livestock as “production-oriented.” U.S. District Court Judge Brian Morris objected. “No statutory language or judicial precedent exists that requires a livestock operation to focus exclusively on production and entirely ignore conservation, range improvement, preservation, or other values,” he stated in the decision. “Congress recognized livestock grazing and livestock management often includes and considers preservation, improvement, and thoughtful development, hand-in-hand with other uses.” The bison will now remain on American Prairie’s leases while the lawsuit proceeds. The decision will delay the BLM’s original removal order, scheduled for September 30. If that order had taken effect, the preserve would have needed to either cull or remove hundreds of bison from the land, as Beth Saboe, American Prairie’s director of public relations, told Backpacker in May 2026 shortly after the BLM announced the changes. “Worst-case scenario, we potentially would have to get rid of hundreds of animals. We don’t want to see that happen,” Saboe said at the time, adding that the organization planned to appeal any adverse final decision. Besides incurring major costs to American Prairie, Saboe said that removing the bison from the public range would have stripped a restorative species away from its native habitat. The uncertainty around the herd also led to the cancellation of American Prairies public bison harvest for 2026. While the permit revocation had support from the Montana Stockgrowers Association and many local ranchers, American Prairie’s tribal partners pushed back. In a January 2026 letter to the Secretary of the Interior, J. Garret Renville, chairman of the Coalition of Large Tribes and Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate of the Lake Traverse Reservation, wrote that American Prairie had provided animals to and worked with a number of tribes attempting to grow their own herds, and that the organization’s methods of raising bison were “largely indistinguishable from the practices and techniques employed by tribal herd managers.” In his ruling, Morris wrote that he “struggle[d] to see” how the BLM’s choice to impose the new regulation while ignoring American Prairie’s evidence could be consistent with the law. With its redefinition, the BLM sought to limit grazing to animals “used as part of an operation to provide output for various purposes, such as meat, milk, fiber, or other products and any animals when they are being used to assist with management of other animals in connection with such operations (e.g. horses that are used to assist with cattle management).” The BLM itself concluded in 2022 that bison grazing would improve rangeland productivity and riparian health on the same lands it now seeks to remove the animals from. If American Prairie ultimately loses the right to graze bison on its leases, it could choose to replace them with cattle. There’s evidence that could compromise the land: Cattle herds often heavily graze one small area before moving on. Bison, on the other hand, tend to graze more gradually while constantly moving over the landscape, covering up to 2-3 miles per day. Studies have shown this can increase biodiversity and even drought tolerance on native grasslands. “These are the ungulates that evolved with the prairie landscape,” Saboe said in May. “They’re one of the main keystone species here and that’s because of how their presence on the landscape improves the rangeland.” The court’s preliminary injunction covers the three federal allotments where American Prairie bison are currently grazing. It did not grant the organization’s request to protect three other tracts where bison do not already graze. “Bison belong on this landscape, and today’s ruling gives them a chance to stay,” said Alison Fox, CEO of American Prairie. “For more than 20 years, our bison have grazed these lands under federal authorization and without grazing violations. The court recognized the concrete harm that removing them would cause, not just to our work, but to our Tribal partners and the broader effort to return bison to their native home.”

item.title: Forget the Camino: Europe’s Newest 191-Mile Thru-Hike Features Wilderness Wine Bars and Zero Crowds
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 4.16
Logar Valley (Photo: Mediaspeed, foto: Jan Godec) The trail passes through the 3,000-foot-high Logar Valley cinematic as a Peter Jackson sequence: Gnarled apple trees and wildflowers line long, narrow fields of bright green grass, and forests of knobby conifers sweep toward a horizon of snow-capped peaks. Historic stone and plaster homes with low-slung shake roofs huddle near the woodline. The path follows the upper Savinja River, which flows clear and aquamarine over a bed of off-white rock. It passes into silvery linden and elm forests as the valley narrows. A tiny, log cabin-style pub offering wild-fermented wines, žganje (berry liquors), and Carniolan sausage plates overlooks the entry to the cirque. Stairs climb toward a high, bowled ridge. The sound of crashing water echoes off stone. Another bend and Rinka Waterfall erupts from a notch in the sheer cliffside, plunging 300 feet into a bright blue pool. Trekkers can admire the action from the deck of a cantilevered, hike-in bar and café that clings to an escarpment about halfway up the falls, or walk another half-mile to take in the view from an alpine meadow where villagers once summered sheep. A Scandinavian-style mountaintop lodge operated by the Alpine Association of Slovenia offers cheap and comparatively luxe overnight accommodations for thru-hikers. The walk and stay are part of the nation’s newly designated Kamnik-Savinja Alps Water Trail (KSAWT). The 191-mile route connects numerous preexisting paths in a loop that showcases the aquatic resources of Slovenia’s second largest mountain range. The trek is divided into 11 stages that link more than a dozen historic villages and towns, and features three lakes, four rivers, numerous waterfalls, and more than 200 springs and streams. “The international backpacking community has started to call Slovenia Europe’s hidden gem,” says hiking enthusiast and Trail Angel Central (TAC) founder, Scott Vanderlip. The retired software engineer and serial entrepreneur operates a seasonal hiker camp on the Pacific Crest Trail. He’s traveled the world to connect with trekking communities for the TAC and logged miles on many of Europe’s most notable long routes—including the new water trail. “To me, Slovenia is a treasure trove for long-distance backpackers,” says Vanderlip. Particularly those who prefer their alpine views with a hardy side of cultural history and traditional foods, yet want to avoid big crowds. Europe’s most popular long trail, the Camino de Santiago, attracts more than 530,000 thru-hikers a year. The Alpine Association of Slovenia, meanwhile, says just 10,350 people have completed the nation’s cross-country Mountain Trail since it was founded in 1953. What’s more, Slovenia—which borders Northern Italy to the west and Austria to the north—is about the size of Massachusetts and home to some 6,200 miles of hiking trails. That gives its 1.7 million annual trekker tourists plenty of room to space out. The notoriously tough Mountain Trail features more than 23 miles of cumulative elevation gain and 14 peaks above 7,000 feet. The KSAWT, however, is a more laid back adventure. Stages average 10.6 miles a day, inviting hikers to soak in the views and indulge in picturesque swimming holes. The route climbs to high points like the overlook above Rinka Waterfall, but forgoes tough-to-reach peaks like 8,392-foot Grintovec in favor of more accessible alpine valleys, meadows, and the banks of the pristine waterways that flow through them. Mountain huts and lodges pepper the route with affordable places to sleep. Electric shuttle vans patrol nearby roads and make it easy to slackpack to and from amenity-packed stopovers like the Medieval fortress town of Kamnik. Points of aquatic interest like Lake Črnava—which is backed by a 16th century castle and bowl of 7,000-foot peaks—are showstoppers. But the trail was actually inspired by less visible resources. The loop was the outgrowth of a 2022 project to map and raise awareness around the region’s abundant springs. Local stakeholders and conservation groups joined forces with the Slovenian Tourist Board and European Union Common Agricultural Policy Network to map and analyze the most productive natural founts. The group identified fifty-four pristine watering holes, including carbonated iron and mineral springs. Infrastructure like hardened treads, stone headwalls, spring boxes, and outflow pipes were added to both invite and protect sites from hiker visits. Annual drinking water festivals were organized to showcase the aquatic wealth and how it influences local products like wine, beer and spirits. “Then we thought, why not connect these amazing resources in a network that provides a very different kind of experience than your usual mountaineering trail,” says Slovenian Tourist Board spokesperson, Maša Puklavec Polutnik. The KSAWT linked trails to the 54 springs and some of the most scenic portions of the waterways they feed into in 2023. Signage provides insight into their geology and historic importance. “These mountains have acted like a natural water tower that supplies clean, potable water to settlements and villages for millennia,” says Polutnik. Hikers are encouraged to challenge their palates and try to distinguish the subtle differences between springs. They can then compare their own observations to scientific breakdowns with exact mineral compositions and taste-notes for each. “It’s a really cool side quest to do as you’re passing through these astoundingly beautiful and historic areas—and unlike anything that I’m aware of in the U.S.,” says Vanderlip. He encourages trekkers to up the culinary ante by immersing themselves in local foodways. “Every town and village you pass through has its own version of popular regional dishes and drinks,” says Vanderlip. “And they all take deep pride in those differences and traditions.” Wines, for instance, feature unique and often much older grape varietals compared to those typically found in western Europe and the U.S. That and ancient techniques like whole-cluster fermentation (where the stems are left on) or the use of native yeasts brings wildly different flavors than your typical chardonnay or merlot. Pair them with traditional cured meats like zgornjesavinjski želodec—a mix of fresh pork leg and shoulder meat, cubed bacon, sea salt, pepper, and garlic water that’s pressed flat during curing—and iconic cheeses like Trnič, which shepherds on the high-elevation Velika Planina plateau craft from cottage cheese, cream, and salt. “There’s just so much to love,” says Vanderlip. “On one hand, the hiking is world-class and filled with scenery that would more than justify a visit without any of the other perks.” But when you factor in refreshing spring water, historic villages, delicious eats, and nifty cultural traditions? That elevates the KSAWT to a bucket list walk.

item.title: PCT’s Northern Terminus Reopens, to Thru-Hikers’ Delight
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 3.83
Monument 78 and the Canada/ US border marks the northern end of the Pacific Crest Trail (Photo: eppicphotography via Getty Images) The northern terminus of the Pacific Crest Trail is accessible again following a weekslong closure that foiled the plans of many northbound (NOBO) thru-hikers. The 50-mile stretch from Hart’s Pass to the Canadian border reopened on September 9 after having been officially closed since July 31 due to the Ptarmigan fire. Since then, finishing northbound thru-hikers have commemorated the finish line in a number of ways: In late July, some built a makeshift monument at the trailhead for Rainy Pass, just south of the closure. Others rerouted to the west, converging on a little-known obelisk at the Canadian border in the Mount Baker Wilderness. As of today, NOBO hikers still on the trail will be able to take the standard route to the border. “We’re overjoyed to know that the PCT up to the Northern Terminus is open again, as it is such an iconic and symbolic portion of the trail,” says Chris Rylee, Director of Marketing and Communication for the Pacific Crest Trail Association. “Appreciation and gratitude goes out to the Methow Valley Ranger District of Okanogan Wenatchee National Forest and all of the other partners, responders, and firefighters who coordinated massive efforts to keep PCT hikers and communities safe.” As thru-hiking season winds down on the PCT, the reopening comes at a difficult time for many hikers who recently left the trail. Last year, the average finish date for NOBO thru-hikers on the PCT was September 12, according to a survey by Halfway Anywhere. “For me it’s tough because all last month I’ve heard that there’s no possible chance they’d open to the terminus, despite the Ptarmigan fire being more and more contained. Because of this I changed my plans to skip that section and go east to the other monument,” says Reed “Steezy” Patricelli, a thru-hiker from Portland, Oregon who reached the Canadian border on September 6, just three days before the terminus reopened. “As much as it’s a bit annoying, to me its also not a huge deal,” he adds. On his reroute to monument 90, a spot on the Canadian border east of the official terminus, Patricelli says he spotted three black bears and 12 mountain goats: “I firmly believe that the trail is a different journey for everyone, and if the end of my journey had to be a different terminus, so be it!” For others still in the final stretch, the reopening means they’ll be able to cross the trail in the way they’d always imagined. Nicola “Sunflower” Whitbread, a NOBOer from England, is one of those hikers. Whitbread was on the trail in northern Oregon when she heard from another hiker that the terminus had reopened. “The PCT for me has always been about the journey and not the destination, but I won’t lie, I’m stoked that I’ll have the finish I’ve dreamed of for a decade.” In an Instagram post, the PCTA noted that lands east and west of the trail remain closed due to ongoing firefighting operations.

item.title: Three Hikers Used AI to Plan Their Mount Shasta Climb—and Ended Up Needing Rescue
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 2.75
Mt. Shasta (Photo: Mimi Ditchie Photography via Getty) In what rescuers called a “mentally challenging” operation, a team of three young climbers safely descended Mt. Shasta over the weekend after spending an unplanned night on the peak with no warm sleep systems or shelter. The group had hunkered down off trail in a potentially dangerous location after running out of food and water—and rescuers say their reliance on an AI chatbot to plan some aspects of their trip contributed to their ordeal. From going too light on food and water to camping in a prohibited location, virtually on top of a mountain headspring, rangers said the three college students came ill-prepared to meet the challenges of the mountain. “These were smart guys,” said Nick Meyers, program manager for the Forest Service’s Mt. Shasta climbing rangers and avalanche center. “But they just missed the mark. It led to spending all day, all night, and all day again walking up and down off the mountain.” The three men, college students in their early 20s, arrived at the Clear Creek Trailhead to climb 14,179-foot Mt. Shasta on Saturday, August 29. They ascended that night to a well-known base camp area at 8,600 feet, arriving around 8 p.m. The next morning, they launched their summit bid with an alpine start at 3 a.m. They advanced very slowly. Ten hours later, they had managed to ascend another 2,600 feet, covering only about one mile. The summit of Mt. Shasta was still another 3,000 feet up and well over a mile ahead. While their slow pace didn’t signal any specific problem, it was becoming a downstream hazard, because their AI-assisted food and water planning had only fueled them for an 8-hour round trip. “We don’t know why they were as slow as they were,” Meyers said, noting that the group did have a conversation at this point about whether to turn around. By 3 p.m., they had reached a distinctive waypoint at 12,800 feet called Mushroom Rock. According to rangers, the group again debated going up or down, consulting two other parties. One said up, one said down. At 7 p.m., they finally summited Mt. Shasta, 16 hours after they had departed base camp. The climbers turned around quickly, reaching Mushroom Rock again by 8, but ran into another problem right away: the phone they had been using to navigate via AllTrails was dead, and the portable charger they’d brought along refused to charge it back up. The men dialed 911, asking for directions. But they mis-navigated nonetheless, wandering significantly off route to the south. After several more hours, they had proceeded in the dark over a neighboring ridgeline into Mud Creek Canyon, an area with dangerously loose rock where there is no established route up or down the mountain. The group had already called rescuers again to report hypothermia and a knee injury when one of them slipped after dark with no headlamp on. “One thing was leading to another on these calls, and we knew they needed help,” Meyers said. Teams reached the group the next morning, Aug. 31, after an exposed bivy near 11,000 feet. A helicopter rescue—often the standard on the steep, uneven and rocky terrain above treeline on Shasta—was unfeasible due to the location. “They were exhausted, but we had to hike them out,” Meyers said. He added that their condition was less than desperate: They had avoided serious hypothermia, and the injured party member was ambulatory. After some food, water, and a pep talk, all three walked down under their own power. Passing their campsite, rangers found the group’s tent pitched damagingly close to the headspring of Clear Creek, among scattered food wrappers and cookware. They reached Clear Creek Trailhead at 6:30 p.m, concluding the planned 8-hour trip after 39.5 hours. Meyers attributed the incident to lapses of information and mentorship. The group said they knew about the robust Mt. Shasta information website, shastaavalanche.org, but didn’t use it to prepare. They also had suitable gear—a solid tent, headlamps, and snow travel equipment, as well as summit passes—but lacked other equipment that would have supported their plan, like a reliable charging system for their phone or a backup method of navigation.. “Our objective is always to give people information,” Meyers said. “We don’t try to influence what people do, but instead give them the knowledge and resources they need to make good decisions in the mountains. “We know people are going to use AI to prepare themselves, and it’s happening more and more – especially with educated young people. But there’s no excuse for ignoring the information when it’s freely available. We just try to encourage everyone to talk to a real person first. We’re here to help.”

item.title: Colorado Bear Euthanized With Trash in Intestines as Food Scarcity Drives Record Conflict
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 2.58
Unsecured garbage cans are a liability for both bears and humans. (Photo: CPW) Wildlife officials euthanized a black bear in Durango, Colorado, on September 9, after it was discovered moaning in pain in a residential yard. The bear had dug itself into a hole, and the homeowner who called Colorado Parks and Wildlife (CPW) said it was acting extremely lethargic and making strange noises. Arriving on scene, CPW Officer John Livingston and his colleagues immediately noticed the bear’s distended, bloated belly. They managed to get it to stand up, but couldn’t get it to move or leave the area. They tranquilized the animal, and as soon as they touched the bear’s stomach, Livingston says they realized something was very wrong. They made the tough call to euthanize and performed a field necropsy. “Immediately upon getting into the stomach, we just started pulling out cleaning wipes and full trash bags that still had the whole drawstring,” Livingston told Backpacker. “It was pretty rough stuff.” This incident comes as human-bear conflicts are peaking across the state. So far this year, Livingston says CPW has logged over 8,000 bear reports—the most they’ve ever dealt with. The agency has euthanized over 294 bears so far this year. In all of 2025, the number was just 98. “It’s definitely going to be a record year,” Livingston says. Between this year’s drought and a late Spring freeze that devastated natural food supplies, he expects human-bear conflicts to continue rising this fall. That’s why CPW is advocating extra caution among mountain residents—not just for their own safety, but for the bears’. Livingston is the CPW public information officer for southwest Colorado and the lead for the agency’s Statewide Bear Working Group. He says that CPW officers have been responding to bear incidents since June, working 18- to 20-hour days, often without weekends. Bear relocation incidents are up 3.5 times the 5-year average, and euthanizations are up 2.7 times, according to CPW. Livingston was preparing to head out on a bear call even as we spoke on the phone. “It’s been a busy year,” he says. “Across the state, we’re seeing more bears getting into homes and crossing lines that maybe, in most years, they’d be too timid or not quite bold enough to cross.” That’s largely due to two factors, he says: food scarcity and habituation. Livingston points to the record-low snowpack that has caused drought across the state and an early spring freeze in May that decimated natural food supplies in the southwest. That drove bears down into the towns early in the season. Now, Livingston says, they’re habituated to that food source. “As long as they are getting trash and human-provided food like bird seed, pet food, or whatever gets left outside, they don’t have the incentive to go back up and look for those natural foods,” he says. That creates a dangerous situation for these ursines. It’s much easier to make a fatal mistake, like breaking into homes or cars, or eating garbage that they can’t digest, when neighborhoods represent their main source of food. It can even mess with their biology. “Bears that get human-provided foods will continue to stay up looking to eat as much as they can for as long as they can,” Livingston explains. It isn’t cold weather that drives them into hibernation; it’s a lack of food. “In some places, there have been instances of a few bears never denning because they continued to access food year-round.” As winter draws nearer, CPW is asking residents across Colorado to exercise greater caution. Many towns and neighborhoods require bear-resistant trash containers, but Livingston points out that they do no good if they aren’t regularly cleaned, as bears will still be drawn to their scent. If they get broken, owners need to fix them, and make sure they’re secured every night. Failing to do so could result in a $100 fine for the first offense and a $200 fine for subsequent offenses. He also says that leaving windows or doors open, or your car unlocked at night, is asking for trouble. “It may not be a person you have to worry about coming into your house or trying to get into your car at night,” he says. “It might be a bear.” Finally, he says, don’t be afraid to haze bears who wander near your home. Livingston suggests yelling at them, sounding your car alarm, banging pots and pans, or using an airhorn. “If you’re going to take the time to take out your phone and record the bear, help send the right message and record it while you’re yelling,” Livingston says. “We shouldn’t want them being around our homes.” If there is any year to exercise greater bear caution, he says, it’s this one. The bears need our help.

item.title: Hiking Norway's heavily monitored Russian border
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 5.47
Hiking Norway's heavily monitored Russian border A series of scenic paths trace the Norwegian-Russian border. But as you trek through the tundra and forests, you may notice watchtowers and cameras hanging in trees. I'm standing at a hillside clearing in the tundra along the Russian-Norwegian border, watching the Pasvik River ripple and writhe below. Maybe it's the rustle of birch leaves overhead or the buzzing sound of mosquitoes circling all around me, but I have an unshakeable feeling that I'm being watched. Then again, those hairs on the back of my neck could be triggered by the nearby military watchtower, and the fact that this public hiking trail is under constant surveillance. Located in the far reaches of north-eastern Norway on a jagged fjord close to where Finland, Russia and Norway meet, the small town of Kirkenes is best known among travellers as the final turnaround port for a number of small Arctic cruise lines. But increasingly, local operators are leaning into another opportunity: leading cruisers on wind-whipped treks along Nato's northernmost land border to the unfenced-but-heavily-monitored 198km-long line separating Norway and Russia. Here, surrounded by taiga forest, travellers can explore a network of public trails where cameras hang in the trees, watchtowers dot the horizon and military patrols ensure visitors are abiding by the periodic pillars (yellow for Norway, red for Russia) marking the international boundary between the two nations. Drawn by the prospect of exploring the Arctic's most closely watched frontiers, I've set out on a three-hour trek through a birch forest strewn with boggy puddles. The trail runs parallel to the Pasvik River for roughly 1km before it reaches the "border corridor": an 8m-wide (26ft) strip of cleared forest that's a veritable no-man's land where travellers can't go. From there, the trek culminates in a scramble up Russehøgda, a hillside overlooking the Storskog border crossing that is the only legal land border between the countries. But as we enter the forest, my guide, Henrik Hoffmann, switches off his mobile to avoid connecting to Russian data networks. He instinctively taps a satellite phone in his pocket, and I'm reminded that this is no ordinary walk in the woods. The lure of Russia's land border Hoffmann has been leading these border-trek trips since 2025 but relocated to Kirkenes in 2021, just before Russia's invasion of Ukraine a year later. Since then, he says that both Russia and Norway have increased security along their respective borders here. Now, seemingly minor offences, like throwing stones towards Russia, risk heavy fines and wandering beyond the marked international boundaries has resulted in detainments. Still, he says that after travelling along Norway's coastline, many passengers who arrive in Kirkenes on Hurtigruten and Havila cruises are eager to escape the confines of ships and shuttle buses and get an up-close look at where these two nations meet. "Many older travellers are particularly interested because they remember the Cold War and have followed relations between Europe and Russia over many decades," Hoffmann explains. "The hike allows them to experience the landscape for themselves while learning about the history and present-day realities of living beside Russia." More like this: While Kirkenes Tours is the newest operator to offer border excursions, it's not the first. Havila Voyages has been leading visitors to this area since 2000, while Hurtigruten told the BBC that its Norwegian Border tour – which also leads travellers through a WW2 atomic bomb shelter – recently became the most popular of its eight Kirkenes excursions. "Interest in the border has definitely increased over the past few years," says Hoffmann. Despite an initial reduction in tourism following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he explained that understanding the border is now a driving motivator for those visiting Kirkenes. Plan your trip: Kirkenes Tours , Havila Voyages and Hurtigruten all offer year-round walking excursions along the Norwegian-Russian border. In addition to Kirkenes Tours' standard May-November hike, it also offers treks that take in the Boris Gleb Church and ones set under the midnight Sun (May-July). Travellers can hike independently on the public trails, but given the strict border rules, it's recommended to book through a regulated company. Littering, photographing military personnel and touching or climbing markers are prohibited by law. Hikers must carry passports, as Norwegian military patrols regularly request formal identification. According to Anja Tellervo Hansen, destination manager at Visit Kirkenes, these border treks allow visitors to "learn more about what everyday life in our region looks like, and how the closeness to the border has shaped the Kirkenes region over the years". Evidence of this shared history is everywhere in Kirkenes. The town is the only place in Norway where street signs are marked in both Norwegian and Russian. Near the centre, the towering Russia War Monument commemorates the day in 1944 when the Red Army liberated Kirkenes from Nazi occupation. And the nearby Borderland Museum highlights how Norwegians, Finns and Russians have intermixed here for generations. Trekking the trail Soon after landing at Kirkenes Airport, I was whisked into a van that cut through the city, past the port where cruisers had already docked for the day and dropped off at an unassuming layby flanked by dense walls of birch and conifer trees. "Ready?" said Hoffman, who was waiting in the layby with a rucksack, beckoning for me to follow along a stony track. An hour later, I'm stepping up a rocky outcrop as Hoffmann nimbly picks the way ahead. As beads of sweat form on my forehead, I pause, taking in the eerie expanse of birch trees dipping down towards the Pasvik River. Soon, the outcrop slopes onto a flattened summit. Standing on Russehøgda, surrounded by desolate tundra and a horizon of hazy peaks, I momentarily forget that I'm at one of Europe's most scrutinised borders and am consumed by the sheer beauty of the terrain. Then I glance to the right, notice a yellow and red set of markers only a few metres away, and am sharply reminded where I am. Hoffman and I throw down a blanket on top of a smooth rock and sit for a drink. "There's Storskog," he says, gesturing towards two lakefront checkpoints below. From a few kilometres away, I can just make out the occasional truck driving along the E105 to cross into Russia. He says that recreational crossings have reduced, but a handful of vehicles still make the journey on a daily basis. He also explains that while more visitors are trekking these border trails, fewer residents are; Hoffmann has seen more military patrols than local hikers. "You don't see many Norwegians here," he says, "Perhaps it's a classic case of not exploring your own doorstep." As we turn away from Storskog and descend Russehøgda, I find myself silenced by the gravity of the experience. I've spent a lifetime crossing borders and collecting stamps, but I could have sat for hours just looking at Storskog. From painted markers to the distant outline of Boris Gleb Church, centuries of politics and negotiations have shaped this terrain. It's easy to understand why more and more cruise passengers are disembarking to witness it firsthand. --

item.title: Five unwritten rules for visiting Spain
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 5.19
'Paella is just for lunch' and other unwritten rules for visiting Spain Spain is famous for its laid-back lifestyle, but beneath the long lunches and late nights are social codes that shape everyday life. Our expert explains how to read them. While Spain is beloved for its beautiful beaches, romantic architecture and delicious food culture, one of its strongest draws is its famously relaxed pace. No hay prisa ("no rush") and tranquilo ("relax") are oft-uttered phrases here; meals are drawn out and nightlife lasts until morning. Even non-Spanish speakers know the meaning of siesta. Get to know your expert Jill Petzinger is a British journalist and professional travel advisor who specialises in Spain and Southern Europe. Based in Valencia since 2021, she has travelled extensively throughout Spain to explore the many regional cuisines and cultural traditions. But "relaxed" doesn't mean there's no order. Beneath Spain's easy-going surface are silent social codes that shape everything from how people queue to how they structure their days. Instinctive rather than explicitly stated, Spain's unwritten social rules are often based on respect for regional identity, a belief that life is best lived sociably in public and a historical need to work with, not against, the searing Sun. Locals might not say them out loud, but that doesn't make them any less important to learn. From relinquishing your personal space to skipping paella at dinner, here are five unwritten rules that will help you understand Spain from the inside. 1. Trust the invisible queue Try to order at a covered market, pharmacy, bakery, bar or local shop in Spain and you'll typically find people standing around randomly, no clear line in sight. It may seem confusing to the outsider, but there's a deeply ingrained system at play, rooted in a cultural preference for interaction, informality and social trust. "Queues" in Spain do indeed exist, but they are typically spread-out crowds rather than prim lines because of space constraints in small premises or market aisles; standing where it's most convenient solves the issue. But how do you know when it's your turn? What to do: When you arrive, approach the closest person and ask "¿Quién es el último?" (Who's last?) or simply "¿El último?" They will point to whomever is. Once you know who's last, you're free to walk along the displays and peruse what to buy without losing your place. But stay alert: you will get asked "¿El último?", too. 2. Don't assume the meal is over when it's over You've just had the last bites of Spanish tortilla and the last drops of Rioja. But before you ask for the bill, look around. The tables next to you, strewn with empty glasses and crumpled napkins, may look like they've finished too, but they're just entering another phase: the ritual known as la sobremesa. Literally translated as "over the table", la sobremesa is the hour (or hours) after the meal when everyone settles in for a long conversation. It may involve another round of coffee or drinks, but there's no pressure: la sobremesa is all about enjoying each other's company. The tradition is thought to stretch back to the agricultural past, when families sat around the table after lunch as it was still too hot return to the fields immediately. Most Spaniards may no longer till the fields, but the sobremesa continues its role in maintaining relationships. The joy of enjoying each meal for as long as possible has never gone out of style. What to do: Simply relax, put away your phone and keep chatting away. Waiters are used to letting people enjoy their conversations, so just raise a hand to ask for the bill when you're (really) ready to leave. And feel free to linger even longer. 3. Follow the Sun Spain's famously late rhythm can bewilder visitors, with dinners that last until midnight and shops that close for hours after lunch. But there's a logic behind the seemingly languorous rhythm. In Spain, people work with, not against, the Sun. Historically, Spanish farmers started the day early to get their work done before the Sun grew too hot, saving lunch until they were through. Then, in the 1940s, General Franco moved the clocks forward to align with Nazi Germany. Though the country now found itself in the Central European time zone, many stuck to the traditional solar schedule: lunch at 13:00 became lunch at 14:00 as the sun reached its zenith an hour later than before, and dinner happened later, too, as the light now lasted longer. More like this: In Spain, the workday is also slightly longer than the EU average: 36.3 hours per week versus 35.9 hours. Perhaps that's why Spain's famous "siesta" is increasingly less the norm, since 80% of its population now lives in cities. Unable to head home at lunchtime and have a nap, workers now often return to the office or use the post-lunch time to tackle chores. What to do: Shape your day around avoiding the worst of the afternoon Sun between 13:00 and 18:00 – a light breakfast. Check shop hours to avoid slogging through the heat to a shuttered destination, and keep in mind that only tourist restaurants open at 19:00. If you can hold off until 20:30 or 21:00 you'll be able to eat at better establishments. Consider a strategic siesta to help you stave off the hunger, or prepare for a long night. 4. Make room for the crowd Spain is a tactile nation, where touching an arm for emphasis, greeting with hugs and (lots of) kisses, bumping shoulders in a bar and standing close to strangers in a line are all everyday aspects of social behaviour – though they can surprise visitors from places with stricter norms around personal proximity. Furthermore, whether you find yourself in the city or the village, Spanish social life has traditionally been lived in public places like plazas, bars and streets. These shared spaces can get quite closely packed, meaning you end up very close to your neighbours by default. What to do: Don't automatically read physical closeness as rudeness. Stake out your own (little) space but accept that you'll still catch accidental bumps and jostles in busy areas. If you need to squeeze past someone, a simple "perdón" (sorry) suffices, and almost always elicits "no pasa nada" (no problem) from the other person. 5. Don't order paella for dinner or sangria at a bar Thanks to Spain's thriving tourist industry, you'll find the same supposed Spanish staples – sangria, paella and tapas – wherever you go. But Spain is a huge country, with 17 autonomous communities on the mainland, and an equal number of regional cuisines. Traditionally, people ate what was produced locally, and that love for and loyalty towards regional identity when it comes to food is still strong today. Embrace the opportunity to enjoy the beloved dishes of the city you're visiting. Paella is revered as a native dish of Valencia and Catalonia, but wherever you try it, do it like the Spanish and order it just at lunchtime, as it is considered a heavy meal to digest. Tapas bars will serve regional specialties depending on the city, but the sheer creative variety of pintxos is best enjoyed in their Basque homeland. If you're in Madrid in the colder months, don't miss the famous meaty chickpea cocido stew; enjoy gazpacho in Andalusia and most of Spain in the summer. Year-round, consider swerving the sangria. Locals do drink it, but it's not regarded a bar drink: it's more commonly consumed as a punch at parties. What to do: If a restaurant has a photo menu, it will likely be a tourist trap. To explore regional dishes, try a three-course menú del dia in local restaurants during weekdays. These menus are dying out in Spain partly because of shorter lunch breaks and the rise of new, trendier eateries, so look out for places full of locals with daily chalkboard menus, generally indicating fresh, seasonal food. To drink at the bar like a local, order the nationally adored tinto de verano, a mix of red wine and lemonade that contains no hard liquor, or tiny caña draft beers, which stay colder longer. --

item.title: Six US drive-ins where you can stay the night
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 5.01
Six places in the US where you can sleep at a drive-in From retro 1950s properties to modern glamping sites, these places are reviving one of the US's most enduring pastimes – and offering travellers one last classic summer experience. At the Frontier Drive-Inn, there are no televisions in the guest rooms. Instead, as the property rather cheekily puts it, the biggest TV in southern Colorado is right outside your door. That would be the outdoor screen left over from the Frontier's first life as a drive-in cinema, which opened in 1955 and went dark three decades later. Today, the former cinema anchors a retro-inspired hotel where guests sleep in Quonset-style yurts and vintage trailers, then gather outside for films beneath the famously dark skies of the San Luis Valley. As Labor Day (7 September) approaches, the Frontier and other properties like it are providing a fresh take on one of the US's most enduring warm-weather pastimes – and offering one last classic summer experience before the season winds down. For generations of Americans, drive-ins have been inseparable from summer. The country's first drive-in opened in 1933, but they exploded after WWII, when rising car ownership, suburban expansion and the baby boom helped push their number to nearly 5,000 by the late 1950s, according to April Wright, a drive-in historian and director of Going Attractions: The Definitive Story of the American Drive-In Movie in which she visits roughly 500 open, abandoned or former drive-in sites. "Going to the drive-in was just something you did every summer," Wright said. Though their heyday may have passed, Wright says the appeal of drive-ins isn't purely nostalgic. Plenty of younger visitors are experiencing them for the first time, drawn to the fact that a night at the drive-in is as much about the ritual around the film as the film itself. "What it's always been about, and what it is still about today, is spending time with friends and family, and creating an experience," Wright said. Now, a handful of hotels, motels and campgrounds around the US are turning that experience into an overnight stay. Some have revived long-shuttered drive-ins, while others let guests sleep within sight of giant screens that have been showing films for decades. At these properties, film night doesn't end with the final credits. Frontier Drive-Inn – Center, Colorado Luke Falcone, co-owner of Frontier, said the screen had survived decades of the San Luis Valley's harsh weather and was too important to the site's history to lose. "When doing historic preservation projects, if you come across something that isn't broken, you've hit the jackpot," he said. Despite the name, the Frontier is no longer a traditional drive-in: guests don't pull up in their cars, but settle into lawn chairs or onto blankets to watch fan-favourite films under the stars. "By bringing folks out of their rooms (and cars), we provide an entirely different experience that we can all bond over," Falcone said. The programming leans into nostalgic cult classics, while the accommodation is decidedly modern. Best Western Movie Manor – Monte Vista, Colorado The motel was built beside The Star Drive-In Theatre, which opened in 1955 as drive-ins were booming across the US, and many rooms face one of its two screens through large picture windows, with the film's audio piped inside. Each room is named after a movie star, from Cary Grant to Robert De Niro, and guests can also head outside and watch from their cars. More than 70 years after The Star first lit up, it still shows films seasonally (generally from spring to the end of September). Sutherlin/Umpqua Valley KOA Holiday – Sutherlin, Oregon The Sutherlin/Umpqua Valley KOA Holiday campground occupies the former Cloverleaf Drive-In, where the original 100ft (30m) screen survived long after the cinema itself closed. When the current owner bought the property in 2006, they chose to keep the screen and eventually added a digital projector and FM transmitter, bringing films back to the site. Today, films are shown most weekends. Some RV sites sit directly in front of the screen (or have private patios angled towards it), allowing guests to watch from their rigs and tune into the film over their radios, much as they would at a traditional drive-in. Tent campers and guests in the rest of the RV sites can bring chairs or blankets to a grassy viewing area just in front of the screen, where the sound plays aloud. Hotel Caravana at Four Brothers Drive-In – Amenia, New York Unlike most of the places on this list, Four Brothers isn't a survivor from the golden age of the silver screen. The Hudson Valley theatre opened in 2013, reviving the format decades after thousands of its predecessors had disappeared. Since then, the family-run property has added mini-golf, fire pits and Hotel Caravana, where guests can sleep in vintage trailers within the drive-in grounds or even pitch their own tent. Ofland Escalante – Escalante, Utah Set along Scenic Byway 12 in southern Utah, Ofland Escalante occupies a former drive-in site within Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument. Guests spend the day hiking, exploring slot canyons or visiting nearby Bryce Canyon and Capitol Reef national parks, then return in time for the nightly film. "The movie starts just after dusk and it anchors the whole evening," said Noah Ellis, CEO of Ofland Hotels. "It's a key amenity, not an add-on." The old drive-in comes with its own fleet of vintage cars – including a 1957 Chevrolet and Ford Thunderbird – that are parked facing the screen.
