Guests grab complimentary popcorn and classic sweets from the concession stand, choose a car and settle in beneath the desert sky. "The site was a drive-in long before it was a hotel, so keeping actual cars in the mix mattered to us," Ellis said. "There's something about a row of vintage cars, climbing in with a bag of popcorn, that stays with people." Overnight options range from modernised vintage Airstreams to a variety of cabins. Tiger Drive-In – Tiger, Georgia Tucked into the mountains of north-eastern Georgia, the Tiger Drive-In first opened in 1954, went dark in the 1980s and then sat abandoned for roughly two decades. It returned to life in 2004, and today guests can stay after the movie in one of three vintage 1960s campervans parked on the drive-in grounds (each with a private deck facing the screen), or camp in a tent or RV. --

item.title: When Russia colonised California
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 4.52
'The forgotten empire': When Russia colonised California For nearly 30 years, part of Sonoma was ruled by Tsarist Russia, and it played a pivotal – if little-known – role in shaping the US. It's a pretty, two-hour drive north from San Francisco to Крѣпость Россъ. After slicing through the Golden Gate fog, I wound past sunburnt vineyards to Sonoma's remote coast and rolled down the windows. To my left, California plummeted into the Pacific and seals barked from boulders cropping out of the foamy surf. To my right, cliffs rose sharply and titanic redwoods shot up from the road's switchbacks. Suddenly, a lonely twin-domed chapel topped with Orthodox crosses appeared against the blue ocean. I got out and followed a footpath past a Cyrillic sign towards a wooden, frontier-like stronghold built 150ft (46m) atop a bluff hanging over the sea. Every year, millions of travellers set out on the Pacific Coast Highway to twist and turn their way along, one of the US's most stunning roads, as it hugs the entire California coastline. But chances are, few of these road-trippers realise that hidden here on a secluded headland 90 miles (145km) north of San Francisco lies a relic from the days when part of California was ruled by Tsarist Russia. I didn't, and judging by Fort Ross's eerie emptiness, it seems I'm not alone. "Even most Californians don't know Russia once had a colony in California," Kent Lightfoot, an anthropologist at the University of California, Berkeley, later told me. "They all know about the Spanish and the Mexicans, but almost no one knows anything about the Russians being here. It's kind of like the forgotten empire." While some Americans may recall that the US's largest state, Alaska, was part of Russia for nearly 70 years, the Russian Empire's only permanent overseas colony, known as Russian America, also extended into California from 1812-1842. In fact, Russians settled in California decades before newly independent Americans did. Innovative and surprisingly cosmopolitan, Fort Ross (short for Rossiya, meaning "Russia") was intended to be a breadbasket for Russia's struggling Alaskan settlements, but it also became the source of hotly debated plans for Russian expansion across North America. The beginning of Russian America As European powers expanded west in the 1500s and 1600s, Russia expanded east. By the 1640s, Russian fur traders and mercenaries had swept their way across Siberia to reach the Pacific coast. This rush led to permanent Russian settlements along Alaska's islands and coasts. In 1799, Tsar Paul I formalised the empire's Alaska claims by chartering the Russian-American Company. Modelled after the British East India Company, the for-profit venture didn't just control the fur trade; it now controlled all of Alaska as a corporate colony. But there was a problem: while the company was growing rich on sea otter pelts, the colonists were growing hungry because they couldn't farm in much of Alaska's frozen landscape. So, the Russian settlers sailed south in search of warmer climates and Spanish trading partners. California dreaming In April 1806, with his colony stalked by starvation and his crew decimated by scurvy, Russian-American Company director Nikolai Rezanov steered the prow of his ship, the Juno, into San Francisco Bay. As the brig limped towards Spain's northernmost California settlement, a Spanish soldier grabbed a megaphone and demanded the strange vessel identify itself. "Russia," a voice called back. It was a response the Spanish had been expecting for nearly 40 years. Though Spain claimed all of California starting in 1542, it didn't actually occupy it until 1769, after getting word that Russian fur traders were rapidly moving east across the Alaskan islands. To prevent Russian and British advancement, Spain created a chain of presidios (military outposts) along the coast, starting with San Diego. "The expansion of all of Alta [Upper] California, in many ways, was stimulated by the Russians," Lightfoot said. "The Spanish were nervous about the Russians coming south. So, the founding of San Diego, Santa Barbara, Monterey and San Francisco were a response to the Russians in Alaska." During Rezanov's six-week stay in San Francisco, the 42-year-old statesman secured enough food from the Spanish to save the starving Alaskan colonists by getting engaged to the 15-year-old daughter of San Francisco's Spanish commandant. As he sailed back through the Golden Gate, Rezanov realised that the entire northern coast of California was undefended and far sunnier than Siberia or Alaska, so he hatched a plan to extend Russian America into California. In 1812, after years of stealthily surveying the coast, 25 Russians and 80 Native Alaskan hunters settled on a shelf-like plateau overlooking the Pacific on what is now Sonoma County's rugged coast. Here, close enough to the area's abundant sea otter population but far enough from the Spanish Empire's sparsely guarded northern frontier, they lived in a Siberian-designed settlement hewn from California redwoods under the tsar's double-eagle flag. Exploring Russian California Today, Russia's far-flung California colony remains a solitary, surreal place. Set 12 miles (19km) from the nearest town or mobile phone service, the weathered wooden remnants of a once-bustling settlement open onto a 180-degree view of the sea. In two days at the 3,400-acre Fort Ross State Historic Park, I counted 14 other visitors, and except for the occasional chime from the St Nicholas chapel, the only noise breaking the stillness was the waves crashing below the bluff. "There's a magical feel to Fort Ross," said Robin Joy Wellman, who worked as an interpreter with California State Parks for nearly 30 years. "It's something of a mystery, but once people discover it, they say it's one of the most beautiful places they've ever visited." The site's dramatic setting straddles the San Andreas fault, and the same earthquake that flattened San Francisco in 1906 also levelled much of the original wooden outpost. But detailed displays of the partially reconstructed fortress paint a vivid picture of frontier life in Russia's wild, wild East. The heart of the colony was the fort-like stockade, where a handful of high-ranking Russian soldiers, officers and company officials lived in barracks enclosed by a 12ft (3.6m) palisade. I followed Kimsey up the steps of two blockhouses armed with enough cannons to command the coast. He explained that while the Russians chose this natural overlook to defend against Spanish attacks, the two empires never actually clashed, and even depended on each other for survival. "The Russians and the Spanish were at the very far edges of their overstretched empires. They both needed things the other side could provide, so they traded illicitly," Kimsey said. In the warehouse, drying sea otter pelts worth $100 each (a year's salary for a Pennsylvania farmer at the time) destined for China, Europe and Spanish California would have hung from the rafters. Under the bulbous dome of one of the oldest Orthodox churches in the Western hemisphere, the little settlement gradually grew into a cosmopolitan colony, complete with banyas, bakeries and some 60 buildings. "It was a bustling, pluralistic mercantile village, with lots of languages and people from different homelands living together," Lightfoot said. "The stockade was just the tip of the iceberg. The real action was outside." Beyond the fort As Kimsey and I walked out of the palisade, he explained that as the colony expanded to include nearly 400 people by the 1830s, it became one of the most diverse places in California – and virtually everyone there worked for the Russian-American Company. Here, where the sloboda (village) once stood at the edge of the cape, paid Aleutian and Kodiak hunters lived with Native California women, mixed-race Russian and European Creoles married local Kashaya Pomo and Coast Miwok workers and people were buried next to each other at the Old Russian Cemetery up the hillside. Compared to other European colonies, it was also largely tolerant. "The Russians didn't come here to 'civilise' like the Spanish," said Kimsey, who serves as the tribal liaison for the area's Native communities. We then followed a steep path down to a crescent-shaped beach where coopers, carpenters and blacksmiths brought in by the Russian-American Company from as far afield as Finland and Hawaii once worked side by side. "This is where the first ocean-going ships in California were built," he said. It's also where the first bricks, glass and windmills in California were made. As workers crafted longboats, forged iron, cast brass and made metal, Fort Ross became the centre of manufacturing in California. The Russians traded these highly coveted goods with their Spanish and (later) Mexican neighbours in exchange for further provisions for their Alaskan settlements – and in doing so, they unwittingly helped their rivals settle California. More like this: This shallow-water cove was also where cargo boats and kayak-bound hunters would set off for the colony's main deep-water port 20 miles (35km) south in Rumyantsev (present-day Bodega Bay) and its sealing station off the coast of San Francisco on the Farallon Islands. As Fort Ross' footprint grew, so did the calls from within the Russian-American Company to heed Rezanov's recommendation of annexing North America's west coast for Russia. In 1821, Tsar Alexander I issued an imperial decree claiming Russian control over modern-day Oregon through Alaska. The US's soon-to-be sixth president, John Quincy Adams, swiftly objected and his warning to Russia that the Americas "are no longer subjects for any new European colonial establishments" established one of the most fundamental principles of US foreign policy: the Monroe Doctrine, which opposes foreign interference in the Western hemisphere. From the beach, Kimsey and I climbed a steep hill past the stockade to the orchard the Russians started with a single peach tree in 1814 and pushed open the gate. Of the hundreds of citrus trees and crops the Russians planted, only a single branch of a 200-year-old Capulin cherry survives. Yet, the Russians actually left a far greater agricultural legacy here than most people realise. "It was the Russians who planted the first grapes in [what is now] Sonoma County in 1817," said Megan Jones, Sonoma's official wine librarian. As Jones explained, while Sonoma is now considered "the birthplace of the modern American wine movement", Russian traders introduced the now-rare Mission grape to Sonoma and produced small batches of light red wine. For all its innovations, however, Fort Ross never succeeded in its two main goals: turning a profit and feeding hungry Alaskans. By the early 1820s, the Russian-American Company's Native Alaskan hunters had speared so many sea otters they wiped out the local population, and a combination of heavy coastal fog and rampant rodents yielded just 13 tonnes of wheat annually between 1826 and 1833. When the British-run Hudson's Bay Company agreed to supply Russian Alaska with provisions from its Pacific Northwest settlements starting in 1839, it was the beginning of the end for Tsarist California. Two years later, a Swiss emigrant named John Sutter purchased Fort Ross' buildings and assets from the Russians for $30,000. He cannibalised parts of the structures to create his new settlement in Sacramento. Seven years after the Russians sailed back to Alaska, a chance discovery on Sutter's property ignited the California Gold Rush. Russia's California legacy Today, reminders of California's Tsarist past are still scattered across the Golden State as you drive north from San Francisco. One of the city's most famous neighbourhoods, Russian Hill, gets its name from the graves of Russian-American Company sailors discovered there during the Gold Rush (look for a plaque near 1120 Vallejo Street). A historical marker at Bodega Bay shows where Russians set sail for their Alaskan capital, Novo-Arkhangelsk (present-day Sitka). And more than a million people visit the Russian River Valley each year to splash, hike and taste some of the US's best wines. "The Russians called this river Slavyanka, and it's one of the main arteries they used to exploit the area," said Suki Waters, a Kashaya Pomo descendant and the owner of WaterTreks, which leads eco-tours along the Russian River. As we kayaked past harbour seals and migrating pelicans, she recounted stories from her great-great-grandmother, who was alive when the Russians sailed in. "Fort Ross was a seasonal fishing village called Metini for thousands of years," she said. "When the Russians first came, the Elders called them the 'Undersea People', because from high on the bluff, it looked like they rose out from under the ocean." Later that afternoon, I walked back through Fort Ross' Cyrillic signs, stockade and sloboda towards a lone bench at the edge of that bluff. Peering across the Pacific, I wondered how many days it would take to reach Russia. But as a distant chime from the chapel echoed in the air, I was reminded of something Wellman told me. "The fact that a little part of Russia was right here in California is amazing. Why would we ever want to forget that?" --

item.title: The 4,554m hike to Europe's highest overnight stay
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.79
Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita: An icy 4,554m hike to Europe's highest overnight stay You can sleep over at this historic mountain refuge straddling the Italy-Switzerland border – but only if you're willing to undertake a days-long, high-altitude icy mountain trek. I'm roped to four strangers, concentrating on the light cast by my headtorch, as I wend my way through the icy labyrinth of crevasses tearing across the Alpine Lys Glacier. We've been here since 05:00, tugging each other ever higher up the Monte Rosa mountain massif towards the highest altitude building in Europe. We've just reached a giant mountain bowl filled with clouds of snow. The milky blue twilight fades to the soft glow of dawn. Our guide squints into the distance. "Up on that ridge" he says, "Do you see it? That's the Margherita refuge." I can't see anything, but the peak he's pointing towards is so sheer sided that I'm convinced he must be mistaken. We press on and, by midday finally arrive at the summit, 4,554m (14,941ft) above sea level. The crystal frosted world of the Punta Gnifetti peak is revealed. I can see the refuge now. I gasp. Somewhat resembling a giant tin can, the narrow three-storey metal building is not so much built onto the mountain as it is balanced on the edge of a precipice. On one side is a steeply falling snow slope and on the other, there's just a vertical kilometre of thin air. A refuge fit for a queen Sharing the Alpine border between Italy and Switzerland, the Monte Rosa massif contains some of the highest peaks in the Alps, including Monte Rosa itself, which at 4,634m (15,203ft) is behind only Mont Blanc. Punta Gnifetti (also called Signalkuppe) comes in sixth. It's here where an Italian scientific research facility and mountaineers' shelter was constructed and named for the then-queen of Italy, Margherita of Savoy. The queen, famed for her adventurous, athletic nature, insisted on climbing to the refuge herself for its 1893 inauguration and spending the night. Plan your trip: When to go: The Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita is staffed only between mid-June and early September. This is a very popular hike, so make guided tour, accommodation and travel reservations well in advance. The refuge sleeps 70 in summertime. How to do it: Most people climb with a qualified local guide on organised tours, which depart daily in summer. To stay overnight at the rifugio, choose the three-day climb. What you need: Winter clothing, sturdy mountain hiking boots and crampons (not micro spikes). More than a century later, the refuge still supports scientific research while also operating as a mountain hut (rifugio) offering rustic accommodation and thrilling panoramic views. Hiking the massif's eternal winter landscapes has become a popular trek in its own right. Roughly 30,000 hikers summit the peak each year and 4,000 stay overnight, ready like me – and Queen Margherita – to say they've slept in the continent's highest beds. I opted for a three-day guided hike, which requires crampons and ropes. As a frequent hiker, this didn't faze me. If anything worried me, it was the altitude. The hike to the refuge involves a dramatic gain in altitude, from 1,200 to 4,554m (3937 to 14,941ft) in just two days, so steady acclimatisation is essential. More than 4,000m into the air My journey began a day earlier in the Italian mountain village of Alagna Valsesia, at the slopes of the Monte Rosa massif – the literal end of the paved road before the mountainous ascent. From here, a series of cable-car rides whizzed me uphill to Punta Indren, (3,275m/ 10,745ft) where I met my guide and the four other members of our climbing group. Since we were all still acclimatising, our first day involved little more than an hour's hiking across rock and ice to where we would spend our first night, the Rifugio Città di Mantova (3,498m/ 11,476ft), a large wooden mountain refuge set just below the start of the Lys Glacier. There was a marked difference in temperature from Alagna Valsesia, but by wrapping up warm from the biting wind, I could enjoy the panoramic terrace with views of the green valley far below. Despite the stunning setting, I slept fitfully – due, I suspect, to excitement about the coming day's 1,000m (3,281ft) ascent and my body adjusting to the altitude. It was almost a relief when the alarm went off at 04:00 and we crawled out of our beds. We strapped the crampons onto our boots to prevent sliding on the glacial ice and roped ourselves up together – just in case someone slipped into a crevasse. We set out over the glacier and, after an hour or so of hauling ourselves through a spiderweb of crevasses, cleared a ridge and trudged across the mountain bowl. Behind us, dawn clouds bubbled in the valleys and ahead stood the walls of 4,000m (13,123ft) peaks. Despite the drama of the Alpine scenery, this middle section of the hike was considerably easier than traversing the steep, ruptured and torn up glacier crossing. Before I knew it, we were starting the final haul up to the refuge. Although I've never suffered major ill effects from altitude, I do struggle with vertigo. As we zig-zagged sharply up the summit cone, teetering alongside a ridge that fell away into the haze, I began feeling the unmistakable dizzy sensation kicking in and, instead of taking in the view, concentrated on where I was placing my feet. But when I next raised my head, we had made it. The vertigo eased as I stepped out onto the snowy dome. Fold after fold of mountain peaks sparkling with icy crowns stretched out around me – and the refuge itself. I was exhausted. But would I be able to sleep in what was easily one of the most hair-raising buildings I had ever seen? The highest sleep in Europe Once inside, the refuge felt more like a safe cocoon, and it was easy to forget how precarious our situation was. A dining room took up almost the entirety of the ground floor while the upper two were filled with dormitory-style beds which, the night of my stay, were completely booked. I dropped my backpack onto one of the bunks and headed downstairs to order a frothy bowl of cioccolato caldo (hot chocolate) topped with a dollop of Chantilly cream. As I savoured the drink, I fell into conversation with Tommaso Bagnati, one of the refuge's four wardens, who told me how the weather conditions can bring the reality of living on the top of Europe into stark focus. "When there's a big storm the building shakes a bit and you can feel very small," he said. "If there's a thunderstorm it can feel like you're right in the middle of it. All our supplies are delivered by helicopter, so when the weather is very bad and the helicopters can't fly, you can feel a bit cut off from the world." As I sat down to dinner, a weather front rolled across the mountains. The refuge became blanketed in clouds and sleet splattered against the windows. Sitting next to me at the communal dining table was Chinese YouTuber Jianpeng Cui, who told me that despite the "end of the world" feel to the place, he was pleasantly surprised. "I thought there'd only be a bed," he said. "No toilet. No kitchen. But it's not at all like that. I can even buy pizza and juice up here!" I was relieved that altitude sickness had missed me this time. But not everyone was so lucky. Mikhail Morozov, whom I met on his way down from the summit, had suffered headaches and nausea. "Coping with the altitude was the hardest part," he said. "I wasn't acclimatised and you go up very fast. After a couple of hours, the altitude started to hit me hard." More like this: Life in the Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita – as with all mountain huts – is very communal. Sleeping at high altitude in a cramped dormitory with seven or eight strangers, sharing two toilets with no shower, means you get far cosier than you perhaps want. But the shared effort of reaching the refuge also creates an easy camaraderie. "The best part for me has been meeting people from all over the world who have come here to climb the mountain," said Craig Shaw, a New Zealander living in Switzerland. "Seeing all these different nationalities together in this refuge is just phenomenal". Perhaps the real magic of this mountain is not just its ability to support a crazily positioned refuge. It's an ability to bring people together. --

item.title: Inside the places that shaped Dolly Parton
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.42
'Everything about her was East Tennessee': The places that shaped Dolly Parton From her Appalachian childhood to Nashville and Dollywood, a journey through the Tennessee she loved – and transformed in return. On a sunny day on 24 June 2026, hundreds of travellers, locals and Dolly Parton fans from across the US gathered in the small rural community of Cornersville, less than an hour's drive south of Nashville, for the unveiling of her Tennessean Travel Stop. It was the country star's last public appearance before her death just two months later. Wearing her signature fringe and rhinestones and a grin as bright as that Tennessee morning, Parton cut the ribbon and welcomed travellers to the new roadside stop, complete with a Southern meat-and-three restaurant, live music and – of course – a Dolly-themed gift shop. It was a fitting final chapter for an artist whose life and career were inseparable from Tennessee. From crooning about the Smoky Mountains to investing in rural East Tennessee where she grew up, Parton spent decades sharing her home state with the world – and transforming it in return. Explore Parton's Tennessee mountain home In 1964, US President Lyndon B Johnson launched the War on Poverty, a federal effort to reduce poverty and expand economic opportunity across the United States. Southern Appalachia, one of the nation's poorest regions, was thrust into the national spotlight. Media portrayals often depicted its residents as backward and destitute, reinforcing the caricature of the "hillbilly", a stereotype that had persisted since the 19th Century. But when Dolly Rebecca Parton came into the spotlight, this daughter of Appalachia who grew up in a two-room cabin with 11 brothers and sisters offered the world a different view of her home: one of joy, dignity and talent. Follow Dolly Parton's story across Tennessee Sevierville: See the bronze statue of Parton outside the Sevier County Courthouse and The Pines, where she performed for a paying audience for the first time at just 10 years old. RCA Studio B, Nashville: Visit the legendary recording studio on Music Row where Dolly Parton and other iconic artists like Elvis Presley recorded some of their greatest hits. The Country Music Hall of Fame, Nashville: A must-visit Nashville institution that chronicles the history of country music through artefacts, exhibits and the stories of the artists who trailblazed the genre. Dollywood, Pigeon Forge: Set in the Smoky Mountains that Parton loved so dearly, Dollywood takes guests on a journey through the singer's roots, from an exact replica of her childhood two-room cabin to the Dolly Parton Experience, which displays childhood memorabilia. "Dolly Parton told a new story about Appalachia that was rooted in her very particular experience," said Dr Jessie Wilkerson, a history professor and Appalachian scholar at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. "Yes, her family was poor, but they weren't desperate or hopeless, and they took care of one another. There was a lot of love and beauty in the place where she grew up, and so we get a different story about Appalachia through her." In the title track of her 1973 album, My Tennessee Mountain Home, Parton describes her Appalachian home as "peaceful as a baby's sigh". The landscape around her childhood home on the edge of the Great Smoky Mountains, along with Appalachia's storytelling traditions and bluegrass heritage, inspired much of Parton's music. In Great Smoky Mountains National Park, a blue-grey mist that gives the Smokies its name settles over the peaks and valleys and waterfalls tumble through the forest. The 522,000-acre expanse is threaded with hiking trails and scenic overlooks, with autumn bringing a canvas of brilliant jewel tones and spring a kaleidoscope of wildflowers to the lower slopes. The landscape was a reoccurring muse, from the mountain blooms that inspired her 1987 ballad Wildflowers to the fog-covered peaks evoked in Blue Smoke, the title track of her 2014 album, and the pastoral idyll captured in My Tennessee Mountain Home. In nearby Sevierville, the main town serving rural Locust Ridge, where Parton grew up, the region's pride in its local legend is evident. A bronze statue on the courthouse lawn depicts her as a young girl playing guitar. Down the street is the Wings of Wander mural, inspired by her hit song Love Is Like a Butterfly, and the Red's Cafe mural, another larger-than-life depiction of Parton as a child, this time getting a cheeseburger from her favourite childhood restaurant. "People in East Tennessee really, really adore her, and it's something that's been important for the region to have someone who's really proud of coming from there, and who's a positive representation of Appalachia, when historically the representations of the region are the opposite," Wilkerson said. Retracing Parton's path in Nashville On the day Parton graduated from high school in 1964, she boarded a Greyhound bus headed west for the neon lights of Nashville. In a letter home shortly after arriving, feeling homesick and uncertain, she wrote, "Nashville isn't what I thought it was gonna be, but I think I'll like it once I get used to it." "When she came to Nashville, she came with a very distinct East Tennessee identity and made that very clear in both her music and her accent," said Robert K Oermann, co-author of her memoir Dolly Parton: Songteller, My Life in Lyrics and a longtime collaborator. "Everything about her was East Tennessee and mountain, and I think that was the message she brought to Nashville." Nashville looks very different today from when Parton first stepped off that bus 62 years ago, but visitors can still trace Parton's path from her early days fresh out of Sevier County to her rise as a country music icon who never lost the Appalachian sound of home even as she became one of Nashville's biggest stars. On Music Row, the city's historic record-industry district, visitors can step inside RCA Studio B where a blue X marks "The Sweet Spot" where Parton recorded hits including Jolene and I Will Always Love You – both of which she wrote on the same day. Nearby, the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum is featuring Dolly Parton: Journey of a Seeker, an exhibition spanning her career and featuring memorabilia like her Gibson five-string banjo and handwritten music drafts. A few blocks away, the historic Ryman Auditorium is where a 13-year-old Parton made her Grand Ole Opry debut in 1959 and earned three encores. Murals of Parton dot the city in her honour, museum exhibits display her stage costumes and in the wake of her passing, fans have left flowers on her star on the Music City Walk of Fame. Visiting Parton's Appalachia Nashville, however, was never the end of Parton's journey. The further her career carried her from the mountains to Nashville and eventually Hollywood, the more firmly she seemed to plant her roots at the centre of her story. In 1982, she told Barbara Walters in an interview about her dream of opening a "mountain Disneyland" in her Appalachian home region. More like this: Today, that "mountain Disneyland" is Dollywood, a major tourist destination in Sevier County that invites visitors into the version of Appalachia Parton spent her career sharing with the world. Beyond the thrill rides and water park are shows featuring Parton's music, some performed by members of her own family. But to Parton, Dollywood was also a way to give back to the mountains and the community that nurtured her. --

item.title: Glamping on Vermont's newest bikepacking trail
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.43
The US's newest bikepacking trail is pioneering a whole new way to see Vermont The Heart of the Greens trail threads through Vermont's stunning Green Mountain wilderness, and is the first part of an ambitious bikepacking adventure that will someday span the state. My mountain bike tyres thud over pebbles and roots as I whizz through the darkening path. Dusk has fallen over Vermont's Green Mountain National Forest and nearly 400,000 acres of woods extend in every direction. In the distance, I spot pinpricks of light. The campsite is finally near. In the last fleeting moments of light, I arrive at the Chittenden Brook campground. As I wheel my bike past the welcome sign, I spy a slick, modern hut with pine siding. I'd planned to simply pitch a tent – to this weary bikepacker, the hut's glass windows and wraparound porch seem like the lap of luxury. Next time, I thought, I'm staying there. This hut is part of the Heart of the Greens Loop, a 38-mile (61km) bike trail loop and the first completed segment of an ambitious, continuous bikepacking network that, when completed, will stretch 485 miles (780km) and span the entire state. Plan your trip When to do it: Spring and summer are ideal, but tackle the trail in autumn to appreciate its stunning changing leaves. Most riders can expect to complete the loop in one to three days. How to get there: Rochester has limited bus service, so it's easiest to drive to the trailhead. Alternatively, park in Pittsfield and start your ride from there. What to eat: Bring your own provisions. The two villages anchoring the trail have a handful of eateries, like Rochester's farm-to-table Maple Soul and Pittsfield's Clear River Inn & Tavern. Sample dishes made with Vermont's famous maple syrup, like the iconic Creemee ice cream. Pittsfield has two general stores. Blazing a path for bikepackers My journey began that morning in Rochester, a picturesque village nestled in Vermont's mountainous White River Valley. I've driven through it dozens of times without stopping, but since it became the official start and end point of The Heart of the Greens when it opened in 2024, the tiny town has become a magnet for bikepackers. Like me, many are eager to blend the escapism of camping with the thrill of cycling through Vermont's glacial-carved wilderness and explosion of autumnal colours. The loop is a closed-circuit preview of the forthcoming Velomont, a bikepacking route through Central Vermont with a twist: it will be connected by 30 cleverly spaced off-grid huts allowing tired pedallers to bed down in protected forest shelter. On track to finish the first 200 miles (321km) within the next 10 years, the project echoes a larger trend in bicycle travel: statewide bikepacking routes are in development in Utah, Massachusetts and along the entire West Coast. I grew up near Rochester and have dreamed of such a multi-day bikepacking route. For now, I'm thrilled to take on the Heart of the Greens. Two huts are already placed along the trail, roughly 19 miles (30km) apart: the Chittenden Brook Hut, featuring simple bunks and a self-service kitchen, and Spikehorn Yurt. The yurt doesn't have electricity, and neither accommodation has running water. The route's huts will straddle a curious middle ground between camping and traditional stays, allowing bikepackers to carry lighter gear and immerse themselves in the wilderness. The Heart of the Greens may be considerably shorter than the Velomont, but with a cumulative ascent of nearly 6,000ft (1,830m) on largely unpaved forest roads and trails, it's no less intense. "It's a big walk on the wild side," says Doon Hinderyckx, owner of Green Mountain Bikes in Rochester, when I stop by before shoving off. Hinderyckx encourages visitors to hire e-bikes for navigating the steeper grades: "You're mixing mountain biking and the adventure of the challenging terrain. You're on and off the seat a lot." It also requires a bike with thick tyres and suspension, a water filter and provisions, since the current route passes through only two small backcountry villages – Rochester and, 9 miles (14km) south, Pittsfield. Like the huts, eateries and general stores along the trail itself are still in development, so I've packed several meals, plus rain gear and insect repellent, despite the beautiful late summer weather. Hinderyckx checks the air pressure in my inner tubes and oils my chain. He's the last mechanic I'll see for the next two days. Next door to Green Mountain Bikes stands the Stable Inn, run by Hinderyckx's wife, Anni MacKay. This handsome two-story guesthouse opened in 2023, with a range of rooms, Nordic-chic decor and rooftop solar panels, converted from a timber-frame warehouse from the 1840s. While not an official hut on the trail, the Stable Inn has become a base for many Heart of the Greens riders to unwind, or bookend their bikepacking journey with jaunts to the village's quaint art centres and shops. "[The loop is] a very strategic, positive thing," says MacKay. "People always want to have access to the backcountry, in a safe way, with the benediction of the community that is providing services. It's a complete win-win." Ups and downs in the Green Mountains I know Vermont well and have bike-toured widely, but this is harder than I expected. On asphalt, a 38-mile ride makes for a pleasant afternoon. The Heart of the Greens is far more demanding – and adventurous. Rugged roads lead to mountain bike trails, which scissor their way up the alpine forest. The first day, I coast south along Route 100 and turn onto State Garage Road, into a residential area. Houses disappear beyond the canopy, and I huff up one shelf of road, then another. All at once, the road transforms into steep gravel. I grind past the Spikehorn Yurt, the Loop's first hut, a rounded fabric enclosure with bunkbeds, a futon, homey furniture and a spacious terrace with views of the mountains. The route then devolves into two dirt tyre trenches cutting through the grass – what mountain bikers call "double track". My temples pound as I climb. Summer mosquitoes drone in the sultry air. After a couple of gruelling miles, the road finally descends, and so do the conditions. Logging lorries have shredded the ground into potting soil, my wheels sink into a mire of turned earth and broken branches. As I struggle, another cyclist pulls up behind me. "This is crazy, isn't it?" he wheezes. "I don't think I'd have made it if I wasn't on an e-bike." I can't help but agree. The grades are tough on my middle-aged thighs, and I frequently dismount and push. I got a late start to begin with, and as I reach the third major trail section of the day – a mile of switchbacks cheekily named "Perspiration" – my legs boil with lactic acid, and the Sun melts beyond the ridge. This is how I come to arrive at Chittenden Brook Campground after nightfall. I pitch my tent onto the cold ground and gaze longingly at the modern hut before me. Riding high After a decent night's sleep, I finally hit my stride. I sail down the smooth pavement of Route 73 and pedal through the pastoral scenery of the quiet, unpaved Bingo Brook Road. Dense trees all around, I pass occasional farmhouses and cottages, but most of this land is national forest. Fog lifts over a pond, and the air is cool and quiet. I try to imagine what the Velomont will look like in future decades. The Heart of the Greens now passes through just two village centres with a loose string of businesses straddling Route 100. As the Velomont expands, it will tether together more towns and country shops, making it easier for cyclists to resupply and interact with locals. Bikepackers will traverse ever-more-varied terrain and, like me, stop in towns they might never notice by car. "You're camping, but you're not really camping," says Georgia Grzywacz, a Maine resident who rode the loop and stayed at the Chittenden Brook Hut in June. She appreciated the kitchen, electricity and bunk mattresses, as well as the nearby brook. "You're without running water, but you have these creature comforts." Even the booking process was easy: "The [Vermont Huts] website is so navigable." I veer off Bingo Brook Road to find a final trailhead. Two mountains remain, totalling 12 miles (19km) and more than 2,000ft (609m) of climbing, but this time, I'm prepared. Teeth clenched, I grind my way up the switchbacks of Swan's Mill Trail, fighting for every foot of elevation. More like this: At last, my reward: Tunnel Ridge is a five-mile-long (8km) flow trail that snakes its way back down to Rochester, for a total of 110 switchbacks. My tyres shudder over washboard terrain and swerve around S-curves. I choke the brakes, my saddlebags bounce noisily over my rear rack. The forest becomes a wash of brown and green. Gravity lures me downward, into the valley. Endorphins flood my brain as I drift into The Stable Inn's parking lot, back to my waiting car. I'm euphoric but exhausted. For now, I'm closing the loop. But in time, there should be many miles, and many huts, more. And I'll be ready. --

item.title: What Is Half-and-Half, Exactly?
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.52
Despite the promise of its name, the half-and-half you buy at the supermarket isn’t actually equal parts heavy cream and whole milk. While the dairy-aisle staple does fall somewhere between the two, and you can get away with substituting it for one part milk and one part cream in most cases, the truth is slightly more complex. By law, half-and-half must contain between 10.5% and 18% milkfat. Most commercial products land on the lower end of that spectrum, at around 11.5%. The result is dairy that’s richer and more luscious than whole milk, but more fluid than heavy cream. Whole milk, meanwhile, has a fat content of about 3.25%, and cream contains at least 36%. Mix the two in equal measure, and you’ll end up with something considerably richer than most store-bought half-and-half. For a closer substitute, combine two parts milk to one part cream (~14%) or three parts milk to one part cream (~11%). What about shelf-stable half-and-half? Your first interaction with half-and-half might have been those tiny cups that get tossed on the table at diners, fast food joints, and other less-than-fancy places. One or two of them does the trick to make even the cheapest, most burnt coffee taste better—or, at the very least, creamier. To keep these thimble-sized cups shelf-stable, manufacturers use ultra-high-temperature processing and may add stabilizers. Similar-looking cups labeled “creamer” may contain little to no actual dairy. What is fat-free half-and-half? Fat-free half-and-half is typically made from skim milk that’s been amended with thickeners and other stabilizers. While the cartons might look similar, the taste and texture aren’t quite the same (not creamy like melted ice cream, but creamy like melted shaving cream). Some manufacturers claim the cooking properties of their fat-free products are equal to those of regular half-and-half, but we generally don’t recommend swapping one for the other. How to cook with half-and-half Half-and-half is an ideal ingredient for soups, sauces, mashed potatoes, and custards when you want richness without the heft of heavy cream. Because it contains less fat, it’s more likely to curdle when added directly to high heat or acidic dishes (such as tomato sauce or lemon desserts). For added insurance, you can temper the cold half-and-half with some of the hot liquid, then add it back in. More often than not, though, you can add half-and-half straight to the saucepan, like in our creamy cauliflower soup, where the dairy is added to hot broth and vegetables and simmered before blending, or our coconut cream pie, where it’s added to reduced coconut milk and cooked. Half-and-half also works well in quiche and other egg bakes, chowders, panades for meatballs or meatloaf, and custardy desserts like our Caramelized Banana Pudding and panna cotta. How to store half-and-half Keep half-and-half refrigerated and generally follow the manufacturer’s guidance for how quickly to use it; recommendations vary by brand. Once opened, some cartons can last up to 10 days. Ultra-pasteurized dairy generally has a longer shelf life when unopened than conventionally pasteurized half-and-half. Unused half-and-half can be frozen for up to 2 months, but may separate upon thawing—shake well and blend into soups or mix into batters. You can also freeze half-and-half in an ice cube tray and add a few cubes straight to a pan sauce. What can you substitute for half-and-half? If you’re out of half-and-half, combine ¾ cup whole milk with ¼ cup heavy cream for a substitute similar to most supermarket half-and-half, or ⅔ cup whole milk with ⅓ cup heavy cream for a slightly richer version. Homemade half-and-half won’t behave exactly like the homogenized stuff you buy in stores and may separate a little. Just give it a shake or stir before adding it to your coffee, sauce, or stew. No heavy cream? Whole milk can stand in for half-and-half in many recipes, though the result will be less rich. For hot dishes, you can compensate by adding a few pats of butter. Going the other direction, heavy cream can generally replace half-and-half 1:1, though the result will be richer (you could also thin it somewhat with water, if desired). If dairy isn’t a requirement, a barista-style plant-based milk works well. Canned evaporated milk can also work in a pinch, but its richness falls somewhere between whole milk and half-and-half, and it has a cooked flavor that may not suit every application. And what if you have half-and-half but the recipe calls for milk or cream? Half-and-half can generally replace whole milk 1:1 in savory dishes like soups, sauces, and mashed potatoes; expect a richer result. It can also replace heavy cream when the cream is primarily there to add richness (like in chowder or custard), though the finished dish will be lighter. Just remember, unlike heavy cream, half-and-half doesn’t contain enough fat to whip, no matter how vigorously you agitate it. Editor’s note: This story was originally published in 2018; it has been updated for style with additional reporting by Anna Hezel and Joe Sevier.

item.title: Blueberry Protein Pancakes (No Protein Powder)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.04
Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Tofu in blueberry pancakes?! Your eyes do not deceive you. Here, silken tofu acts as a binding agent in these protein-packed vegan blueberry pancakes. As there are no eggs in this recipe, you’ll need as much help with leavening as possible to cut through the density of the tofu. This means adding both baking powder and soda—and a lot of it. Baking powder (make sure to use the aluminum-free kind to mitigate any unpleasant flavor) will activate with the water and again when the batter hits the heat; baking soda will react with the water and the acid in the brown sugar. The result is a fluffy, crisp-edged pancake with a slightly chewy, almost mochi-like interior. Small wild blueberries are best, but whatever kind you find at the store will work. As is the case with most baked goods—even those that technically don’t go into the oven—these pancakes are most successful when the ingredients are measured by weight with a scale. If measuring by volume with measuring cups, it can be easy to pack in a little extra flour. If so, you may need to add about a tablespoon or so more water; you want the batter to be the approximate consistency of pourable whole-milk yogurt (not thick Greek-style). Discover more Good for You recipes here: Veggie Club Sandwich; Berry Protein Smoothie; Chopped Salad With Sardines and Preserved Lemon Read More: How I Make Protein Pancakes Without Protein Powder Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour 15 minutes - Yield Makes about 16 Ingredients 1½ ½ 3 2 1 1 1 5 ½ Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Whisk 1½ cups (188 g) all-purpose flour, ½ cup (62 g) whole wheat flour, 3 Tbsp. light brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. aluminum-free baking powder, 1 tsp. baking soda, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Step 2Blend tofu and liquid from one 16–17-oz. package silken tofu in a blender until very smooth. Scrape down sides and add 1 Tbsp. avocado oil or vegetable oil and 1½ cups water; blend until mixture is very smooth. Scrape into bowl with dry ingredients and gently fold in with a whisk. Step 3Heat a dry large nonstick skillet over medium for 3 minutes. Drizzle in 1½ tsp. avocado oil or vegetable oil. Pour 2 scant ⅓-cupfuls of batter into skillet, leaving space around each. Top each pancake with about 1½ tsp. fresh or frozen wild blueberries. Cook pancakes until tops start to look matte, about 4 minutes. Gently flip and cook until golden underneath, about 4 minutes. Transfer pancakes to a plate or wire rack. (Alternatively, transfer to a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet and keep warm in a 300° oven while you make the rest). Working in 7 more batches, repeat process with remaining oil, batter, and blueberries, adjusting heat as needed to keep pancakes from absorbing too much oil or burning. Step 4Serve pancakes with pure maple syrup. Do Ahead: Pancakes can be made 3 months ahead. Let cool, then stack between sheets of parchment paper and place in an airtight container or resealable plastic bag and freeze. Reheat in a toaster or toaster oven until warmed through.

item.title: 19 Margarita Recipes for Any Season
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.71
A great margarita is hard to beat: tequila, fresh lime juice, orange liqueur, and salt in sweet-tart harmony. But the classic margarita recipe is also an excellent starting point for experimentation. Small tweaks—swapping triple sec for agave syrup, say, or tequila for mezcal—can create a whole new drink. Perhaps even more compelling is the margarita's ability to veer into maximalism. Blend yours with frozen mango, muddle in fresh blackberries, or infuse the tequila with chiles. Below you’ll find 19 of our best margarita recipes, including frozen margaritas, spicy margaritas, fruit-forward riffs, and a few less traditional variations. There’s a salted watermelon margarita for summer, a blood orange version for winter, and an avocado margarita that blends up remarkably creamy. Whether you like yours on the rocks, straight up, or frozen, there’s a margarita here for you.

item.title: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.25
These lettuce wraps with spicy crumbled chicken, fresh herbs, and lime are a longtime favorite of Bon Appétit readers (and staff). Inspired by larb, the saucy filling gets its savory-sweet heat from a blend of soy sauce, fish sauce, brown sugar, and sriracha, with plenty of garlic and scallions. The combination of warm, spicy ground chicken, cool, crisp lettuce, fresh cilantro or mint, crunchy store-bought fried shallots, and bright citrus comes together in just about 20 minutes. It’s a high-reward dinner for very little effort. Chicken lettuce wraps FAQs What kind of lettuce should I use? Bibb lettuce is our first choice: Its leaves are tender and pliable enough to fold around the spicy chicken filling without tearing. Boston and butter lettuce are good substitutes, while romaine “boats” will give the wraps more crunch. Can I make these lettuce wraps with a different ground meat? Absolutely. Ground pork, beef, turkey, or lamb can be swapped for the ground chicken without otherwise changing the recipe. For fattier meats, like ground beef and lamb, you can start with 1½ Tbsp. oil. What should I serve with chicken lettuce wraps? These lettuce wraps make a complete light dinner on their own, but steamed jasmine rice or coconut rice will make the meal more substantial. You can also skip the lettuce and spoon the chicken, herbs, fried shallots, and lime over rice for an easy rice bowl. Recipe information - Total Time 20 minutes - Yield 2 servings Ingredients 3 2 2 2 3 6 4 1 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Mix 3 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. light or dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. sriracha, and 2 tsp. fish sauce in a small bowl to combine; set aside.x Step 2Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a skillet over medium. Add 6 scallions, thinly sliced, and 4 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and cook, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened (a little color is okay), about 3 minutes. Add 1 lb. ground chicken and lightly season with kosher salt. Cook, breaking up meat with spoon and tossing occasionally, until cooked through, 5–7 minutes. Add reserved soy sauce mixture and cook, tossing occasionally, until liquid is reduced by half, about 2 minutes. Step 3Serve chicken mixture with Bibb lettuce leaves, mint leaves and/or cilantro leaves with tender stems, lime wedges, store-bought fried shallots, and more sriracha for making lettuce wraps. Editor’s note: This recipe was first published in 2019; it has been updated based on reader feedback to increase the sauce and reduce the saltiness. Head this way for more of our favorite weeknight dinners →

item.title: Listen to BA Bake Club's Podcast on Plum Karpatka (Polish Cream Puff Cake)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.12
For the past six years, senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewyczk has been trying to get a karpatka recipe published. Even though he’d never made one in its entirety before. But he knew BA’s Bake Club was the perfect place to showcase what he calls the drag queen of Polish desserts. “I’ve made every component before,” Jesse tells his cohost Shilpa Uskokovic. “I just haven’t arranged the puzzle pieces in this fashion.” “We hope that that's what people in Bake Club take away,” Shilpa adds. “That by having these building blocks, you can make all these things, even if they’re the first time you’re making them.” Jesse’s version has an American twist (a no-bake cheesecake filling) and a nod to his Polish roots (the plum compote). Listeners also weighed in with questions about and photos of their sky-high desserts, and we awarded our Baker of the Month. We also had a visit from a beloved star baker in The Great British Baking Show (a.k.a. Bake-Off for those in the UK). Season nine finalist Ruby Bhogal stopped by the podcast to talk about her new book Around the World in 80 Cakes. And yes, there is a karpatka in it! Find Ruby Bhogal @rubybhogal and on Substack. Shilpa Uskokovic: I'm Shilpa Uskokovic. Jesse Szewczyk: And I'm Jesse Szewczyk. SU: We're both senior test kitchen editors at Bon Appétit. JS: And this is BA Bake Club. SU: Bake Club is Bon Appétit's community of confident and curious bakers. JS: We're creating the nerdiest and most wholesome corner of the baking internet. SU: Every month, we publish a recipe on bonappetit.com that introduces a baking concept that we think you should know. JS: Then you'll go bake, and you can send us any questions you have or pictures of your finished creations. SU: And we get together here on the podcast to talk about the recipe. JS: The September Bake Club recipe for glazed apple pie fritters is live now on bonappetit.com, and we'll tell you a bit more about those at the end of the episode. SU: But today, today we're diving into Jesse's Polish roots with his recipe for a Plum Karpatka. JS: Listen, I've been pitching of Karpatka for years. SU: You have? JS: Okay, I'm going to be real. I didn't grow up eating Karpatka. And we'll explain to you what this is. I feel like I'm building suspense here. SU: Yes. JS: But it's this Polish cake that I stumbled across several years ago, and I was like, "This is cool." SU: How do you describe it in your text? I love the phrase that you use. JS: Oh, and they let me keep it. I called it the drag queen of Polish desserts because it's just big, boisterous, and kind of silly. SU: Showy. JS: Yeah. SU: It's a lovely dessert. JS: Thank you. SU: And you gave it a really nice ... In a way, it was almost like a very New York spin with a cheesecake. JS: Yeah, yeah, yeah. SU: That's the whole thing. Okay. The photos that our Bake Clubbers have sent in of the Karpatka have been absolutely incredible. JS: They're big. Yeah. SU: I feel like there were a lot of skills that came together in this one from past Bake Club bakes. JS: Yeah. Those of you who have been around for a while, we did a Paris-Brest, which is this big kind of tire of choux that you fill with a sweet filling. SU: And for those who are listening, it's choux, as in choux pastry. JS: Choux paste, yes. SU: Okay. Sorry, Jesse. Didn't mean to cut you off. JS: Not the gym shoes, a big tire of choux. And that was a traditional way to cook pâte à choux, you can make cream puffs, éclairs. And this is baking choux in a cake pan, which I feel like is a very unique way to bake it. And then I use that to assemble the inside, and it really helps. And you can bend it back, whatever. It's fine. SU: You can't. JS: It's a work spoon. I'm not paying for it. SU: It's a little freak of a spoon. JS: Save it for later. SU: It is very helpful in this application. JS: Yeah, you can use it for other things. SU: Yes. If you make a lot of layer cakes, you should definitely be bending your spoon into an L shape. JS: I agree. I agree. SU: Okay. And finally, from Christina, "What is the leftover situation for the cheesecake? Should I wait to make it until I have enough people to eat it all at once, or can it last in the fridge for a bit?" JS: It totally lasts. Yeah. I think since it's that we're leaning into the crisp/gone soggy of it all, I think that it will last for several days, and you're good. SU: Ooh, okay. Okay, perfect. And before we take a break, it's time for our new tradition. JS: Okay. SU: The Baker of the Month Award, in which you get nothing but a shoutout. Jesse, who gets the shoutout this month? JS: Okay. Listen, I know Mark, you didn't cook your jam far enough, but that top choux you got, that looks like a nasal cavity. It is giant, and I feel like you get the award because your choux is the wonkiest, the craziest. I love it. SU: Wonderful. JS: Yeah. Mark, you win. SU: Mark and your nasal cavity, Karpatka won our Baker of the Month Award. JS: We're having the wonkiest bake. You win. SU: Okay. We are going to take another break on that note. JS: And when we get back, we're going to introduce you to a baker we think you should know. SU: Welcome back to BA Bake Club. JS: And it is time to meet a baker that we think you should know, although she might already be a familiar face to many of you, if you are online, or if you watch the British Baking Show. SU: We have a lot of British Baking Show fans. JS: A lot of fans. SU: Ruby Bhogal survived the Bake Off tent. She was a finalist on season nine of the show, and she now has a very exciting, very beautiful book called Around the World in 80 Cakes. JS: So, Ruby, we are so excited to have you. Ruby Bhogal: Thank you so much for letting me gatecrash your podcast today. JS: No, not a crash. It is an enrichment. SU: Oh, God, enrichment is really lovely. RB: You're being too kind. SU: No, thank you for sending the book, Ruby. We both really love the book, and I love that there's such a nice variety of things in there. JS: Yeah. I'm curious what the inspiration was, because it sounds really difficult to write, honestly. SU: Yeah. RB: Yeah. I didn't make my life easy for myself when I started the second book. And in all honesty, the series started online, I can't believe I'm going to say this, three years ago, which is mind-boggling, because people have followed the journey from the very start and have now had kids who are three years old. And that honestly makes me, A, very happy, but B, also mortified that I've taken so long to make 80 cakes. JS: You can't think about it too much. RB: No. You know what? It's done, it's done now. It's fine. But I initially started the series as a bit of light relief. I had just finished writing my first book, and was looking for something to kind of reignite my baking mojo. I had poured every last bit of me into my first book, and I was talking to one of my friends, and she was like, "Oh, have you seen this list? This is the top 10 cakes in the world." And I was like, "Oh, this would be really fun just to try out on social media. No pressure, just having a little bit of fun with it and see what we can do." And then my brain was like, "Well, 10 doesn't sound really exciting, and 10 also sounds like I could do that in a weekend. Why not make it 80, because it's obviously a catchy title?" And honestly, when I first thought of that, "I thought this is going to be easy. I will get 80 cakes made in about a couple of months, seriously, we'll be done, and then I'll move on to something else." Lo and behold, it's taken me three years to make 80 cakes. And I've done my best to deep dive really quickly into the history of each cake and learn about the origins. And it's so much more than just my sassy quips that people normally see on Instagram. SU: What was the most challenging, or maybe unfamiliar, region of bakes that you tackled? RB: Honestly, all of it. Even the cakes that I'm familiar with, I think, especially in the UK, like our beloved Victoria Sponge and Lemon Drizzle, I really wanted to go above and beyond just what we normally get or what we normally know. I really wanted to understand the history about it, and learn a bit more about where it originated from, and the initial variations that people used to make of it. And that was quite hard. And people are very patriotic about their cakes, which has honestly been endearing, but also mind-boggling, because people get really upset if you don't make it how their nan has made it. And I think for me, in my book, I've tried to be respectful to tradition, but then also wanted to add my own tweak to it, my own kind of twist to a recipe, because otherwise then it's just me regurgitating a lot of stuff that already preexists. But it's been a really wild journey. I really have loved being able to explore different continents and different countries all from the comfort of my own kitchen, and really being able to showcase cakes from regions that really just don't get shown enough or people are aware of. For instance, there's this Fijian honey cake, which features in the book, which is stunning. It's so easy to make. It's a real distillation of that country in carb form, and I really love that. JS: Not to overaggrandize, but it's almost like you're kind of decolonizing baking education, because I feel it's so rooted in French technique, and that's "The proper thing we're taught." But it's like the world is huge. SU: Yeah. JS: Yes, and this is such a beautiful tone. SU: An encyclopedia. JS: Yeah, so I love what you're doing. RB: Thank you. JS: Okay. Taking it back to Karpatka. RB: Yeah. JS: So, you made a traditional one, and you liked it. And as a proud Polish person, I say thank you. But you also made a PB&J ones. So, I also riffed on Karpatka for this. So, I'm wondering where your riff, the inspiration came from. RB: I have wanted to make one for so long. Love choux pastry, think it was delicious, and then have seen iterations of it on social media for a very, very long time. Because I think the first time I made it, I just rippled through a rhubarb and strawberry compote in there. And it was so delicious, but people got so mad at me because, obviously, you can't beat tradition, you can't beat what's original. But honestly, I think you can in certain circumstances. And then the PB&J one was really just a bit of fun. It was just something where I wanted to bring classic flavors, or a classic flavor combination of a peanut butter and jelly, into something that is quite traditional. Choux pastry is such a wonderful vehicle for stuffing with lots of wonderful things. So, yeah. JS: I'm excited to try it. SU: Yeah, and I think it's brilliant. It's like PB&J, like a PB&J sandwich essentially. JS: How can you not like it? SU: Yeah. JS: Yeah. SU: I think it's great. We endorse, and I think that really governs a lot of stuff we do at Bake Club, which is we take- JS: Yeah, if you give credit and you honor it- SU: Yes. JS: ... yes, you can riff. SU: Yeah. Since we're in the Karpatka zone, Ruby, we have a listener question that Jesse's going to- JS: Sure. Yeah. So, this comes from a listener named Ashley, and she wrote, "I loved making this recipe. The Karpatka was stunning. One slight issue was the weather. It's been really hot lately, and it started to look a bit sad in the heat. I don't have air conditioning. Any tips to help deal with hot weather?" We thought you might be perfect, as I feel like everyone's like, "The tent, it's so hot." RB: And also, no one in the UK has air conditioning. Let's be real. That was a whole topic on social media over the summer. But especially, when it comes to something like choux pastry, I don't really feel like there is much movement for it, in terms of choux pastry is akin to something like a sponge. It loves moisture, and so the only way you can really keep choux pastry nice and crisp for a long time is to only fill it before you're about to eat it. So, maybe this is, you tackle it in a way of making smaller Karpatkas, or individual Karpatkas, where it's essentially just a filled choux bun. But another way you can maybe tackle that, in a not so traditional way, is by adding craquelin on top of there, which will kind of give the top of the choux pastry a bit more of a crunchy texture, which may work if you're eating it straight away, or you are eating it the same day. But then, alternatively, again, if you are going to be putting it in the fridge, once again, it will still soak up and locks that moisture. So, my tip would be maybe make smaller Karpatkas, or smaller choux buns, if that's what you want to do and keep them for a longer time period. And then before you're about to eat them, pop them back into the oven for about 5, 10 minutes, just to crisp up again, just on something low and slow, just to help draw out any of that excess moisture. But choux pastry is choux pastry. How you've got anything left over once you've made it is beyond me, because that stuff goes within a blink of an eye. JS: I like the idea of making tiny Karpatkas too, because then you just eat it before the filling will melt too if it's crazy hot. SU: Yeah, that's true. RB: Absolutely. JS: And I wonder if you could use a little muffin tin and make little baby ones. SU: That would be so cute. RB: That would be so cute. JS: Yeah. SU: That is cute. JS: I've never tried. SU: Thanks, Ruby. That was actually a very helpful tip. JS: I want to make little baby ones now. RB: I know, me too. SU: Okay. Now, we're going to talk about Bake Off stuff, which I'm sure a lot of listeners want to hear about. And we want to know what the experience taught you about yourself. RB: Oh, I mean, what a phenomenal experience, particularly, as I'd only started baking, I'd say a year before I got in the tent. I honestly applied, I remember filling out the application form in a very jokey manner. It was like I was having a conversation. It's also a very rigorous application to get into Bake Off. So, if you're not serious about baking, you'll get found out pretty quickly. But I had just gone through a period of unemployment. I was like 28 years old, 30 was on the horizon, started to have a bit of a mild panic about that. Spoiler alert folks, she did not find a job. She was unemployed for about 12 months. And then, for some reason, and I don't know why, because neither my mom or my dad bakes, but there was a baking book on the shelf. And I hate to credit him with this, but it was a Paul Hollywood book. I would never say this to his face, but it did teach me the foundations of baking. And I literally baked my way from my unemployment. I tackled everything from making croissants to attempted sourdough very terribly, but I did everything just to wow my days away because I had so much time. It would make me feel good that I was actually doing something useful. Fell into a job, and then I remember seeing the Bake Off audition, the bit of fun that I had with the application form turned quite serious when then they called me up and was like, "Oh, loved your application. Just got a few questions for you." And I was like, "Great. I literally know nothing about baking. How am I going to get through these questions?" And then they were asking me these questions, and every time they'd ask me something, I'd be like, "Oh, I'm really sorry. My phone line has gone so bad." Put them on mute, and I was furiously typing away on Google like, "Oh my God, please help me. What is this? What are they talking to me about?" Sorry, Bake Off if you hear this, but yes, I did cheat my way for the- JS: Fraud. RB: Loud and proud, can I just say? And then next thing I know, I was in the tent with people who had been baking since they were five, or been baking with their granny all their life. And everyone was like, "Oh, so how long have you been baking for?" And I was like, "About a year." But I think my inexperience actually really helped me in the tent because I had no expectation. I had none of this. I want to get to halfway point, or I want to get to the final, or I want to win. I was like, "I'm just counting my lucky stars that I made it into the tent." So, it was wonderful. I've made some incredible friends from there. I've had an incredible experience, and it's given me such a wonderful, joyful platform, that it will always be one of my most cherished memories, I think. JS: Are you still in touch with your fellow bakers? RB: There's one in particular who, no matter what I do, I just can't get rid of him. This guy is invited to my family weddings. He came to my cousin's wedding. He baked a cake for my own wedding. He's my best friend, and I couldn't see my life without him. Antony, he was only in the tent for about three weeks, but we bonded from the minute that we first met. Very, very grateful for that. JS: I'm like, "Damn, I need to fill out an application." SU: I know. RB: It's an incredible experience. SU: Is it safe to say that Paul Hollywood doesn't get invited to any family weddings? RB: Oh, absolutely not. That guy will be lucky if he gets a hello here and there. JS: Damn. SU: Okay. We'll move on to a rapid fire question. JS: Yeah. Are you down to answer some? RB: Oh, yeah, absolutely. Let's go for it. JS: What are you bringing to a bake sale? RB: Oh God, this is like asking someone who their favorite child is. This is terrible. Chocolate cake, something like my Brooklyn Blackout from my book. JS: Crowd pleaser, yeah. SU: Yeah. Who do you call in a baking emergency? RB: My friend Antony, for sure. I mean, very rarely will he give me good advice, but he will calm me down. JS: That's me for Shilpa. RB: Yeah. SU: That's both of us. JS: What do you think the best baking smell is? RB: Oh God, laminated pastry, for sure. It's just that waft of butter in the kitchen that really just gets me every single time. Just nothing but butter. Fantastic. SU: Do you have a motto or words that you live by in the kitchen? RB: What's the worst that can happen? JS: Fair enough. Yeah. RB: Literally, every time I have a disaster in the kitchen, I take it as a lesson and a step closer to perfecting something that I wanted to. So, yeah, definitely that. JS: I like that. SU: A great lesson for life. What is the best compliment you've ever received on something you've baked? RB: I remember on Bake Off, everyone would strive for getting a Hollywood handshake, or some praise from Paul, but for me, Prue was a tough cookie to crack. And there was one cake that I made, and she said that she wanted the recipe for it afterwards, and then she came up to me afterwards and said, "Please send that to me." And that for me was a huge compliment. Someone who I've admired in the food industry, she's a strong, fierce woman, who's really made a name for herself in the food industry. And so, to get a compliment like that so early on in what I didn't know then was my baking career was phenomenal. JS: That's a good one. SU: Did you send her the recipe? RB: Well, I sent it on to the production company, so whether she got it or not- JS: Who's going to say? RB: I don't know. But you know what? I did my bit, girl. SU: Yeah, yeah. You certainly did. Okay, that's the end of our rapid fire. Ruby, we really loved having you. JS: Yeah, thank you so much. RB: Thank you. SU: This was such a good conversation. JS: Where can our listeners find you if they want to follow you? RB: You can find me on Instagram and TikTok @rubybhogal, where you can keep up to date with the latest cakes. Hopefully, by the time you hear this, I've finished the cake series, but you never know. We could have another three years in it. Or you can also grab a copy of my new book, which will be out in the States towards the end of September at your local bookstore, on Amazon, at Barnes & Nobles, or your local independent. JS: Beautiful. Thank you so much. SU: Thank you. RB: Thank you. Thank you so much for your time today. JS: That's it for this month's edition of BA Bake Club. Shilpa, do you want to tell our bakers about the September Bake Club recipe? SU: Okay. September's Bake Club recipe is probably the one recipe that we're not actually baking. JS: Oh. SU: September's recipe is for glazed apple pie fritters, because I'm thinking of state fair fritters, and I've never been to a state fair, and I've always wanted to go to one. JS: They're fun. SU: Oh my God, I'm so jealous that you've been to one. How many have you been to state fairs? JS: A handful. SU: Oh my God. JS: Yeah. SU: Anyway, I've always been thinking about these state fair fritters and how they have these big chunks of fruit in them, and I wanted that same sort of chunkiness, but in the texture of a cider donut that you get at the farm stand. JS: Oh, yes, yes, yes, yes. SU: So, this is my version of that. JS: I can attest to their deliciousness. And is there any special equipment or ingredients that bakers should have on hand? SU: Ingredients, I would say get some nice ricotta. I generally like the ones that are in a tin with some holes. JS: Oh, with a big bulbous top? SU: Yeah. JS: Yeah. SU: Can I just name the brand? JS: Yeah, sure. SU: It's Calabro. Calabro has the best ricotta that I had. JS: Yeah, sure, sure, sure. SU: So, that's as far as ingredients go. Get yourself some nice apples. Jesse and I are very partial to Honeycrisp apples, after a few failed attempts with Granny Smith, and you should be good. JS: Yeah. SU: Yeah. JS: Cool. Well, Bake Clubbers, once you bake through the fritters, send us your pictures and questions. There are so many different ways to get in touch. SU: You can comment on the recipe on the Epicurious app, or on the Bon Appétit website. You can comment on our Substack, or you could email us at [email protected]. And if you've made it and loved it, please rate and review the recipe on our site. JS: Or you can tell a friend. If you have a buddy that should be in the Bake Club, share this episode. SU: Oh, good. Are we buddies, Jesse? JS: Oh, baking buddies. We got a package sent to us that said Shilpa and Jesse today. SU: I know. That was our first joint package. JS: Yeah. SU: I'm so touched. JS: Okay. Well, we're your hosts, Jesse Szewczyk. SU: And Shilpa Uskokovic. JS: This month's episode was produced by Emily Elias. SU: Pran Bandi is our studio engineer, and we had editing by Rhiannon Corby. JS: Research editing by Ryan Harrington. SU: This episode was mixed by Amar Lal at Macro Sound. JS: If you like this show, leave us a rating and review, and hit that follow button so you never miss an episode. SU: And if you're not already part of the club, head to bonappetit.com/bakeclub to find all the information you need to join. JS: Thanks for listening to BA Bake Club, and we'll see you next month.

item.title: A Really Big Chicken Parm
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.05
When Senior Test Kitchen Editor Jesse Szewczyk first came across Chef Skyler's giant chicken cutlet that went viral on TikTok, he knew he wanted to put his spin on it. His take? This supersized chicken Parmesan topped with marinara, melted mozzarella, and fresh basil. (Turns out Chef Skyler also had the same idea; check out her version here.) To make it, you’ll start by rolling out ground chicken between two sheets of parchment paper until it’s as thin as a ruler. You’ll coat the top of it with flour, eggs, breadcrumbs, and Parmesan—just like you would a typical cutlet. The next step is the only one that takes effort, and one that requires a burst of confidence to pull off: You’ll flip the entire disk in one swift move, exposing its undressed underbelly so you can bread the other side. If this process does not go as planned, don’t fret: A misshapen “cutlet” will bake up just as delicious (and hidden underneath all the toppings, no one will see its flaws). Serve it as is, tuck it between slices of crusty bread for a filling sandwich, or serve it alongside a simple salad for dinner. Check out more winning weeknight dinners here: Pad Kra Pao; Sheet-Pan Feta With Tomatoes and Chickpeas; and Spaghetti With So Much Zucchini. Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour - Yield 4 servings Ingredients 1 2 3 1 4 1½ 8 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Place 1 lb. ground chicken in the center of a large sheet of parchment paper cut to fit a rimmed baking sheet. Place a second sheet of parchment paper (the same size) on top, then roll out chicken until very thin and it covers parchment, leaving 1"–2" border around sides. Carefully and slowly peel off top sheet of parchment; set aside. Step 2Whisk 2 large eggs in a small bowl with a fork to combine. Mix together 3 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (½ cup), 1 cup panko, a pinch of kosher salt, and a pinch of freshly ground pepper in another small bowl. Step 3Generously season top of chicken with salt and pepper. Scatter 2 Tbsp. all-purpose flour over and rub into an even layer to completely coat surface. (It’s easiest to use your hands for this.) Brush half of eggs on top with a pastry brush or your hands. Scatter about half of panko mixture over, pressing in with your hands to adhere. Generously coat entire surface with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Place reserved sheet of parchment on top of chicken, then hold both sheets together and turn over in a swift, confident motion. Peel away top layer of parchment and discard. Generously season top of chicken with salt and pepper. Scatter remaining 2 Tbsp. all-purpose flour over and rub into an even layer to completely coat surface. Brush half of egg on top. Scatter remaining panko mixture over, pressing in with your hands to adhere. Generously spray entire surface with nonstick spray. Step 4Transfer chicken with parchment paper onto a rimmed baking sheet. (It’s easiest to hold baking sheet flush against the counter and drag parchment paper with chicken onto it.) Bake chicken, rotating baking sheet front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown all over, 28–35 minutes. Remove from oven, turn cutlet over with tongs, and spread 1½ cups homemade or store-bought marinara sauce over. Scatter 8 oz. mozzarella, coarsely grated (1–1½ cups), on top, then bake just until cheese is melted and browned in spots, 14–18 minutes. Remove from oven and top with basil leaves and drizzle with extra-virgin olive oil if desired.

item.title: Magical Midnight Margarita
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.81
Fans of the cult classic film Practical Magic may recognize some version of this cocktail. The “Midnight Margarita” is inspired by a scene in which two characters blend up a witchy brew to the soundtrack of Harry Nilsson’s “Coconut.” Some fans even start the movie at exactly 11:12 p.m., so the pivotal moment arrives at the stroke of midnight. While the movie’s cocktail appears to be a standard standard frozen margarita—no eye of newt or toe of frog, (maybe hair of the dog if you prefer tequila and lime in the morning)—but our version leans into the magic. Blackberries give the drink its deep purple color, while coconut water adds a subtle sweetness and makes the frozen version especially refreshing. Serve it on the rocks or blended. If serving on the rocks, garnish with a torched rosemary sprig for a smoky, spellbinding flourish. More tequila drinks to cheers to at midnight: Paloma; Citrus Slushy; Aperol-Kombucha Cocktail How to make a frozen version: Because freezing can dull flavors, adding a little extra lime juice perks this version up. We’ve also increased the coconut water so you won’t have to dilute the drink with plain ice. | Yield: Makes 1 | Total time: 10 minutes plus chilling | Ingredients - 1 cup coconut water - Flaky sea salt - 3 limes - 5 blackberries - 2 oz. tequila blanco - 1 oz. orange liqueur (such as Cointreau or triple sec) - ½ tsp. sugar Method - Pour 1 cup coconut water into an ice cube tray. Freeze until solid, at least 2 hours or, ideally, 12 hours. - Pour some flaky sea salt on a small plate. Halve 3 limes and rub a cut side of 1 half around rim of a rocks glass; dip rim into salt to coat.
