Squeeze juice from limes into a small measuring glass or bowl (you should have about 3 oz). - Place 5 blackberries in glass and muddle berries just to break up. - Blend coconut water ice cubes, 2½ oz. lime juice, 2 oz. tequila blanco, 1 oz. orange liqueur (such as Cointreau or triple sec), and ½ tsp. sugar in a blender until smooth. Pour into glass with blackberries. (Save any remaining lime juice in an airtight container in the fridge up to 3 days.) Recipe information - Total Time 10 minutes - Yield Makes 1 Ingredients 2 5 2 2 1 ½ Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Pour some flaky sea salt on a small plate. Halve 2 limes and rub a cut side of 1 half around rim of a rocks glass; dip rim into salt to coat. Squeeze juice from limes into a small measuring glass or bowl (you should have about 2 oz). Step 2Place 5 blackberries in glass and muddle berries just to break up. Step 3Combine lime juice, 2 oz. coconut water, 2 oz. tequila blanco, 1 oz. orange liqueur (such as Cointreau or Triple Sec), and ½ tsp. sugar in a cocktail shaker filled with ice. Cover and shake until outside of shaker is very cold, about 30 seconds. Step 4Fill glass with blackberries with ice cubes. Strain cocktail over and garnish with a rosemary sprig, briefly singed over a flame, if desired.

item.title: 26 High-Protein Breakfasts for Any Day of the Week
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.51
There’s more to high protein breakfast than protein bars and cottage cheese egg bites. (No offense intended, bars and bites: I love your work in a pinch.) When one is not at the airport, though, there are many more options. A high-protein breakfast should give a long-lasting sense of mesatiety and keep energy levels high, of course; but it should also taste good. That’s where our vast Bon Appétit recipe archive comes in. Before we get to the good stuff: What the heck makes a meal high in protein, versus one that simply contains the macronutrient? Depending on who you ask, it should contain about 15 to 30 grams of protein—a rough range based on your body type and activity levels. I’m not going to give you a full macro breakdown of each meal (I’m sure you have an app for that). I will, however, share some suggestions to turn up the protein-dial in these recipes, so you can adjust them to what feels best for you.

item.title: 3 Best Bread Knives, After Testing 35 Blades (2026)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.70
Serrated bread knives may seem like specialized kitchen tools, but you’d be hard-pressed to slice that beautiful loaf of sourdough you brought home without one. Unlike standard kitchen knives, serrated knives have, well, serrations—a line of individually sharpened teeth along the edges that dig into whatever you’re cutting with each stroke. This sawing action easily cuts through a soft bread crumb without smooshing it, and it’s also helpful for slicing delicate tomato skin or peeling a watermelon. Our top picks - Best bread knife overall: Mac Superior Bread Knife - The best cheap bread knife: Mercer Culinary M23210 10" Bread Knife - A worthy splurge: Shun Classic 9" Bread Knife For years, the common thought was that a good serrated knife didn’t have to be expensive, and we generally agree—you can find an affordable bread knife that’ll do the job well and free up more of your knife budget to invest in the rest of your knife set. Some of that is because part of what makes a chef’s knife expensive, the high quality steel forged to hold a fine, sharp edge for a long time, isn’t as much of a thing for serrated knives. The design of the teeth makes it so that the blade can still function even if it isn’t that sharp; that’s not really the case for straight edge knives. And, because sharpening a serrated knife is a much more involved process than sharpening a a straight edge knife, some people think it’s better to replace a serrated knife after several years rather than try to maintain it. However… After testing over 35 bread knives over the last few years, I think it’s worth investing in a higher-end bread knife that’ll stay sharper longer, with blade geometry that makes slicing as easy as possible. And so I recommend one of those along with a variety of more affordable picks below. Regardless, the best bread knives at any price point are sharp, long enough for large loaves of bread, and sturdy in the hand. The top picks below all aced that criteria even with long-term testing. New in this update: We adjusted replaced the top pick in this piece after long-term testing of our favorite knives, and because of pricing and availability issues with a longtime favorite brand Tojiro. We also updated additional reviews, including on knives from Made In, Winco, and Mac after more testing. Finally we added a section on serrated knife sharpening and tested a well-liked serrated knife sharpening rod. Best bread knife overall: Mac Superior Series 10.5” bread knife Pros and cons Pros: - Long blade makes slicing through wide bread loaves easy - Curved shape offers extra leverage Cons: - On the pricier end of the spectrum Specs Knife length: 15.38" Blade length: 10.75" Weight: 6.6 oz. What we love: Mac’s Superior Series bread knife features an extra-long curved blade that makes slicing bread a breeze. Even the crustiest, oversized miche loaves were no match for this knife. It features rounded teeth that cut easily into the crust without snagging, making each stroke smoother and more deliberate. It also sliced neatly through tomato skin and glide effortlessly through the pulp, delivering perfectly uniform tomato slices. The Mac is made from high-carbon stainless steel that will keep an edge longer—a plus because serrated knives are so labor-intensive to sharpen. The curve to the blade is another excellent design choice. That curve adds cutting force to the knife because the belly extends about half an inch beyond the handle, creating immediate leverage with each stroke. In long-term testing, I found that Mac’s Superior Series offered sustained performance that cheaper knives just couldn’t match, bumping this knife into our top-pick slot. What we’d leave: My biggest gripe about this knife is the price point and handle construction. While the blocky handle scales are comfortable, it seems reasonable to expect a $100 knife to have an integrated bolster and nicer finish. For those looking for a nicer handle and are willing to spend money, you can check out the Mac Professional Series below. NOTE: The Mac Superior series is sometimes listed as the Mac Professional series on Amazon and other large marketplaces. It is not! The Professional series has a metal bolster between the blade and the handle. No bolster, not Professional. The actual Professional series knife should also cost about 50% more than the Superior series model. A cheap (but very good) bread knife: Mercer Culinary M23210 10" Bread Knife Pros and cons Pros: - Great value knife Cons: - Not full tang - Plastic handle Specs Knife length: 15.5" Blade length: 10" Weight: 5.9 oz. What we love: Premium bread knives have their perks, but a good one doesn’t have to break the bank. The Mercer Culinary Millennia 10" bread knife is less than $20, and it’s the one we use most frequently in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen. “This bread knife came in the kit bag I got in culinary school, and I am still using it today,” food director Chris Morocco says. “It won’t split atoms, but it is dependable, and for this price, you will love it all the more.” It has deep, wide serrations, also known as a wavy edge, as opposed to the pointy teeth you see on the Wüsthof or Tojiro. Instead of a wooden handle, the ergonomic handle of the Mercer is made from a combination of rubber and plastic. While this knife isn’t full-tang (no knife at this price is), it still feels stable and comfortable to hold. Our editors have used this knife for every slicing task you can imagine: crusty bread, pineapple, ripe tomatoes, overstuffed BLTs—and it always gets the job done. What we’d leave: This knife performed admirably for its price point, but it was the least sharp of our other two winning bread knives, requiring a bit more effort to cut crustier loaves. Some people also didn’t like the Mercer’s plastic handle, which wasn’t as comfortable as our other picks. A beautiful bread knife splurge: Shun Classic 9" Bread Knife Pros and cons Pros: - High carbon steel will stay sharper longer - Beautiful knife Cons: - Pricey Specs Knife length: 14" Blade length: 9" Weight: 6.8 oz. What we love: While chef’s knives are often praised for their steel quality and appearance, bread knives are typically prized for their functionality. While you don’t need to spend as much on a bread knife to get top-tier performance, we really loved the total package from Shun’s Classic line bread knife. It’s made from Damascus steel with a VG-MAX core, which is a much higher-carbon-content steel than most bread knives. This means that the serrated edge of the knife is less likely to dull over time—key for a knife that needs to be maintained professionally to keep sharp edges. In testing, it sliced tomatoes beautifully thin, and even the crustiest sourdough provided almost zero resistance. We also appreciated the height of the blade, which provided some extra heft and cutting force without adding extra weight. Finally, the Japanese wa-style handle was comfortable to grip when you needed a little extra leverage. Because there’s no palm swell or shape to the handle, it lets the user find the position that’s most comfortable for them. Shun’s bread knife might be pricier than our other top picks, but the price definitely matches the performance and knife quality. If you’re looking for a serrated knife that will stay sharper for longer, then this might be the right pick for you. What we’d leave: The 9" blade was plenty long for most loaves of bread, but wider boules were tricky to cut all the way across without having to angle the knife. It’s hard to ignore how expensive this knife is. While it does have the highest quality fit and finish of our winners, its performance boost over our two budget picks might not quite be enough for some people. Still, if you’re picky about the details of knife construction and steel quality, this knife justifies its price point. How we tested bread knives We spoke with our Test Kitchen editors to find out which blades they’ve relied on throughout their careers. Then we tested more than two dozen bread knives on crusty sourdough and winter vine tomatoes—ideal examples of that tricky firm-outside, soft-inside texture that serrated knives handle so well. We also conduct long-term testing on our top picks to evaluate how they hold up with daily use, noting whether the blades retain their sharpness and if the handles show any signs of cracking. What makes the best bread knife We focused on evaluating the following factors when it came to making our selections: How effectively it cuts The ideal knife practically does the work for you, creating clean cuts with minimal downward pressure. In our testing, we found that thin knives usually got the job done best. Weight Your knife should have enough heft to cut through foods that have a firm exterior and a delicate interior. A too-heavy knife, however, will be cumbersome to wield. Shape of teeth A serrated knife is defined by its toothlike edge, but there are a few variations on the design. A serrated knife can have rounded, scalloped teeth; pointy teeth; and even double serrations that feature a combination of the two. While scalloped teeth might seem like the least effective option, our testing proved that this is not always the case. In fact, knives with teeth that were too pointy risked snagging and tearing on bread interiors or tomato flesh. How it feels to hold We considered the knife as a whole—from the tip of its blade to the end of the handle. We looked for knives that had ergonomic handles that fit the natural contours of our hands and paid attention to the balance of weight between the handle and the blade. We wanted a knife that felt hefty enough to give us proper leverage when slicing hardier loaves, but not so heavy as to become unwieldy. The ones we picked above were the most stable and comfortable to hold, the easiest to work with, and they made the cleanest cuts. Other bread knives we like Dexter Russell Basics 10" Scalloped Bread Knife This knife from Dexter-Russell was a top contender for the best budget spot thanks to its super sharp scalloped blade, which made easy work of slicing through tough sourdough crusts and delicate tomato skin. In the end, the Mercer edged out the competition because of its grippy, more comfortable handle, slightly sturdier construction, and (just barely) lower price tag. That said, this would be a good option if the Mercer is ever out of stock. Hedley & Bennett 8.6" Bread Knife Senior test kitchen editor (and Bon Appétit’s resident baking expert) Shilpa Uskokovic loves this bread knife from Hedley & Bennett because it’s sleek and light. While it has a smaller 8.5" blade, its angled, serrated edge becomes more pointed at the tip, making it easier to maneuver and offering heightened precision for more fragile slicing tasks. It’s relatively affordable at $90 at the time of writing, and it comes in a variety of colors. However, for all those positives, the Hedley & Bennett doesn’t offer quite the force you get from a longer blade. MAC Professional Series 10.5" Bread Knife After long-term testing, this knife is a personal favorite of Bon Appétit writers and editors—but the price makes recommending it tricky. With nearly the exact same blade as MAC’s Superior series, MAC’s Professional Series bread knife is also a high performer. The slight curve on the spine gives you tons of leverage to get through crusty bread with little effort, and the sharpness of its rounded teeth lets it slice without snagging. The big thing that sets this knife apart is its fit and finish. With a full bolster that has enough room for a pinch grip, full tang construction, and three handle rivets, this knife is built to withstand heavy-duty wear and tear. Is it overkill for a bread knife? Absolutely. But for knife aficionados, the high price tag might be worth it. Performance-wise, the MAC Professional bread knife easily sliced through the crustiest loaves and glided through tomatoes. It also felt great in the hand, even if it was a little heavy. Overall, the price-to-performance ratio kept this bread knife from the top picks, but if you want an upgrade on our top pick, it is a great option to consider. Wüsthof Classic 9" Double Serrated Bread Knife This German-made knife is another pricey blade, but it justifies that price tag with its interesting and super-effective design. While this one has a shorter 9" blade, it’s double serrated, which means it has mini teeth within the larger, scalloped serrations. All those extra sharp points give it a better grip on waxy surfaces like the exterior of a tomato or watermelon and make for fast, easy slicing. It’s also a knife that asks very little of you—during testing, the double set of serrations cut through hard crust with very little exertion from the tester and produced such thin slices of tomato that we could see right through them. One final advantage of a double-serrated blade: because there are more of them, each individual serration will wear less, so the knife stays sharper for longer. The shorter blade did make it tricky to cut wider loaves straight across, though it was an adequate length for most batards and pan loaves. Mercer Culinary 8" Züm Bread Knife Sharp and with a comfortable handle, the ZüM knife from Mercer Culinary excelled in our testing. It neatly sliced through the tomatoes, piercing the tough skin easily without smashing the delicate flesh. It also perfectly sliced through the sourdough crust and crumb without snagging. The only thing we didn’t like was the 8" blade length, which was a little short for bigger sourdough loaves, but for around $50, it’s an effective budget option with high-end handle construction and a full bolster. Not quite our favorite budget pick, but a good alternative, and a good option for people who want a very comfortable handle. Misen 8" Serrated Knife Misen’s bread knife was a mid-tier performer in our tests, cleanly cutting through tomatoes and bread without any notable issues. We also thought the handle was comfortable, and its overall build quality was high. The blade’s taller heel also meant it performed well slicing through larger sourdough loaves. However, its performance didn’t quite match our top picks, and our two budget models performed better at half the cost. We recommend either spending a little more for a nicer bread knife, or saving a bit of cash instead—unless you can find this knife on sale. Bread knives we don't recommend A former top pick, I still stand behind this knife’s performance and build quality. What I don’t love, however, is its spotty availability and fluctuating price. At around $60, I thought this knife was a steal. Now that its price has rocketed up to match Mac’s Superior Series bread knife, I can’t recommend it when the Mac offers better build quality and consistency. Still, if you can catch this knife on a deal, go for it—it’s sharp and nimble, but sturdy enough to tackle most tasks. Like its sturdier cousin, this bread knife from Tojiro is sharp and swift. But when we originally picked this serrated knife, its price was around $40. For that price, this knife was a great pick. But its cheaper build quality, lack of a full tang, and slightly smaller wood handle mean we don’t see much value in recommending this knife now that it’s price has nearly doubled. Bob Kramer is a legendary knife maker, but the Bob Kramer Essential Bread Knife by Zwilling felt like overkill for a serrated knife. Its $400-plus price point is excessive for a tool with such a narrow set of uses (no matter how often you bake homemade bread), and because this knife is made from carbon steel, it'll be prone to corrosion and rust. Does it work well? Definitely; it was one of the better tomato knives we used. But is it worth the sky-high price? In our opinion, no. This knife has a nice weight to it—stable without being heavy—and it's easy to control through longer cuts. However, it wasn't as sharp or efficient as the top performers. Global's great knives have won the hearts of many a BA staffer. That said, their metal handles are divisive—some people think they're comfortable to hold and others find them too thin and slippery. While our testers say this knife is well-balanced and decently sharp, they ultimately disqualified it from our winners list due to its handle shape, short blade length (8.5"), and less-than-perfect performance in the tomato test, where its large teeth snagged just a bit on the tomato's flesh. IKEA's $25 bread knife handled bread and tomatoes competently without excelling at either. The serrations weren't the sharpest we tested, but they cut cleanly enough for everyday use. We were impressed by the sharpness of Kuhn Rikon's serrations, which allowed for precise cuts. Its limitation is its reach; at under eight inches, wide bread loaves demand more back-and-forth. But if you're not into sourdough boules, this will be an impressive performer. This is a beautiful knife (just look at that gorgeously curved handle grip), but the Lamson's teeth weren't sharp enough. The knife snagged on crusty sourdough boules and required a lot of force to make cuts. Its 8" blade was also too short to cut through entire loaves, and it snagged slightly on tomato skin. Lamson does offer complementary sharpening for life, but for this price ($90 at the time of writing), we feel the bread knife should be sharper out of the box. Sharp and well-made, we do like Mac’s Chef’s Series bread knife. But it’s only slightly cheaper than our top pick and doesn’t feature a curved belly. Again, the decision not to recommend it comes to value; you’ll get a much more better slicing experience if you drop an extra $10 on the Mac Superior. Though it was razor sharp, MAC's offset knife was too short to effectively slice bread. At only 7.5", we had to maneuver it to make it through an entire sourdough loaf. We also didn't like its offset blade, which made it hard to intuitively feel where the blade was compared to the handle. It did excel as a tomato slicer, but it would be hard to recommend it at this price point. The first time we tested Made In’s bread knife, we found it lacked sharpness. That’s no longer the case—their slightly updated model has sharper serrations and slices through bread and tomatoes with ease. The big issues are with the weight and the price—the heftier handle does balance well against the blade, but overall it’s a heavy knife. It’s also more expensive than our top pick while having a shorter, straighter blade. This knife is fine, but there are plenty of others that offer better value. A little too flimsy, this knife struggled to neatly slice through sourdough bread. Even though it was sharp, the blade tended to flex when cutting, creating uneven slices of bread. We also didn't like the cheapness of the handle or the offset blade shape, but it did offer solid performance at a very affordable price. For how pricey this knife is, we were disappointed in how dull the blade appeared to be. Since it's difficult to sharpen a serrated knife, initial sharpness is a key factor in picking out the best option for your kitchen. This knife snagged on tomato skin and tore apart the delicate sourdough bread crumb. Though the handle was beautiful and felt nice in the hand, this knife was the most expensive model we tested and had some of the worst performance. Considering it's one of the most expensive bread knives we tested, we were hoping for better performance out of the Miyabi Kaizen 9.5" Bread Knife. Instead, it crushed most loaves of bread instead of cutting them, and it got stuck on tomato cores. The Opinel Intempora fell short—in some cases, literally—in a few areas. Its 8" blade is shorter than we'd like, making it hard to cut through sourdough boules without changing the slicing angle. Its teeth weren't quite as sharp as we'd like either. It didn't mangle the tomatoes (a win!), but we had difficulty keeping the blade straight—the knife typically snagged on the fruit's core, creating wobbly, inconsistent tomato slices. We do like the round polyurethane handle and the high-quality high-carbon stainless steel, but we expect better performance from a knife of this price. The Shun Classic Master Serrated Knife has a unique wavy edge that adds to the overall serration pattern. It excelled at slicing paper-thin tomatoes and was comfortable to hold, but its edge shape didn't consistently cut through bread well. Its blade was also on the shorter side, making this knife less well-suited for large loaves. This knife has a lot going for it: The Shun Ultimate Utility looks almost like a toy shark and, accordingly, has plenty of bite—we loved how sharp its rounded teeth were. Its flat sides and curved tip mean that this knife is able to both slice your sandwich toppings and spread mayo on a piece of soft bread. It also sliced tomatoes perfectly and slid right through the crust of the sourdough boules. But its tiny 6" blade, which is more similar to a santoku than a typical bread knife, made it hard to cut even slices. And when you factor in the price ($140 at the time of writing), we just can't recommend it. This model from Victorinox, the makers of one of our favorite budget-friendly chef's knives, performed pretty well overall. Testers found that while the plastic handle looks flimsy, the knife cut really well and felt sturdy. However, this is an incredibly light knife—so much so that it verges on too light—and at more than double (or triple, at some stores) the cost of our affordable picks, it costs more than we think is worth spending. The Victorinox Swiss Army 8" knife sliced bread okay, but it required more effort than most other models; worse, it crushed tomatoes. It was also too lightweight to maneuver comfortably. Sharp, well-made, and great at cutting, there's a lot to like about the Wüsthof Classic bread knife. It easily sliced through tomatoes, and it cut swiftly through crusty sourdough bread. But its 8" length struggled to span the entire loaf, and then there's the price. As one of the most expensive bread knives we tested, we think there's better performance for less money—or, you can upgrade to the double-serrated version, which was one of our top picks. The double serrations of this Ikon series knife performed as well on waxy surfaces as the Wusthof Classic double serrated knife above, but struggled a bit against crusty bread. The bigger issue is that this knife regularly retails for about $200 (30% more than the regular Classic series knife). You're paying for the Ikon finishes, which are lovely, but if you're interested in double serration, we think the standard Classic offering (listed above) is a better bet at a slightly more affordable price. Although billed as a "13-inch" bread knife, Zulay's blade is only 8 inches. The short blade struggled with thick, wide sourdough loaves. It was also hard to control; the blade wandered during cuts, making it difficult to produce straight, clean slices. Both bread and tomatoes eventually yielded, but the process felt imprecise compared to most knives we tested. We struggled to make clean cuts with Zwilling's entry-level Gourmet series. While it sliced tomatoes just fine, its teeth often caught on crusty sourdough loaves, interrupting the sawing motion and requiring more force to power through. During testing, its handle scales felt clunky, making the knife awkward to hold and even more awkward to wield, and it failed to perform as well as our two budget picks—both of which are significantly less expensive. Zwilling's double-serrated knife is a good slicer, and its double-serrated edge is similar to the Wüsthof model we recommend. It performed well in testing, yielding thinly sliced tomatoes and perfectly straight slices of bread, but ultimately, this knife's overall weight and high price tag kept it from being a winner. A bit heavier than much of the competition, Zwilling's bread knife was trickier to wield comfortably, and its longer handle made it hard to find a good balance point. Offset knives are awkward to cut with because they remove the leverage you can create with the handle. While this knife from Winco slices tomatoes nicely, it struggles with crustier bread and dulls more quickly than other serrated knives we tested. It does have a bargain price tag though, so there’s that. Serrated knives feature dozens of individually sharpened teeth, meaning that, if you do want to sharpen your bread knife, you need to sharpen dozens of edges instead of the single edge most kitchen knives have. While this process can be tricky and is generally best left to professionals, you can pick up a serrated knife sharpener that lets you add more bite to your blade. These sharpeners work best with pointy serrations that create neat half-circle teeth—simply run the diamond-coated rod in the interior of each curve until they’re sharper than they were before. The only issue? The rod is shaped to work best with pointy serrations, so rounded scalloped edges won’t easily sharpen with a tool like this. Also, even the finest diamond surface is still rougher than ceramic—you can sharpen each pointy tooth on a bread knife with this thing, but it won’t be as highly polished and smooth as a professionally sharpened bread knife. Overall, I recommend these tools for budget-tier bread knives that you want to breathe some life into. Since bread knives don’t smack against hard cutting boards the same way as chef’s knives do, they also don’t dull as quickly. And if you have a higher-end bread knife made from harder steel, it’s likely your knife will hold an edge for a long time without any intervention from you. Fill out the rest of your knife block - The best chef's knives to serve as your daily driver - A nakiri knife is a blade you didn't know you needed - How much do you need to pay for a good knife anyway? Get to know the experts Jesse Raub: I’ve been a professional kitchen product tester since 2021, where I tested nearly everything: espresso machines, wooden spoons, bread proofing baskets, pizza stones, garlic presses, and more. My fascination with kitchen knives began in 2003 when the chef at the kitchen where I worked let me use his personal Wüsthof knives during prep work one day. Over the last two years, I’ve tested over 70 different knives for Bon Appétit and written about the best knife sharpeners and how to best sharpen your knives at home. If you’re ever on the phone with me and hear a light scraping noise in the background, just know that I’m likely touching up my kitchen knives on a whetstone and testing their sharpness by slicing sheets of paper. Additional reporting and testing by Alaina Chou and Jamie Thilman.

item.title: How I Make Protein Pancakes Without Protein Powder
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.11
Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. The thing about protein powder is that it doesn’t taste good. And that makes sense—it wasn’t designed to be a joyful culinary experience. As with many dietary supplements, it began with nutrition in mind, and morphed into an athletic performance enhancer. For this, we can thank two so-called “fathers” of their time and industries: German bodybuilder Eugen Sandow, a 19th-century proponent of neutral-tasting milk-based protein powderPlasmon, initially used to fortify packaged food products like porridge and cookies; and Bob Hoffman, a 20th-century American weightlifter who’s credited with the first successfully marketed soy- and whey-based “Hi-Proteen,” which was eventually flagged by the FDA for misleading health claims. Decades later, the supplement has become steadily more mainstream, from an almost-fatal smoothie on The White Lotus to Ballerina Farm’s viral Farmer Protein. Show me a person in 2026 who has never consumed a protein-powder-enhanced shake, bar, or “dessert,” or at the very least, wondered if they should. Whether made from whey, soy, peas, or beef, I find protein powder chalky and synthetic-tasting, only valuable in hangry emergencies. And with most powders costing well over a buck per serving, I’d rather just get my protein from food I’ve already purchased. Meat and fish are well-known sources, but plenty of meatless options—like eggs, beans, yogurt, and quinoa—can provide the body with ample protein. Today, I want to highlight one of my favorites: tofu. A beloved vegan protein, pressed soybean curd has graced plates for centuries. You’ll often see American recipes highlight firmer varieties of tofu (which are also the highest in protein), like stir-fries and nuggets. But just as, if not more, versatile is silken tofu. It can be the star of a dish, like this five-minute dinner or an eggless scramble; or sneakily blend into the background, like in this nutty dressing. Thanks to its neutral flavour, it can be even further camouflaged into sweet dishes, like 2-ingredient chocolate mousse or my new Blueberry Protein Pancakes. When blended with usual pancake ingredients, like flour, sugar, and leaveners, silken tofu acts as a binder, much like eggs in a standard recipe. The result is a thick, accidentally-on-purpose-vegan batter, creating fluffy pancakes that fry up with crisp edges. Studded with tart blueberries, they’re hearty and flavorful, and yes, protein-rich. On mornings when I’m craving something more fun for breakfast than my usual bowl of yogurt and muesli or boiled eggs on toast, I’ll reach for a couple of these. Pancakes take a little longer to make, of course, so I’ll whisk up a batch on a weekend and freeze the extras. (Stack between squares of parchment and tuck in a zip-top bag or airtight container.) A quick trip in the toaster and I’m ready to eat. Do tofu pancakes pack the same protein-punch as a powder-fortified shake? Of course not. And that’s okay. We can all stand to remove some of the pressure of optimizing every meal to the highest degree. But if you’re really in it for the gains, you still have the rest of the day to keep chipping away at that protein goal. In the meantime, pass the maple syrup.

item.title: TSA’s New PreCheck Perk Allows Non-Ticketed Visitors to Accompany Friends and Family at the Gate
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.44
TSA’s newest PreCheck perk is intended for people who aren’t flying at all. Gateside by TSA PreCheck, which began rolling out this month at 13 US airports, allows eligible non-ticketed visitors to pass through security after receiving advance approval. That means they can accompany someone to a departure gate, meet an arriving traveler airside, visit a friend or relative during a layover, or access the restaurants and shops beyond the checkpoint. The program marks an expansion of an idea that several individual airports have experimented with in recent years: allowing some people without boarding passes back into the secure side of the terminal. But Gateside also raises a more practical question—who actually wants to go through airport security on their own volition when they don’t have a flight to catch? Jennifer Yellin, managing editor at travel rewards platform Points Path, expects the answer to be mostly people helping or meeting someone they know. “I think families will be the ones to use this the most,” Yellin says “I foresee this being the most beneficial for parents accompanying their child for an outbound flight as well as welcoming home family members.” She also sees potential for older travelers, nervous or infrequent fliers, and people navigating unfamiliar airports with the help of a friend or relative. In those cases, Gateside could make it possible for someone to stay alongside a traveler all the way to the gate, rather than saying goodbye before security. “If you have a child, parent, spouse, or even friend who is a nervous flier, being able to walk them to their gate and see them off could help put their nerves to ease,” Yellin says. “It can also be useful to help the same younger or older family member navigate an airport, which might otherwise be challenging. For some travelers, having someone there with you to the very end can put them at ease.” That doesn’t mean Gateside will replace existing assistance available to travelers who need it. Airlines already issue escort or gate passes in certain circumstances, including unaccompanied minors, and airports and airlines offer assistance for travelers with disabilities. Gateside is broader: A visitor doesn’t need to be escorting someone who qualifies for one of those services. Instead, access is based primarily on the visitor’s eligibility for TSA PreCheck screening and approval for Gateside. How Gateside by TSA PreCheck works Gateside is currently being offered as an “operational assessment” at 13 airports, including major hubs such as Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport, and Salt Lake City International Airport. To use it, visitors need to be eligible for TSA PreCheck screening and have a Known Traveler Number. That includes TSA PreCheck members as well as eligible members of trusted traveler programs such as Global Entry, NEXUS, and SENTRI. The pass itself is free, but visitors have to apply online one to three days before their intended airport visit and select the participating airport they plan to enter. Those who are approved bring an acceptable form of identification to the airport and go through a TSA PreCheck checkpoint; they are still subject to normal security screening and restrictions. An approval is valid for the designated calendar day and allows the visitor to leave and re-enter the secure area that day. Gateside isn’t the first way for a non-ticketed visitor to get beyond airport security. Airports including Seattle, New Orleans, Orlando, Tampa, Palm Springs, and Tulsa already operate their own visitor-pass programs, each with its own rules. Detroit and San Diego have existing visitor programs in addition to being among the first Gateside airports. The distinction with the new TSA program is that Gateside is tied to PreCheck eligibility and gives approved visitors access through the PreCheck screening lane. For the average traveler, Yellin says, the program is still likely to remain fairly niche. “While it's a meaningful change, it's only beneficial for a small group of travelers,” she says. “For the average traveler, it won't change the airport experience since this is limited to a very small subset of airports and advance approval is required.” Seeing off a family member is perhaps the most obvious use for the program, but Gateside could also make it easier to spend time with someone who isn’t beginning or ending their trip in your city. “If you have a friend or family member traveling with a long layover in your home airport, meeting them during their connection is the perfect situation,” Yellin says. “This allows the traveler to stay near their gate without having to leave security.” Currently, meeting a connecting passenger generally requires the traveler to leave the secure area of the airport, then go through security again before continuing their trip. That may not be practical on a shorter connection, particularly at a large airport where getting between the gate and terminal exit can itself take time. With Gateside, the local visitor goes through security instead. Still, Yellin doesn’t expect non-ticketed visitors to start heading to airports simply because they now can. “The airport experience today is tiring for many and extremely different than what it once was,” she says. “Because of that, I do not believe too many people are going to choose to park their car and navigate their way through security, without actually traveling that day, unless they have a very real reason.” The program’s arrival also comes 25 years after the September 11 attacks transformed who could access US airport gate areas. Before 9/11, people without tickets could generally accompany passengers through security; afterward, access to the secure side of terminals became largely limited to ticketed passengers and those with specific authorization. However, Yellin doesn't believe Gateside is a signal that TSA is returning to the old airport model. “Now that it's been 25 years, TSA is experimenting to see how the overall experience can be better for travelers, while still keeping safety in mind,” she says. Airports offering Gateside by TSA PreCheck - Mesa Gateway Airport (AZA) in Arizona - John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH) in Ohio - Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) in Texas - Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) in Michigan - Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport (ICT) in Kansas - Indianapolis International Airport (IND) in Indiana - Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) in Nevada - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in California - Bill and Hillary Clinton National Airport (LIT) in Arkansas - Will Rogers International Airport (OKC) in Oklahoma - Eppley Airfield (OMA) in Nebraska - San Diego International Airport (SAN) in California - Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) in Utah

item.title: A New Museum, Cruise Haute Couture, and Gorgeous Glassware: Here's What's Exciting Us in Travel Right Now
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.40
Whether you're on land or at sea, in a bar or in Bahrain, there are myriad reasons for design lovers to get excited about travel right now. In the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler, we went long on a number of these stories—how Como's enduring craft traditions help make it one of the planet's most luxurious destinations, why Fort Worth is the sartorial epicenter of the rise of ranchcore in fashion. But we also collected a few juicy morsels worth sharing in brief. There's a new museum in the Middle East to earmark if you're interested in the intersection of craft and history, and a French cruise line has launched a new itinerary that will bring haute couture to the high seas. Read on for all we think you should know. A gem of a new museum on Bahrain's pearling path “Inside an elegant home formerly owned by a wealthy merchant family in Bahrain's coastal city of Muharraq sits the two-year-old Siyadi Pearl Museum. The space is the latest addition to the Pearling Path, which connects important structures from the city's pearling history. Along its two miles are 17 significant sites; public squares shaded by flame trees; and a pedestrian bridge that reconnects Muharraq with its original shoreline, which has been mostly lost to development. Terrazzo lampposts topped by pearl-shaped light bulbs double as trail markers. Tales of wealth are told in the grand living quarters of merchants and traders; those of hardship in the display of the simple tools pearl divers relied on (nose clips, stone weights, leather finger covers) during arduous months aboard dhows at sea.” —Nicola Chilton High fashion comes to the high seas “In September 2027, French line Ponant will sail a commonly traveled route along Italy's coast with an entirely unique agenda: placing the country's fashion maisons at the center of the passenger experience. Sailing down the coast from Tuscany and then up to Venice, guests on board the intimate Le Boréal will experience five major haute labels. They will chat with a Brioni tailor about making the perfect alterations; observe a master craftsperson cut precious gemstones at iconic jeweler Pomellato; and explore two historic sites in Florence tied to Gucci via the Palazzo Gucci and the 15th-century Palazzo Settimanni, home to the Gucci archives. Think of this as high fashion on the high seas.” —Erin Florio Drinks wear designer around the globe “Striking, artisanal glassware that upstages the concoction it holds is the coolest thing in cocktail culture these days. Here, bars around the world and the gorgeously unique vessels you may just encounter while there.” —Michelle Tchea This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: Thousands of Flights Disrupted at UK Airports Due to Air Traffic Control Issue
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.84
Several major UK airports are continuing to experience delays and cancellations following an air traffic control technical failure on Tuesday, September 8. The National Air Traffic Services (NATS) has now resolved the issue, which affected its flight processing system, but the disruption is expected to continue through Wednesday as airlines and airports work through backlogged flights. The failure caused widespread disruption across the UK on Tuesday, with FlightRadar24 reporting around 1,300 cancellations to and from UK airports. Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester, and Stansted were among the airports affected, while the disruption also had knock-on effects at airports across Europe. NATs boss Martin Rolfe has apologized for the disruption, telling the BBC there would be a full investigation into what had gone wrong, after the firm said resolving the issue had taken “longer than hoped.” An official statement on the NATs website reads: “This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.” London Heathrow was particularly impacted. Arrivals were suspended for the remainder of Tuesday, while departures resumed later in the day. The airport has warned that disruption will continue and is advising passengers to check directly with their airline before traveling. A statement on the airport's X account on Wednesday morning reads: “Following yesterday's NATS technical issue, flights are operating today, but some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew. Please check your flight status with your airline before traveling to the airport and only travel if your flight is confirmed to be operating.” FlightRadar24 is currently reporting that 177 flights scheduled for Wednesday, September 9 have already been canceled, with the vast majority at Heathrow, while further delays and cancellations are expected as aircraft and crew displaced by the disruption are repositioned. Can I get a refund if my flight was disrupted? If your flight was delayed or canceled following Tuesday’s air traffic control issues at NATS, you may be entitled to flight compensation. According to the UK Civil Aviation Authority, passengers can claim compensation ranging from £220 (approximately $300) per person to £520 (approximately $700) per person if the delay causes you to reach your destination airport more than three hours late. If the delay is more than five hours, you can choose not to travel and receive a refund. Because air traffic control issues are typically considered “extraordinary circumstances” outside the airline's control, cash payouts aren't likely in this scenario. However, many airlines will still provide food and drink vouchers, airport transfers, and hotel accommodations for overnight delays. If your flight is canceled, the airline is required to provide an alternate flight or full refund. Flight delay compensation in the UK is not automatic, and the procedure for submitting a claim varies by airline. Because the UK is no longer part of the European Union, EU passenger rights only apply to UK flights if it arrives in an EU country and is operated by an EU airline (for example, if you were flying from London to Paris with Air France). Or, if your flight departs from an EU country and arrives in the UK (operated by either an EU or a non-EU airline). Passengers should check the status of their flight and compensation policies directly with their airline and monitor the NATS website and X account for further updates. UK airports reporting disruptions: - London Heathrow Airport - London Gatwick Airport - London Luton Airport - London Stansted Airport - Manchester Airport - Birmingham Airport - Belfast City Airport - Edinburgh Airport - East Midlands Airport - Jersey Airport This is a developing news story and will be updated with more information. This article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: Shoulder Season on Paros: Ceramicist Christiane Smit Finds Inspiration at a Slower Pace
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.51
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to ceramic artist and owner of Moonhouse, Christiane Smit. For Netherlander and artist Christiane Smit, a holiday on Paros in 2008 rerouted the course of her life. “It wasn’t a carefully planned life decision, it was something I felt instinctively,” she says of her unplanned move to the Cycladic island. “I listened to that feeling, stayed, and started building a completely new life on the island.” Having lived all over the island since then, she now operates a ceramics atelier in the village of Lefkes and owns the stunningly minimalist clifftop villa rental Moonhouse—both of which are open to visitors. She is currently completing the restoration of a nearly 100-year-old stone house in the village of Kostos. Here, the now-local shares the shoulder-season delights that keep her on-island year-round as well as her favorite hotel-slash-taverna for a warming meal and stay. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit—when the travelers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? For me, the sweetest time in Paros is late spring or early autumn. The island feels wonderfully balanced: Everything is open, but life is still unhurried. I love walking through the villages in the morning, when the streets are still quiet. The air smells of jasmine, fresh bread from the bakery, and the sea. You hear church bells, neighbors greeting each other, and the wind moving through the olive trees. The light is what inspires me most. It changes constantly, making the whitewashed houses glow and bringing out every texture in the stone. As a ceramic artist, I find myself collecting those colors, textures, and moments every day. They’re as much a part of my work as the clay itself. What do you love most about being there during this season? The season allows me to slow down and notice everything. The colors of the landscape, the textures of old stone walls, the shifting light on the sea—those details naturally find their way into my ceramics. I don’t have to look for inspiration here; I simply have to pay attention. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travelers at all? It’s mostly locals. The cafés are filled with familiar faces, fishermen are heading out in the morning, and shop owners have time to stop and chat. You also meet a small number of travelers: The people who aren’t looking for the typical summer vacation, but who want to experience the island more slowly and authentically. There are also Greek visitors escaping the city for a long weekend or visiting family. It’s a lovely mix, but the locals set the rhythm, and that’s what gives Paros its real character. What’s notable about the locals in Paros; do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? What I’ve come to appreciate most about the people of Paros is their warmth and sense of community. Even though it’s a popular island in summer, life outside the season is very local. People know one another, and there’s a genuine willingness to help each other. As someone who lives here year-round, that’s something I’ve really come to value. There’s also a deep respect for craftsmanship—from marble carving, for which the Cyclades are famous, to fishing, farming, and handmade work. Where would we find you eating during this time? One of my favorite places is the family-run taverna at Hotel Julia in Drios. I love it because it feels authentic and unchanged—a place where generations have welcomed people with simple, honest food and genuine hospitality. My perfect day always starts with a swim in the crystal-clear waters just below the taverna. Afterwards, I walk up for a long, leisurely lunch. There’s something so special about sitting there, the sound of the waves below and nowhere else to be. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? Winter on Paros is the season for revithada (slow-baked chickpea stew), hearty bean soups, and goat or lamb braised with local wine—dishes that are more like daily specials rather than menu staples. But if there’s one meal that defines the island’s quieter months, it’s whatever is cooking in the pot that day (mageirefta). That’s what locals order, and every taverna has its own depending on the day. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off-season? I wouldn’t say any one area suddenly comes alive in the off-season; it feels more like the island returns to its natural rhythm. While Parikia is the social hub for year-round residents, it’s the villages—Lefkes, Marpissa, Prodromos, Kostos, and Dryos—that reveal the character of Paros through seasonal festivals, religious celebrations, and community events. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? You get cooler temperatures; crisp, sunny days; and the occasional rainstorm, which turns the landscape unexpectedly green. The island feels softer and more vibrant. For me, one of the greatest advantages is the sense of calm. Of course, there are a few trade-offs. Stronger winter weather systems can occasionally disrupt ferry schedules, and many seasonal businesses close until spring. But these are minor inconveniences. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? My perfect Saturday begins slowly with a coffee in my house, catching the first sunlight. From there, I’ll often wander through Lefkes, Marpissa, or Prodromos before a long lunch at a traditional taverna. In the afternoon, I usually head back to my ceramic studio. The quieter months are when I’m most creative. Without the intensity of the summer season, there’s space to observe, reflect, and create. At sunset, I love taking a walk along one of the beaches or coastal paths. Even in winter, there are many clear, sunny days, and the light over the Aegean is extraordinary. I usually end the day with friends over a simple meal and a glass of wine. Do you have any favorite activities during this time of year? I love walking the ancient Byzantine paths that weave between villages. With few people on the trails, the silence becomes part of the journey. This winter is especially meaningful, as I’ll be putting the finishing touches on a small renovation project in the village of Kostos, a space I’ve been shaping with the same care and intention that I bring to my ceramics. Creating a home is, in many ways, another form of making, and I find great joy in both! This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: On California's Central Coast, an Indoor-Outdoor Museum Connects Visitors With Centuries of Chumash Heritage
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.32
The Chumash Heritage Marine Sanctuary was featured on Condé Nast Traveler's Bright Ideas in Travel 2025. Read the full list of winners here. I am greeted by cast iron doors, engraved with spiraling pictographs and cool to the touch, even in the morning heat of June. I grip the handle—shaped, I'll learn, like a clapper stick, a traditional Chumash percussion instrument—and push it open. The sounds of birdsong, layered and ambient, rise toward a curved ceiling where light moves like cloud shadow. Here, what lies indoors simulates the beauty of the natural world. I have entered an 'Ap, the Chumash word for home, reimagined at monumental scale. The traditional version would have been made of willow branches and tule reeds, but this one is steel and stone with the same circular, embracing shape: This is the 14,000-square-foot Santa Ynez Chumash Museum and Cultural Center, which opened on May 15, 2025, after 20 years in the making. Every detail has been designed with intention by Native American architect Johnpaul Jones. The ancestral home of the Chumash, the Indigenous Native American people who have lived along California's central coast for more than 13,000 years, spans from Malibu to Paso Robles, including the Northern Channel Islands. In 2024, Chumash stewardship of more than 4,500 square miles of sea and coast in this region was formalized on the federal level as part of the Chumash Heritage National Marine Sanctuary, the first-ever Indigenous-led marine sanctuary in the US. The new museum is the most visible piece of a broader, sustained effort to connect visitors to California's central coast with Chumash culture. The tribe's Culture Department runs a state-credentialed language program—two of its teachers hold the specialized credential that California created in 2008 for Native language instruction—alongside basket weaving classes, an archery club, a youth camp, and a cultural resource management team that protects tribal sites and artifacts. "The circular shapes of the buildings, the model of the oak tree where the coyote lives in the Maria Solares Discovery Center, and the west-facing direction of the buildings represent important symbolism to our people," says Kenneth Kahn, Chairman of the Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians. The museum faces the Western Gates, or Point Conception—a spot on the cliffs overlooking the Pacific Ocean, which tribal beliefs describe as the place one departs this world and enters the spirit realm. Felicia Cogorno, Education Programs & Volunteer Manager and tribal member, tells me that if I stand in exactly the right place in the center of the museum's main room, I'll hear my own voice come back to me. I find the spot—a subtle seam in the floor's inlaid pattern—and say something small and ordinary. For a moment, my voice and the birdsong, and the fire and the Sʰamala (Santa Ynez Band native language) words floating from a nearby speaker, are all one sound, indistinguishable from each other. Cogorno grew up on the reservation, on whose lands the center now stands, and manages its education programs and volunteers. She points to the ring of painted figures along the upper walls, each mid-movement, each representing a different animal, each placed at a different ancestral village along the central California coast. "If you were being welcomed to our village," she says, "you would be welcomed with singing and dancing." I wave my hand near the fire. The movement activates the walls where animals light up—deer, bear, condor—each one accompanied by a voice pronouncing its name in Sʰamala, the language of the Santa Ynez Band. The polished stone floor, meanwhile, is inlaid with a seasonal round: concentric rings mapping harvests and hunts and gathering times, labeled in Sʰamala and English, with a bit of Spanish woven in. As Cogorno explains, the arrival of the Gregorian calendar required new words for things that hadn't needed naming before. Before going further into the museum, I stop at a photograph of a woman hanging on the wall. I continue to see her image, reappearing throughout the galleries like a thread you keep finding in the weave. Her name is Maria Solares, I learn. In the early 1900s, she was one of the last fluent speakers of Sʰamala. Between 1914 and 1915, she worked with linguist John Peabody Harrington, sitting for sessions that produced wax cylinder recordings of the languages and more than 100,000 pages of notes. The language survived because she sat in that room and spoke. "She's my five-times great-grandmother," Cogorno says, matter-of-factly. "Many of our volunteers are also descendants of Maria." The permanent galleries are accessed off the ‘ap lobby area through a set of iron doors whose design, Cogorno mentions, was made by her aunt. Inside, the ceiling rises and the light changes, cooler, darker. The exhibit moves through the Chumash cosmology of three worlds—Upper, Middle, and Lower—stacked like basket trays. Most of what surrounds me is the Middle World, the et ya shoop ("here world") display. Cases hold stone tools, hunting materials, and abalone ceremony regalia. Paintings that line the walls show figures fishing, gathering, and paddling. The objects in the cases mirror what the figures carry. I stop at a case of abalone shells, cut into jewelry and adornments, and polished to a high shine, almost iridescent under the gallery lights. "My cousin made those," Cogorno says. Nearby, there's a swordfish headdress with intricate shell work—her aunt, who cast the door handles at the entrance, made that, too. In the Upper World gallery, a taxidermied California condor has her own case, her own story. In 1986, when only 27 California condors remained on earth, she was the last wild female of her species before she was captured, then put into a breeding program. Because of this, she raised the next generation and was released with them, teaching the young birds, somehow, to be condors in a world that had nearly erased them. Nearby, a painting depicts the Condor dance, one of the newer dances in the Chumash tradition. "To me, [the condor return] represents a cultural resurgence," Cogorno says. "We're still here. We're still thriving. We're not static." Outside, the Culture Park opens wide across the landscape. Native plantings—dogbane, yerba mansa—border brooks and pools that are fed by greywater, which the tribe recycles on-site. The limestone underfoot came from a quarry twenty minutes away. Further down the path stands the Tomol House, an open-slatted building that holds its namesake: a 950-pound plank canoe known as a tomol. It is not a relic, but a vessel that regularly hits the water. This very tomol has made what is known as “the crossing”—a culturally significant journey across 26 miles of open Pacific water from Ventura to the Channel Islands—multiple times. The crossing takes 10-13 hours, with 6 people sitting on their knees to paddle. Moving by feel and tradition toward an island they could reach in twenty minutes by motorboat. Jennifer, one of the museum's volunteers and one of the only women to captain a tomol, joins me inside. She talks about the crossing the way any athlete talks about a journey that changed them. "You really connect with past ancestors," she says. I continue on, following an audio narration, drawn from the voices of tribal leaders, that guides me through the middle of the museum, chronicling the mission period—a traumatic era that involved the boarding schools, the forced silencing of language, and the cutting of hair. A time when children were taken away and conditioned into believing their heritage shameful. But as I walk further, the room shifts to contemporary photographs. Ceremonies, children, laughter, a tomol coming into shore. A collection of moments that show the Chumash thriving. On my way out, I pass the seasonal round again—the acorns of fall, the fishing of summer—and I grip the clapper stick door handle one more time. The birds still sing overhead. I push through into the heat and the light, back into the valley the Chumash never left. The Santa Ynez Chumash Museum and Cultural Center is located in Santa Ynez, California, and is open Thursday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

item.title: RF Kuang's New Novel Takes On the Angst of a Diaspora Kid on a Study-Abroad Trip to Taipei
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.28
In RF Kuang’s latest book Taipei Story, the genre of the campus novel outgrows its name. The novel follows Chinese-American college freshman Lily Chen, who leaves the pale, male, and Yale environs of New Haven, Connecticut, for an intensive Mandarin-language program in Taipei for the summer. While her own family has never stepped foot in Taiwan, Lily holds onto the belief that perfecting her Mandarin will finally reconcile the shortcomings of being a diaspora kid. And when it came to choosing a place to study the language, traveling to Taiwan conveniently didn’t require her to apply for a visa. But on this quixotic mission to achieve total fluency, she finds that the gulf between her and her complicated family history won’t simply mend itself through diligent study. Her presumptions quickly unravel as she seeks answers in the gaps between economy seats on the flight from Boston to Taipei; in the uncertain, stilting words of Chinese heritage speakers; and in arthouse cinemas and concert halls she’s drawn to for the promise of blending in. From the seasonally inappropriate hot springs of Beitou to the glossy, souvenir-flogging halls of Taipei Taoyuan International Airport, the plot of this coming-of-age story doesn’t shy away from the uncomfortable realities of traveling abroad. Compounded by the sudden passing of Lily’s grandfather—which renders her initial motivation to study Mandarin moot—these follies only deepen beneath a veil of complicated mourning. And yet, they are also softened and forgiven with a grace that comes uniquely from allowing ourselves to be vulnerable in foreign places. Condé Nast Traveler recently spoke with Kuang about how home, identity, and being split between two places inspired Taipei Story, which is available in bookstores now. This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity. Walk us through your research itinerary for Taipei Story. The first place I looked was personal experience. When I started jotting down notes for what would become this book, I didn't know what it was going to be. I was just trying to make legible a tough time in my life when my Gong Gong passed away and I was in Taiwan. I was also in an intensive language program where I was wandering aimlessly around Taipei, meditating on [concepts of] home and cultural alienation. I wasn't walking around with a research agenda. I was just following crowds into places to see what they were seeing. If a long line of people was swarming, I would just join it. I would end up at screenings of movies I'd never heard of, or bookstores that I didn't know existed because I felt so blank, confused, and empty. I wanted somebody else to show me the answer to, “what is your city?” and if I became a ghost in its wake, was there a way I could totally erase myself? A lot of the descriptions in the novel where Lily ends up going to a place by accident, like the National Concert Hall, are places I also encountered by accident. Then, I started thinking about turning all those notes into an exaggerated, fictionalized version of what this experience would be—like if I were even younger and more dim-witted about how the world works. I read a lot of the major modern Taiwanese authors [like Kaori Li, Bai Xianyong, Chen Yingzhen, Wu Ming-yi, and Yang Shaung-zi—all mentioned in the author’s note and available in English translation] and wondered how they were thinking about home, identity, and being split between their mainland cultural heritage, and what it meant to be Taiwanese. How does this novel interface with—the sometimes impossible—expectations of homecoming? I'm fascinated with fantasies of homecoming and the narratives we buy into about how certain cultural experiences can return you to the fold. A lot of Chinese heritage speakers end up getting these flattened experiences in the US that feel like touch points, but are actually silly ways to reconnect—distilled cultural simulations such as Lunar New Year, red envelope parties, and film screenings. I say this not to mock diasporic kids; it makes total sense. You get so little, so you take whatever you can have, even if it's not region-specific or what your parents experienced. In Lily's case, I'm fascinated by the promises of heritage speaker-study abroad programs (editor’s note: these are linguistic immersion programs designed for students who grew up in households speaking a second language) because they hold so much promise and meaning for many people attending them. With Taiwan in particular, if you think about it just on the logical level, every step of this premise that you could, as a Chinese-American, go to Taiwan, to study Mandarin, to feel closer to your family on the mainland—is crazy. Lily's family has never been to Taiwan. She's the only person who's ever stepped foot there until her mom has a layover. When she finally gets there, she starts learning all the ways in which she is so wrong and how her experiences of Chineseness and the trajectory of her family history has absolutely nothing to do with Taiwan. In the end, she is a little more aware of this complexity and moves towards a more genuine, honest encounter of a strange place. She's like, I'm a foreigner, this is a weird summer, and maybe that's okay. In what ways does foreignness, or a lack of fluency, act as a source of fuel for travel and exploration in this novel? I definitely think [feeling out of place] is generative because I’ve felt like an outsider culturally for most of my life. My family immigrated [to the US from Guangzhou when Kuang was four-years-old], and I never felt like I quite belonged in the world of Dallas, Texas. I was a pretty happy kid, but when you're on the periphery, observing how people behave, I think you just get more perceptive. When I go back to China, that’s also not home, which is not a unique perspective. I think almost every immigrant kid feels this way. When I'm in China, I am looking at my family, and I observe cultural codes that they're following, and I have to figure out how these rules work because I didn't grow up understanding them innately. Being reflective about all of this makes you a good writer. In Lily's case I don't think she perceives her bumbling and ignorance as virtues. For her, it’s a barrier between her and the rest of the world. Because she's so afraid of getting things wrong, she never asks for help and never willing to embarrass herself. The ethical argument that the book is making is that embarrassment is really good for you. To admit, “I don't know what's going on,” and also “somebody helped me,” is an attitude I wish we all embraced more, not just when we're traveling, but in our entire lives. I find it a strength, and Lily finds it a weakness, and by the end of the book, she's at least accepted that she's gonna mess up, and she might as well own it. From the Poppy War trilogy to your last novel Katabasis, you often take on the perspective of being a student. Why return to the eyes of an undergraduate for this story? This book was very different because it's the first book of mine where the protagonists weren't growing up with me. When I was working on the Poppy War trilogy, I was a teenager, and they're teenagers, then they're undergrads, grad students, and in their late-20s. I was writing very reflexively to try to understand the world from my vantage point in life, but I had a couple of life changes in the past few years that made me more interested in going back. With the maturity of turning 30, I have more comfort in making fun of the person I used to be. When I was writing Taipei Story, it was like, I could write a memoir of what I experienced, or I could make things even more ridiculous, even more embarrassing, and reach back to the person I was when I was 18 going to Beijing for the first time and overwhelmed with everything I didn't know. The key to writing from the point-of-view of adolescence is not from this position of condescension that the youths are so silly, but to be kind to your younger self and recognize that all of your insecurities, all the things that you were failing at, everything that you got wrong, are deeply hilarious and also a really shared experience. There's a lot of humanity in cringe. By setting a story in modern-day Taipei, the narrative acknowledges Taiwanese-Chinese geopolitics, and beyond that, the country’s past with Japanese colonialism, the Chinese Civil War. How did you want to depict Taipei as a city with those layered histories? I wanted to be really cautious here, because I'm not Taiwanese. I'm not an expert in Taiwanese history or literature. As I pointed out in the author's note, this is not a voice from the inside but the very filtered perception of an American teenager who’s learning about all of this for the first time. I did want to poke gentle fun at the way that people generally take Western ideological frameworks that are very binary and project them onto local histories with no attention to what locals are actually saying. There's the first chapter where her little cohort of friends are running around the city, and there’s a pecking order based on assumptions about race. People would ask her where should we go? What should we eat? And she’d always pretend to know the answers and go Google them in the bathroom. They do the same thing when they're at Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall trying to understand, is he a good guy or a bad guy? Is he like George Washington? Should we be taking selfies with him? I wanted to give the experience of somebody who feels like they ought to be an expert by virtue of the ethnicity that they were born into, but who’s actually totally detached from genuine knowledge of the place or history. How did grief form your characterization of Taipei? [When Lily’s grandfather passed] it was a snapping moment for her. Up until that point, she is trying to slot all of her experiences into this predetermined narrative that this is getting her closer to the person she could have been if her family had never left China. After her grandfather passes, she is thrown into this weird grief and confusion, and she gives up on that goal altogether. She recognizes the futility of trying to go back and becoming a version of herself that never existed. Paradoxically, this frees her up to take in the things she closed her mind off to before. Now, she's okay with being a tourist. She goes on these Klook experiences [to Pinglin Tea Museum and Yehliu Geopark]. She’s on a bus with American families from Philly doing all the canned, predetermined activities just thinking, “oh, this is fun,” and learning a lot. Despite all the complex grief that is in this novel, it’s also very funny. Is Taipei a place that is particularly funny to you or has its own language of humor that you wanted to capture here? I think every place has surprising, inexplicable quirks if you know how to pay attention to them. One in particular I'm obsessed with is Taiwan English. I was inspired by a blog post by Tao Lin, an author who also wrote a novel called Taipei. It was just a series of pictures that he took walking around of ridiculous translations, and some of them are accurate on a very literal, character-by-character level, and some of them, I can't believe you would get this result if you ran it through any translation app. But it's not just in Taiwan either. You see it on the mainland. For instance, my mom was wearing a shirt, that just said, “GO FUCK” in repeating block letters. She bought it at a clothes market with her sister when she was in China, and she was only paying attention to the fabric, and she was like, “Oh, it's so lovely. Does this color look good on me?” and didn't register the text at all. I said, “Mom, do you know what that says?” She turned it inside out and wore it that way for the rest of the day.

item.title: 'The Gentlemen' Season 2 Takes Us From English Country Estates to Italian Palazzos in Mob Territory
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.28
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The second season of Guy Ritchie’s hit Netflix series, The Gentleman, is here. The first series introduced us to Eddie Horniman (Theo James), a young British aristocrat who had inherited his father’s grand country estate, only to discover that behind the family money was a secret cannabis empire. In Season 2, Horniman, now the Duke of Halstead, is keen to expand the operation, alongside his business partner, Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario). This will take them out of the English countryside and subterranean criminal worlds of the East End and Liverpool, and thrust them instead into the world of the Mafia, as they attempt to go international and do business with the dangerous Capo dei Capi, Marco Moretti (Sergio Castellito). “The madness of Italy’s beauty, its culture, its history and its traditions was something I felt would fit perfectly into our show,” says Ritchie. “I had wanted to expand the canvas of The Gentlemen in this season. Italy was just an obvious choice. British gangsters colliding with the Italian Mafia just feels so right for our world. Some fruit hangs low and looks so tasty you just can’t resist for very long.” Here are some of the key locations used in the filming of The Gentleman Seasons 1 and 2, from Ritchie’s Ashcombe Estate to Lake Maggiore in Italy. Is The Gentlemen based on a real-life story? Both the film of the same name and the two seasons of The Gentlemen are not based on a true story, though of course, they borrow elements from the criminal underworld and its cast of characters. The situation that Eddie Horniman and his family find themselves in – of having to find new ways to monetise their vast aristocratic estates – is a reality, however. There are no real life examples of aristocrats running cannabis empires that we know of though. The main thrust of the action in Season 2 of The Gentlemen takes place in Lake Maggiore, connecting Horniman and his business partner Katie Glass to Italy’s criminal gangs – the mafia. Historically, the area has not been known as a mafia heartland – unlike regions like Sicily, for example – but it does have a relationship with organised crime. In particular, the ’Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, have reportedly used the area for cocaine and weapons trafficking, thanks to its close proximity to the Swiss border. Where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The Badminton Estate, Gloucestershire While some scenes of The Gentleman were filmed on stage sets at Alperton Studios in Wembley, London, the exterior of Halstead Manor, the fictional home of the Horniman family, is The Badminton Estate. The real-life home of the Duke and Duchess of Beaufort is a popular filming location and wedding venue in the south Gloucestershire countryside. Viewers with a keen eye may recognise the property from Netflix favourite Bridgerton and movies including Pearl Harbour and 28 Days Later. The sprawling estate has been occupied for thousands of years, and the remains of several Roman villas surround the main home. The medieval property was owned by the Boteler family before Edward Somerset, fourth Earl of Worcester, purchased the manors of Great and Little Badminton in 1612. It’s his son, Sir Thomas Somerset, who made significant alterations to the original house, and the property has captured the imagination of high society and even the royal family over the centuries – Charles II stayed in the house, and the late Queen Elizabeth II was a regular visitor to the annual Horse Trials. “Badminton felt immediately right for Halstead,” says supervising location Manager Iggy Ellis, “because it’s a proper, lived-in home rather than a National Trust museum. So inside, there’d be some walking sticks by the door or a few shotgun rounds from where they’d been out shooting. There were cracks and tired bits, as you’d get in every family home. But there was also oil painting and history and majesty. It felt perfect for our story.” Ashcombe Estate, Wiltshire In episode one, Ritchie made his own country estate, Ashcombe Park, available for filming a shooting party scene. “That was a lot of fun but tricky at times too,” says production designer Martyn John. “You’re in the middle of nowhere with no phone signal or internet. We had to take everything in; so, flowers, food, dogs, guns and also… frozen partridges.” Ashcombe is a working farm set in 1,100 acres of rolling chalk land, and is named after the ash trees and the valleys (‘combes’) that monopolise much of it. It has been the family home of Ritchie since 2001 (when he bought it with ex-wife Madonna for £9 million), and was previously the home of photographer Cecil Beaton.
