item.title: The Best Hotels in Berlin at Every Price Point
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.58
More than three decades after the wall came down, Berlin remains a city in constant flux, where the past and present intertwine in wildly innovative ways. A booming capital brimming with youthful energy and creative ideas, it is reinventing itself brick by brick—and nowhere is this more evident than in its dynamic hotel scene. New life has been breathed into landmark properties, and dilapidated buildings have been rescued and refashioned into chic boutique stays. Famed global brands such as Rocco Forte and The Hoxton have arrived on the scene, joining timeless classics that have stood for the past century. From the splashy west to the grittier east, property choices in every style and at every price point span the city. Here are the best hotels in Berlin that are open for check-in now, as chosen by our local editors. Our top picks: - Best for luxury: Waldorf Astoria Berlin - Best for a central location: Telegraphenamt - Best for families: Michelberger Hotel - Read Full ReviewHoused in a late 19th-century building, Irish lifestyle hotel brand The Dean brings its “vibe first” philosophy to the German capital, pairing bold design with cultural connectivity and a food concept that draws in more than just overnight guests. Interiors channel Berlin’s creative energy and avant-garde spirit from the moment you step inside. Historic architectural details sit alongside saturated colors, sculptural lighting, and a confident, contemporary design language. Room numbers are handwritten on the doors rather than printed—an intentionally imperfect detail that nods to Berlin’s slightly rough-around-the-edges character. In the bathrooms, original black-and-white tiles have been preserved, punctuated by red shower frames and boldly framed mirrors. Toiletries are by D.S. & Durga, lending a subtle spa feel. For food, Benedict is the heart of the hotel—a bakery, restaurant, and bar combined in one lively, open space. Breakfast is served until 4 p.m. on weekdays and all day on weekends. The focus is, naturally, on eggs Benedict in multiple variations: with ham and cheese, avocado, or pulled beef, served on brioche or a buttery croissant. The brand’s Irish roots are also present in the drinks offering: whiskey in every minibar, the Irish cocktail “Ól,” and even a dedicated Guinness tap behind the bar—a small but unmistakable nod to its heritage. —Susanna Gunst - Read Full ReviewThis sophisticated hotel in Mitte’s bustling center, steps from the Brandenburg Gate, features one-of-a-kind guest rooms decorated by local and international artists. The prominent neon sign on the façade is strategically placed above a self-portrait done in bronze by artist Alicja Kwade, and once inside, you’re transported into a moodily lit living room reminiscent of an art patron’s salon. Refined couples, having just finished their cocktails, chat quietly while on their way out to the Staatsoper (German State Opera). It all feels very calm and grown up, like an idealized version of Berlin’s past artistic glories, updated with a buzzy sense of creative present. Bed down in a room with hand-painted wallpaper or a hand-carved folding screen; each is uniquely decorated and may have a one-of-a-kind large-scale painting on the wall, or even a funky video installation. Bathrooms are lined in glazed subway-style tiles and have heated floors and large walk-in showers. The property is an easy to walk to the Reichstag; if you’ve come to shop, Friedrichstrasse is a block away; to run or bike, the large green expanse of Tiergarten is a hop and a skip. —Liz Humphreys - Read Full ReviewWith an exceptional location on Monbijoupark in the Mitte district, this grand neo-Baroque building once housed the city’s vast telegraph office—built between 1910 and 1916, and at one time the most sophisticated postal building in Germany. It has since been meticulously restored and transformed into a posh destination for discerning travelers looking to stay close to a huge selection of trendy restaurants, bars, and shops, as well as beloved Hackesche Höfe's old courtyards-turned-commercial spaces. The 97 guest rooms all have an industrial look, with brick-barrel vaulted ceilings divided by metal beams and exposed brick walls. Art Deco design elements like illuminated glass capsules, which display the room numbers, nod toward the building’s history, and hanging lamps adorn each side of the bed like a movie star’s chandelier earrings. Though occupied by digital nomads during the day, the bar at ROOT buzzes after dark, and a DJ spins techno beats nightly starting at 8 p.m.—this is Berlin, after all. —L.H. - Read Full ReviewFans of the flagship Waldorf Astoria New York will feel right at home in this Berlin outpost, set in an elegant skyscraper in City West and just around the corner from the exclusive shopping boulevard Kurfürstendamm (Ku’damm). Rooms are seriously big—starting at 452 square feet—and designed in a contemporary style, with neutral gray velour furnishings, swirl-patterned rugs, and a statement-making gold wall behind the beds. Large marble bathrooms have separate tubs and showers in every category, and the in-mirror televisions and Aesop toiletries add a luxurious touch. Reached by a separate elevator, the Tower Suites (floors 22 to 31) are worth it for the views—of the city, the Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church, or the neighboring Tiergarten park and Berlin Zoo. For a true splurge, the massive 30th-floor Astor Suite (with floor-to-ceiling windows, a balcony, and a separate dining room and kitchen) or the 31st-floor Presidential Suite (complete with a grand piano, open fireplace, and two balconies) boast sweeping city views. —Jennifer Ceaser - Read Full ReviewA neoclassical 19th-century bank houses this five-star Rocco Forte property, which enjoys an unrivaled location on Bebelplatz, right in the historic heart of East Berlin. Many of the building’s original details—graceful marble columns, skylights, an intricate iron staircase—have been retained, most notably down below in the pool area, formerly the bank’s jewel vault. A contemporary design streak runs throughout the lobby, which is dotted with oversized black velvet sofas, towering red-lacquer vases, and dangling globe lights, plus a playful pink neon birdcage as the centerpiece. Book one of the higher-end suites and get perks galore, including personalized concierge service, luggage unpacking, free pressing of one garment, and in-house movies. There's a standard minibar in all rooms, but you can request a bespoke Rocco Forte Nourish minibar in advance, stocked with a selection of healthy snacks and drinks. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewBuilt in 1891 as a private residence and converted into a hotel in 1911, Hotel Zoo has been one of West Berlin’s poshest stays for more than a century. In the 1950s, it served as the VIP hotel for the Berlin International Film Festival and was a haunt for A-listers like Grace Kelly and Sophia Loren. So it’s fitting that the hotel’s glamorous history has been reinterpreted by two Hollywood designers, Dayna Lee and Ted Berner. The cool design aesthetic and location on Ku'damm, Berlin's best shopping street, make it a covetable stay for anyone. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewToday, there’s that sense that Hotel Adlon Kempinski Berlin—having withstood the vicissitudes of a tumultuous century—is armor-plated, as unassailable as the bulletproof floor-to-ceiling windows of the presidential suites. Under the Kempinski aegis since the 1990s, it bottles that sense of timelessness and offers a feeling of security and tradition as something that is as precious as it is soothing. The past is present here, exuding patrician-style grandeur and elegance: the Art Deco floor gauges in the elevators, an old-fashioned bicycle that the bellboys use, the panels of walnut wood in the Michelin-starred Lorenz Adlon Esszimmer restaurant, acres of marble for a grand staircase, and gold flakes even on the lobby lounge’s currywurst. Old-school perfectionism calls for the three types of caviar and Champagne at breakfast, as well as butler-ironed newspapers brought to the table. It all contributes to that illusion that you are in a cocoon, away from the travails of the world. —Catherine Fairweather - Read Full ReviewKPM is the vision of Berlin banker Jörg Woltmann, who helped save the 18th-century Royal Porcelain Manufactory Berlin complex on which the hotel has stood since 2019. The ultra-modern, cube-like building has picked up multiple design and architecture prizes and was nominated as Europe’s Leading Design Hotel by the 2021 World Travel Awards. Rooms are minimalist, chic, and smartly designed, with functional desks, high-tech wall control panels, and clever built-ins that make the spaces seem larger than they are—aided by the floor-to-ceiling windows. If weather permits, take advantage of the rooftop terrace with great views over Berlin—just remember to bring your own drinks, as there is no bar. Major sites like Tiergarten and the Berlin Zoo are 10 and 15 minutes by foot, respectively. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewSet in a restored 1913 Art Nouveau building along leafy Oranienplatz, Orania is one of the few hotels—and the only upscale option—in the edgy, nightlife-filled Kreuzberg. A large, open-plan "Living Room," which functions as a restaurant-bar-lounge, is bookended by two roaring fireplaces (in winter) and surrounded by enormous windows; a raised corner stage sports a Steinway piano (there's classical or jazz most nights). The rooms and suites vary in size and layout, but all are similarly designed: lots of rich woods, deep red textiles featuring the hotel’s signature gold elephant, handmade Persian carpets, and curvaceous lamps from Catellani. If you're a frequent visitor to Berlin and love nightlife, this hotel is ideal for you. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewA renovated 1950s high-rise is home to the Berlin outpost of this hip German hotel chain, which is sandwiched between the Berlin Zoo and the trendy concept mall Bikini Berlin. There's a fun energy as soon as you walk into the third-floor reception area, dubbed Bikini Island, which sports a playful jungle-themed design, with tropical plants, stuffed monkeys, and hammocks perfectly positioned to look out over the zoo’s monkey and bird cages. All rooms, even the ones called XL, are on the smaller side, but the funky Jungle Rooms, many with their own hammocks overlooking the zoo, offer an escape different from others you can find in the city. The hotel is also home to the Monkey Bar, one of Berlin's most popular cocktail spots, and guests can cut the line by taking a private elevator straight to the door. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewThis five-star property, long known for its impeccable white-glove service, has a sophisticated look that nods to 1920s Berlin. Entry-level Deluxe Rooms are plenty spacious, measuring a generous 430 square feet, but it’s worth trading up to a Deluxe View Room for fantastic views overlooking Potsdamer Platz. For even more exclusivity, the 42 Club Level rooms and suites on the 10th and 11th floors offer 24-hour access to a lounge with panoramic city vistas, complimentary food and drink, and a private concierge. The elegant sandstone tower fits right in with the neighboring skyscrapers on bustling Potsdamer Platz, and guests are a short stroll from the Holocaust Memorial, the Brandenburg Gate, and Tiergarten park's 519 acres of tree-lined paths and flowering gardens. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewFrom the outside, the circa-1970s building housing The Hoxton doesn’t look like anything special. But step into the oversized lobby chock-full of comfy places to sit (with your choice of chairs and sectionals arranged around tables of various shapes and sizes, along with one long communal coworking table), and you see why the young (and young at heart) could spend all day here. When the mood strikes for a drink, the sophisticated bar lies right behind the lobby, separated by staggered shelves displaying artfully arranged vases, jars, books, and other design knickknacks. And since the Hoxton also has its own coffee shop (technically a teahouse) and Indian restaurant, it’s truly a place that invites lingering. Each of the 234 guest rooms has a similar look, with scalloped headboards in muted pink and green, speckled terrazzo side tables, Art Nouveau lamps, and hardwood floors. —L.H. - Read Full ReviewBuilt in 1914 in the style of a French palace, this magnificent villa has served as a private residence, embassy, naval officers’ club, and later, a luxury hotel, hosting notable guests such as Romy Schneider and Paul McCartney. In 2014, late Berlin fashion designer Patrick Hellmann acquired the property and began renovations, restoring its glorious historical details while bringing much of the design—previously done by Karl Lagerfeld in the 1990s—firmly into the 21st century. The 43 rooms and 9 suites feature particularly impressive details: A dual-bedroom Kaiser Suite boasts an antique library with original frescoes, and the first-floor Karl Lagerfeld Suite has lovely Art Deco touches and a stone balcony overlooking the gardens. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewVladimir Nabokov, Brigitte Bardot, and Alain Delon have all stayed at this luxury hotel at some point in its history. It opened in 1913 on a quiet, leafy square in posh Charlottenburg and was renovated a century later as part of Marriott’s Autograph Collection. It was just spruced up again in 2025 after its takeover by the Germany-based, design-focused Roomers brand. The boutique property retains its alluring Art Nouveau flourishes, including a sinuous canopy above the entrance, Moorish arched windows, and exquisite stucco work throughout. The flawless redesign integrates historic decorative elements with contemporary touches. The luxurious boutique vibe and ideal location—just a short walk to the shops along Kurfürstendamm and the Berlin Zoo—make it an enduring draw, even after the redo. —J.C. FAQ: What is the best area to stay in when visiting Berlin? For first-timers who want to get a true feel for the city, Mitte is the beating creative heart of Berlin, and where you'll find some of our favorite locally-grown hotels, including Telegraphenamt and Chateau Royal Berlin. Another ideal option is Charlottenburg, in western Berlin, which is home to upscale shopping, the grand Charlottenburg Palace, and hotels like The Hoxton. How do we choose the best hotels in Berlin? Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. It was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller UK. Recommended

item.title: The Quiet Magic of Greece in the Off Season
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.58
Few eras of Greek history compare to the ancient times that the country has become so synonymous with—the cinematic fables of Odysseus, comic-book lore of Leonidas, and philosophic creeds of Socrates are ever-present in pop culture. But anyone who’s been to Hellas in the past few years can tell you that something new is brewing here—current-day Greece is coming close to a similar precipice, one that could be nearly as definitive as the Bronze Age, as visitors arrive in droves higher than ever before. Arrivals to the nation of 10 million people were up by 38% in the first few months of 2026, the highest increase on the continent for that period by far (Italy was second, with a 21% rise). Now, more than ever, it feels like everyone is planning a seafaring escape or mountain adventure to Athens and the islands—or, if you’re in-the-know, to the serene coastal towns of the Peloponnese peninsula or the northern Aegean’s sparkling Thermaic Gulf. One decade after the country’s financial crisis peaked, and a half decade since the pandemic-era halt in tourism that had so many here pleading for the long-despised cruise ships to return, you would think this is good news for a state as tourism-dependent as Greece. And you could be right—but the unfortunate reality, according to the Bank of Greece, is that the crescendo coincides with mounting climate disasters that threaten the infrastructure of a nation still in the throes of recovery; a particularly harrowing warning ahead of this year’s El Niño; not to mention during their Mediterranean neighbors' unprecedented fire seasons. The seasonal pressure has become a balancing act. The good news, though, is that summer is far from the only time to visit. Outside the grip of sweltering summer heat lies some of Greece’s most delicious adventures: tasting early spring’s olive oils straight from the groves right after harvest; fall parties with small-island locals celebrating another season of panigiria wrapped; perusing the treasures of Athens’ open-air ruins in the soft, pre-winter light. There is so much more to Greece than the postcard islands—and the packed ferries to get to them—and with the mainland about to have its moment in the sun (we’re looking at you, Christopher Nolan), there’s no better time than the off-season to uncover every corner’s most spectacular self—the one without the heaving crowds. To prove it, we’ve tapped the best local creators to share how they do it, and how you can, too, siga siga (more slowly). —Shannon McMahon, senior destinations editor Over the last 30 years, Nikos Tsepetis has made Ammos Hotel (and its beloved on-site Red Jane Bakery) one of Crete’s most talked-about hotels. Born and raised in Chania, the owner’s joyful, design-led approach to hospitality is rooted in his hometown, with 80% of his staff also locals. From its high-quality cuisine to its warm, home-away-from-home atmosphere, Ammos reflects Tsepetis’s deep connection to Chania. Here, he shares why spring is his favorite time to experience the city. For Dutch artist Christiane Smit, a vacation on Paros in 2008 changed the course of her life. Drawn instinctively to the Cycladic island, she stayed and has lived in villages across Paros ever since. Today, she runs a ceramics atelier in Lefkes and owns minimalist clifftop villa Moonhouse, while restoring a century-old stone house in Kostos. Here, Smit shares the shoulder-season pleasures that keep her on the island year-round, and where to eat and stay. For winemaker Michael Kouloglou, moving to Santorini from Greece's mainland 11 years ago was an easy choice: “It is the mecca of Greek white wine.” Since then, he has worked across the island’s wineries before launching Orycton, a small-batch Assyrtiko made with grapes from old vines. Now based in quiet Monolithos, Kouloglou has lived throughout Santorini, gaining an intimate understanding of its villages, landscapes, and rhythms. Here, he shares why autumn is his favorite season to explore the island. Greek family recipes are often passed down by instinct rather than instruction—a pinch here, a glug there, learned at the kitchen table. Food writer Anastasia Miari has spent nearly a decade documenting these dishes and the older generations and remote villages that have kept them alive. Her cooking celebrates Greece’s culinary traditions, while her latest book, Mediterranea, expands the journey across the region, from Moroccan tagines and Turkish breakfasts to Sicilian pasta. “Alive. That’s how Athens feels to me,” says Agapi Sbokou, co-owner and CEO of Greek hotel brand Phāea. Having lived in the capital since she was 18, Sbokou has watched the city continually evolve, while retaining its irresistible energy. For her, the joy of visiting somewhere lies in understanding its local rhythm. Here, she shares why autumn is so magical in Athens, alongside some of her favorite places to explore in the city. Lead editors: Sarah Allard, Shannon McMahon, Arati Menon, Lisa Riehl Writers: Shannon McMahon, Chadner Navarro, Noo Saro-Wiwa, Olivia Morelli Visuals and social media: Sophie Knight, Mercedes Bleth, Lucy Bruton Syndication editors: Kat Chen, Skyli Alvarez This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: The Best Luxury Cruise Lines Now Rival the Finest Hotels
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.53
The luxury cruising landscape—or seascape, rather—has grown tremendously over the past few years. And it's no longer just traditional ocean cruises. Travelers accustomed to the finer things in life can now have their pick among expedition vessels plying previously inaccessible polar regions, sumptuous river ships sailing from the Amazon to the Mekong, and flashy new superyachts worthy of Page Six. Aboard, passengers can expect all the same perks they'd find at the world's most exclusive hotels, from personal butlers to multi-story penthouses. This year alone has seen a boom in ultra-luxe yachts, built not by established names in the cruising industry but rather by hotel brands. Sailing with far fewer passengers, they give the vibe more of a private charter or a floating hotel than a traditional cruise ship, with thoughtful approaches to dining and design. Scheduling, too, is shifting. Many posh lines are extending Mediterranean itineraries into the shoulder season and even winter, meaning there are more options for luxury voyages than ever before. Not to be left behind, the old guard—Regent Seven Seas Cruises, Seabourn, Crystal—are continuously making adjustments to meet the needs of today's luxury traveler. Regent is reducing the passenger count on Explorer Class ships to expand cabin sizes while readying to unveil the opulent Seven Seas Prestige ship in December. Seabourn will soon announce a fleet-wide makeover of its culinary programs. Crystal, which has dropped “Cruises” from its brand name, is readying the new-build Crystal Grace for June 2028. Luxury is also creeping aboard expedition ships. Silversea extends its all-suite, butler-outfitted, complimentary caviar philosophy to four exploration vessels, including the Galapagos-only 100-passenger Silver Origin. Scenic Luxury Cruises & Tours, now sailing two sleek 270-passenger yachts capable of polar cruising, debuts 270-passenger Scenic Ikon with two helicopters, a submersible, and 15 dining venues in April 2028. Luxe French line Ponant scores with 245-passenger Le Commandant Charcot, the only luxury icebreaker at sea and can sail to the true North Pole. Seabourn sails the 264-passenger Seabourn Venture and twin Seabourn Pursuit, two lavish all-suite polar-class expedition ships cruising remote itineraries, each with two submarines. All of this to say, there’s never been a better time to hop aboard a luxury cruise line. Below, we round up the names to know across all categories. Yacht The 94-passenger Amangati, which is now open for reservations and will set sail in spring 2027, embodies the hotel brand’s space and privacy design, and even offers a two-deck spa with a Japanese serenity garden. It’s so catered to the one-percenter that it offers “host suites” for passengers’ personal service or security staff as well as two helipads. Consider this ship particularly ripe for charter. The 95-suite, residential-leaning Four Seasons I, which debuted in March 2026, has a one-to-one passenger-crew ratio, meaning your needs will never go unmet. The 79-suite Four Seasons II will arrive in May 2028 for further Med sails, showcasing two-to-four-bedroom suites on the upper decks and a whopping 11 culinary concepts. Only breakfast is included in cruise fares, a luxury cruise first. (Passengers should plan for about $250 per day, per person for food and beverage.) Late stays and overnights in ports, deep dives into well-being (including the Lanserhof Reset, a longevity experience on the November inaugural transatlantic crossing courtesy of the renowned medi-spa group), and personalized shore excursions are among the amenities. This line’s stunning bespoke ships feature three fully automated rigs capable of delivering 100% wind-powered propulsion in favorable conditions. Dynamic positioning and LNG propulsion are among its energy-efficient and environmental accomplishments. The 54-suite Orient Express Corinthian features five restaurants under the culinary direction of superstar chef Yannick Alléno, whose restaurants have won multiple Michelin stars, and sails the Med until autumn. Twin Orient Express Olympian sets sail next spring. Some excursions are included in the price, others are not. From the hotel brand known for its luxe amenities, personalized service, and fine dining, find three all-suite, all-inclusive ships—149-suite Evrima, 224-suite Ilma, and 226-suite Luminara. Each offers five restaurants and a marina for watersports. Menus from the brand’s Michelin-star-earning chefs are de rigueur, as are personalized spa therapies, and high-end boutiques such as Cartier. Expedition Le Commandant Charcot, the only luxury icebreaker, can travel to the true North Pole and other ice-bound destinations. This French ship offers Le Nuna, the only Alain Ducasse fine-dining restaurant at sea. Ponant also features six bilingual explorer ships for warmer climes. This elegant ocean-going line sails two twin expedition ships, 264-passenger Seabourn Venture and Seabourn Pursuit. Both possess PC6 Polar Class standards, meaning they are capable of pushing through ice. All-suite accommodations, excellent dining, and crew pampering enhance expedition adventures. Scenic currently possesses two sleek 228-passenger ultra-luxury vessels dubbed “discovery yachts” excelling at polar cruising. Both feature 10 dining venues, a spacious spa, two helicopters, one submersible, Zodiacs, kayaks, and stand-up paddleboards. Beyond its classic ocean liners, Silversea’s four expedition ships include three venturing to Poles, Kimberley, Australia, and other remote locales, and one in the Galapagos. Silversea is also opening The Cormorant at 55 South, the Earth’s southernmost hotel in Puerto Williams, as an easier waystation to Antarctica, in October 2026. Ocean Crystal’s two ultra-luxurious ships, 740-passenger Crystal Serenity and 606-passenger Crystal Symphony, feature butler service for all, pillow menus, a Nobu Matsuhisa-affiliated Asian restaurant, and 24-hour room service. Owned by Abercrombie & Kent Travel Group, Abercrombie & Kent partners with Crystal for special voyages combining land elements. With three 922-passenger ships already sailing, EJ unveils Explora IV in summer 2027 with 461 suites, five heated pools, and seven restaurants. This ship and Explora III feature a private dining chef’s table, beach-club-style Shore Club eatery, wine-tasting cellar, and an expanded kids club with family-oriented destination experiences. Near-twin Explora V sets sail in December 2027 and Explora VI in August 2028. Oceania’s seven ships are devoted to culinary superiority. Beyond Oceania Sonata, discover Oceania Aurelia, with just 238 accommodations, in November 2027, and Oceania Arietta in 2029. Oceania Cruises teams with Condé Nast Traveler editors for insider tips on activities ashore. Bilingual French line Ponant is hailed for intriguing itineraries across 12 intimate ships, from sailing vessels to expedition. English-only cruises sail in partnerships, often with Smithsonian Journeys. The December debut of Seven Seas Prestige heralds the newest of the line's seven-ship fleet. Lavish new suite categories feature accommodations with in-suite elevators, private gyms, and personal butlers. These three ocean liners feel more quiet luxury than over-the-top opulent—just the way devotees like it. The all-suite 600-passenger Seabourn Encore and Seabourn Ovation offer multiple fine-dining venues and a fee-extra Retreat for extra privacy and service. The 458-passenger Seabourn Quest just underwent an extensive refurbishment. With two twin mega-yachts, 112-passenger SeaDream I and SeaDream II sport a relaxed yachting lifestyle. Signature elements include sophisticated cuisine, attentive crew, and a watersports marina platform. SeaDream III promises a somewhat bigger and more elevated sailing experience to more destinations in 2029. Beyond exploration vessels, Silversea sails eight all-suite ultra-luxury ships where butlers pamper passengers and complimentary caviar abounds. Expect multiple other included amenities, too. River The three all-suite ships in this European line arguably deliver the best gastronomic experiences on rivers. Included outings might range from an al fresco candlelit dinner at a French winery to private palace concerts in Vienna. Ever-expanding Uniworld will count some 24 distinctly designed ships by 2028, each reflecting the sailing region. The design-forward riverboats mirror charming boutique hotels, with itineraries in Europe, Vietnam, Cambodia, and Egypt. Not as uber-luxury as some of the other names here, AmaWaterways is a more affordable luxury river cruise option that still offers an incredible sense of intimacy and low-impact cruising thanks to the ships' small sizes. Most notable recently is the line's launch of an itinerary on Colombia's Magdalena River, the first of its kind since the days of the steam ship. With one of the most extensive fleet of river cruises vessels in the world, river cruising is Viking’s bread and butter. While Viking falls on the more accessible end of the luxury cruise spectrum, it’s frequently voted the best river cruise line in the world by CNT readers thanks to its Scandanavian design, exceptional service, Nordic spas, and adults-only atmosphere.

item.title: From Kendall Jenner to the Clooneys: This is Where the A-list Stays for the Venice Film Festival
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.48
For over 80 years now the Venice International Film Festival has attracted the world's most glamorous and famous crowd. In the 1950s, it saw Brigitte Bardot pose for paparazzi while sitting on grass, and Elizabeth Taylor take a dip in the lido at Hotel Excelsior Venice. Fast forward to today and it's just as star-studded, with the 83rd Venice International Film Festival hosting an array of actors, supermodels and musicians, from Laura Dern to Robert Pattinson, Irina Shayk and Liam Gallagher. Much of the red carpet action takes place at Hotel Excelsior Venice, which has hosted the main event since 1932. Notably, following a three-year closure, the hotel reopened last year (2025), to reveal a grand renovation and thus many of this year's attendees – Kate Mara, Claire Foy, Maggie Gyllenhaal – have also chosen to stay in the boldly striped suites. It's not the only top hotel in Venice that is known to host film festival attendees. The A-listers that prefer something more private often book into one of the 24 opulent rooms within Aman Venice – not only do the Clooneys love to stay here, they also married in the Palazzo Papadopoli location in 2014. To be even further removed and escape the flashes of paparazzi, Hotel Cipriani, A Belmond Hotel, Venice sits on the eastern tip of the Giudecca island. Its peaceful location has been a long- time favourite for the world's most famous stars, with previous guests including Sophia Loren, Cary Grant, and more recently Jennifer Lawrence and Lady Gaga.

item.title: Off-Season Greece: To Avoid the Crowds on Crete, Hike and Ski in Early Spring
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.25
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to hotel owner Nikos Tsepetis. For 30 years, Nikos Tsepetis has run Ammos, one of the most talked-about hotels in Greece. The seaside boutique hotel in Chania, northwest Crete, is a manifestation of the man himself: joyful and design-focused with a commitment to high-quality cuisine (including his Red Jane Bakery) and local roots. Tsepetis’s improvisational approach to hospitality creates a home-away-from-home warmth that keeps many of his guests returning, year after year. Born and raised in Chania, Tsepetis is deeply connected to his hometown, which he believes is different from other towns in Crete, because “we are more international and welcoming to foreigners, and it's a multi-layered city." Yet, 80 percent of his staff are locals, he says. “It adds to the experience, because you always meet people who were born here, who remember the past, so there is this continuity." Here, Tsepetis tells us why spring is his favorite time of year in Chania. What would you say is the sweet spot time of the year to visit? Just before high season. April and early May are my favorite time of year because the climate is amazing. Chania is on the western end of Crete and is the prettiest part of the island because it's greener, and we still normally have snow on the Lefka Ori [White Mountains]—you can see them from the sea while swimming. In spring, everything is very fresh, everything is well painted; you can go to the villages and monasteries, and all the flowers are out. Also, spring often coincides with Easter, which is important in the Greek Orthodox religion. I don't care at all about religion, but it's still very spiritual and beautiful. What do you love most about being there during this season? It's less busy. The rain cleans everything and the snow melts, so we are greener than other parts of the island. Everything's fresh and new; you can feel the rejuvenation, so spring is a very sweet time. Who’s around this time of year? Traditionally, Chania benefited from the presence of foreigners, even before it became touristy. It’s very urban, with more than 100,000 permanent residents, so you have everyone from hipsters and freaks to lefties living here—not the expected Greek island crowd. It's always very lively, and what sets it apart from some other towns in Crete is that the locals are a driving force with a very loud voice. They are not here to serve the foreigners. Where would we find you eating during this time? My all-time favorite local is Evgonia Tavern. Only a very simple tavern, it has fish and meat in a non-fish environment. I love Periplous Restaurant for its unbeatable location at the beautiful Tanneries Hotel. It’s one of the old buildings by the water where they used to process leather. In spring we go to the villages, because it's still very mild and there aren’t too many people. I always go to Ntounias, a very old, well-known rural taverna in the middle of nowhere near Drakona in the mountains. There's a crazy guy there, Stelios Trilyrakis, who has been involved with slow food for 30 years. You don't know what you’ll eat or when you’ll eat it. It's very inexpensive, and he cultivates everything himself. In Greece, we love French fries. And Stelios makes amazing chips by cooking them in olive oil in a ceramic pot. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? We're famous for doing a traditional Tsoureki Easter brioche, a kind of braided bread that's sweet but not too sweet. Once a year we also eat a special soup called magiritsa made from lamb intestines, lungs, and liver. We normally eat it at home—it’s not so much a restaurant dish—but we do a very good one at Ammos. Also, Nyketerida is famous for it. Spring is about beans and greens—we have beautiful asparagus and the best artichokes—and goat roasted in the oven with potatoes, zucchini, and tomatoes. We also have a very famous dish called dakos, a barley rusk with tomato sauce and this amazing goat’s cheese called mizithra. One of the best places to eat it is Costas Cafeneion, a family-run cafe in village Maza, which is between Chania and Rethymnon. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off-season? In January and February, people from around the world come here for the mountains and skiing, including the annual Pierra Creta ski mountaineering race. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Summer is very hot and can be dry, and then we have the winter, which is rainy. But in spring, the weather is cooler and you can hike, ski, and swim. The sea is actually colder in spring than in winter because of the snowmelt. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? I’m biased, but Saturday is a great day to hang out at my Red Jane Bakery early in the day. I think it's very pretty. At around 2:00 p.m., I’ll visit my small wine shop next to Red Jane, and I always have one cigarette per day with one glass of wine. On Saturdays, it gets busy and the crowd is very interesting. They’ll have wine with a sandwich in our beautiful, small yard. I also love hanging out at a small, humble taverna called Kafeneio Fix in the old Turkish neighborhood, or I’ll go to Tamam, an amazing taverna inside a beautiful Turkish hammam dating back to 1645. Spring is also the beginning of the open cinema season. My favorite open-air theater is Attikon. Another one, Kipos, shows mostly old Hitchcock-style films in a public garden created during the Ottoman era. If I want to have a final drink before going home, I’ll go to Fagotto, a jazz bar that has been there for 40 years. Do you have any favorite activities during this time of year? I love hiking all the way down to Chora Sfakion, a small coastal town in the south. From there, you can either take a boat or walk for an hour along a very steep and narrow path—not for the faint-hearted—to Sweetwater Beach, a tiny cove made up of very tiny pebbles. If you dig your hand in it, sweet water from the mountains comes out. This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: 16 Best Resorts on Private Islands for an Ultra-Exclusive Getaway
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.22
For many, true relaxation looks like dropping off the map—settling down on a secluded, sparsely populated island where no one knows anything about you, save for your favorite tropical cocktail. The very best private island resorts balance downtime and adventure; personal space and hospitality; rugged, natural beauty and state-of-the-art facilities. Scattered across the turquoise waters of Indonesia, the Maldives, and Turks and Caicos, some of these properties are wonderfully far-flung, while others, like Little Palm Island Resort & Spa in Florida and Lovango Resort and Beach Club in the US Virgin Islands, don’t even require a US passport. No matter where you decide to book your bungalow, you can rest assured that exclusivity and quietude take top priority at the properties on this list. Offering everything from fresh meals tailored to your preferences to bespoke spa treatments, these resorts are built on the idea that it’s all for you. Whether you’re seeking an open-air villa that floats above crystal-clear water, a luxury ecolodge powered by wind turbines, or a safari-style escape where jungle hikes are always on the table, these are the world’s best private island resorts—each the very definition of paradise. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Tetiaroa, French Polynesia Actor Marlon Brando’s legacy lives on at his former private getaway in French Polynesia, now a hyper-exclusive, eco-minded retreat where travelers come to escape it all. Relax in one of 35 stylish, palm-thatched villas, each a grand fusion of indoor and outdoor space, the beach just footsteps away (alternatively, go even bigger with the island’s sole over-the-top residence). Enjoy island bike rides, treatments in the stickwork cocoons of the Varua te Ora Polynesian Spa, and French-tinged, Polynesian-influenced dining by French celebrity chef Jean Imbert. Nature tours led by in-house researchers offer a deeper connection to the island, while daily cultural experiences like Polynesian dance classes, ukulele lessons, and traditional weaving sessions introduce guests to local traditions. Make sure to save time to explore the other islands of the Tetiaroa Atoll, which also belong to the Brando family, where untouched beaches, preserved reefs, and thriving seabird colonies are as gorgeous as when Brando first encountered the location in 1960. All meals, libations (including Champagne), in-room dining, and daily spa treatments are bundled into the all-inclusive rate, allowing for carefree indulgence at every turn. And although The Brando immerses guests in barefoot ultra-luxury, it also quietly stands as one of the world’s most sustainable resorts—powered by solar energy and cooled by innovative seawater systems—preserving the paradise Brando so deeply loved for generations to come. —Antonia Quirke - Read Full ReviewLocation: Little Torch Key, Florida This adults-only private island is a study in tropical chic, redefining the castaway fantasy right on American soil. There are a total of 30 thatched-roof bungalow suites (some freestanding, some within larger bungalows) across the four-acre island, many with four-poster beds and outdoor copper bathtubs. Thanks to a smart layout and smarter landscaping, you’ll encounter other people less often than you’d expect (a strict cap at 60 guests helps). All suites have water views, outdoor showers, and furnished decks; most also overlook private slivers of white-sand beach and are kitted out with hammocks, loungers, and firepits. The Dining Room has sweeping sea views, and the spectacular SpaTerre complex is underscored by a breezy two-story atrium. Paddleboard or kayak through mangrove mazes as eagle rays swim by, laze the day away on a beachfront hammock, or simply enjoy the day resting on a poolside lounger. Also, don’t miss a snorkeling trip to Looe Key Reef, part of the third-largest living coral reef in the world and site of ongoing reef restoration efforts by MOTE Marine Laboratory & Aquarium, a Florida-based nonprofit marine research institution. Little Palm Island has partnered with the organization to create the “Paradise with a Purpose” package, which includes a half-day in Looe Key Reef, a donation to MOTE Marine, accommodations, and breakfast. —Paul Rubio - Read Full ReviewLocation: Yaukuve Levu Island, Fiji Located in the untouched Kadavu Islands, a 45-minute seaplane flight from Nadi International Airport, this private island balances romance and multigenerational travel in Fiji. Straddling the renowned Great Astrolabe Reef, the waters near Kokomo teem with colorful fish, manta rays, sea turtles, and thriving coral gardens, making underwater exploration a must for any visit (don’t miss the marine biologist–led manta snorkel excursion). Twenty-one beachfront villas range in size from a couples-friendly one-bedroom to larger two- and three-bedrooms, each with a private plunge pool, private walled garden with outdoor shower, and direct beach access. Meanwhile, five hilltop luxury Grand Residences welcome larger families to multi-bedroom homes, inclusive of a private butler and nanny. Guests can also anticipate other water activities like sailing and kayaking, and three memorable meals daily, made of locally sourced produce from Kokomo’s 5.5-acre farm and hydroponics garden, and seafood from a sustainable, caught-to-order island initiative. —Adam H. Graham - Read Full ReviewLocation: Anambas, Indonesia There are drop-dead gorgeous private island resorts, and then there’s Bawah, an entire nature and marine reserve comprising 6 islands, 3 blue lagoons, and 13 unspoiled white beaches in the heart of Indonesia’s Anambas Archipelago. Sustainability lies at the core of the reserve with no compromises on luxury. In fact, the entire resort was constructed by hand using sustainable bamboo and locally sourced natural building materials, and decorated with works from local artisans. The reserve oozes natural splendor, which can be enjoyed from the comfort of a swoon-worthy rustic-chic tented suite, overwater bungalow, or pool villa. Come here for Indonesian coastal cuisine perfected, dinners in the treetops, spectacular sunsets, hikes through the jungle, island-hopping via transparent kayaks, and sublime snorkeling. To access Bawah’s remote location with ease, the reserve offers a door-to-door transfer from Singapore airport with short components by road and ferry, followed by a 75-minute seaplane that lands directly in paradise. —Michelle Jana Chan - Read Full ReviewLocation: Peter Island, British Virgin Islands From the moment the resort’s yacht glides into the serene waters of Yacht Harbor in Sprat Bay, the transition from passenger to prized guest is practically instantaneous. Peter Island, the largest private island in the British Virgin Islands, turns up the volume on the wellness-minded, pastoral strains of Caribbean life, and in no time, you might just find yourself humming along to the tune. With just 52 rooms and 2 villas, you’ll never have to battle for privacy and discretion, yet the company of fellow guests is always welcome. In 2017, Hurricane Irma tragically destroyed homes and upended lives throughout the Virgin Islands. The resort strives to be as sustainable as possible; it has a reverse osmosis water purification plant and two wind turbines that can generate up to 75% of the island's power. And yet Peter Island still doesn't mess with what works, and leans into a familial flavor of hospitality that feels like you’re at your favorite aunt and uncle’s for the holidays. —Kat Chen - Read Full ReviewLocation: Mnemba Island, Tanzania Just shy of two miles off the coast of Zanzibar’s main island, Mnemba is a tiny, casuarina-forested sanctuary surrounded by a private marine reserve. Home to just 12 shell-shaped, thatched bandas, designed with understated elegance by Fox Browne Creative and Jack Alexander Studio, it’s the antithesis of bling. A seven-month rebuild in 2024 expanded the villas into curvaceous, nautilus-like spaces, blending natural materials with breezy open-air design. Guests can explore turquoise shallows on catamarans, dive vibrant reefs, or simply lounge in private beach bandas watching noddies and plovers whirl above the sandspit. The spa, yoga deck, and Oceans Without Borders education center enrich the experience, while chefs curate custom menus that range from sushi boxes to lobster ravioli served under the stars. Service is impeccable, with a charming butler, a jovial bar team, and Tanzania’s first local dive master leading ocean explorations. Despite Zanzibar’s tourism boom, Mnemba feels like a world apart—exclusive, untouched, and deeply serene. With a staff-to-guest ratio of over 3:1, every detail is handled, leaving you to do exactly what you’re meant to here: absolutely nothing. —Lisa Grainger - Read Full ReviewLocation: Nosy Ankao, Madagascar A nothing-is-impossible hideaway for adventurous high-fliers, Miavana by Time + Tide is set on remote Nosy Ankao in northern Madagascar, only reachable by helicopter. With ease, the private island merges barefoot luxury and a deep commitment to conservation and community support. Just 14 villas, built from sun-bleached Malagasy wood and hand-hewn limestone, sprawl across private gardens and powder-soft beaches. Interiors channel a beachy Palm Springs vibe, with sunken bathtubs, pastel Smeg appliances, and fully stocked kitchens, offering a luxurious home-away-from-home feeling. The central Piazza serves farm-fresh menus that change daily, while off-menu requests are happily fulfilled. Though there’s no stand-alone spa, therapists deliver seashell massages and herbal body wraps directly to your villa. Service is breezy yet impeccable, with butlers anticipating every need—whether folding laundry, crafting green juices, or lending sunglasses. Miavana by Time + Tide’s eco-efforts are serious: villas rely on natural ventilation, solar panels power much of the resort, and local conservation programs protect turtles, lemurs, and coral reefs. While private island life is great, take time to explore mainland Madagascar’s iconic baobab forests or Tsingy formations (both can be arranged by helicopter safari from the island). —Chris Schalkx - Read Full ReviewLocation: Islas Secas, Panama Set within the jungle-cloaked splendor of Panama’s Gulf of Chiriquí, Islas Secas offers an exclusive, eco-friendly escape across a private archipelago of 14 untouched islands. At its heart, the resort’s eight light-footed accommodations—including casitas, safari-style tents, and open-air mansion Casa Cavada—blend flawlessly into the landscape, each with sweeping hilltop views and living spaces that celebrate the outdoors. Guests have exclusive access to this entire island chain, blanketed in tropical flora and fringed by white- and gold-sand beaches. Days unfold as you please across the various islands: kayak through emerald waters, snorkel vibrant coral gardens, hike jungle trails to ancient artifacts, or island-hop to wide, sparkling beaches where staff can arrange private beach barbecues. Water adventures abound, too, from fun on pricey water toys like hydrofoils, flyboards, and Seabobs, to fishing and whale-watching, all included in the resort’s personalized, all-inclusive program. On the main island of Isla Cavada, find a stunning open-air beachfront restaurant, a swoon-worthy jungle spa, a Hemingway-inspired bar, and an infinity pool perched high above the rainforest coastline. —Andrea Whittle - Read Full ReviewLocation: Necker Island, British Virgin Islands Necker Island is the creation of Virgin Group founder Sir Richard Branson, who has transformed what was once a scrubby, 74-acre British Virgin Island cay into a fortress of lush greenery, serene Balinese villas, exotic animals ranging from local flamingos to endangered lemurs and tortoises, and solar panels and wind turbines that make the island self-sustaining. The resort is accessible only by boat from nearby Tortola—no private-plane runway here—which makes it feel more approachable and refuge-like, especially compared to some other private-island hospitality projects. Every inch of the place feels like a Bond hideaway: Tropical canopies give way to white-sand beaches all your own, lagoons filled with flamingos, infinity-pooled suites, and cozy lounges. A sprawling hilltop Great House has far-flung views of the azure waters around the island; there's also a billiards table, board games, a bar (just one of many on the island, including the self-serve one in your own villa), and dining nooks with incredible views where five-star, family-style dinners and healthy à la carte breakfasts are served. —Shannon McMahon - Read Full ReviewLocation: Turks and Caicos Located off the main chain of Turks and Caicos, Ambergris Cay achieves billionaire-level relaxation with its serene azure waters, rugged nature, and waterfront villas. The 1,100-acre island is home to a collection of expansive villas, from 1-bedroom beachfront bungalows to 10-bedroom homes. All meals and house beverages are included, meaning you’ll never go hungry—or thirsty—with cocktails made from fresh ingredients and a floating rum bar called The Hangover accessible only by boat. Suites sit on the sugar-sand beach leading into the Caribbean Sea, while sprawling villas are perched on craggy hilltops overlooking the Atlantic Ocean. Interiors are beach house chic, with wood-plank floors and shiplap walls. Guests roam the island via golf cart between the spa, tennis courts, beach activities, and state-of-the-art fitness center encased in 180 degrees of glass. Service is breezy but attentive, with 24/7 concierge support via WhatsApp. The private island resort also houses one of the longest runways in the region, making it easy for outdoor-minded billionaires and professional athletes to arrive in private jets for instant immersion into the tropical good life. —S.M. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Lovango Cay, US Virgin Islands Located across St. John’s legendary Caneel Bay on an island all its own, this unpretentious seasonal resort (open December through July) features the USVI’s only private island beach club and eco-chic accommodation in the form of wooden treehouses, explorer-style tents, and one- to three-bedroom villas. Views of the surrounding jewel-toned waters abound, peaking at Treetops Lobby Tent, where bird's-eye views of St. John proper and St. Thomas can be admired in a single panorama. Indulge in island cuisine and rum-spiked fun at the resort’s Waterfront Restaurant (get the smoked pineapple old- fashioned and the signature Caribbean lobster paillard) or its fast-casual counterpart, Sand Pit, which services Lovango’s Beach Club and its cabana-lined swimming pool. For active and gastronomic pursuits in greater St. John, take the ferry to Cruz Bay, which runs regularly; for another incarnation of beach bliss, hop on the five-minute ferry to St. John’s Honeymoon Beach, which runs on select days. —Todd Plummer - Read Full ReviewLocation: Lhaviyani Atoll, Maldives This Yuji Yamazaki–designed property in the Maldives’s Lhaviyani Atoll is a next-generation ultra-luxury experience like no other, underscored by a mind-blowing “Anything, Anytime, Anywhere” fixed price policy, where few things are off-limits—nor cost extra—from floating breakfasts to most top-shelf Champagne to private fitness training. The island’s 15 ryokan-inspired overwater residences epitomize contemporary Japanese ocean elegance, offering ample room to relax and play against the backdrop of the Maldives’ lazuline beauty (units start at 3,300 square feet). At Kudadoo’s core lies The Retreat, an impressive open-air minimalist overwater pagoda crowned by 984 solar panels (that power the resort in its entirety) and housing the island’s bar, restaurant, spa, fitness facilities, and lounge areas. Thanks to the Anything, Anytime, Anywhere policy, your residence, The Retreat, and the surrounding nature become your muses for fulfilling the utmost island fantasies. Request to be marooned on nearby Dream Island for a luxury-draped Robinson Crusoe experience or ask for a private toes-in-the-sand beach lunch on Kudadoo itself. Snorkel with giant mantas alongside a marine biologist or try your hand at jet-skiing, parasailing, or fishing. Pencil in plenty of time for spa treatments—they are unlimited, after all—before or after you figure out how to manage an entire staff of butlers, cooks, personal trainers, and yoga masters at your beck and call. Suffice to say, Kudadoo is the ultimate castaway narrative come to life—and the script is yours to write. —L.G. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Moskito Island, British Virgin Islands While everyone knows about billionaire Richard Branson’s original private retreat, Necker Island, the Virgin founder purchased another exclusive playground just two miles away called Moskito Island. But instead of using it for himself and his high-powered pals, the mogul built a home and sold nine other plots for others to build their dream beach houses. While most are only inhabited by the estate owners themselves, three of the remarkable properties—The Branson Estate, The Oasis Estate, and The Point Estate—became available for rent in October 2021. Although more expensive than your average luxury hotel, Moskito Island makes living the life of a billionaire a tiny bit more accessible. Five-star restaurants are swapped for private chefs, hotel suites for exclusive estates, and concierges for dedicated house managers capable of making nearly anything you want possible. The only guests in sight are those in your immediate party—that is, unless you decide to venture to the communal Manchioneel Beach, complete with a floating trampoline and bartenders at the ready, or the Beach House, a community recreational area where you can play a round of tennis and mingle with estate owners (you may even spot Richard Branson himself). —Jordi Lippe-McGraw - Gold List 2018, 2019, 2020Readers' Choice Awards 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025Read Full ReviewLocation: Turks and Caicos As COMO’s sole property in the Americas, Parrot Cay's renowned luxury experience makes it an unrivaled property in Turks and Caicos. The pinnacle of bespoke solitude, it's located on a private island enmeshed in the wilderness. You arrive after a 15-minute chauffeured drive from Providenciales International Airport, then a 20-minute panoramic boat ride through cays and turquoise waves hugged by mangroves. It’s primeval in nature and worlds away, despite its ease of access from the main island. The private, white-sand beach—with miles of clear-water sandbars inviting you to walk across, float around, and laze about for ages—is the main reason why the property has been dubbed by locals as "the Maldives of the Americas," despite being entirely singular in the impression it makes. If you’re seeking a romantic getaway inspired by an itch for an immersive nature escape, this is the place to go—and I recommend booking a private beach house with your own plunge pool for the full immersive experience. —Bridget Knowles FAQ: How we choose the best private island resorts in the world Every resort on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: Off-Season Greece: Athens Comes Alive in Fall, According to Hotelier Agapi Sbokou
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.13
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to Agapi Sbokou, co-owner and CEO of Greek hotel brand Phāea. “Alive. That's how Athens feels to me,” says Agapi Sbokou, co-owner and CEO of the Greek hotel brand Phāea. Sbokou grew up in Crete but has lived in Athens since she was 18. “There was never really a debate about where to live. We go back and forth between Athens and Crete, but the city just feels so buzzy. It’s a place that is constantly transforming.” Sbokou knows a thing or two about why people are drawn to a particular destination. “When you go to a place, it should be about understanding the local rhythm,” she tells me. “I'm in love with Athens. It’s a place that you can continue exploring your whole life.” Here, Agapi explains why autumn is so magical in the Greek capital, and lets us in on some of her favorite places to visit at this time of year. Tell me what you love most about Athens. Walking around and exploring. The city transforms with the seasons, and it feels completely connected with nature. For example, my neighborhood is full of these beautiful trees called jacarandas, which have very small, lilac flowers. They completely transform the whole neighborhood when they bloom. Elsewhere in the city, some areas are filled with bitter orange trees, which also have a strong scent when they bloom. There are a lot of young people here, and recently a lot of young travelers are coming to stay and live in Athens. They all come with a very open heart and the desire to explore as we, the locals, do. Athens is not about what’s cool and what’s not—it’s about discovering new things, revisiting old places, and watching the city transform over time. That’s what I love. When is the best time to come to Athens? When it’s not too busy, but local life is buzzing. I would say April and October or November. I've always been a summer person, but to be honest in Athens spring and autumn are the most beautiful seasons. In April, the blooms are starting to appear. There are beautiful scents around the city. But autumn is great because the weather is very mellow. There's still the warmth from the summer, and there is very little rain, so it's very pleasant and you can walk around all day. What makes autumn so special in Athens? There's a different light about the city, which is not that classic Greek light that you see during summer. It's more yellow and soft. The city starts preparing for winter, so there is a kind of excitement with the locals—people are returning from the islands, they still go swimming in the sea, and still it's quite warm. It's the perfect season because it combines it all. Who’s around this time of year? There are travelers year-round. But in autumn, it's a different kind of traveler. People who come during this season have a slower appreciation of the city, which I love. I think that's what tourism should be. We should spend more time exploring a place and really getting a sense of it to understand its rhythm, rather than going in and out, just ticking off things. Do as the locals do. Maybe spend two hours in a coffee shop. Get to know the person sitting at the next table and start a conversation. Spend three hours in a museum, not one. There are so many museums here, and not just the big ones. The Benizelos Mansion is the oldest house in Athens, or, of course, the Benaki Museum with the Nema Collection. There are so many things to discover, and it shouldn't all be packed into one trip. The kind of travelers who appreciate this tend to come off-season. What’s notable about the locals in Athens? Do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? An appreciation for a slower way of life, I guess. Athens is very much about its neighborhoods, which is characteristic of the city and its people. You start your day at your local coffee shop, then visit your local barber, grocery store, and dry cleaner. You stop for a few minutes, you exchange a few words. That's very typical of people here. You have a sense of community. Sometimes you buy things and you don't need to pay—they know you, and write it in a notebook and you pay at the end of the month. Athens feels like a village, even though it's a city of four million. Where would we find you eating in autumn? I love exploring new places, but I also love going to the same places again and again, because then you begin to know the people. There is a new generation of fantastic restaurants that embrace Greek cuisine, but I’d rather visit the ones that have been around for 20, 30, or even 50 years. I go to Manári Taverna a lot, which is in the city center. It's right by a Byzantine church, and it has very traditional cuisine with strong Cretan influence. There is Pharaoh, a very cool restaurant where everything is slow-cooked over a wood-fired grill. It has the best music and the coolest bar, so it's really fun to visit. Plus, it belongs to a friend, so it's always fun to see him and catch up. There’s a place called Dourambeis where I've been going with my dad since I was a kid. It's very traditional, and it has the most delicious fish. In autumn, these places are perfect because they are traditional and laid-back, but have really good food. They all use excellent, seasonal ingredients. Speaking of seasonal ingredients, what is the most traditional dish that people should eat when they come in autumn? That's a good question. It's hard to say, because the weather in Greece stays warm into autumn, so we tend to drag summer dishes into the year. For example, one very traditional dish we continue to eat in autumn is gemista. It’s often made with very ripe tomatoes—you empty them, and fill them with rice, mince meat, and other ingredients like herbs and nuts. You could replace tomatoes with zucchini, or eggplant, or peppers. It is very, very Greek and very traditional. And then, of course, in autumn, we eat a lot of pastries and pies. The most typical one is spanakopita, a cheese-and-spinach pie. Those are more home-cooked recipes, though. Athens is like the melting pot of the whole of Greece, so a lot of wider Greek traditions are incorporated in the restaurants. Skioufichta is a specific thick pasta dish, made by hand. You boil it in a broth, and then it's sprinkled with cheese. And it's the most delicious dish, very soothing, very appropriate for autumn—perfect with a glass of red wine. Order this at Manári—it's one of my favorite dishes there. Are there any areas of Athens that really come alive in autumn? I've always lived in and around Kolonaki. It's an area that's quite buzzing and quite well-known, but I love the streets that are purely residential. There are a couple that are quite high, with amazing views, because Kolonaki is at the bottom of Lycabettus Hill. From those streets, you can see straight down to the Acropolis, in between buildings. In the autumn, when the light is right, it just feels amazing and very Athenian. It's almost like a secret—you know that if you turn down a specific street, you’ll suddenly get this view. That feeling always makes me feel very lucky to be there. In autumn, it’s easier to be more spontaneous in Athens, because it’s not as busy. It feels like normal life is back, so you can access museums, galleries, exhibitions, and restaurants more easily. Us Greeks are very welcoming. We want to share the best of what we have. It’s the perfect time to do that.

item.title: How to stay at the real life 'Sterling Point' cottage
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.68
It’s been quite the year for TV shows and movies both set and filmed in destinations that have captured our attention and tempted us to hop on set-jetting adventures. Among the shows that have truly captured our wanderlust is Sterling Point, the young adult Prime series that follows Annie (played by Ella Rubin) and her brother Connor (Keen Ruffalo) as they unexpectedly find themselves in possession of a remote island in Ontario’s Muskoka region. Aware of their late mother’s love for the area, but taken aback by the unlikely situation they find themselves in following the passing of a grandfather they were unaware existed, Annie travels north from her hometown to experience a Canadian summer and seek answers. The series shines a spotlight on Muskoka’s breathtaking scenery and natural beauty, but there’s one question that many fans of the series were left wondering: is Sterling Point's Gordon’s Cottage a real place, and is it possible to stay there? Up until now, despite plenty of sleuthing from entertainment and travel insiders, it wasn’t possible. However, that’s set to change as the historic cottage country retreat that became an unexpected summer star is landing on Airbnb. In response to unprecedented travel demand, with searches from outside Canada for check-ins through November 2026 up almost 110 per cent year on year, the cottage is opening up to jet-jetters for just three special stays. The cottage first opened in 1902 as a summer hotel, with travellers captivated by its lakeside charm and position among the towering trees. Now, a few lucky holidaymakers will find themselves plunging into the water off the dock, sharing long meals on the 800-square-foot screened porch, and keeping an eye out for local wildlife such as loons and chipmunks. Other highlights include watching blazing sunsets that turn into spectacularly starry nights thanks to the clear Muskoka sky, morning yoga sessions and plenty of opportunities for curious guests keen to kayak, canoe and paddleboard their way around the lake. Guests can book one of three special stays between 2 - 5 October, 9 - 12 October and 16 - 19 October as of 9am ET (12pm GMT) on 15 September at a cost of $180 CAD (£96) per night.

item.title: UK airport latest: thousands of flights delayed and cancelled at UK airports
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.40
Several major UK airports are continuing to experience delays and cancellations following a major air traffic control technical failure on Tuesday 8 September. The National Air Traffic Services (NATS) has now resolved the issue, which affected its flight processing system, but the disruption is expected to continue into Wednesday as airlines and airports work through the backlog. NATs boss Martin Rolfe has apologised for the disruption, telling the BBC there would be a full investigation into what had gone wrong, after the firm said resolving the issue had taken "longer than hoped". An official statement on the NATs website reads: “This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.” The failure caused widespread disruption across the UK on Tuesday, with FlightRadar24 reporting around 1,300 cancellations to and from UK airports. Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted were among the airports affected, while the disruption also had knock-on effects at airports across Europe. Heathrow was particularly impacted. Arrivals were suspended for the remainder of Tuesday, while departures resumed later in the day. The airport has warned that disruption will continue and is advising passengers to check directly with their airline before travelling. A statement on the airport's X account on Wednesday morning reads: “Following yesterday's NATS technical issue, flights are operating today, but some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew. Please check your flight status with your airline before travelling to the airport and only travel if your flight is confirmed to be operating.” FlightRadar24 is currently reporting that 177 flights scheduled for Wednesday 9 September have already been cancelled, with the vast majority at Heathrow, while further delays and cancellations are expected as aircraft and crew displaced by Tuesday's disruption are repositioned. Passengers should check the status of their flight directly with their airline and monitor the NATS website and X account for further updates. UK airports reporting disruption include: - London Heathrow Airport - London Gatwick Airport - London Luton Airport - London Stansted Airport - Manchester Airport - Birmingham Airport - Belfast City Airport - Edinburgh Airport - East Midlands Airport - Jersey Airport Can I get a refund if my flight was disrupted? If your flight was delayed or cancelled following Tuesday’s air traffic control issues at NATS, you may be entitled to flight compensation. According to the UK Civil Aviation Authority, passengers can claim compensation ranging from £220 per person to £520 per person if the delay causes you to reach your destination airport more than three hours late. If the delay is more than five hours, you can choose not to travel and receive a refund. Because air traffic control issues are typically considered “extraordinary circumstances” outside the airline's control, cash payouts aren't likely in this scenario. However, many airlines will still provide food and drink vouchers, airport transfers, and hotel accommodations for overnight delays. If your flight is cancelled, the airline is required to provide an alternate flight or full refund. Flight delay compensation in the UK is not automatic, and the procedure for submitting a claim varies by airline. Because the UK is no longer part of the European Union, EU passenger rights only apply to UK flights if it arrives in an EU country and is operated by an EU airline (for example, if you were flying from London to Paris with Air France). Passengers should check the status of their flight and compensation policies directly with their airline and monitor the NATS website and X account for further updates.
