The result is a distinctive bright-red apple also known as ‘Disney Snow White Apple’ due to its shiny skin. This variety is ready in early September but can last a few weeks after picking if properly stored. This is a great farm to visit with children as its trees are low and easily reachable. You don't have to purchase a ticket to enter and are welcome to show up during PYO weekends – the only request is that you pick only what you intend to buy. For 2026, Castle Farm currently confirms PYO on the weekends of 4-6 and 11-13 September, but additional dates may be added. Ampleforth Abbey, Yorkshire At Ampleforth Abbey, you can pick your own apples during September and October and learn everything about how Ampleforth Abbey apple juice and cider are pressed in the Abbey’s own Cider Mill. This orchard is one of the biggest in England and boasts sixty apple varieties, making it the perfect place to spend a full autumn day out. After you have picked your apples, you can visit the abbey, explore the grounds and indulge in an afternoon tea in its tea room. Craigie's Farm Shop and Cafe, Scotland Craigie’s Farm is only a stone’s throw from Edinburgh and makes for a gorgeous day trip from the city. During autumn, you can pick your own apples (and blueberries) at the farm or buy some farm-made delicacies from its shop. This family-run business also organises lots of events and this year it’s launching its very first Apple Fest on 19 September. The festival will feature live music, child-friendly entertainment, food and drink, farm experiences and plenty of apples ready to be picked! Lathcoates Farm, Essex If you are looking for variety, Lathcoates Farm has over fifty different varieties of British apples – from Chelmsford Wonder and D’Arcy Spice to Discovery – with more than ten available to pick during PYO days. You can spend the day picking your favourite apple varieties, have lunch at The Bee Shed, the farm’s restaurant, and do some shopping at its well-stocked farm shop. Lathcoates Farm is a lovely place to spend a whole day out with children, but pets are not allowed. Blackmoor Estate, Hampshire Blackmoor Estate organises apple picking days during autumn, but there is one specific event that has brought people to Hampshire for the last fifty-four years and that’s its popular Apple Tasting Day. This year, the Apple Tasting Day will take place on Sunday 11 October from 10 am to 4.30 pm. The event brings the community together to learn about apple varieties and taste the farm’s produce, with a craft fair, food and drink stalls, Morris dancing and plenty more for adults and children. If you can’t make it to the party, you can pick your own apples on weekends throughout September and October. Drove Orchards, Norfolk At Drove, you can transform your day out apple picking into a full holiday. This orchard is located next to the sea on the Norfolk coast and allows visitors to pick their own apples – or whatever else is growing, depending on when you visit – shop for local produce, have lunch and even stay the night in one of its cosy accommodation options. No booking is required for apple picking – you can simply show up and choose what you want to take home. Drove is a great orchard to visit if you are not quite ready for summer to be over. Long Meadow Cider, Northern Ireland The McKeever family has been growing apples on this 28-acre farm near Loughgall village in Northern Ireland for more than 50 years. Since adding cider production in 2014, the family has made a name for itself thanks to its award-winning ciders made from apples grown and handpicked on the farm. During autumn, the farm offers interactive tours during which visitors can learn about the production and pick their own apples to take home. The best apple-picking essentials You can go apple picking no matter the weather, but what you bring will depend on the forecast. From waterproofs for rainy days to picnic essentials for sunny days, a few well-chosen items can help you make the most of your day.

item.title: Off Season Greece: Hotelier Nikos Tsepetis on how to explore Crete's green heart during spring, without the crowds
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.35
This is part of Off Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favourite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to hotel owner Nikos Tsepetis. For 30 years, Nikos Tsepetis has run Ammos, one of the most talked-about hotels in Greece. The seaside boutique hotel in Chania, northwest Crete, is a manifestation of the man himself: joyful and design-focused with a commitment to high-quality cuisine (including his Red Jane Bakery) and local roots. Tsepetis’ improvisational approach to hospitality creates a home-away-from-home warmth that keeps many of his guests returning year after year. Born and raised in Chania, Tsepetis is deeply connected to his hometown, which he believes is different from other towns in Crete, because “we are more international and welcoming to foreigners, and it's a multi-layered city”. Yet 80 per cent of his staff are locals, he says. “It adds to the experience because you always meet people who were born here, who remember the past, so there is this continuity”. Here, Tsepetis tells us why spring is his favourite time of year in Chania. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit? Just before high season. April and early May are my favourite time of year because the climate is amazing. Chania is on the western end of Crete and is the prettiest part of the island because it's greener, and we still normally have snow on the Lefka Ori [White Mountains] – you can see them from the sea while swimming. In spring, everything is very fresh, everything is well painted; you can go to the villages and monasteries, and all the flowers are out. Also, spring often coincides with Easter, which is important in the Greek Orthodox religion. I don't care at all about religion, but it's still very spiritual and beautiful. What do you love most about being there during this season? It's less busy. The rain cleans everything and the snow melts, so we are greener than other parts of the island. Everything's fresh and new; you can feel the rejuvenation. So spring is a very sweet time. Who’s around this time of year? Traditionally, Chania benefited from the presence of foreigners, even before it became touristy. It’s very urban, with more than 100,000 permanent residents, so you have everyone from hipsters and freaks to lefties living here – not the expected Greek island crowd. It's always very lively, and what sets it apart from some other towns in Crete is that the locals are a driving force with a very loud voice. They are not here to serve the foreigners. Where would we find you eating during this time? My all-time favourite local is Evgonia Tavern. Only a very simple tavern; it has fish and meat in a non-fish environment. I love Periplous restaurant for its unbeatable location at the beautiful Tanneries Hotel. It’s one of the old buildings by the water where they used to process leather. In spring we go to the villages because it's still very mild and there aren’t too many people. I always go to Ntounias, a very old, well-known rural taverna in the middle of nowhere near Drakona in the mountains. There's a crazy guy there, Stelios Trilyrakis, who has been involved with slow food for 30 years. You don't know what you’ll eat or when you’ll eat it. It's very inexpensive, and he cultivates everything himself. In Greece, we love French fries. And Stelios makes amazing chips by cooking them in olive oil in a ceramic pot. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? We're famous for doing a traditional Tsoureki Easter brioche, a kind of braided bread that's sweet but not too sweet. Once a year we also eat a special soup called magiritsa made from lamb intestines, lungs and liver. We normally eat it at home – it’s not so much a restaurant dish – but we do a very good one at Ammos. Also, Nyketerida is famous for it. Spring is about beans and greens – we have beautiful asparagus and the best artichokes – and goat roasted in the oven with potatoes, zucchini and tomatoes. We also have a very famous dish called ‘dakos’, a barley rusk, with tomato sauce and this amazing goat’s cheese called mizithra. One of the best places to eat it is Costas Cafeneion, a family-run cafe in Maza village, which is between Chania and Rethymnon. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off-season? In January and February, people from around the world come here for the mountains and skiing, including the annual Pierra Creta ski mountaineering race. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Summer is very hot and can be dry, and then we have the winter, which is rainy. But in spring the weather is cooler and you can hike, ski and swim. The sea is actually colder in spring than in winter because of the snowmelt. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? I’m biased but Saturday is a great day to hang out at my Red Jane Bakery early in the day. I think it's very pretty. At around 2pm I’ll visit my small wine shop next to Red Jane and I always have one cigarette per day with one glass of wine. On Saturdays it gets busy and the crowd is very interesting. They’ll have wine with a sandwich in our beautiful, small yard. I also love hanging out at a small, humble taverna called Kafeneio Fix in the old Turkish neighbourhood, or I’ll go to Tamam, an amazing taverna inside a beautiful Turkish hammam dating back to 1645. Spring is also the beginning of the open cinema season. My favourite open-air theatre is Attikon. Another one, Kipos, shows mostly old Hitchcock-style films in a public garden created during the Ottoman era. If I want to have a final drink before going home, I’ll go to Fagotto, a jazz bar that has been there for 40 years. Do you have any favourite activities during this time of year? I love hiking all the way down to Chora Sfakion, a small coastal town in the south. From there you can either take a boat or walk for an hour along a very steep and narrow path – not for the faint-hearted – to Sweetwater Beach, a tiny cove made up of very tiny pebbles. If you dig your hand in it, sweet water from the mountains comes out.

item.title: Off Season Greece: Author Anastasia Miari on Corfu's thriving food scene and why spring is the best time to savour the isle
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.30
This is part of Off Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favourite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to food writer and author Anastasia Miari. Whenever I’m feeling disconnected from myself or from Greece – the place my mother’s family is from, and whose traditions I grew up with – I muster up the energy to make a comforting Greek meal. But whether it’s my yia yia’s old-school-style avgolemono soup, my mom’s traditional pastitsio, or my thea’s Americanised spanakopita, the recipe is rarely ever already written down. As with so many other cultures’ time-tested family dishes, they’re usually passed on by doing; surmising how many box grater’s-worth of tomatoes you'll need, or eyeballing the number of glugs of olive oil to add. Enter Anastasia Miari, a food writer and author who has spent the better part of a decade travelling all over the Mediterranean to document not only Greek recipes, but create an extensive, photographic encyclopedia of the many octo- and septuagenarians (and their often-remote villages) who passed those very dishes – and their way of life – to younger generations. Nowadays, when I want to try a new or lighter Greek dish than the handful of rib-sticking ones I know, I crack open my stained copy of ‘Yia Yia,’ Miari’s first cookbook. Better yet, when I want to explore the cuisine of the broader region – Moroccan tajin, Turkish breakfast, Sicilian pasta – there’s now also her newer iteration, ‘Mediterranea.’ To say Anastasia is an expert in all things Greek would be an understatement – she was born and raised on the Ionian island of Corfu in Greece’s northwest, and is currently renovating a historic cottage on the Cycladic island of Tinos to enjoy with her family in the summers (and filming a web series about it all). Here, the British-Greek Corfiot shares her guide to the Italian-leaning island’s Venetian traditions, natural splendour, and seasonal dishes – all of which are best experienced in the off-season. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit – when the travellers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? I would say May, springtime. Because of all this rain that we get then, the island is fully in bloom in May – it's stunning. It's like being in a Disney movie here. What do you love most about being there during this season? If you have in mind to do the Corfu Trail, which is a hiking trail that runs all the way from the south of the island to the north of the island, the month of May is a particularly incredible month to come in because you tend to have the best weather, but it's also not incredibly hot. You're still able to hike, especially in the morning and evening hours. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travellers at all? Corfu is really interesting because it doesn't have this sort of off-season, on-season vibe as much as the Cycladic islands do. What I mean by that is the island doesn't shut down when it isn't summertime. We have a university and we have a music school on the island, and because it is very cosmopolitan and because it's so big, we tend to retain our residents. People don't tend to move to Athens or to Saloniki as much as they might in more remote Cycladic islands. So of course, there are a few travellers, but it's not as many as you'll find in July and August. And I think it's usually people who love to hike and people who like to be in nature, so it's a different kind of traveller. What’s notable about the locals; do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? What's notable about the locals in Corfu is that, supposedly, we're the craziest in all of Greece? [Laughs] Other Greeks tend to say that Cretans and the Corfiots are the crazies of the nation. But I do think we are quite distinct in Corfu because we have this incredible heritage that comes from Italy, and we love to align ourselves with the Italians. The Venetians came and colonised 500 years ago, and many vestiges of our Venetian past are still visible, not just in the architecture and in our food. Where would we find you eating? The places that eat in the summer tend to also be open in the winter, and I think that's great because you are always able to rub shoulders with local clientele. One of my favourite places to eat is Marina's Tavern in Corfu Town because they do all of the classic yia yia home-cooked dishes in a really great home-cooked style – eating a pastitsada or a stifado at my léas table. So I love Marina's Tavern for all of the traditional home-cooked dishes that they serve. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? The dish to order is tsigarelia, which are like wild greens that you find at that time of year. And here in Greece, we sauté them with lots of spices. Again, this is a sort of vestige of the Venetians, and [a result of] our being put on the spice trail by the Venetians. So it includes lots of spices like cinnamon, cloves, and cayenne pepper. So cigarella, that's a great dish to have. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off season? In the off-season, I think Corfu Town is the place to be because even everyone else from the rest of the [surrounding] island tends to sort of congregate in Corfu Town. It’s really popping off, especially because of the universities there: there's a high concentration of people hanging out in town; it's very much alive. Any coffee shop you go into will be full of people. Again, Corfu isn't one of those sort of Disneyland islands that shuts down in the winter and opens up this sort of like fake display of life in the summer. It's very much alive all year round. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Corfu is one of the wettest islands in Greece, so if you try and come in May you’ll have the occasional rain shower. But generally, it's just a very pleasant temperature and really great to experience the best of the island, which is its nature. September or October can be the trickiest months. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? It's fantastic to go into the mountains and visit mountain villages on weekends because I think much of the coastline has been marred by mass tourism. The real secret and beauty of this island is actually inland, in the mountains. Do you have any favourite activities during this time of year? It absolutely has to be hiking. And I think the most incredible way to live and experience this island is by doing the 112-mile Corfu trail. You don't have to do the whole of it, of course. You could just pick one part of the whole trail because it takes like seven days to hike it in full. It took me a bit longer, but you can pick a section of the trail and do just that. It's unmissable, really. Where to stay: Snugly in a pine-studded cleft beneath Mount Pantokrator, the island's tallest mountain, The Merchant's House has six guestrooms carved out of the stunningly renovated stone-walled shell of a 14th-century Venetian building. High ceiling rooms with chunky stone walls are far from mediaeval, however: there are Coco-Mat mattresses and large balconies with spectacular views over to the Albanian coast opposite.

item.title: I spent a night in Kenya’s remote bush, and it changed how I think about safaris
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.21
It’s the night of the blood moon in northern Kenya. We sit in a loose semicircle around a crackling bushfire, our canvas chairs settled into the sand of a long-dried riverbed. The flames warm our faces as embers drift up into the starry sky. Gin and tonics sweat in our hands while the bush comes alive at night. Somewhere nearby, hyenas giggle and whoop in the darkness, and a silent group of giraffes glides across the riverbed ahead, their tall silhouettes graceful in the half-light. As the moon slips into the earth’s shadow, soft rhythmic chanting rises from the surrounding manyattas. Samburu women sing, their melodic voices carrying across the plains as part of a ritual to mark the eclipse and guide the moon back to life. We sit quietly, listening as it glows crimson and is slowly reborn. In that moment, caught between moonlight, wildlife, and Samburu tradition, it’s impossible not to feel the captivating pull of Sarara. Sarara sits within the vast Namunyak Conservancy in northern Kenya. It’s more than just a safari destination; it’s a community-led conservation project run with the Samburu people, who have lived here for generations. The project protects over 850,000 acres of wilderness and creates sustainable livelihoods for the local community through tourism, conservation, and cultural programs. The people are at the heart of the experience. Many guides, hosts, and team members come from nearby villages, bringing a deep knowledge of the land, wildlife, and traditions that no guidebook can match. Life beyond the game drive Head out on guided walks and game drives with Samburu trackers, swim in natural rock pools tucked into the hills, or ride on horseback across the open plains. But time here offers a window into life beyond the safari, too. Sarara opens the door to the community behind it, with opportunities to visit the nearby Reteti Elephant Sanctuary — Africa’s first community-owned elephant orphanage — where rescued calves are raised by local keepers before eventually returning to the wild. I fell in love with Long’uro, a baby elephant found trapped in a well, his trunk badly injured after a hyena attack. Seeing him now, with a shortened trunk, gently cared for by the keepers who rescued him, says everything about the sanctuary’s work. There’s also the chance to meet the women behind the Milk Mamas programme, one of the first initiatives in the conservancy to provide women with their own independent income by selling goat milk used to feed the orphaned elephants. One afternoon, I joined a circle of beading mamas, sitting cross-legged together with a translator as we stitched bright beads into ankle bracelets and shared stories about our lives. The conversation was relaxed, curious and open — one of the most memorable experiences of the trip. Spending time in a traditional Samburu manyatta offers a glimpse into daily life within these small homestead communities. Visits to local schools and healthcare projects supported by the conservancy give a deeper understanding of life in this remote region and the work being done to support the community. A handful of hideaways Sarara is a small collection of places to stay scattered across the conservancy. Each offers a slightly different way to experience the landscape, from the privacy of Reteti House to the treetop hideaways of Sarara Treehouses and the remote simplicity of Sarara Wilderness, alongside the original Sarara Camp that first put this remarkable corner of northern Kenya on the safari map. Across them all runs the same design philosophy – open, earthy spaces built from natural materials that blend delicately into the surrounding landscape. Sarara Camp Set on the slopes of the Mathews Mountains, Sarara Camp is the original lodge at the heart of the conservancy, comprising six spacious canvas tents with solar-heated outdoor showers and wide terraces overlooking the valley. At the centre sits a beautiful natural infinity pool overlooking a permanent waterhole. One afternoon, we counted nearly twenty elephants from two different herds gathered there, alongside zebras, giraffes and warthogs, like something out of the opening scene of The Lion King. Wildlife moves easily through camp too; one evening, a zebra grazed quietly outside my window, and most mornings I woke to a giraffe browsing just beyond my tent. Reteti House A short drive from Sarara Camp, Reteti House feels altogether more private, bookable by a single group, meaning the space is entirely your own. It’s a secluded hillside retreat with just four tents and sweeping views across the plains below. The main house is a beautiful gathering space filled with African artefacts and rustic details. A small infinity pool is tucked into the rocks beside it, shaded by trees and looking out across the plains. Down below, a waterhole draws wildlife through the night; more than once, I woke to the unmistakable sound of elephants slurping away in the darkness. Reteti is also known for its resident leopard. My first night alone in the tent was slightly nerve-wracking, but the nerves soon turned to excitement as the distant rasp of the leopard echoed through the cliffs and baboons wailed their alarm calls. Sarara Treehouses Sleeping high in the canopy, Sarara Treehouses is one of the most unique stays in the conservancy. Eight tented suites sit among the branches, linked by wooden walkways that wind through the trees while wildlife moves quietly along the forest floor below. Spending the night in the treetops felt completely magical, something I’d never experienced before, and it brought a surprising sense of luxury to the wilderness. Monkeys chatter constantly overhead, while elephants often wander beneath the decks. The main house is the largest of the camps, its heavy timber beams and striking bar creating a beautiful space for long evenings. Amarula on ice quickly became the drink of choice, best enjoyed while listening for another resident leopard, said to nap in a branch within view from my bed. Sarara Wilderness Sarara Wilderness is the most remote of the camps, reached by a short hop in a small plane with Scenic Air Safaris - an experience in itself. The pilots fly low over the plains, pointing out wildlife and Samburu manyattas below, giving a completely different perspective on the landscape as wildlife moves across the savannah beneath the wings. Landing on the remote airstrip, the sense of isolation becomes immediate. The spacious tents are intentionally temporary, designed to move with the landscape over time, which adds to the feeling of being somewhere truly wild. Days are spent exploring the conservancy with Samburu guides whose knowledge of the land is extraordinary. The wildlife encounters were some of the most memorable of the trip - watching a line of lionesses stride past our vehicle, sitting quietly among an unbothered herd of elephants with a week-old calf and spotting cheetah, leopard and even the rarely seen serval cat. Out here, the wilderness feels closer, wilder, and totally unfiltered. In the end, what defines Sarara is not just the wildlife or the landscapes, but the people. Days quickly turn into friendships with the Samburu guides, hosts and staff who share their knowledge, humour and stories so generously. There’s a genuine sense of connection here, and plenty of opportunities to give back - whether through community projects or simply supporting the people who make this place what it is. It’s that spirit of shared stewardship that makes Sarara feel less like a destination and more like something you become part of, even if only for a little while. Return domestic flights from Nairobi to Namunyak airstrip with Scenic Wilderness start from $600 per person, or alternatively, you can opt for a private air charter with Scenic Air Safaris for up to 9 people at a cost of $3,470 for the aircraft.

item.title: Condé Nast Traveller invites you to A Taste of the Cayman Islands at Wild by Tart this month
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.17
September has long been synonymous with back to school. But in the world of Condé Nast Traveller, it also means making exciting plans for the year ahead – and these typically revolve around the hottest restaurants on the horizon and travel. In the spirit of prolonging the summer sun that is suddenly setting earlier in London, there might be no time more perfect than the turn of the month to join Condé Nast Traveller for an evening celebrating the Cayman Islands at Wild by Tart, Belgravia's chicest coal station-turned-eatery. Set to be hosted by acclaimed Caymanian street food chef Diego Smith, who will be bringing the island's vibrant culinary Caribbean culture to life through an array of cocktails, canapés, and a dinner with wine pairings, we already expect this to be the kind of event where guests will leave happily debating their favourite dish. Not to mention, we'll take any excuse for an evening with a compelling culinary voice from an equally covetable location. Over the course of the evening, Chef Diego Smith will bring the islands to the table via an expertly-curated menu inspired by Cayman’s exceptionally fresh and flavourful produce, all steeped in local traditions and deep sense of place. You can expect anything from mahi ceviche in fresh orange marinade, jerk pork belly on cassava charcoal, grilled chicken papaya salad and traditional Cayman snapper, coconut and breadfruit run-down stew. And if dessert (we won't spoil it) isn't enough to convince you to book a one-way ticket to George Town in your cab home, we don't know what will. From stories behind the kitchen door to the zingy flavours you'd expect straight of a grill on a turquoise water-hemmed beach, we're already counting down the days to this evening that'll be the perfect way to settle back into the bustle of London, all while dreaming for what's ahead. When: Wednesday 30 September from 6.30pm Where: Wild by Tart, 3-4 Eccleston Yards, Belgravia, London, SW1W 9AZ Tickets: From £100 per person, including a cocktail-and-canapé reception and dinner with exceptional wine pairings. Book here.

item.title: 8 cheapest nicest hotels in Menorca for an affordable, but still elevated, Balearic getaway
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.16
Crystal-clear waters, whitewashed villages and unforgettable sunsets – that’s what you’ll find on any of the beautiful Balearic Islands. But if you’re looking to escape the crowds that flock to Mallorca, Ibiza or Formentera during peak season, the best option is to choose the least-populated island of them all: Menorca. Here, you’ll discover the purest version of Mediterranean living and some of the region’s most unspoiled nature, in secluded coves and charming villages where centuries-old traditions live on. Personally, I love Menorca for its effortless Mediterranean charm and relaxed vibe. One of the island’s best surprises is its collection of enchanting hotels. As a local Spanish and a longstanding fan of the island, this is my curated selection of the cheapest and nicest hotels in Menorca. Editor's picks - For the old town: Can Alberti 1740 Boutique Hotel - For countryside: Alcaufar Vell - For sea views: Barceló Nura How we choose the best affordable hotels in Menorca Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. For more information on how we review hotels and restaurants, please look at our About Us page.

item.title: My favourite farm stay in the UK: Tewinbury Farm, Hertfordshire
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.13
It’s a rare treat to be able to take my two small children away for the weekend without having to strategically pack and mentally prepare for the journey. On a particularly sunny weekend in July, we hopped on the tube and wound our way to Finsbury Park station before boarding a Great Northern train for 25 minutes to Welwyn Garden City. From there, we strolled up to the taxi rank outside the shopping centre and a 7-minute drive later, we arrived at Tewinbury Farm. Suddenly the air was fresher, time slowed down, and the only sound was the trickling of the chalk stream. What originally started as a dairy farm of just 50 cows in 1931 has grown and evolved into a 700 acre estate with a hotel, restaurants, a cookery school, a wedding venue, farm shop and a shiny new fitness centre. The impressive set-up is still owned and operated by the William family who originally owned it, now three generations later. The hotel itself is expansive with an array of rooms scattered about from cosy woodland huts to lakeside lodges and generous rooms in the main building. My brood and I checked into the spacious King Edward room in the main building – in a previous life the building operated as the farm's potato shed, and thus all the rooms are named after potatoes. While I eyed the plump primary bed and countrified details, my son dashed up the stairs to discover a delightful mezzanine kid’s bedroom, all kitted out with toys, a rocking horse, tent and farm books. All the details are beautifully considered and elevated, right down to the old-fashioned Polaroid camera on offer to capture family memories during our stay. Elsewhere, the lakeside, woodland and shepherd’s huts are equally slick and all impressively built and renovated by an in-house team. If I was returning sans-children, I'd be booking into one of the lakeside huts, all pine-green wooden slats, petite kitchenette and private hot tubs. Just outside are fire pits for roasting marshmallows and mini pontoons with seating overlooking the lake. The latest coup for Tewinbury is the freshly opened (2026) Farm Club, a sprawling fitness and wellness space. Hotel guests and club members can use the show-stopping open-gym, book into a group class including reformer pilates, and relax in the recovery yard featuring ice baths and saunas. With children in tow, there was no sadly time for a sauna. Instead we skipped off to explore the estate – there’s the central courtyard with a snooker and foosball table, plus a nearby vintage tractor to climb and play on. Further exploring will lead you to plenty of lawn to run around on and an ample wooden playground that will keep wee ones entertained. But of course the starring attraction is the animals – there’s a herd of friendly cows that will plod over to say hello, some pedigree pigs and three quirky alpacas. For grown ups, the real drawcard for the farm though is the fresh produce. This is the kind of place where a steak and simple garden salad will knock your socks off; the distance from farm-to-fork is mere steps. Fittingly, Tewinbury has a cookery school headed up by chef Lee Maycock. Or you can leave it to the pros at Cowshed, where everything is seasonal, homemade and feel good, from farm-reared pork chops to chargrilled trout caught from the local chalk stream, and sourdough bread ingeniously served with chorizo butter. For more casual bites, there’s the Granary Kitchen, while on the weekends the pizza oven is fired up in the courtyard, making it the ultimate hangout for all ages. Before checking out, pop into the farm shop where you can take some of the farm’s current seasonal hits home with you.

item.title: New London restaurants to try in September 2026: our editors' honest opinions on the openings everyone's talking about
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.13
We've always got one eye on any new restaurants opening on the London food scene. Our editors are on the ball for the latest openings in each London neighbourhood, from Covent Garden restaurants to Shoreditch hotspots. For the ultimate list of places to eat in the city, check out our definitive guide to London's best restaurants. These are the places that we consider the crème de la crème, from generations-old spots that have stood the test of time and Michelin-starred dining rooms that get better each year to mind-blowing new openings from this list that we decided deserved a spot on the ultimate round-up of the best restaurants in London. For new restaurants opening in London recently, we've seen follow-ups from some of the city's biggest-name chefs and a handful of restaurant openings that have stopped us in our tracks: from London's newfound love for BBQ to a Turkish restaurant that's turning heads. These are our favourite openings of the past six months. How we choose the tastiest new restaurant openings in London The best new restaurants in London are the most exciting places to eat that have just opened in the capital city. Ranging from small affairs with daily changing menus from up-and-coming chefs to Michelin-starred spots with fresh new menus, these are London's new restaurants we've got our eye on right now. Every restaurant on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has eaten at that restaurant. When choosing new restaurants, our editors consider both high-end and affordable eateries that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for stand-out dishes, a great location, warm service, and serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new restaurants open in London. Best new London restaurants in September 2026 Waterhouse Project, Bethnal Green At the start of September, husband-and-wife team Gabriel Waterhouse and Patricia Wakaimba opened the doors to Waterhouse, a much-anticipated restaurant, wine bar and garden set inside a Victorian warehouse on buzzing cobbled Ezra Street, just off Columbia Road Flower Market. Following the closure of The Water House Project in June, their new home is an impeccably designed space, flowing from raised beds outside, where the chefs pick fresh herbs, into a bar area with stainless steel countertops and handcrafted oak furniture, and through to the dining room, which serves 24 covers in an intimate nightly sitting. The food measures up to the space. Chef Gabriel draws on his Northumberland upbringing and the region’s traditional cooking techniques, while adding a playful touch with in-house ingredients such as miso, koji and garums. Start with a punchy, syrupy fig leaf martini at the bar before embarking on the 11-course tasting menu. The ensemble hits a high note immediately with a rich, comforting cep and Madeira tea, before moving into bites that challenge the palate while remaining comforting and, ultimately, delicious. The courses balance refreshing zing, like the oyster with cucumber and sorrel, with familiar but elevated mouthfuls, like the moreish onion crumpet. Larger plates, including a smoked haddock porridge (oyster mushroom for vegetarians), hit a hearty note. The meal ended on singing hinnies, a traditional griddle cake, with boozy-forward lavender and Laphroaig cream. If you manage to have some room left, the seasonal cheese selection isn’t to be missed. This is a savoury, umami-rich tasting menu that has immediately risen to the top of my list for celebratory meals. The team have nailed the difficult task of creating fine-dining plates without a stuffy atmosphere. Gabriel and Patricia’s history of supper clubs, where their journey began, can still be felt in the environment they’ve curated at Waterhouse. Chloe Laws Address: 7A Ezra Street, London, E2 7RH Website: waterhouse.com Bar Blondie, Queen's Park Queen's Park is having a little moment in the limelight of late, preening and showing off as curious eyes turn its way thanks to a slate of clever openings (Don't Tell Dad, where a queue forms for glossy cinnamon buns and plump pains au chocolat every morning; The Salusbury, a smart pub with a dining room that punches above its weight; Naples-inspired joint Casa Felicia) joining some long-standing favourites like Harry and Meghan's favourite Italian Ida and brewery Wolf Pack. Now, everyone's talking about a wine bar that's taking interiors inspiration from Spaghetti Westerns and looking to four imaginary muses – the writer, the actor, the architect and the director – to pull together its cellar book. The Bar Blondie site used to be Milk Beach, an Antipodean all-day restaurant which kickstarted the Queen's Park foodie revolution eight or so years ago. The space is still owned by Aussie Elliot Milne, who's given it a tip-to-toe renovation. Interiors, designed by Macaulay Sinclair (also behind Dishoom's Permit Room and Hawksmoor, among others), are now mid-century sexy with a masculine edge: nutty woods, dark greens, art curated by The Other Art Fair founder Ryan Stanier. The menu looks to France and Italy: delicate grilled artichokes with pecorino di fossa and honey and silky Cantabrian anchovies in puddles of Provençal olive oil are perfect to share, while heartier pastas (we especially liked the paccheri alla vodka with nduja) are the smart choice if you're settling in for the evening. Award-winning sommelier Alexandra Price has curated a wine list that celebrates everything from well-known, beloved estates to emerging producers. I visited earlier in the summer, on opening night, but live close enough to confirm that the buzz has sustained into autumn, too – this is a smart Act II for a cosy neighbourhood joint. Sarah James Address: 19-21 Lonsdale Road, NW6 6RA Website: barblondie.co.uk Best new London restaurants in August 2026 Oudh 1772, Borough Chef Aktar Islam is something of a Brummie legend. He was the first British-born Bangladeshi chef to be awarded a Michelin star in 2019, just one year after opening his debut restaurant, Opheem, in Birmingham's Jewellery Quarter. A few years later, Opheem became the joint-first Indian restaurant to receive two stars, alongside London's Gymkhana, in the 2024 ceremony. Opheem's status as the city's go-to Special Occasion table to book is firmly cemented. So when news of Islam opening in London reached me, a native Brummie, I was naturally a) very proud (how often do chefs find success outside of London and then transplant to Zone 1?) and b) desperate to get through the door. And it is quite the door. Oudh 1772, Islam's Borough restaurant, is set across a Grade-II listed Victorian townhouse, where each storey sits sort of wonkily on top of the next. That's not to say it's not beautiful: designer Polina Sychova collaborated with Islam on the soft, sumptuously layered spaces – all curvy arches and thick drapes, peppered with antiques from Lucknow and even a bespoke hand-painted ceiling in the attic bar. Rather than bouncing across the Indian subcontinent, Islam's menu focuses on the flavours of Awadh, a historic region in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh. Regional street food is a playful place to start: chaat with white peas and potato or gol guppa (better known here, perhaps, as pani puri) are crispy and best eaten with your hands, a perfect way to start any evening. We boldly take on the mutanjan dum biryani with oxtail, a king prawn kebab and the Awadhi monkfish curry – be warned that while this might certainly be a white tablecloth sort of establishment, the portions are hearty. They're also, luckily, all perfectly pitched – perfumed biryani, garlicky prawns, creamy curry. Like Opheem before it, this is undoubtedly somewhere for a properly nice supper – prevented from ever becoming too proper by the friendly team and Islam's plucky menu. Add it to the list for your own next Special Occasion. Sarah James Address: 66 Union Street, London SE1 1TD Website: oudh1722.com Kismet, Borough Somewhat unexpectedly located above The Globe Tavern, a buzzy pub on the corner of Borough Market, is Kismet. After passing a throng of pint drinkers, visitors climb a winding staircase and enter a Turkish meyhane – a traditional tavern known for live music and family-style meals. Kismet has captured that atmosphere perfectly: dark, glittering mahogany benches, delicate lace curtains and vintage photographs make the restaurant feel wonderfully homely. Turkish music bubbles away in the background, with live performances on the qanun, a traditional string instrument, even hosted every Thursday evening. The menu follows Turkish meyhane cooking, so come prepared to share. Start with Atom, a thick buffalo milk yoghurt topped with chilli butter; cool and tangy against the gentle heat, it is particularly good scooped up with bread or piled onto Sigara Böreği, a crisp pastry filled with salty white cheese. From the charcoal grill comes Tavuk Şiş, smoky chicken thigh with red pepper, alongside Patates Kizartmasi, fried Cyprus potatoes. Wash it all down with Basketcase, a bottled lager brewed in partnership with Coalition Brewery, or, my personal favourite, a glass of raki. The Turkish anise-flavoured spirit is made for sipping alongside food, its clean, herbal finish acting as a refreshing palate cleanser between bites. The final flourish comes with dessert, when waiters glide between tables carrying silver trays above their heads. Lowered on request, they reveal rows of Turkish tea in delicate tulip-shaped glasses and slices of pistachio baklava drowned in syrup. Kismet is only a year-long residency in the space, so visit while you can. Amelia Dhuga Address: Upstairs at The Globe Tavern, 8 Bedale Street, London, SE1 9AL Website: kismet.london Cue Point, Latimer Road Cue Point is determinedly not a newcomer to the London restaurant scene. For a decade, the hybrid Afghan-Texas BBQ of Kabul-born chef Mursal Saiq and head chef Joshua Moroney has been making a name for itself through pop-ups, residencies and stints at breweries. This summer, they've finally found a permanent home for their low-n-slow, fired-up cooking. Cue Point at The Garden Bar is set inside an unchic West London boozer with, as the name hints, a truly enormous garden out back. Here, meat – Wagyu brisket, oak-smoked lamb shank, black lime pepper chicken bites – is smoked to meltiness, or else cooked over licking flames. Saiq's immaculate Afghan flavours are anything but shy and retiring, and a perfect match for Moroney's expert BBQ techniques. Those chicken bites' gnarly exteriors give way to soft meat – we boldly paired ours with the smoked pimento garlic chilli cheese flatbread to start. Wagyu brisket steak served with fluffy Texas naan and cowboy butter is a non-negotiable, although we'd also recommend ordering the flaky chilli-citrus seabass for something a little (emphasis on the word) lighter. The sticky toffee pudding with Bertotti kulfi was a surprise standout: moreish and sweet, Saiq works with West London gelataria Bertotti to perfect the kulfi. The team serve a special menu on Sundays, when Saiq tells me that people try to sneak in the door; advance reservations are so hard to get. This is West London's opening of the summer, and a must-book for anyone seeking serious flavour. Sarah James Address: Garden Bar Grill & Smokehouse at 41 Bramley Road, Notting Hill, London, W10 6SZ Website: cue-point.co.uk Rosina, Wandsworth It's been 20 years since chef Adam Byatt opened Trinity, which in restaurant years is practically ancient. In that time, the Clapham Old Town spot has not only survived but thrived, earning a Michelin star and cementing itself as a south London favourite – its signature beef tartare is still one of the best dishes I’ve ever had, and I don’t even like beef tartare. So when Byatt opened his latest table, Italian-inspired Rosina, in Wandsworth Common, it was busy from day dot. Busy but effortlessly breezy, with smart couples seated at white linen tables adorned with plates of bread, lemons and olives, and single white candlesticks. Antipasti comes to the table with a vibrant flurry – crimson tuna crudo, smoked sardines on toast, and a heavenly bowl of rainbow Datterini tomatoes with basil, nectarine and buffalo mozzarella. This is the kind of place where everything is confidently simple, and the bread basket is put to good use mopping up every sauce and vinaigrette. For mains, a pillowy turbot is roasted on the bone and swimming in lemon, capers, parsley and wilted spinach. The intriguingly named ‘post-service pasta’ was my favourite; an understated yet masterful bowl of spaghetti with anchovy, chilli, garlic and parsley, essentially the dish Byatt likes to make for himself after a shift in the kitchen. Wonderfully oily and crunchy in equal measure, I ate every tiny crumb and noodle. Pudding is served from the marble trolley that holds court in the centre of the restaurant, with tiramisu rustically served with a generous dollop tableside. If there’s room to try two, the not-too-sweet but cheese-heavy Rosina's torte is a worthy option; the torte and the restaurant are named after Byatt’s daughter Rosie, who also works in the kitchen. Lauren Burvill Address: Rosina, 35 Bellevue Road, London SW17 7EF Website: rosinarestaurant.co.uk All Roads, Brixton I visited All Roads during one of London's many 2026 heatwaves, so it says something about how delicious the food is that I wasn't remotely overwhelmed by the plates of mac and cheese, lamb from the house pot or fried wings that were placed in front of me on one of the hottest days of the year. While the rest of London was digging into light salads, or maybe a barbecue, I was more than happy to get stuck into the hearty dishes from chefs and partners Malika Green and Paschelle Brown, who have finally put down roots in Brixton following three years of sold-out supper clubs. The menu blends Caribbean cuisine with British, European and Southern American influences, resulting in a list of dishes that are hearty, moreish and full of flavour. Split into snacks, smalls, grill and plates (with just two or three dishes to each), it's tempting to order the whole menu – take three friends, and you probably could. Unfortunately for me, I was with just one friend, so we had to be discerning (albeit still rather greedy). Having tried over half of the menu, I truly think it would be difficult to order badly here, but my favourites were undoubtedly the chilli parm clams, served in a sweet and salty tomatoey-soy sauce, with crispy pancetta and topped with parmesan, or the impossibly cheesy baked mac and cheese. We ordered a fresh tomato salad to break up the dishes, and ended with homemade sorrel cheesecake ice cream. In the end, despite the heat, there's nowhere I'd rather have been on a Wednesday evening than here in Brixton Village, soaking up the vibe, flavours and fun of this memorable new spot. Abigail Malbon Address: 44 Atlantic Road, London SW9 8JN Website: allroadsldn.com Hon’s BBQ, Hackney Wick After earning a fiercely loyal following during his two-year residency at All My Friends, chef Man Hon Luk's first bricks-and-mortar restaurant – in the spot formerly occupied by Silo above Crate Brewery – was a natural next step. I never made it to the pop-up, but just knowing that Hon perfected his craft at world-renowned, Michelin-starred Interstellar BBQ was reason enough to clear the diary, hotfoot it over to Hackney Wick and see what all the fuss was about. The space is cool, casual and buzzing – high ceilings, whitewashed walls and simple red wooden tables and chairs let the food do the talking. Hon’s cooking is clearly shaped by his time in Texas, but what lands in front of us is something entirely his own: smoky, low-and-slow meats elevated with Chinese flavours and techniques. Every bite melts in your mouth, with just the right hit of spice and sweetness and the kind of deep caramelised crispy bits you’d fight your fellow diner for. The beef short ribs with Sichuan peppercorn sauce are the star of the show (tender, peppery and sticky) but don’t sleep on the sides; perfectly crunchy green beans with an umami-rich glaze, and a silky mac and cheese with a tangy mustard-laced sauce. Our only regret? Opting to share a bowl of the creamy mango coconut pudding – one each is a must. Sarah Allard Address: First floor, Unit 7, The White Building, Queen's Yard, London E9 5EN Website: honsbbq.com Best new London restaurants in July 2026 Vesper, Exmouth Market When Jackson Boxer opens a new London restaurant, it’s safe to assume it’ll be a smash hit. The chef and restaurateur behind buzzy Brunswick House, Dove and Henri has just opened a new neighbourhood spot on Exmouth Market. Interiors are industrial, with bare brick walls, a metal bar in the centre and curtains hiding candle-lit tables in intimate corners. There’s also plenty of tables that spill onto the sun-drenched street. We dined at Vesper a full month after opening, as tables really are that hard to come by. We made sure to book an early 6pm reservation, as the infamous burger you may have seen plastered all over your Instagram, often quoted as one of the best burgers in London, is ordered off-menu to 10 lucky customers on a first-come, first-served basis. We secured the fourth burger of the evening. The bun is covered in sweet glaze, hugging a hefty slab of seared and torched beef with a rare centre, layered with caramelised onions and oozing gorgonzola sauce. We’d recommend sharing, or you’ll be rolling home without a chance to try any of the other delicious plates. Our favourite dish of the night was the fried potato pizzette: a little circular pizza bread topped with pineapple, stringy stracciatella cheese and mortadella. Other highlights include the green bean salad coated in goat's cheese and gooseberry tahini, the chicken agnolotti – al dente pasta pockets bursting with fragrant chicken liver in a madeira jus. For pudding, order the punchy poached apricot flavoured with ginger and amaretto. Plates were scraped clean, as were our little gimlets, previously filled with the Vesper martini finished with a little squirt of citrus oil. Sophie Knight Address: 8-10 Exmouth Market, London EC1R 4QA Website: vesper.restaurant Langosteria, Whitehall Italian seafood restaurant group Langosteria has a knack for attaching itself to smart addresses in glamorous European locations, from Milan's Design District to St Moritz and the waves at Paraggi near Portofino. So it’s no surprise that the Milanese group’s first UK outpost has made a beeline for Raffles London at The OWO. Whitehall's neoclassical Portland stone grandeur doesn't quite evoke the summery spirit of the Ligurian Riviera, but once you pass through its doors, you're transported to that familiar Langosteria world, with its signature animated wallpaper and matching ambience. Here, everything is bold and impactful with a touch of experimentation – including the bar cocktails. From the concise list, the Pomodoro Mezcal, a smoky take on a Bloody Mary, confused my vodka receptors, but the Spicy Margarita with jalapeño was the unequivocal star. Food-wise, Langosteria casts a wide net in pursuit of freshness and quality, hauling its catch from Italy, Spain, France and Scotland. Locavore advocates will scream, but the quality is undeniable. My Sicilian red prawn starter – butter-soft and topped with wafer-thin slices of pecorino – was beautiful. The mains included Langosteria classics like the King Crab Special Edition 2007 and the Brittany Lobster "Spicy Blue”; I plumped for the crispy-skinned black grouper Chateaubriand, its saltiness offset by tangy-sweet caponata (Sicilian aubergine, olive and caper relish). My langoustine with lobster in a puddle of zingy lemon butter was perfectly al dente, but the Milanese turbot with asparagus and saffron proved somewhat immemorable. I chased it all with a glass of Ferrari Brut from a wine list that features most of the Champagne heavy hitters alongside an impressive, Italian-dominant selection of reds and whites. Portions are generous throughout, and for guests of the Raffles hotel, it's just a short stagger to their rooms upstairs. Noo Saro-Wiwa Address: Langosteria, Whitehall Place at The OWO, London, SW1A 2BD Website: langosteria.com Willet's, Chelsea At the back of The Cadogan, A Belmond Hotel, is an elegant wooden staircase that King Edward VII (when he was the Prince of Wales) ascended to visit his lover, the Victorian actress and socialite Lillie Langtry. It still stands as a testament to the history (and discretion) of this particular 1880s Chelsea townhouse, and today, though less steeped in scandal, it is as regal and luxurious as ever. The Cadogan is also home to Willett’s, a new British bistro that seems set to become a hotspot in its own right, even amongst those not staying upstairs. Studio Shayne Brady, the interiors team behind the renovation, has modernised while remaining true to the hotel's history – bathing the space in calming blues and greens. Executive chef Michael Turner (a Gordon Ramsay alum) is producing à la carte dishes that showcase the very best of British produce in unfussy, delicious dishes. The sourdough crumpets with gentleman’s relish and dressed Dorset crab were the definite showstoppers and are destined to become signature dishes. Mini but mighty, I’d have been more than happy with plates of those alone. Seasonality and locality are buzzwords thrown around quite loosely these days, but Willett’s really does do credit to everything that is brilliant about the produce of the British Isles. I'd also recommend the succulent Beef Wellington and the Colchester oysters. We’ve no doubt that this restaurant will become as legendary as some of the hotel’s historic residents. Cass Farrar Address: 75 Sloane Street, London, SW1X 9SG Website: belmond.com Dante, Mayfair Devotees of all things Stateside were intrigued when one of America's best cocktail bars, New York City's Dante, jumped across the pond in 2025 to pop up at grand dame Claridge’s. Rather than tire and bloat at yet another cross-Atlantic collab, the gourmands kept coming. And so, a year later, the hotel restaurant closed its doors for a facelift any Mayfair resident of a certain age would approve of, led by Bryan O’Sullivan Studio, with a fresh palette of green-and-blue tones and fantastical, botanical murals by Beth Rodway, to welcome Dante as a permanent resident of the neighbourhood's slickest hotel. We follow Billecart-Salmon Champagne with a taster of the Negroni Rosa, a watermelon concoction that tastes like a swig of the summer to come. A host of NYC favourites are now on the menu – we sample delicate caviar tarts and champagne pearls and are taken aback by the gargantuan grilled king prawns, their smoky, chilli-butter scent enveloping our booth. If a dish is preceded by the restaurant’s name, you know it’s one the chef’s hedging their bets on. And so the Dante smash burger arrives: a juicy patty coated in provolone cheese and topped with sweet caramelised onion, beside perfectly crispy chips awaiting their saucy demise. Burger devoured and Parmigiano Reggiano-doused veal Milanese inhaled between us, we call on our second stomachs for pudding with a side of spectacle. An espresso martini arrives, my face staring back at me in cocoa dusting courtesy of the bar’s cocktail-printing sorcery, alongside an uber-indulgent sticky toffee doughnut that illuminates our woozy cheeks with a whiskey flambé. It's a fiery finish to a meal I’ll be dining out on for a long time to come. Connor Sturges Address: Dante Mayfair, Claridge's, Brook Street, London W1K 4HR Website: maybourne.com Best new London restaurants in June 2026 The Sea, The Sea, Chelsea When we walk into Pavilion Road’s The Sea, The Sea – already a familiar name in Chelsea, but now a restaurant serving far more than just drinks and oysters – we don’t know what to expect. Above the ground-floor raw bar, tables are bathed in light, and the design is minimalist, but we quickly learn that all attention is poured into the fare. The menu spotlights lesser-known fish, plus whatever catch is locally abundant from the seafood suppliers they've built trusted relationships with. We start with cold sake and a tin of Imperial (as a caviar enthusiast, I love that the sour cream comes pre-topped with chives), followed by butter-soft Isle of Skye scallops with flowering currant. Often, the raw bar usually outshines everything else to me, but three warm dishes – cuttlefish ragu with green almond, smoked Chalkstream trout on a Jersey royal mash, and a rice vinegar-steeped John Dory with maitake – are impossible to top. The ragu is nothing like we imagine: no pasta, just clean-cut cuttlefish with an unbelievably flavourful squid ink salsify that results in an immediate repeat order. Come dessert, don’t look beyond the potato ice cream with smoked eel. It sounds hard to wrap your head around, and for that reason, you must order it. Tamara Southward Address: 243 Pavilion Road, London SW1X 0AW Website: https://theseathesea.net MA/NA Mayfair A new opening in Mayfair comes with glitzy high expectations, which we immediately felt as we were swept through the doors of MA/NA by a suave-suited doorman. He guided us through the long, winding bar space with a house DJ and down to our table under huge bonsais and gold statement lighting. A martini is poured table-side as we browse the extensive menu divided into small plates, robata (meats from the Japanese grill), sushi, steak cuts and large plates. We ordered to share: rock shrimp tempura in a glazed sticky sauce, juicy chicken thigh skewers from the robata grill, a 12-piece sushi platter with fresh cuts as selected by the chef (which could also pass as a piece of art) and the crunchy duck salad with sweet pomegranate. But, our favourite dish, which – fair warning – comes with a big price tag, was the Japanese A5 Wagyu slices served on a hot Himalayan salt stone, which not only flavours, but sears the meat from its heat. Melt-in-the-mouth slices of the finest beef, packed with flavour. MA/NA is on par, if not tastier than some of London's favourite high-end Japanese spots, with equally flashy guests and interiors. Sophie Knight Address: 30 Upper Grosvenor Street, London, W1K 7PH Website: manarestaurants.com Buvette London, Neal's Yard 14 years since its New York debut, chef Jody Williams has brought Buvette (and with it, the spirit of the West Village) to the cobbled streets of Covent Garden – slap bang in the middle of Neal's Yard. This charmingly chic bistro – complete with curated antiques and a black bicycle parked out front – somehow manages to strike just the right balance between familiar and fancy, with a day-to-night menu focusing on locally-sourced produce. We start with a crisp glass of bubbles as we make our selection, following the house suggestion of sharing three to five dishes between two. Plates are indulgent yet remarkably delicate; a vibrant ratatouille, fresh steak tartare, garlicky escargot, and decadent dauphinois. The standout is, unsurprisingly, Buvette's signature croques; we opted for the forestier, a vegetarian riff on the original, paired with a generous pour of white wine (French, naturally). To end, tarte tatin and a mousse au chocolat, followed by a perfectly chilled martini made just the way you like – a highlight among the well-executed classic cocktails on offer. I can’t wait to visit again, whether for a flaky morning croissant and espresso or another evening encounter with that croque... Drew Burns Address: Buvette London, 2 Neal's Yard, London WC2H 9DP Website: buvette-london.com Ornella, London Fields Foodies and film fanatics flocked to Lupa when it opened its doors in Highbury – an Italian feeding frenzy from restaurateur Ed Templeton and chef Naz Hassan, fuelled by The Gentleman star Theo James’ involvement. The reviews were promising, and bookings soon became hard to come by, so it came as no surprise when the trio announced a follow-up – Ornella. On the corner of a leafy suburban street in London Fields, this new arrival is an edible love letter to Milanese fare that the capital’s food scene has long been crying out for, named in honour of the late singer Ornella Vanoni. Inside, it’s simultaneously cosy and sexy, diners tucked into banquettes and huddled around circular tables illuminated by flickering candlelight. Proceedings start over punchy sbagliato and caffè amaro cocktails – easy on those, mind – before the fluffiest focaccia in town arrives, warm and doused in glittering olive oil, alongside wafer-thin slivers of salty mortadella and coppa. There’s a choice of four starters – shoutout to the sea bream tartare, I hear, from my companion – followed by five ‘primi’ dishes. We slurp on salty onion broth and twirl our forks to catch shavings of cheese in the simple yet moreish butter and Parmesan tagliatelle, all washed down with generous pours of Venetian Manzoni Bianco. Naturally, onto secondi, a satisfyingly crisp chicken Milanese, used mostly to mop up heaps of silky mashed potatoes that likely contain more butter than potatoes (no complaints from us). We saunter into the night, hands in circular motions on our stomachs, remarking on how beige and calorific our spread became. No regrets at all, mind, as we plot our return to get snug in one of Ornella’s corners when the mercury drops, if not before. Connor Sturges Address: Ornella, 51 Wilton Way, London E8 1BG Website: ornella.restaurant Mezzogiorno by Francesco Mazzei It’s no small feat bringing Italian summers to London, so it comes as no surprise to any Italophile that Francesco Mazzei is the one leading this charge for the foodie moment that’s taken root within the grand dame walls of London’s Corinthia Hotel. Designed to transport, its namesake and menu are inspired by the southern regions of Italy, where the sun is the most intense at midday, translated as ‘Mezzogiorno’. Personally more accustomed to London’s shades of grey, I was surprised to enter the opulent Northall bar and find myself in a nonna-esque open kitchen that doubles as a walk-through to the main restaurant. Here, a communal oval table sits opposite the kitchen, where an intimate group sit watching folds of dough being expertly handcrafted into pasta and breadsticks by the chefs in their whites. Inspired by the Baroque palazzos of Southern Italy, the restaurant is adorned with custom-made Murano chandeliers hanging from tall ceilings, held up by dramatic pillars adjoined to a waffled terracotta ceiling, which makes me think of a gelato cone. The scene here on a Tuesday evening is mostly out-of-town pals sharing plates, business comrades and on this occasion, a Hollywood A-lister, but the winning majority here were couples holding hands across tables and huddled in booths. We start by nibbling on the longest breadsticks I’ve ever seen - simple and all unique, the only concern is filling up on them, but they are surprisingly light. Next comes an injection of colour with the Pipi Cruski Limone Di Rocca Mayo, a traditional dish of fire-red peppers that are fried and best enjoyed slovenly dipped into lemon butter. Despite the colour, these aren’t spicy and have the most excellent crunch. Among the tables, we tuck into an antipasti of Orkney scallops, which are tender but fragrant alongside Batutta Di Manzo Inglese, a refreshing mix of chopped beef, salad leaves, pomegranate seeds and large shavings of black truffle. Mouths still full but contentedly chatting, it’s easy to see the inspiration behind this place. With excellent company and ambience, come and come again, but definitely share the hand-made pasta with native blue lobster sauce and T-bone among the table, while you snack on humble traditional Sicilian vegetables and of course, an entire bowl of zucchini sticks. To finish, the showstopping Tiramisu is necessary - presented to the table in a family-style bowl, the friendly server affectionately spoons the dessert onto our plates, like they are welcoming us to the family. Megan Wilkes Address: Whitehall Place, London, SW1A 2BD, United Kingdom Website: corinthia.com/en-gb/london/mezzogiorno/ Kumori, Soho Slap-bang in the heart of Soho, Kumori is a 30-seat handroll bar where most of the action happens at the counter, creating an intimate, immersive feel. Inside, the space feels a little like stepping into a spaceship – all brushed-metal surfaces and iridescent pink and purple lighting. From the plump made-to-order handrolls to the carefully curated soundtrack, everything about Kumori feels cool, fresh and considered. Knees brush as we pore over the tick-box menu, leaving me spiralling as I weigh up how many of the handrolls I can reasonably fit in; there are simply too many good options. The cocktail list is an equally delicious debate, eventually landing on a yuzu mezcal margarita and sitting back to settle in for the show. Behind the counter, chefs move with speed and precision through a menu curated by head chef John Randy De Guzman (formerly Nobu, Tobi Masa and Katsuya). Each roll is served from chef to patron the moment it’s made, turning dinner into a kind of live theatre. Lucy Bruton Address: Kumori, 26 Denman Street, London W1D 7HX Website: kumorirestaurant.com Best new London restaurants in May 2026 Tavern, Shoreditch I’m still thinking about those little melted cheese-filled choux buns that kicked off dinner (the chunion puff), and the dense brown butter muffin that we finished on. But also every course we inhaled in between, which was cooked on open flames from the team behind Michelin-starred Restaurant St Barts in Farringdon. Nest, the high-end tasting-menu restaurant that once sat on this site, is no longer open. The trio behind it, Johnnie Crowe (Co-founder), Brendan Appleby (executive chef), and Kirsty Easterbrook (head chef), have moved away from fine dining, rebranding and reopening as Tavern, a much more casual affair with a nose-to-tail concept using seasonal British produce. I loved the new bistro-style interiors mixed with oldy-worldy pub furnishings. Dark, mismatched wooden chairs, scattered with shaggy sheepskins, are tucked beneath linen-topped tables with flickering candles. Kick things off with a Tavern Pickleback cocktail – a dirty martini infused with pickle juice, served with a cocktail stick of cured meat inside. Small plates (actually on the larger size) are flung out of the kitchen quickly; order the fire bread coated in wild garlic and, obviously, the chunion puff to start. For mains, we loved the asparagus with a dollop of buttery hollandaise and cured egg yolk, the pork and cuttlefish sausage with squid-ink mustard and the huge joint of smoky sirloin with a side of charred leaves, beetroot and horseradish. For dessert, have the black koji custard tart, bitter and sweet at the same time. Sophie Knight Address: Tavern, 374-378 Old Street, London, EC1V 9LT Website: tavernlondon.co.uk The Latimer, North Kensington The Latimer is a true family effort. It's been recently brought to life by Rochelle Canteen co-founder Melanie Arnold, St John and Sessions Arts Club partner Jon Spiteri, and their three children, Lorcan, Fin, and Molly, who have brought their own prowess to London hotspots Caravel and Koya, respectively. Given this resume, I already knew I’d be in good hands when it came to the food, but the clan have also captured a remarkably warm neighbourhood feel. Though it’s been open for just over a week, when we visit, guests here walk around comfortably with a sense of knowing the place. We ordered grilled asparagus in a herb sauce we’d drink by the bowl if we could, confit trout with green beans and new potatoes, and our must-have: unbelievably tender pork belly skewers braised in cider, served with a dollop of applesauce. Grilled-to-perfection sea bream with tiny green and yellow tomatoes in a delectable aioli, and a courgette linguine tossed in stracciatella followed. There are two desserts – an amaretti crumble and a chocolate mousse. Plus, I’m impressed by the drinks here – at £12, they’re decently priced for West London and the chicest thing about the pub. I opt for the Westway, a tequila-and-blood-orange shrub short drink, but mentally bookmark South of the Border, a black coffee-and-reposado tequila drink, for when I’m next here on a weekend. Tamara Southward Address: 274 Latimer Road, London W10 6QW Website: thelatimer.co.uk Bar Etna, Newington Green Does London really need another hype-y pizza joint? Having been left as cold as a next-day margarita by a couple of recent openings, I was sceptical – but having spent the evening being charmed and carbloaded by the team at Bar Etna, I can attest that it absolutely does. Perhaps I shouldn’t have been surprised – this is the dream-team project from Four Legs’ Ed McIlroy (Finsbury Park’s Tollington and The Plimsoll) and Joe Beddia (owner of Philadelphia-based, Bib Gourmand-garlanded Pizzeria Beddia). Their special relationship has resulted in an East Coast pizza bar with mid-century Milanese design and top-notch seasonal British ingredients. The downstairs bar is reserved for walk-ins, while upstairs is (slightly) more formal tables, where we huddle knee-to-knee with strangers in front of an open kitchen from which servers twirl out piping pizzas. The menu is no-fuss: three spritzes plus a special (a tomatini-inspired affair on our visit); negronis or vermouth on tap; an Italian-focused wine list; a couple of snacks; and four thin-crust, Italian-American style pizzas to choose from. Creamy “judion” (butter) beans arrive floating in silky olive oil and liberally doused with salt and lemon zest – perfectly simple and perfectly done, a hint of what’s to come. The must-order tomato pie is a Philly staple of salty, herby tomatoes spread on springy focaccia. My fellow diner deems it “the best, most upscale version of primary school traybake pizza you’ve ever had”. For pizza, we go for a simple Number One (tomato, mozzarella and Neal’s Yard coolea), which elegantly manages the dance between a thin, crispy base and a satisfying amount of flop. The Number Two (cream, cantabrian chillis, greens, coolea) is our favourite, with just the right amount of chilli heat, but the appropriately volcanic Etna Curry Pizza blows my socks off with one bite; it’s not for me, but those made of stronger stuff might enjoy this playful tribute to a curry house saag paneer. A stainless steel coupe of espresso soft serve is tiny and chic and just right to cut through all the carbs. One night after opening, Bar Etna was heaving, with a real house party feel. With plans for late-night pizzas by the slice on Fridays and Saturdays, I can already tell that the pavement outside will be spilling over this summer – and with the recently opened The Gold Tooth (from the pair behind London Fields’ Papi) and existing favourites Cadet and Yield nearby, Newington Green is fast becoming one of the buzziest food spots in this part of town. Olivia Squire Address: 47 Newington Green, London N16 9PX Website: instagram.com/bar.etna.london Idalia at Pillar Hall, Olympia There’s something sparkly happening in West London. Last month saw the opening of Pillar Hall – a landmark new live music venue, 30,000ft restaurant and speakeasy set within a truly magnificent Grade II-listed space, as part of Olympia’s tidy £1.3 billion regeneration. Originally designed in 1886 by architect Henry Edward Coe, it was built for exhibitions, concerts and even the circus. Vivienne Westwood staged her first catwalk show here; Britain hosted one of its earliest film screenings; and now, 140 years on, it’s back with a new outfit for a fresh dose of razzle-dazzle. At its heart sits the sweeping restaurant, Idalia. The name is an alternative moniker for Aphrodite that was rather more in vogue in the 1880s. The vast, gleaming dining room is all verdant glamour, inspired by the nearby gardens of Kensington and Olympia, with space for 300 – so not your quiet Tuesday supper spot. The sparkling wine list is all English and excellent, but do start with one of the cocktails, which are playful, theatrical things served in everything from pink-crusted globes to glass handbags as an homage to Dolce & Gabbana. Of course, it’s a fine dining experience. In the kitchen, Samantha Williams – formerly Angela Hartnett’s executive chef – delivers a modern British menu with the odd Asian interlude. Reasons why, unsure, but why not, I say – and to be fair, the Asian stuff is really good. A bowl of Gochujang chicken thighs are juicy, crispy and drizzled in zesty sriracha mayo, while the whole roasted Turbot, which arrives theatrically and is deboned tableside, comes with a heaping scoop of shichimi togarashi butter oozing atop the skin and some fresh pickled daikon. It’s melty-soft and perfect for sharing, best served with a side of the beef tallow chips – the swankiest fish and chips you’ll eat all year bar none. Finish with the pistachio cheesecake, which is truly humongous and has famously racked up quite a reputation in only the first week of opening. This is a thoroughly grand affair perfect for your next big do – and such a glitzy night deserves a little flourish. Charley Ward Address: Pillar Hall, Olympia Way, London W14 0EY Website: pillarhall.co.uk Fenix, Mayfair I’ll never say no to a Greek salad, but a salad plus endless dips, pittas and charcoal-fired meats and seafood? Count me in. Fenix is a smart Greek-Mediterranean restaurant in the heart of Mayfair (right next to Green Park station), serving sharing plates with a slightly modern twist. The menu is split into spreads, salad, cold dishes, meze, open fire, pasta and rice and sides, and the choice is overwhelming – in the best way. At first glance, I knew I'd have trouble choosing from the vast menu, and there were multiple extra dishes I’d have chosen if I had endless stomach space, but in the end, we went for a little bit of everything. Start with the dips – the spicy feta is creamy with a bit of a kick, but the smoked taramasalata was the real star of the show; full of flavour, a perfect smooth texture and just gorgeous spread across pillowy pita. We saved a little bit of our dips for the meze (the halloumi tempura and caramelised aubergine with tahini miso are must-orders) and added spicy sea bass carpaccio, spicy sweetcorn and orzo with langoustine and feta to finish things off. There wasn’t a dish I regretted, although in hindsight I was probably too stuffed for the crème brûlée – but who can say no to a sweet treat? The space is massive, but it still feels intimate. During our Thursday night dinner, we were catered to by multiple members of staff (all of them friendly and knowledgeable) and our reservation was stretched out for nearly three hours, without ever feeling rushed. The decor is clearly slightly themed towards a taverna (think raffia and wood, plenty of greenery and paved flooring) but avoids being gimmicky thanks to the chic combination of textures and light colour palette. I’d come back here with friends visiting London to show them a cool spot in the city, and for a menu with an endless list of crowd-pleasers. Address: Fenix, Stratton House, 80 Piccadilly, London W1J 8HX Website: fenixrestaurants.com Café Jikoni, Stratford It’s rare for a toastie to be anything more than a rushed, forgettable meal, but at Café Jikoni, that all changed. The Goan aubergine achaar and Mony’s cheddar toastie was one of the best bites I’ve had this year, and without question the finest toastie I’ve ever eaten. The staff insisted we try it, and despite my initial scepticism at choosing a sandwich over something more elaborate, I was quickly proved wrong. It was spicy, oozing, and bright with freshness. To me, the mark of an exceptional chef lies in their ability to elevate the humble. Ravinder Bhogal is a clear master of this, able to refine even the most staple of dishes. Born in Kenya to Indian parents, she is an award-winning food writer, TV presenter, journalist, cook, and restaurateur, and her breadth of experience is evident in every dish. Jikoni Marylebone has long been an essential part of London's dining scene, and now Bhogal has expanded the concept with an all-day café and restaurant housed on the lower ground floor of the new V&A East Museum in Stratford. The striking building feels like a natural home for her food: elevated yet relaxed, inclusive, and creative. Standouts ranged from the nibbles – such as the Shambaa pickles and umami-rich oregano fries – to larger plates like butter beans aglio e olio, topped with irresistibly crunchy pangrattato, and a deeply comforting massaman curry. As someone who eats predominantly plant-based, I found Jikoni sets a high bar for vegetarian cooking, proving it can be just as inventive, flavourful, and satisfying as any meat-based dish. The tofu massaman and butter beans were particularly vibrant and memorable. From the drinks list, the sweet, smoky strawberry margarita and a satisfyingly dry martini are both worth your time. To finish, I watched the sun set over the canal while indulging in an intensely rich Vietnamese coffee brownie, alongside a picture-perfect yuzu, pandan, and strawberry iced bun. Address: Café Jikoni at the V&A East Museum, 107 Carpenters Rd, Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, Stratford, E20 2AR Website: jikonilondon.com Best new London restaurants in April 2026 Teal by Sally Abé, Hackney Tucked along a leafy Hackney street, Teal by Sally Abé feels immediately at home among neighbourhood pubs, cafés and delis, just a short stroll from London Fields.
