item.title: Arc’teryx Wants the Sperro SV to Be the Last Jacket You Ever Buy—Seriously
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 5.01
Engineered for versatility across high-stakes mountain environments, the Sperro SV underwent rigorous testing during ski tours and ice climbing ascents. (Photo: Courtesy of Arc'teryx) Tucked alongside the interior chest pocket of a two-toned magenta Arc’teryx jacket is a laser-etched QR code—but instead of pulling up the menu at your local pub, it prompts you to register your new purchase, immediately kicking off a record of the jacket’s materials, origin, and, eventually, repair history. A QR code seems simple enough—after all, you encounter dozens of them weekly—but a QR code on a mountain-grade hardshell requires a different level of engineering than the laminated square on your bartop. The internal placement makes it near-impossible to destroy or remove; the laser etching, adapted from the electronics industry, underwent multiple trials to ensure it left a permanent mark without degrading the fabric. So why spend so much time, money, and engineering on a single square inch of jacket? For Arc’teryx, that QR code is the entry point into System 0™, a new framework that reimagines how products can be designed, manufactured, used, repaired, and ultimately regenerated. In fact, the QR code is just one of many updates and innovations Arc’teryx built into its first System 0 jacket, the Sperro SV. Among the others: an easily repairable zipper, a nylon face fabric and backer engineered for chemical recyclability, and reinforcement at common failure points. System 0 started as a “what if” conversation between Arc’teryx CEO Stuart Haselden and VP of Advanced Concepts, Alex Plante, brainstorming what circularity would look like for the company. At that point, Arc’teryx’s ReBIRD program already existed, with a solid infrastructure for product repairs, resale, trade-in, and upcycling, but the team knew they were still missing an actual process—a viable, repeatable way to create products that can be used for longer and ultimately regenerated into something new. “We landed on what product we wanted to develop within that [circularity] concept, and then, while we were developing the product, realized that we didn’t have all the pieces of the system,” says Andrew Yip, Senior Director of Materials Innovation at Arc’teryx. That meant building capability as they went, bringing in people like Kyle Wood, Vice President of Strategy, to focus on circularity. They also recruited for other supporting roles, like sourcing manager for raw materials. Throughout the circularity initiative, Yip and his colleagues used one principle as their North Star: Sustainability alone isn’t a reason for a product to exist. Anything they created had to live up to Arc’teryx’s sky-high standards for technical excellence and durability. “Most sustainable materials and products are just less bad than their incumbent,” argues Yip. “If you’re just going to make something less bad from a sustainability perspective but make it worse in terms of performance, then there really isn’t a justification for it to exist.” To that end, Arc’teryx prioritized abrasion resistance on both face fabric and backer, while refusing to compromise on tear and tensile strength, waterproofing, and breathability—all the things that determine whether a jacket becomes a one-season purchase or a mainstay in your gear closet. They also intentionally aligned on nylon 6 as the key material instead of polyester; even though polyester has more recycling opportunities, the team knew that nylon 6 fabric would perform best. To find the exact nylon content ratio—the perfect number that would make the fabric functionally and financially recyclable—Arc’teryx worked closely with Aquafil, the manufacturer of ECONYL® regenerated nylon. According to Aquafil, the textile is known for high wear resistance and impact strength (aka extreme durability). Finding the perfect jacket material was one thing. But that wasn’t the hardest problem the Arc’teryx team had to solve, says Yip. You already know Arc’teryx for its insanely technical, single-purpose shells like the Alpha SV—a scalpel, according to Yip. “It’s really a precision tool, and it was designed for ice climbing,” he explains. “It doesn’t have hand pockets for a reason—you don’t need hand pockets when you’re ice climbing.” On the contrary, the Sperro SV had to be a jacket-of-all-trades, working in a variety of environments and use cases. “With the Sperro SV, we wanted to make something that was multi-environment, multifunctional, and multi-activity,” details Yip. They needed a Swiss Army Knife, not a scalpel—but that Swiss Army Knife couldn’t compromise on durability. To ensure the Sperro SV was worth its mettle, Arc’teryx tested the jacket on ski tours, hiking trips, snowshoeing expeditions, and even ice climbing. They also partnered with the North Shore Search and Rescue, a volunteer-led organization and one of Canada’s oldest search-and-rescue teams, to make sure the jacket performed in high-stakes scenarios. All that engineering ultimately serves one purpose: creating a jacket worthy of what Yip refers to as custodianship, rather than ownership. “Hopefully, the person who’s purchasing this jacket is somebody who cares about their stuff and is going to take care of the garment, bring it in for repair, and extend its lifetime as much as possible,” says Yip. “And only after many, many years and many, many repairs, when something is no longer repairable, only then is when we take it back.” Hence, the QR code. Arc’teryx hopes that by making it as seamless as possible for customers to track the Sperro SV’s lifespan, materials, and repair history, customers will view themselves as custodians with a responsibility to their gear—instead of temporary owners of a disposable item. If all goes according to plan, the Sperro SV might be the last jacket Arc’teryx ever sells you. At a gulp-worthy $1,200 retail price, most customers are probably praying that they never have to buy another jacket again, but it’s not exactly a sound business strategy in an industry that counts on customers to replace old gear. Yip is strangely okay with that. “When we’re developing new products and prototypes, we know we have something when our athletes and field testers don’t want to give it back,” he explains. “Similarly, I think we’re onto something if we have a commercial product that people can buy and they don’t want to replace it. So personally, I would have no problem with that.” When asked to comment on the price, Arc’teryx reps note that the Sperro SV is priced in line with their most advanced hard shells, and the price reflects the design effort and materials that went into this sustainable jacket. “Circularity at this level of performance requires significant investment across materials, manufacturing, certification, and end-of-life infrastructure,” Arc’teryx acknowledges. They believe that the price reflects the value of three years of unlimited repairs, a product they’re backing to last for years, and eventually, an end-of-life offramp. “When you factor in the total life of the jacket, the value calculation looks different than a traditional purchase,” reasons the brand. Whether consumers will find the price a fair trade-off for the total package remains to be seen. The Sperro SV is just the first “statement of intent,” as Yip puts it, for what System 0 can do within the Arc’teryx playbook. With the streamlined processes and internal philosophies Arc’teryx has now aligned on, they’re free to explore further iterations of circular gear. “We started with a hardshell because it’s what we know, what we make, and what we’re known for—so you can imagine that the other things we’re known for and make well are coming down the pipeline,” hints Yip. And for the Arc’teryx loyalists who worry this new iteration of a hardshell won’t live up to their high standards—you’ve got nothing to worry about. “If anyone were to put on the jacket and close their eyes, it really shouldn’t be different at all compared to anything that we’ve made before. And I think that’s the point,” says Yip. “It’s everything else around it that we’re trying to change.”

item.title: The High-Altitude Journey of the World’s Most Famous Adventure Cat
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.31
Simon the adventure cat (Photo: Courtesy of JJ Yosh) Had JJ Yosh, an adventure content creator based in Boulder, Colorado, simply taken his cat, Simon, on a handful of hikes and posted the videos online, I would have dismissed it as a pet-thetic social media stunt. But a decade after adopting the black Bombay cat, the duo—better known to millions as Backpacking Kitty on Instagram and TikTok—has built something far more remarkable. Together they’ve hiked the Austrian Alps, whitewater rafted California’s Sacramento River, climbed a volcano in Guatemala, and traveled to more than 15 countries and four continents. They’ve flown on over 100 flights, including on a seaplane, and kayaked some of the most remote waterways in the world, taking an audience of 11 million followers along with them, and making Simon less of a novelty and more like a bona fide field companion. Now Yosh has something even more ambitious in mind. He’s preparing to take Simon on a multi-year Seven Summits spree. “I’m positive he’s the only cat who has summited a dozen of Colorado’s 14ers,” Yosh says of Simon who he rescued from euthanasia in 2016. Yet even those accomplishments, and, arguably, the title of one of the most famous cats in the world, pale beside this latest odyssey. Over the next three years, they plan to tackle the tallest mountain on every continent: Denali, Mount Kilimanjaro, Aconcagua, Mount Elbrus, Vinson Massif, Puncak Jaya, and the world’s highest peak, Mount Everest. Before you picture a cat being hauled into Everest’s notorious Death Zone—a place so hostile to life it contains only about a third of the oxygen available at sea level—rest easy. “I’m definitely not taking Simon to the summit. I’m not risking his life,” Yosh says. While Yosh makes his push for the top, Simon will be living the considerably cushier life at Everest Base Camp with a dedicated pet sitter, people he already knows and trusts. Yosh is emphatic that Simon’s health and safety come first. “How high he goes depends entirely on the mountain,” Yosh says. That means, for Everest, Base Camp is his ceiling. “Nothing above it, no exceptions.” For Kilimanjaro and Aconcagua? Those are non-technical walk-ups, so there is more room. “He could go higher than base camp on those, and how much higher gets decided on the ground rather than promised in advance.” As for everywhere else, Yosh will assess each peak one at a time, and veterinary opinions will inform each decision. Yosh says, “ If the answer is that it is too high for a cat, that is the end of it. He does not go.” It’s all part of the careful balance Yosh has spent the past decade striking with his feline partner. Simon may be born for adventure—while he does trek via leash, he’s happiest riding Yosh’s shoulders through forests and across alpine trails, even snowboarding—he’s still a cat, with very real limitations. For example, while Yosh was on a Mount Baker crevasse rescue training ahead of his Seven Summits bid recently, Simon wasn’t practicing self-arrests. Which begs the question: How do you prepare a house cat for extreme altitude? After all, Everest Base Camp sits at a breath-stealing 17,598 feet. The answer starts at home. In Boulder, where the pair live at roughly 6,000 feet above sea level, acclimatization is woven into everyday life. Yosh’s home—playfully known as “the house his cat built”—is tucked into a rocky cliff and outfitted with an indoor climbing wall scaled by both owner and pet. Outside, Colorado’s high country is Simon’s natural conditioning ground, where regular mountaineering outings have gradually exposed him to thinner air—one might say the purrfect conditions—long before the Himalayas come into view. Yosh has even taken Simon on technical rope climbs, securing him a small-dog harness. And when it comes to gear, Simon is just as outfitted as his owner: Yosh has assembled a wardrobe for Simon to rival any serious adventurer’s, with specialized gear for seemingly every climate, condition, and expedition. Add to that the deep relationship these two have built. Even talking about the possibility of something happening to Simon makes Yosh visibly shaken. The depth of that bond was forged early. Not long after Yosh adopted Simon, he left the cat with a friend while filming a commercial in Bolivia. What Yosh didn’t learn until later was that Simon had gone missing for three days. “Thankfully, they didn’t tell me at the time,” Yosh says. “They’d put up missing posters everywhere, but I had no idea.” Even now, the memory rattles him. “If that happened today and I found out while I was on a mountain, I’d turn around. I wouldn’t be able to finish the climb,” he says. “You have to be in a good mental place to climb a mountain, and I wouldn’t be.” “This work can be so taxing and draining. You question why you’re doing it over and over again,” Yosh says. “That’s where having Simon is such a huge emotional pillow. The hardest moments usually aren’t the scary, high-adrenaline ones. They’re when the weight of the whole expedition catches up with you.” Whether he’s just finished an ultrarun or a grueling climb, Yosh knows there’s one constant: Simon, curled up in the tent ready for a cuddle at the end of the day. In a life all about relentless forward motion, that ritual has become the reset that keeps him going. It will be tested during their next challenge. But first, there are the logistics to work through. Namely, the travel concerns of hop-scotching the planet with a cat. Fortunately, this isn’t Simon’s first rodeo. He has a U.S. ID card and an E.U. pet passport that allows him to easily cross borders, and he doesn’t fly cargo. “But of course he has to get all of these health certificates for each country,” Yosh says. Then there’s the tricky reality of lengthy flights and layovers. Naturally, I had to ask, does Simon get jet lag? “Simon gets so excited every time we reach a new hotel or destination,” Yosh says. “He’s like ready to go.” Apparently, when you’re an international adventuring cat of mystery, the only thing tougher than Everest is waiting for room service. That, and then clawing your way into mountaineering history.

item.title: Colorado’s Maroon Bells Are Closed After a Second Climber Has Died in Less Than a Week
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.30
Responders with Mountain Aspen Rescue evacuated a deceased climber on September 6 using a technical lowering system (Photo: Photo courtesy of MRA) The U.S. Forest Service temporarily closed all climbing access to Colorado’s Maroon Peak on September 8, 2026, to recover the body of a climber who had fallen off the mountain. The death marked the first of two fatal mountaineering accidents on Colorado’s famed 14er summits in less than a week. Officials have not released the names, sex, or ages of either person. On September 8, authorities embarked on a recovery mission for the body of a climber who went missing six days earlier, on September 2, according to the responding agency, Mountain Rescue Aspen (MRA). To aid the recovery, the U.S. Forest Service closed climbing access to Maroon Peak, including the standard route from West Maroon Creek and the traverse from North Maroon Peak. After the climber was reported missing on September 2, rescuers found notes in their vehicle parked at the trailhead. Based on these notes, responders conducted aerial searches in the Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness, a remote alpine area that contains six peaks over 14,000 feet, including the iconic maroon-colored twin peaks known as the Maroon Bells and Snowmass Mountain. “During the aerial search, the climber was located deceased and tentatively identified in very technical and difficult terrain to access,” MRA wrote in a statement. In an unrelated incident on September 6, a second climber died after falling from the north face of Castle Peak, located about 12 miles south of Aspen. An all-volunteer team of 21 members responded on the ground and by helicopter. Rebecca Rees, a dental anesthesiologist, witnessed the September 6 fall while hiking with a group between Castle and Conundrum Peaks. Rees, 44, lives in a suburb of Denver and has been climbing Colorado 14ers since 2017. She said she had been on this specific climb around five times. “There had been a rockfall all day from Conundrum going into the lake, so we were used to hearing these rocks fall into the lake,” she said. “At 12:25 P.M., we heard the rocks again but it was a different sound. I looked over and I saw this gentleman tumbling down the mountain. It was horrifying because it was not a fall that would be survivable.” Rees estimated that the man initially fell about 30 feet, and then continued to tumble hundreds more down the mountain. It’s not clear how or why he fell, she said. Her group called emergency services, and yelled at the man, but he was unresponsive. Looking up-slope, she said they saw his sunglasses and water bottles in a debris field. “Mountain Rescue Aspen personnel reached the climber at approximately 3:58 P.M. and determined the individual had sustained injuries that were not survivable,” MRA wrote. “Team members then carefully evacuated the climber from the mountain using a technical lowering system.” Located in Colorado’s Elk Range, the Maroon Bells are one of the most photographed destinations in the state, and encompass Maroon Peak and North Maroon Peak. The peaks have earned their nickname “Deadly Bells“—the mountains are highly technical, dangerous, and extremely difficult, according to the nonprofit that does service work on the state’s highest peaks, Colorado Fourteeners Initiative. “These mountains are known for having a lot of loose rock and being fairly dangerous,” Rees told Outside. “Up close, the rock is very loose and unforgiving. Route-finding is difficult, and it’s very easy to take a wrong step or have the wrong handhold and fall,” she said. Incredibly steep terrain also means seemingly innocuous mishaps can quickly become deadly. In May, a hiker slid 200 feet down the Maroon Bells after slipping at an elevation of around 11,300 feet. In August, Colorado hiker Brandon Hinkle was completing the Maroon Bells Traverse when he tumbled 500 feet down a sheer rock face and suffered multiple serious injuries. Rees reiterated the importance of traveling with a buddy, especially in dangerous terrain. “Without even realizing it in the moment, you’re constantly checking in with each other when you’re hiking up,” she said. “Having that constant feedback and another opinion is helpful checks and balances.” And if you’re not feeling it, Rees said known when to turn around can save lives. “The mountain will be there forever, and it’s okay to get to a certain point and realize today is not the day,” she said. MRA also reminds backcountry travelers to leave a detailed itinerary with a trusted person before departing, including the intended route, expected return time, and contingency plans. Anyone traveling in the backcountry should also carry appropriate equipment, be prepared for rapidly changing mountain conditions, and always bring a reliable two-way satellite communication device when traveling in areas without cell service. “We’re not going to stop hiking these peaks,” Rees added. “It’s traumatizing but, just be safe and be prepared. Know when to stop, and know your limits.”

item.title: How Skin Tone Affects Wearable Accuracy—and How Tech Giants Are Responding
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.87
(Photo: Hill background: Fond, Magnus; Fitness Watch: simplehappyart/Getty; Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva) Wearables have become a near-constant companion for many Americans. According to a 2026 study, nearly 107 million people in the United States own one. People track their steps, workouts, and recovery, and increasingly look to those numbers to tell them how their bodies are doing. But for some—particularly people with darker skin tones—there’s a nagging question: Can I trust what my device is telling me? There’s a good reason to ask. A 2025 review of smartwatch accuracy studies found significant variability in how wearable devices performed across skin tones. According to one study included in the review, a major smartwatch brand measured heart rates within five beats per minute (bpm) across a full spectrum of skin tones. Other devices, however, underestimated heart rate by ten to 15 bpm in darker-skinned users during moderate to vigorous exercise. Researchers also found large discrepancies in heart rate readings during cycling and resistance training in people with dark skin. While heart rate metrics help people gauge workout intensity and how quickly their heart recovers after exercise, heart rate readings can also be lifesaving. An irregular heartbeat may indicate serious cardiovascular issues that can lead to blood clots, stroke, and heart failure, and should be flagged to a doctor. An inaccurate reading could miss these red flags. This issue is not news to wearable companies as getting accurate data from darker skin is a known challenge—one that requires extra effort from wearable makers to ensure the data is reliable. Outside contacted eight major wearable tech companies, including Oura, Apple, WHOOP, Google, and Polar, to find out how they’ve worked to address the wearable skin-tone problem. Here’s why wearables can struggle to get accurate readings on dark skin, and how these companies say they’ve improved their tech to ensure better accuracy across skin tones. Most smartwatches and rings rely on a type of technology called photoplethysmography (PPG), which uses optical sensors. Those sensors detect light to measure blood flow. A typical PPG device shines green light into your skin. (If you take a peek at the underside of your fitness watch, you can probably spot those green flashing lights.) Hemoglobin—a small protein in your blood that carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body—absorbs some of that light, and the rest is reflected back onto the sensor. As blood moves through your vessels, the device measures changes in the reflected light to estimate your heart rate. The catch is that melanin, the pigment that gives skin its color, also absorbs and scatters some of the device’s light. The more melanin in the skin, the more light is absorbed. This makes darker skin tones more vulnerable to data loss compared to lighter skin tones, according to that 2025 review. Categorizing skin tone can be tricky because it’s subjective. But dermatologists often rely on the Fitzpatrick Scale. This scale is the dermatology industry standard classification for skin tone groups, according to a study published in the HCA Healthcare Journal of Medicine in February 2026. The scale is based on people’s self-reported observations of how likely they are to sunburn and tan. That data helped classify skin tone into six categories, from Type I to Type VI. Type I skin is the lightest and burns easily and doesn’t tan; Type VI is the darkest and tans easily and almost never burns. Despite the scale’s widespread use, it’s considered flawed, as that same 2026 study noted that its reliance on self-perception and cultural and societal influences complicates categorization. Even though skin tone can affect watch accuracy, it’s not the only factor that can lead to an inaccurate reading. “Noise is the biggest issue,” Michael Rosenberg, MD, a cardiac electrophysiologist who studies wearables in the division of cardiology at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, told Outside. Noise, Rosenberg said, includes tattoos, body hair, hydration levels, sweat, and residue from lotions or sunscreens. He said that wrist size, skin temperature, and even freckles can impact readings. Improving wearable tech accuracy takes real intention; however, Apple, Oura, WHOOP, Polar, Google, and other wearable companies have made it a priority. Emily Capodilupo, senior vice president of research, algorithms, and data at WHOOP, said they’re intentional about ensuring their studies include people across all six Fitzpatrick values. WHOOP is a wearable company that sells a tiered membership, where customers pay an annual fee that includes their screenless device and access to their app’s metrics and analysis. “When we notice a population—skin tone, gender, age—where we think we’re struggling performance-wise, we overrepresent that group in the data collection efforts, and that’s a very effective technique for improving algorithms,” Capodilupo told Outside. Capodilupo also said WHOOP has specifically designed an algorithm to compensate for how melanin absorbs light. She said that algorithm is constantly validated and updated. The device monitors how much signal it gets back and adjusts the LED brightness accordingly. If the signal is weaker, the LED intensity increases. This approach comes with a trade-off, she explained. More powerful LEDs use more battery. “That’s a trade that we’re willing to make because we want to make sure that we can stand by the data that we provide,” Capodilupo said. Apple’s strategy is similar. The company says that it addresses the issue at the software and hardware level, including by adjusting how much light is transmitted into the skin and how strongly the return signal is amplified. They also said that in every generation of Apple Watch, software and hardware design factors are driven by ensuring users with the darkest skin tones get a strong signal and equivalent performance. At Oura, the company’s smart ring uses the same PPG technology. Senior vice president of science Shyamal Patel, PhD, said the product’s advantage is that the palm side of the finger tends to have more consistent pigmentation than the wrist. The finger, he said, also provides access to larger arteries, which can produce a stronger signal than what you can measure on the wrist with the same kind of hardware setup. That doesn’t solve for everything, though. Patel said the ring’s “smart sensing” capability means there are a number of paths the light can travel through the skin. The device continuously evaluates which path is producing the strongest signal and adjusts accordingly. In a statement via email, Raija Laukkanen, PhD, said that optical heart measurements have improved over the years largely due to better sensor technology, ergonomics and algorithms. Laukkanen is the director of science collaborations at Polar, a wearable tech company that offers watches based on activity types and other products like chest straps. “Optical measurement remains a practical and effective option for continuous heart rate tracking and everyday training. For situations where precision is the priority, electrocardiogram (ECG) remains our recommended approach,” she wrote. Unlike PPG tech, which relies on light sensors to collect heart rate data, ECG or EKG measures electrical heart signals directly through the skin, so it isn’t affected by pigmentation and is considered the gold standard in heart rate testing. The Polar H10 chest strap uses ECG to monitor heart rate during physical activity where real-time data is necessary. (Some Apple Watch, Polar watches, and WHOOP models offer on-demand ECG readings.) Patel said Oura is exploring new ways to characterize skin tones, such as the Monk skin tone scale (MST), which is a ten-tone visual scale that captures a fuller spectrum of darker skin. Patel’s team focuses on improving algorithms to better translate sensor data into useful metrics that can tell users about their overall health and well-being. Patel also said they intentionally collect data in a broad range of locations worldwide to support diversity. “We need to continue expanding the standards and then continue innovating on how we measure and validate the data,” Patel said. Apple also incorporates a spectrophotometer, which helps measure color more objectively. In addition to the standard Fitzpatrick assessment, researchers can use this lab instrument to measure the exact amount of light reflected at different wavelengths. In a statement via email, a Google spokesperson said, “Google Health takes accuracy very seriously and continuously conducts studies to rigorously test the accuracy of our products among diverse groups of users. We also focus on recruiting a diverse testing population from around the globe for wear testing during our development cycles for Google wearables including Fitbit and Pixel Watch devices.” Though wearables provide a wealth of data on users’ health and wellness, Rosenberg said it’s important to remember that wearable devices are still commercial products, not medical ones. So, it’s reasonable to expect occasional inaccuracies, but he said they do detect overall trends pretty well. To get the most accurate readings, the experts contacted for this story said there are a few things that are within your control: keep a snug fit so that the sensor is in contact with the skin, make sure the sensor isn’t sitting directly on a bone, wipe the sensor regularly so it remains free of sweat and residue from lotions, try to keep the sensor away from any tattoos, and install recent device and app updates. If your device isn’t working properly or starts producing strange results, it’s probably best to ditch it for a new one. Wearables aren’t one-size-fits-all. As the technology evolves, continued research and more representative data will be key to ensuring everyone can trust the numbers on their devices. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: Recent Research Says That Climbing Can Reduce Depression and Anxiety
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.48
(Photo: Canva) My eyes shot open two hours before my alarm, again, and the anxiety train that is my postpartum brain pulled out of the station right on schedule. I’m a journalist and Outside‘s former health history columnist, and I work full-time. I’m also a new parent. Naturally, my work hours and personal life are all over the place. Four months into motherhood, I find myself managing everything from moments of crushing anxiety to bouts of depression any time I question my parenting abilities. On top of that, as a runner and someone who loves to ski and do anything outdoors, I’m feeling a bit of cabin fever these days and trying to figure out when the hell I can get back on my workout schedule or do any kind of physical activity at all. That said, you can imagine my surprise—and subsequent elation—when I came across a study, published this year, where people with anxiety and depression climbed rocks to work through it. I interviewed the paper’s lead author and a psychologist who specializes in sports and performance. Here’s what they had to say. The study, published in the scientific journal BMC Medicine, is the latest from a German research team that has spent over a decade testing bouldering as therapy. Bouldering is a type of rock climbing done on small rock formations (or indoor rock walls) sans rope and harness. For safety, rocks are generally no more than 20 feet high. Researchers in this 2026 study randomly assigned 128 adults with diagnosed depression into three groups: one did structured bouldering therapy, another tried a newer talk therapy, and a third received standard care as a comparison. That newer talk therapy is called WISE-T, which stands for What’s Important: Schedule and Engage Therapy, and it focuses on identifying what actually matters to you and following through on it, instead of reacting to whatever feels most urgent. The goal of that therapy is to help combat symptoms that accompany depression, including anhedonia—the inability to feel joy or pleasure. In this study, bouldering involved climbing moderate heights, up to ten feet, without ropes or harnesses. Thick pads at the bottom broke falls. Each bouldering session involved three parts: a mindfulness exercise beforehand, the climbing portion, and a relaxation component at the end of class. The two therapy groups ran for ten weeks, once a week, in real settings: a bouldering gym for the bouldering therapy group and a psychiatric clinic for the WISE-T group, led throughout by trained therapists. Both WISE-T and bouldering therapy cut anxiety scores significantly compared with standard care, which barely changed over the same ten weeks. Depression, the study’s main focus, dropped in both groups. On average, people went from moderate depression to mild. Bouldering’s effect was considered moderate; the talk therapy’s was slightly larger, though the gap is small. What matters most is that two very different approaches, one physical, one purely cognitive, both worked. Self-efficacy also improved, most clearly in the talk therapy group. Self-efficacy refers to people’s belief in their ability to handle hard situations. The bouldering group’s effect on self-efficacy appeared, too, but only after some statistical untangling. As expected, only the bouldering group showed a jump in mindfulness during physical activity, and lead researcher Katharina Luttenberger has a theory as to why. “Thought can never be in the here and now, because thoughts necessarily always deal with the past or the future. Therefore, it makes perfect sense to me that mindfulness is fostered through physical activity rather than through cognitive engagement,” she told Outside. Because the participants were randomly assigned to groups, the results are more than a coincidence, but researchers can’t say that bouldering itself caused every improvement. Scientists can conclude, however, that there is an association between fewer depression symptoms, reduced anxiety, and bouldering therapy. The researchers have a clear explanation for why climbing specifically works: a boulder problem forces total, immediate attention. Every route is a specific puzzle you have to solve with your body, right now, leaving no spare processing power for anything else. That’s different from running or cycling, where your mind can wander for miles. Add real but manageable risk, a fall that’s expected, cushioned, and pretty safe, and you get practice handling uncertainty in a contained space. A 2025 survey on bouldering found that nearly three-quarters of American climbers said the sport had a real, positive effect on their mental health. Over 70 percent of 748 people surveyed said climbing was more effective at improving their mental state than medication, and nearly 65 percent said bouldering was better than therapy. Teresa Behrend Fletcher, a psychologist at Adler University who studies sports and human performance, explained that metaphors work in therapy because clients get stuck rehashing a problem the same way, and a metaphor forces a different angle. Bouldering works especially well for this, she said, because a client isn’t just imagining a solution; they’re finding one in real-time. Standing back and reading a route, then adjusting mid-climb when the first plan fails, mirrors the process of working through anything hard. As she put it, the goal is ensuring that “every problem has a solution,” Fletcher told Outside. A few limitations in Luttenberger’s study are worth noting. This study took place in one city, at one gym, and participants were employed and already getting some kind of treatment for their anxiety or depression. But the appeal here isn’t just the sport itself. It’s finding anything that demands your full attention long enough to interrupt rumination and anxious-thinking loops. Trail running a technical descent might do it. So might reading whitewater, or skiing a double black diamond trail. It’s not the rock that matters. It’s what engaging with the rock or other outdoor entity takes off your plate. When you’re trying to survive, your worries tend to fall away. Now, is bouldering therapy going to be a widespread method for alleviating anxiety and depression? Not quite. Luttenberger said that it depends on therapists’ qualifications and national regulations. “In Germany, for example, where the study took place, group psychotherapy is covered by health insurance, and under certain conditions, certified therapists can offer group sessions in various settings,” she said. One of the biggest hurdles in group bouldering psychotherapy, she said, is that “therapeutic climbing with a group of people with mental health issues is very demanding and should not be underestimated.” For it to be feasible and effective, “thorough training in all three areas—psychotherapy, climbing safety, and therapeutic climbing—is required.” I personally haven’t been bouldering, and I’m not claiming it would fix anything. But a researcher and a psychologist, working independently, landed on the same idea, and it’s got me thinking that heading to a climbing gym or even tackling a small boulder on my own might be that way out of my postpartum fog. Whether I climb or find time to get back on the running trails, my goal is to move my body in a way that pulls me out of my head for a while. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: Review: Berghaus Pendower Wind Jacket Review
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 4.80
The Berghaus Pendower Wind Jacket is a lightweight windbreaker for hiking, trail running, and outdoor activities where you don't need full waterproof protection. Its main strength is its breathability and simplicity: it blocks wind effectively while retaining body heat without the bulk or restriction of a heavier shell jacket. - Gender: Men's (Women's – only available in UK) - Weight: 4.0 oz - Fit: Easy to layer with - Material: Nylon - CFM 1.2 (very windproof) - Fit: true to size The jacket has a clean, understated appearance that works well both on the trail and around town. Its lightweight construction makes it easy to pack into its zippered chest pocket, while the fit leaves enough room for layering. It works especially well over a Polartec Alpha fleece, for example. This creates a warm, highly adaptable system for cool, changeable conditions. The fleece insulates while staying breathable, and the Pendower helps block wind without adding much weight. The Pendower hood is pre-cinched behind the head to keep it snug and has a brim to keep the sun out of your eyes. I have a small hat size, so it's a bit slack on me, but it fills out when worn with a fleece beanie (or if you have a larger head). Fully adjustable windbreaker hoods are pretty rare, especially these days in the race to make the lightest weight gear and clothing. The chest pocket is large enough to hold a Smartphone and has a fabric key fob inside, while the stretch cuffs are wide enough to roll up your arm. The exterior fabric is thin and very quiet, even in gusty wind. These details make the jacket easy to wear and use as a windbreaker. As a windproof outer layer, the Pendower performs well in windy and exposed conditions. It is particularly useful when conditions are too cold and breezy for a fleece alone but not wet enough to justify a heavier waterproof shell, which would retain too much body heat. Breathability is reasonable during gentle to moderate activity. When walking quickly or climbing steep hills, heat can build up, especially when worn over a warm midlayer. This combination is best managed by adjusting layers as activity levels change. Unzipping the central zipper, removing the hood, or rolling up the sleeves all let you dump excess body heat without stopping to remove garments. The low weight is one of the jacket’s biggest advantages. It is easy to carry until needed and takes up little space in a pack. The simple construction also makes it practical for regular use, whether walking, traveling, or wearing around town. Rather than a standalone warm jacket, it works best as part of a layering system. Comparable Wind Jackets | Item | Weight | Price | |---|---|---| | Patagonia Airshed Pro Hoodie | 3.7 oz /105g | $139 | | Patagonia Houdini Jacket | 3.7 oz /105g | $119 | | Enlightened Equipment Copperfield Wind Shirt | 2.05 oz / 58g | $120 | | Mammut Aenergy WB Hooded Jacket | 4.7 oz / 132g | $149 | | Katabatic Gear Crest Windshell | 1.8 oz / 51g | $129 | | Rab Vital Windshell Hoody | 4.6 oz /160g | $100 | | Montbell Hooded Tachyon Jacket | 2.5 oz / 71 g | $130 | | Mountain Hardwear Kor Airshell Hoody | 4.7 oz /133g | $165 | | Arc'teryx Squamish Hoody | 5.3 oz /150g | $200 | | Black Diamond Distance Wind Shell | 3.2 oz/91g | $199 | Recommendation Overall, the Berghaus Pendower Wind Jacket is a dependable and versatile wind layer. It works best over a breathable insulating midlayer such as a fleece or wool pullover in cooler conditions, where it helps turn a lightweight midlayer into a more weather-resistant system. Disclosure: Berghaus donated a jacket for review. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides.

item.title: Hyperlite Mountain Gear Unbound Backpack Review
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 4.61
The Hyperlite Mountain Gear Unbound 55 Backpack is an ultralight backpack weighing 29.8 oz (819 g) made with Woven Dyneema fabric and Dyneema mesh. This new version is a substantial upgrade from the previous model, with more durable fabrics, a better frame system, and female-friendly (S-shaped) shoulder straps. Together, they make the pack much more comfortable and functional, enough so that existing Unbound owners should consider upgrading to the new model. - Color: Grey - Spec Weight: 29.8 oz (819 g) - Actual Weight: 29.8 oz (819 g) in a size large - Gender: Unisex - Volume: 55L internal storage, 9L external storage - Sizing: Multiple torso and hipbelt lengths - Frame: Contoured aluminum stay, foam back panel - Load lifters: None - Pockets: 6 (2 side, 1 front, 1 bottom, 2 hip belt) - Hydration Compatible: No - Material: Dyneema Woven Composite, 100D Dyneema Gridstop, Dyneema Stretch Mesh - Seam-taped: Yes - Pros: Tougher fabrics and mesh, effectively waterproof, good pockets, multiple torso lengths, excellent attachment points Backpack Pockets and Storage The Unbound 55 is a rolltop backpack that can be buckled together on top or along the sides using webbing straps, which are girth-hitched to the daisy chains along the sides so you can remove them if you don't need them. I prefer securing a roll top with them because I find that they provide better compression than just rolling the extension collar (the top of the pack) and buckling it on top. The top of the extension collar has a stiffener, making it easy to roll shut and helping it stay shut. The Unbound comes with huge side pockets that are great for storing multiple bottles, securing a tent along the side, and holding the bottom of a snowshoe if you hike in winter. The top of the side pockets has an elastic cinch cord for securing the contents. The Unbound does not have an internal hydration pocket or hydration ports, so you'll need to carry water in these pockets or in accessory sleeves attached to the shoulder straps. The hipbelt pockets are similarly large and can easily fit a Smartphone and snack bars or gloves. HMG expanded its hipbelt pocket size a few years ago, so this isn't a net new change. The pack also comes with two open stretch mesh pockets, one on the front and one on the bottom of the pack, which is a feature that's become popular with thru-hikers. The front mesh pocket is pretty unique: it has a top opening and a lower one about halfway down, held shut with elastic. It lets you access items at the base of the front pocket without unloading everything. For example, I keep my tent stakes at the base of the front stretch pocket, and this lets me access them easily. Both the front mesh pocket and the pocket at the base of the pack are made with highly durable Dyneema stretch mesh, since these zones experience considerable contact with the ground. The bottom pocket is a convenient place to store small snacks and trash, or hats and gloves, as long as you don't mind crushing the contents or getting them wet when you take the pack off and set it on wet ground. It has two openings: one on the right when facing forward and a small hole on the left, called a trash port, so you can stuff used wrappers into it. Backpack Frame and Suspension The Unbound 55 has dual contoured aluminum frame stays augmented with foam padding behind the shoulder straps for increased comfort. They terminate behind the lumbar pad at the base of the pack, providing much better load transfer to the hips. This is a major upgrade from the previous version, which had only one internal stay and is more comparable, in terms of load transfer and stability, to the HMG Southwest and Windrider backpacks, making the Unbound comparable to those mainstays of the Hyperlite product line in functionality and comfort. Take, for example, the UnBound hipbelt, which you tension by pushing the straps forward using what's called a Scherer cinch, named after Michael Scherer, who first designed it at Kelty. I get a much better hipwrap with the Unbound than the Southwest, which has been my backpack of choice for many years. The Unbound's shoulder straps, like HMG's other packs, are now S-shaped, making them more female-friendly. They are covered in front with daisy chains so you can easily attach accessory best-of-breed pockets, like the HMG shoulder strap pocket shown, bottle sleeves, or electronics to your shoulder straps. Hyperlite sells a full range of pack accessories. External Attachment Points and Compression The Unbound 55 has low-profile daisy chains sewn along the main compartment's side seams that you can use to secure bulky gear like fishing rods or packraft paddles to the sides of the pack. The pack comes with elastic cords for this purpose, but you can use your own instead. This is more difficult on Hyperlite's other packs, which offer less flexibility in strap placement. If you've ever lost a fishing rod because it's popped out of a backpack's side pocket, you'll really appreciate the intricate webs you can design to keep from losing precious cargo. Comparable Ultralight Backpacks w/Frames | Make / Model | Weight | Fabric | Price | |---|---|---|---| | Hyperlite Mtn Gear Southwest 55L | 29.8 / 845g | Dyneema Woven Composite | $395 | | Durston Kakwa 55L | 31.5 oz / 880g | Ultra 200X, UltraGrid | $279 | | Gossamer Gear Gorilla 50L | 31.9 oz / 904g | Robic Nylon | $275 | | Zpacks Arc Haul 60L | 20.9 oz / 593g | Ultra 100X | $399 | | Granite Gear Crown 3 60L | 32.6 oz / 1040g | Robic Nylon | $260 | | Osprey Exos Pro 55 | 34.6 oz / 981g | Robic Nylon | $330 | | ULA Ultra Circuit SV 48L | 35.8 oz / 1015g | Ultra 200X, Ultra400X | $380 | | REI Flash 55L | 45 oz / 1276g | Robic Nylon | $229 | | Atom Packs Notch EP40 | 29.6 oz / 840g | Ecopack EPX200, EPX400 | $303 | | SWD UL Long Haul 50 | 30.2 oz / 856g | Ultra 200X | $379 | Recommendation The Hyperlite Mountain Gear Unbound 55 is an excellent ultralight backpack for multi-day backpacking trips, excelling across a wide range of trail conditions and gear needs. It differs from Hyperlite's other backpacks in pocket size and placement, offers a more adjustable hip belt, and provides more flexible external attachments. This new version also represents a major upgrade in two key components: a switch from a single aluminum stay to dual stays and the use of woven Dyneema as the pack fabric, making it significantly tougher and abrasion-resistant. The new grey-silver color is also pretty cool. The upgraded Unbound 55 is so impressive that owners of the previous version should consider upgrading if their existing pack is nearing the end of its life. It also wouldn't surprise me if the Unbound becomes the most popular pack in Hyperlite's backpacking line, even outshining the Southwest and Windrider backpacks, because the hipbelt is easier to tighten and fit and the pack is more functional with no added weight gain. Disclosure: Hyperlite Mountain Gear donated a backpack for review. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. Thanks for the review. Could you easily get a bear canister into it? Yes, of course. Anyone you want, vertically. It’s a 55L pack. But here’s a jedi tip – pack your food/smellables in a plastic bag inside your pack and carry the empty canister under the Y strap on top of the pack. At night, put your food into the bear canister. This makes it much easier to carry a bear canister because it won’t be top heavy and throw you off balance without losing pack volume or increasing gear weight. I like that Jedi tip, thanks!

item.title: ‘Fabulous museums and no queues’: five of the best under-the-radar city breaks in Europe
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.43
Nantes, France As dilemmas go, it’s an unusual one: saddle up a giant squid or board a submersible for a voyage to the bottom of the ocean. In the end, I find myself drawn to a fierce-looking merhorse and tentatively take the reins. High above, my daughter glides by on a flying fish, metallic fins flapping, while her Dad is battling stormy seas at the helm of a huge conch shell. A ride on the Carrousel des Mondes Marins (marine worlds carousel) – a three-storey steampunk merry-go-round inspired by Jules Verne’s novel Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea – is one of the highlights of a visit to Nantes. A surreal fairground ride, a work of art and a homage to the city’s most famous son. It’s also a lot of fun. On the banks of the Loire, 30 miles from the Atlantic ocean, Nantes is a city whose fortunes were built on the sea. As a young boy growing up near the docks in the 1830s, Verne dreamed of being a ship’s captain, but it wasn’t to be. Instead, he embarked on a series of journeys of the imagination, channelling his wanderlust into novels such as Around the World in 80 Days and Journey to the Centre of the Earth. The last of Nantes’ shipyards closed in the 1980s, but Verne’s unique vision provided the inspiration for a radical art and regeneration project, Les Machines de l’Île, that has breathed life into the abandoned quays and warehouses of the Île de Nantes, the river island that was home to the city’s docks. This is now the stomping ground of the Grand Éléphant, a 12m-high mechanical pachyderm that carries passengers on tours of the island, spraying bystanders with water from its trunk. I’d seen photos but nothing prepares you for the thrill of turning a corner and seeing the real thing lumbering towards you. You can learn about the magic behind the machinery at the nearby Galerie des Machines, where the creators bring a mechanical menagerie of strange creatures to life. The Verne connection also inspired the name of the city’s summer arts festival, Le Voyage à Nantes, which transforms streets, parks and public spaces into an open-air art gallery from July to September. Our visit coincides with the festival’s opening weekend, and the squares and avenues of the elegant Graslin district are busy with DJ sets, food stalls and people checking out the new artworks. In the Place Graslin, a beautiful square built – like much of Nantes – from chalky-white tuffeau stone from the Loire valley, some kind of cataclysmic eruption has been conjured up in front of the opera house. Huge ammonites appear to have been forced up from beneath the earth, engulfing cars in a mountain of rubble, their doors wide open, radios playing, as though abandoned in haste. Just yards away, children are playing in the dancing water fountains of the square, while the white-aproned waiters of art nouveau brasserie La Cigale weave through the pavement tables delivering seafood platters to diners unfazed by the apocalyptic scene before them. Titled Fossil Opera, the artwork is a commentary on consumerism and the fleeting nature of human endeavour, and is one of about a dozen site-specific installations that have appeared in the city, as if by magic. Even outside the summer months, there is plenty to discover in France’s sixth largest city. Each year, a handful of the festival installations are selected to become permanent fixtures, which has resulted in an impressive collection of contemporary public art, from Les Anneaux, a series of 18 giant steel rings on the Quai des Antilles, which frame views of the Loire and light up at night, to Tadashi Kawamata’s Belvédère de l’Hermitage, a viewing platform inspired by a swallow’s nest, which juts over a sheer cliff. All of these cultural highlights, old and new, are linked by the Ligne Verte, a 12-mile (20km) green line painted on the pavement. We follow the trail through the Passage Pommeraye, an exquisite 19th century glass-roofed shopping arcade; past the imposing Château des ducs de Bretagne, a moated 15th-century castle; stop off at the excellent Musée d’arts de Nantes, which houses an impressive collection of international art spanning seven centuries; and finish up at the peaceful Jardin des Plantes, a charming (and free) botanical garden which is home to a handful of modern art installations and a good cafe. From here it’s a short stroll to the Lieu Unique, a cultural space and concert venue in the factory that once produced the city’s beloved buttery LU biscuits. And there’s more to come. The Jardin Extraordinaire is a newly created garden and climbing wall in a disused granite quarry in the Bas‑Chantenay district. The exotic planting, waterfall and paddling pools were inspired by descriptions in Verne’s novel, The Mysterious Island. The nearby Chantenay docks have been colonised by studios, music spaces and the Little Atlantique Brewery, housed in a 19th-century former oil mill. Opposite the quarry, a derelict industrial building is being transformed into a new riverside cultural hub, the Cité des Imaginaires, which will eventually provide a home for an expanded Jules Verne museum. It’s an ambitious project: creative, unconventional and looking to the future. I’m sure Jules Verne would approve. Joanne O’Connor The trip was supported by Le Voyage à Nantes. Oceania Hôtel de France, just off the Place Graslin, has air‑conditioned doubles from €101 room-only Winter’s Journey, a seasonal festival of concerts, temporary light installations, artworks and gastronomic events, runs from 21 November to 3 January. Basel, Switzerland Unless you’re a professional who makes their way to the Art Basel fair every year, chances are Switzerland’s third largest city will have passed you by – or rather you will have passed it by. Basel is one stop before Zurich on the fast train from Paris, but to whiz through would be a mistake. For art and design lovers, it is the perfect city to explore on a long weekend. Basel bills itself as “the city of art and culture on the Rhine”, and it lives up to its boast. Stroll around the charming old town and marvel at the cathedral before enjoying a cold beer at one of the many cafes. If temperatures soar, you might want to join local people with a dip in the Rhine. Once you’ve done all that, you need to engage with the area’s art offerings. Within the city, the Kunstmuseum holds more than 300,000 works spanning eight centuries, with big hitters such as Monet, Van Gogh and Warhol, while Museum Tinguely is home to the work of the idiosyncratic Swiss sculptor Jean Tinguely and his dada-esque machines. But the two real draws are on the outskirts of the city. Fondation Beyeler in the suburb of Riehen is home to an impressive collection of modern and contemporary art, and always has a blockbuster exhibition (currently Pierre Huyghe) to check out. A short bus or train ride across the German border in Weil am Rhein is the Vitra Design Museum, home to one of the world’s largest permanent exhibitions of modern furniture design. Before you admire the furniture collection, take a walk around the campus, where you can marvel at the main museum building designed by Frank Gehry; the Vitra Schaudepot – which houses the furniture collection – designed by Herzog & de Meuron; Zaha Hadid’s former fire station; and Tadao Ando’s conference centre. There is a beautiful garden by the Dutch designer Piet Oudolf, and the recently added Doshi Retreat for a moment of quiet reflection designed by the Indian architect Balkrishna Doshi, his first completed project outside India and the last he worked on before he died in 2023. That’s half the day gone, so time to head inside. In lots of ways, exploring the Schaudepot is like walking through a giant doll’s house, with the rooms filled with instantly recognisable furniture icons from the 19th century to today, including works by Verner Panton, Le Corbusier, Alvar Aalto and Charles and Ray Eames. The museum also puts on temporary exhibitions. And if all of that has exhausted you, head to the VitraHaus Café, which serves a delicious lunch. Max Benato The Volkshaus, a boutique hotel in the old town, has doubles from 152 swiss francs (£138) room-only Lübeck, Germany Unless you’ve read Buddenbrooks, Thomas Mann’s epic family saga, you may not have heard of Lübeck. But in the middle ages, this port city in Germany, 70km north-east of Hamburg, was one of the richest and most powerful places on Earth. Today, despite the best efforts of the RAF to destroy it in 1942, it remains a beautifully intact medieval gem. The old town is a Unesco world heritage site. It sits on an island in the centre of the city, encircled by the rivers Trave and Wakenitz, and the water is a good place to start exploring. My boyfriend and I hired an electric boat (€49 for up to six people) and spent an hour circumnavigating and gazing at its distinctive seven church spires. Back on dry land, we set off on a guided walking tour, starting at the imposing – if wonky – Holsten Gate. We took in the five red brick churches the spires belong to (two have doubles), and climbed one of them, St Petri’s viewing tower, for a panoramic view. We also stopped at the 800-year-old town hall on the marketplace. But just as fascinating was what lies behind the gothic splendour. At one time, there were 180 hidden alleyways and courtyards threaded through the old town, and about 80 remain. These labyrinthine lanes were built behind wealthy merchants’ mansions to house the poor. Today, the restored cottages are sought-after and the flower-filled, cobbled alleys are charming to explore. To better understand Lübeck’s past, we visited the European Hansemuseum in the old castle monastery. It tells the story of the Hanseatic League, the powerful trade network that stretched from England to Russia and gave Lübeck (“the Queen of the League”) its wealth in the middle ages and its status as a free city state right up to 1937. In a nearby palace, the Museum Behnhaus Drägerhaus displays 19th- and early 20th-century German and European art, including work by Edvard Munch, who visited Lübeck and painted its salt warehouses. Just round the corner is the Günter Grass-Haus, where the writer regularly stayed (he died in Lübeck in 2015). We visited in June during the HanseKulturFestival, when the quarter around St Jakob’s church was full of live music stages, food stalls and outdoor bars. The next festival isn’t until 2028, but there are annual museum, theatre and literature nights, and popup live music in the summer. Lübeck has three natural open-air swimming areas, one on the island. And the seaside isn’t far away – we had a day trip to Travemünde, a historic resort town with miles of sandy beach, taking a scenic river ferry there (90 minutes) and a 20-minute train back. In town, the medieval Schiffergesellschaft (Seafarers’ Guild) is now a traditional Hanseatic restaurant, with long communal tables. Alongside North Sea fish and Holstein meat dishes are vegetarian versions of labskaus, a sort of hash. Sadly, we couldn’t visit Buddenbrookhaus, the museum dedicated to the novel, as it is being renovated. It is expected to reopen in 2030 – which gives you plenty of time to read Mann’s 864-page doorstopper. Like Lübeck itself, it is worth the effort. Rachel Dixon The trip was provided by germany.travel and luebeck-tourismus.de. Accommodation was provided by Liho Lübeck, doubles from £73 room-only Parma, Italy Parma is just far enough off Italy’s main travel routes to discourage the huge crowds of tourists that flood the likes of Venice and Florence. Most travellers reach this tranquil Italian gem by flying into Milan or Bologna, followed by an hour’s train ride. It is definitely worth that extra effort, as I discover a city that ticks every box for a weekend getaway: fabulous museums and frescoed churches without long queues or the need to book a timeslot in advance; friendly, affordable trattorie and osterie showcasing a feast of local food and wines; and, if you time it right, the chance to catch an opera composed by locally born Giuseppe Verdi in the intimate Teatro Regio. The historic centre of Parma is small and easily explored on foot, taking me past an array of architectural masterpieces. I kick off at the grand Piazza Duomo, dominated by the imposing 900-year-old romanesque cathedral. Everyone’s eyes are drawn up to the ornate cupola, decorated with a captivating illusionist fresco by local Renaissance artist Antonio da Correggio. Next to the cathedral stands the early gothic Battistero, an octagonal baptistery whose bare, minimalist exterior contrasts with an incredible explosion of colours from the 13th- and 14th-century paintings that cover the interior. Then, tucked away behind the Duomo, I come upon the entrance of the medieval Monastero di San Giovanni Evangelista, whose cloisters and garden are a peaceful oasis. Entry to the monastery and cathedral is free. Parma’s big must-see is the monumental Palazzo della Pilotta, a baroque complex of palatial museums, a library and remarkable 400-year-old theatre, all included in a single €18 entry ticket. Just by the Parma river that slices the city into two, the palazzo was built by the Farnese family, whose patronage created most of the city’s Renaissance monuments. The Teatro Farnese, made almost entirely of wood, is rarely used as a venue today, but a visit remains an incredible experience. I leave most sightseeing time, though, for the Pilotta’s landmark Galleria Nazionale di Parma, a treasure trove of old master paintings. It may not quite rival the collection of the Uffizi, but I enjoy the chance to just turn up without booking in advance and quietly appreciate works by Leonardo da Vinci, Fra Angelico, Canaletto and Tintoretto without being surrounded by crowds. Sightseeing is only part of Parma’s attraction, however, as this is one of Italy’s food capitals. I walk into the rustic, raucous OsteMagno bar, where everyone is tucking into tagliere – wooden boards piled with razor-thin slices of cured ham, the famous prosciutto crudo di Parma, artisan salami and crumbly aged parmigiano reggiano cheese, accompanied by a glass of the local’s favourite tipple, fizzy red Lambrusco wine, which is a lot more drinkable than I expect. This is not a city to seek out chic, gourmet restaurants, but rather one of the many traditional trattorie such as Da Antonia, whose eponymous owner has overseen the cucina for more than 50 years, or the 120-year-old Trattoria Corrieri, serving up generous plates of homemade pasta for less than €15. John Brunton Palazzo Dalla Rosa Prati has doubles from €80 room-only Santander, Spain Often dismissed as little more than a ferry terminal – somewhere to stop overnight if you want to take your dog to Europe or lower your carbon footprint – the port city of Santander is undergoing something of a cultural renaissance. It’s already blessed with a spectacular bay facing the Cantabrian mountains, wide sandy beaches, grand, colonnaded plazas and superb food, but the opening of new art spaces and museums in the coming months will put the Cantabrian capital firmly on the weekend-break map. Leading the way on 8 September is Faro Santander – a new cultural centre in a grand historical building housing a 1,000-piece art collection belonging to Banco Santander, including works by Velázquez, Goya, Titian, Rubens and Picasso. Different parts of the collection will be shown at different times. With its ornate white facade facing the bay, the Pereda building was previously the bank’s headquarters, but has been transformed into a striking, 21st-century museum space by Pritzker prize-winning British architect David Chipperfield. Santander’s moment in the spotlight will extend into 2027 when Madrid’s Reina Sofia Museum opens its first outpost, set in a similarly grand neo-Renaissance building just a few metres away from Faro Santander. The museum will house the Archivo Lafuente, with paintings, sculptures and manuscripts, including major collections on dadaism and the Spanish civil war, as well as art from Spain, North America and Latin America. Faro Santander and Archivo Lafuente will form two points on a kind of “art triangle”, along with architect Renzo Piano’s 2017 Centro Botín contemporary art centre just over the road. With a bijou but impressive permanent collection, including works by Matisse, Juan Gris, Joaquín Sorolla and Mark Rothko, the Centro Botín sits on the waterfront like a giant, stilt-mounted, 60s alarm clock sawn in half. Spaniards cottoned on to Santander’s charms long ago, and the seafront is lined with elegant fin-de-siècle villas built when well-heeled Madrileños discovered that the city’s Atlantic breezes were the perfect respite from the Spanish capital’s infernal summer. More than 100 years later, while Britain was experiencing its own heatwave, I followed their lead. Temperatures were in the balmy high 20s as I ambled past toddlers building sand castles and teenagers frolicking in the surf on El Sardinero beach, just 15 minutes by bus from the city centre. The centre itself is wonderfully walkable and there’s an unhurried, laid-back vibe in the streets, grand plazas and narrow alleys near the gothic cathedral, lined with bars serving pinchos – the Cantabrian equivalent to tapas. After tucking into tender, grilled squid, laced with gutsy garlic and olive oil, at Mesón Rampalay on a leafy square, I spent a fascinating couple of hours at Mupac – the Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology of Cantabria, just a few minutes’ walk away from Faro Santander. The museum, which is home to one of Spain’s most important prehistoric collections, features excellent interactive displays, and in 2027 it is moving to a brand new, multimillion-euro building. By next year, it seems, Santander will be not just the capital of Cantabria, but a capital of culture too. Eddi Fiegel The trip was provided by Faro Santander. Abba Santander, near the Centro Botín, has stylish doubles from €66 room-only

item.title: You can now go through TSA without a plane ticket at these airports
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 6.28
You can now go through TSA without a plane ticket at these airports The Transportation Security Administration now wants you to visit the airport without a plane ticket. Twenty-five years after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks changed airport security and largely put an end to non-ticketed visitors meeting loved ones at the gate, the TSA is rolling out a new program welcoming non-ticketed visitors at 13 airports. The program, called Gateside by TSA PreCheck, invites non-travelers with TSA PreCheck status and Known Traveler Numbers to apply for an airport day pass and use the dedicated TSA PreCheck lanes for expedited entry to the airport. "This new program makes it easier to return to the gate for welcomes and send-offs, meet friends during a layover, and enjoy dining and shopping along the way," TSA said in the program announcement, adding that the program brings back "the moments that once defined air travel." The program could be particularly useful for people who want to help family members navigate the airport. Parents could accompany children all the way to their departure gate, while family members could escort older relatives through security or meet them at the gate when they arrive. How it works Gateside by TSA PreCheck is free and is open to TSA PreCheck members and those with Known Traveler Numbers. To use the program, you'll need to apply one to three days before your planned visit, log in using your Login.gov account (or create one), enter your personal information on the form and wait for approval. Kids are welcome to join you, but be sure to enter their information on your reservation. Once approved, you'll need to bring a Real ID or other acceptable form of ID to a PreCheck lane at the airport and be prepared to log in to the application portal to show the TSA officer your approval status. Keep in mind that TSA says screenshots or printouts of your approval status won't be accepted for this program. For now, the Gateside by TSA PreCheck program is only available at 13 airports, with more promised by TSA in the coming months. If you don't have TSA PreCheck or know that your membership will soon be renewed, here's the TPG guide to everything you need to know about TSA PreCheck and some ways to get free or discounted TSA membership. Airports rolling out Gateside by TSA PreCheck - Mesa Gateway Airport (AZA) in Arizona - John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH) - Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) - Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) - Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport (ICT) in Kansas - Indianapolis International Airport (IND) - Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) - Bill and Hillary Clinton National Airport (LIT) in Arkansas - Will Rogers International Airport (OKC) in Oklahoma - Eppley Airfield (OMA) in Nebraska - San Diego International Airport (SAN) - Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) Gateside by TSA versus other airport gate pass programs At least 20 airports already welcome non-ticketed guests to apply for gate passes to visit the non-secure side of the airport. These programs go by different names at each airport; for example, there's the Hopkins Hang Out Pass at Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) and the Wingmate Pass at Philadelphia International Airport (PHL). These programs differ from Gateside: While they do run an applicant's name through the TSA database, anyone can apply for a pass, and no PreCheck membership is required. And for these gate pass programs, using the TSA PreCheck lanes to enter the airport is prohibited. Related: The best credit cards for TSA PreCheck and Global Entry Some of those gate pass programs also differ in that applications for same-day access are often permitted, the application windows can be much longer, and screenshots and printouts of approved passes are often allowed. Here's a list of airports with their own gate pass programs: - Albuquerque International Airport (ABQ) - Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) - Kansas City International Airport (MCI) - Louis Armstrong International Airport (MSY) - Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) - Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) - Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) - Nashville International Airport (BNA) - Palm Springs International Airport (PSP) - San Antonio International Airport (SAT) - Tulsa International Airport (TUL) - John Wayne Airport (SNA) in California - Ontario International Airport (ONT) in California - Capital Regional International Airport (LAN) in Michigan - Tri-Cities Airport (PSC) in Washington - San Francisco International Airport (SFO) - Orlando International Airport (MCO) - Shreveport Regional Airport (SHV) in Louisiana - San Diego International Airport (SAN) - Tampa International Airport (TPA) Note that two of the above airports — SAN and DTW — are also on the Gateside by TSA PreCheck list. We checked with the airports to see whether anything about their gate passes will change. Matt Morawski, director of communications and external affairs at DTW, said the DTW Destination Pass is available to anyone who meets the program requirements and has a valid government-issued ID. "We do not anticipate that the Gateside by TSA PreCheck program will have any impact on our DTW Destination Pass program," Morawski said. "We're pleased to continue offering this safe and convenient option for our customers." As for SAN, the airport's public information officer, Nicole Hall, said: "While both programs offer a similar experience by allowing access to the gate area without a boarding pass, they operate independently of one another, and there are some differences." She noted that TSA's Gateside program is only available to TSA PreCheck members, while the SAN Pass program works with TSA to approve applicants to use the normal (non-PreCheck) TSA security checkpoint line. "The timeline for requesting passes also differs between the programs," Hall said. "Our SAN Pass Program allows applicants to apply for the SAN Pass as early as seven days prior to their visit date and as late as the day of the visit." Bottom line Gateside by TSA PreCheck brings back an airport experience that largely disappeared more than two decades ago: the ability to accompany loved ones all the way to the gate even when you aren't flying yourself. Beyond meeting friends during layovers or taking advantage of airport dining and shopping, the program could be particularly valuable for families who want to accompany children or older relatives through the airport. And unlike existing airport visitor-pass programs, eligible Gateside visitors get the added benefit of using TSA PreCheck lanes to get through security.

item.title: Hilton American Express card offers worth up to 200,000 bonus points
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.23
Hilton American Express card offers worth up to 200,000 bonus points Editor's Note If you've been considering a Hilton credit card, you're in the right place. That's because there are great welcome offers on Hilton's American Express cards right now, for new cardmembers to earn a swath of Hilton Honors points. This includes a highest-ever offer on the Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card: Earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Jan. 13, 2027. Depending on how you redeem them, these bonuses could cover anything from several nights at budget-friendly Hilton properties to a luxury award stay at aspirational resorts. Let's take a look at the current Hilton card offers and which one may make the most sense for you. Comparison of Hilton credit card welcome offers Here's what to know about the current offers at first glance: | Card | Welcome offer | Annual fee | Bonus value* | |---|---|---|---| | | Earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Jan. 13, 2027. | | $800 | | | Earn 150,000 bonus points and a free night reward after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Jan. 13, 2027. | | $600, plus the value of the free night reward | | | Earn 130,000 bonus points and a free night reward after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Jan. 13, 2027. | | $520, plus the value of the free night reward | | | Earn 70,000 bonus points and a free night reward after spending $2,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Jan. 13, 2027. | | $280, plus the value of the free night reward | *The bonus value is based on TPG's September 2026 valuations and is not provided or reviewed by the issuer. Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card The Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card is the brand's top-tier card and offers the most benefits when staying at Hilton properties. Current welcome offer Earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Jan. 13, 2027. TPG's valuations place Hilton points at 0.4 cents each, making this bonus worth $800. This is the best-ever offer we've seen on this card, so we recommend applying now. This card has an annual fee of $550.
