Apply here: The Hilton Honors American Express Business Card Hilton Honors American Express Surpass Card The Hilton Honors American Express Surpass Card is the mid-tier option for Hilton loyalists who want to receive more perks. Current welcome offer Earn 130,000 bonus points and a free night reward after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Jan. 13, 2027. According to TPG's valuations, this welcome offer is worth $520 plus the value of the free night reward, which is a solid value for a card with a reasonable annual fee. Although we've seen higher points bonuses on the Hilton Surpass, don't overlook the free night reward included with the current offer. Depending on where you redeem it, that single night could add hundreds of dollars in value to the 130,000 bonus points. If you've been eyeing this card, now's a great time to apply. Additional benefits With this card, you'll earn: - 12 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases made directly with a hotel or resort within the Hilton portfolio - 6 points per dollar spent at U.S. supermarkets, U.S. restaurants and U.S. gas stations - 4 points per dollar spent on U.S. online retail purchases - 3 points per dollar spent on other eligible purchases It also comes with some nice perks: - Complimentary Hilton Gold status - A free night reward after you spend $15,000 on eligible purchases each calendar year - National Car Rental Emerald Club Executive status* - A path to Hilton Diamond status through the end of the next calendar year after spending $40,000 on eligible purchases per calendar year - Up to $200 in statement credits (up to $50 quarterly) on eligible Hilton purchases To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Surpass. *Enrollment in the National Car Rental Emerald Club is required. Apply here: Hilton Honors American Express Surpass Card Hilton Honors American Express Card The Hilton Honors American Express Card is the simple no-annual-fee card that offers entry-level benefits. Current welcome offer Earn 70,000 bonus points and a free night reward after spending $2,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Jan. 13, 2027. According to TPG's valuations, this offer is worth $280, plus the value of the free night reward. We've seen more valuable offers on this card. However, the free night reward gives the current offer some upside, particularly if you can use it at an expensive Hilton property. Unless you have a booking in mind that would maximize the free night reward, we recommend waiting for a better offer. With this card, you'll earn: - 7 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases made directly with a hotel or resort within the Hilton portfolio - 5 points per dollar spent on dining at U.S. restaurants, U.S. supermarkets and U.S. gas stations - 3 points per dollar spent on all other eligible purchases This entry-level card also offers: - Automatic Hilton Silver status - No foreign transaction fees (see rates and fees) — a rarity for a card with no annual fee - A path to upgrade to Gold status through the end of the next calendar year when you spend $20,000 on eligible purchases in a calendar year To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Amex. Apply here: Hilton Honors American Express Card Bottom line The current Hilton Amex welcome offers are a great chance to earn a large stash of Hilton Honors points, especially since the Hilton Aspire is currently offering its best-ever welcome offer. With these limited-time Hilton Amex welcome offers available now through Jan. 13, 2027, now may be a good time to consider applying — especially if you're looking to boost your Hilton Honors balance or unlock elite status perks. Just remember that Amex generally limits cardmembers to earning a welcome offer on each card once per lifetime. Apply here: Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card Apply here: The Hilton Honors American Express Business Card Apply here: Hilton Honors American Express Surpass Card Apply here: Hilton Honors American Express Card For rates and fees of the Amex Hilton Honors Aspire, click here. item.title: New York to Dusseldorf, nonstop? All-biz carrier La Compagnie will give it a try
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.17
New York to Dusseldorf, nonstop? All-biz carrier La Compagnie will give it a try New York City-based travelers will have a new business-class option to Germany next spring. The all-business-class airline La Compagnie will launch service between Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) and Dusseldorf Airport (DUS) on April 23, it announced Monday. The carrier will offer five weekly flights, operating on Mondays, Tuesdays, Thursdays, Fridays and Sundays. La Compagnie will fly an Airbus A321LR with 76 lie-flat, business-class seats in a 2-2 layout on the new EWR-DUS route. All La Compagnie flyers have access to its lounge, Lounge&Co, at EWR and the DUS Sky Lounge at DUS. "La Compagnie is bringing a clearly defined product to our airport: nonstop, comfortable and designed for people who want to cross the Atlantic efficiently and in a relaxed way," Lars Redeligx, CEO of Dusseldorf Airport, said in a statement. Filling a gap from New York DUS, a large business and industrial center in northwestern Germany, lacks a regular nonstop to New York City. Only Condor offers limited seasonal flights in September and October, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows. "Dusseldorf represents a natural next chapter in La Compagnie's development," Christian Vernet, CEO of La Compagnie, said in a statement. "At the heart of one of Europe's most dynamic economic regions, with strong international businesses and long-standing ties to the United States, North Rhine-Westphalia is well suited to our unique all-business-class model." Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, DUS boasted regular daily flights to New York City. Lufthansa flew to EWR from at least 2004 until 2018, when its budget subsidiary, Eurowings, took over the route, Cirium data shows. Eurowings suspended flights in 2020. And now-defunct Air Berlin flew from New York City's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to DUS from 2008 until its shutdown in 2017. La Compagnie's EWR-DUS route complements its existing flights from EWR to Milan Malpensa Airport (MXP), Nice Cote d'Azur Airport (NCE) and Paris Orly Airport (ORY). Tickets on the new route start at $2,428.50 one-way, according to the airline's website. That compares to $2,313 one-way on United Airlines from EWR to Frankfurt Airport (FRA) in April 2027.

item.title: 11 ways to use points and miles for an incredible trip to Costa Rica right now
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.13
11 ways to use points and miles for an incredible trip to Costa Rica right now Editor's Note Gorgeous beaches, lush rainforests, dramatic volcanoes, incredible biodiversity and phenomenal hotels ranging from sprawling seaside resorts to intimate jungle lodges … Costa Rica is truly one of the most unique, welcoming destinations in the world. The coffee is pretty phenomenal, too, if you're into that (and I am!). To travel there is to fall in love with its natural wonders and cultural riches — I have yet to meet anyone who has visited and not wanted to return. Costa Rica pioneered the ecotourism trend, protecting over a quarter of its territory as national reserves and parks, both on land and in the ocean. It's also a beacon of stability in a region that has been volatile at times, making it a safe bet for a hassle-free vacation. While many folks flock to its Pacific and Caribbean beaches, its world-class surf breaks and golf courses, others are enchanted by its teeming forests, where you can spot unique fauna like snuffly tapirs foraging for food, dazzlingly colorful resplendent quetzals, quizzical toucans and languorous sloths sunning themselves in the canopy. Just to name a few. So, if this little Central American nation has been on your travel to-do list, now might just be the right time to plan your visit, especially once the summer heat has dissipated and the days turn dry and sunny. Here are some of our best tips to make the most of your trip to Costa Rica, and how to get the most out of your points and miles while doing so. What's the best part of Costa Rica for a trip? Although it's the third-smallest country in Central America (and that's not saying much!), Costa Rica still clocks in at over 19,000 square miles, which means most travelers will likely want to stick to one or two spots during their visit. The capital of San José offers plenty of flights to and from U.S. hubs, but for many vacationgoers, the main arrival point is Liberia on the country's west coast thanks to its proximity to the beach resorts of Guanacaste, the rainforests of the interior and the national parks to the south. For the purposes of this guide, we'll just stick to the regions around Liberia, though if you're interested in exploring other parts of the country, let us know in a comment and we'll write up guides to those as well. Related: The 13 best all-inclusive resorts in Costa Rica Mix and match Alaska Airlines and American Airlines awards One of the best ways to fly from the U.S. to Costa Rica is to take either American Airlines or Alaska Airlines, two U.S.-based Oneworld airline partners that, between them, fly to Liberia from the following airports (though note some of these are seasonal): - Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) - Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) - Miami International Airport (MIA) - New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) That gives flyers a lot of choices when it comes to redeeming miles. In some cases, you're better off redeeming Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points for shorter American Airlines flights, but in others, redeeming American Airlines AAdvantage miles for its own flights as well as those on Alaska is the better choice. So … you have to do a little homework, but it can be worth it to save thousands of points or miles. For instance, you can book American Airlines' flights from Miami to Liberia for as few as 7,500 Alaska points plus $44 (or $76 in the other direction), while American's award rates start at 9,000 miles plus slightly lower taxes and fees. However, Alaska will charge you 17,500 points and the same taxes and fees from other hubs like DFW, JFK and LAX ... Whereas American AAdvantage rates tend to start at around 10,000-11,500 miles each way plus $24 in taxes and fees (or $56 coming from Costa Rica). Use a tool like seats.aero to compare rates quickly and determine which is best. So that you're stocked up and ready with the specific types of points or miles you need when you're ready: Alaska is a 1:1 transfer partner of Bilt. If you have the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card or the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card, you can earn 3 Atmos Rewards points for every dollar spent on eligible rent when paying through Bilt, on up to $50,000 per calendar year; terms apply. Related: The best credit cards for Alaska Airlines flyers American Airlines is a transfer partner of Citi ThankYou, so you can transfer points to your AAdvantage account if you have one of the following cards: - Citi Strata Elite℠ Card (see rates and fees): Best for Citi Travel users and American Airlines flyers - Citi Strata Premier® Card (see rates and fees): Best for earning full-fledged ThankYou Rewards points with a low annual fee - Citi Prestige® Card: Best for restaurants, airlines and travel agencies The information for the Citi Prestige Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. You also might want to check out one of the following American Airlines cobranded cards to rack up miles quickly with a large welcome offer and keep your account stocked thanks to earning miles on everyday spending: The information for the Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Related: The best credit cards for American Airlines flyers Use Virgin Atlantic Flying Club and Flying Blue miles for Delta flights Delta flies to Liberia, Costa Rica from its megahub at Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL). The airline also recently announced it would be relaunching weekly nonstop service from JFK from Dec. 19, 2026-Apr. 10, 2027. The Delta SkyMiles program prices awards dynamically, so the higher the cost of airfare, the more miles you'll need for tickets. However, the airline is also partners with other carriers including Virgin Atlantic and Air France-KLM, so you can often find lower-priced awards using miles from their loyalty programs instead of SkyMiles. For instance, this flight from Atlanta to Liberia would cost 31,700 SkyMiles plus $25 in taxes and fees in economy. But it would only cost 18,500 Virgin Atlantic miles plus the same taxes and fees. Even better, Air France-KLM Flying Blue would only charge you 16,500 miles, though the taxes and fees are $52. Still, that could be worth it to save nearly half your miles compared to using Delta SkyMiles! Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is a 1:1 transfer partner of: Flying Blue, meanwhile is a 1:1 transfer partner of: Even if you don't regularly fly Virgin or Air France-KLM, or fly Delta for that matter, you have tons of ways to top up your frequent-flyer accounts. Book United flights using Air Canada Aeroplan points United Airlines flies nonstop to Liberia from its major hubs, including: - Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) - Denver International Airport (DEN) - Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) - Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) United MileagePlus prices award tickets dynamically based on airfare, too, so the more tickets cost, the more miles you can expect to redeem. That's why it pays to keep Air Canada's Aeroplan program in mind since you can redeem Aeroplan points for United flights. For instance, this flight from Chicago to Liberia requires just 15,000 Aeroplan points. But the same flight would cost 20,000 United MileagePlus miles, unless you have elite status or a cobranded United credit card. That's the lowest price discrepancy I could find — typically, United flights to Costa Rica start closer to 22,500 miles each way. Now, the taxes and fees on United MileagePlus awards are just about $80 round-trip, versus $180 with Aeroplan, but it could be worth spending the extra cash to save miles, as well as the fact that round-trip airfares on this route typically run anywhere from $760-$2,200 over the next several months. Also keep in mind that if you do have elite status or a cobranded United Credit card, that you often have access to award prices that are cheaper than general MileagePlus members. That 20,000-mile award drops down to 18,000 miles, so be sure you're logged into your account to see what pricing is available to you. United is transfer partners with Chase Ultimate Rewards and Bilt, so even if you don't fly the airline regularly or have a United credit card, there are plenty of ways to stock up on miles. Air Canada Aeroplan is a transfer partner of: Whether you want to go with United miles or Aeroplan points, you have plenty of options for stocking up on them. Related: The best United credit cards Stay true (blue) to JetBlue For East Coasters, JetBlue is also a contender since it flies to Costa Rica from its hubs at: - Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) - Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL) - New York-JFK Even better, the airline's flights can be downright bargains when redeeming its own JetBlue TrueBlue points. You can find flights from JFK, in particular, for as few as 11,900 TrueBlue points plus $24-$63 each way instead of $195-$229. Like Delta and United, JetBlue prices awards dynamically based on airfares, but you can count on a solid fixed value per point of about 1.4 cents apiece. JetBlue is a transfer partner of the following programs at the following ratios: - American Express Membership Rewards (250:200), - Chase Ultimate Rewards (1:1) - Citi ThankYou Rewards (Varies from 1,000:700 to 1,000:1,000 depending on your card) Related: The best credit card for JetBlue flyers Use Marriott points at these Costa Rica hotels There's no shortage of resorts where you can redeem Marriott Bonvoy points to save on hotel rates. You can stretch your points and your budget even further by redeeming points for all-inclusive hotels. While this is not an exhaustive list, here are three great Marriott-affiliated hotels where your points can come in handy. The Westin Reserva Conchal, an All-Inclusive Golf Resort & Spa is a favorite with families and couples alike since it has an adults-only area and one for guests of all ages as well as dreamy pools and a beach club. Guests can also enjoy over a dozen bars and restaurants serving everything from tapas and pizza to Asian fusion and seafood. Rates at the Westin Reserva Conchal start at $512 or 88,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night. For something a little sultrier, you can opt for the nearby W Costa Rica-Reserva Conchal, which has just 132 rooms and 18 suites, for a more intimate, design-forward feel. While away an afternoon in one of the poolside cabanas or relaxing at the Away Spa and then celebrate with a predinner cocktail at the seaglass-inspired Living Room and dinner at the lively Zona Azul Beach Club. Rates at the W Costa Rica start at $350 or 59,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night. Marriott's latest Costa Rica resort will open later this fall. The JW Marriott Costa Elena Resort & Spa is a sophisticated new all-inclusive making its debut along the Guanacaste coast with 415 rooms and suites and a 44,000-square-foot pool among its hallmarks. Guests will also find 11 bars and restaurants and a huge spa. Rates at the JW Marriott Costa Elena start at $580 or 112,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night. Related: The best Marriott credit cards Use Hilton points at these Costa Rica hotels Hilton points turn out to be versatile whether you want to stay near the beach or up in the mountains. One of the most exciting recent additions to Costa Rica's hotel scene in recent memory is the Waldorf Astoria Costa Rica Punta Cacique, perched above beautiful Culebra Bay, about a 45-minute drive from Liberia's international airport. The resort comprises 148 guest rooms and 40 suites spanning 20 room types, so there are choices for every configuration. The hotel also offers several distinct restaurants, including Tico Tica for seafood and pasta, La Finca for upscale Costa Rican cuisine and, of course, an outpost of Waldorf's signature Peacock Alley for coffee, tea and cocktails. The Waldorf Astoria Spa is another selling point in its favor. Rates at the Waldorf Astoria Costa Rica start at $622 or 120,000 Hilton Honors points per night. Looking for something a little more niche? Remember that you can also redeem Hilton Honors points at many boutique lodges thanks to the program's partnership with Small Luxury Hotels, including the captivating Rio Perdido, which has just 38 stilted bungalows constructed of timber and volcanic stone and surrounded by lush jungle on a 1,500-acre reserve. Guests can go on wildlife hikes, zipline through the forest and swim in a geothermal river, among other distinctive activities. Rates at Rio Perdido start at $290 or 90,000 Hilton Honors points per night. Related: The best Hilton credit cards Use Hyatt points at these Costa Rica hotels Hyatt beckons with classic beach retreats as well as more unique offerings thanks to its acquisition of Mr & Mrs Smith. One of TPG staffers' all-time favorite Hyatt redemptions is the beautiful Andaz Costa Rica Resort at Peninsula Papagayo, located in a lush private development along Culebra Bay, just 45 minutes from Liberia. The hotel sprawls along a ridgeline overlooking the inlet and features a swanky cocktail bar, high-end restaurants, a peaceful little spa and plenty of pools, not to mention a private beach club to which guests can catch a free shuttle boat. Rates at the Andaz Papagayo start at $512 or 35,000 World of Hyatt points per night. Prefer an all-inclusive where you don't have to watch your dining budget? Consider the adults-only Secrets Papagayo Costa Rica, which has a more casual, but still intimate feel with just 202 rooms and suites, not to mention a beautiful oceanfront location. The hotel has a whopping 12 bars and restaurants, including an alfresco deck with a health-focused menu, a pan-Asian eatery and an Italian cucina. Rates at Secrets Papagayo start at $560 or 25,000 Hyatt points per night. Finally, for a nature-filled, off-the-grid experience in the heart of Costa Rica's rainforest, consider a visit to Origins Lodge, which is tucked up in the highlands near the country's northern border with vistas that stretch all the way to Nicaragua, about 90 minutes' drive from Liberia. The hillside bungalows are at one with their surroundings, with plenty of natural light as well as private decks with woodfired jacuzzis. Guests can enjoy gourmet meals of locally-sourced ingredients with daily changing menus in between activities like guided nature hikes to spot sloths and visit thundering waterfalls, horseback rides, whitewater rafting and more. Rates at Origins Lodge start at $885 or 76,750 World of Hyatt points per night. Related: Which credit cards should you use for Hyatt stays? Avoid resort fees when redeeming hotel points in Costa Rica Unfortunately, resort fees are a fact of life and can add hundreds of dollars to your trip cost depending on the hotel and the length of your stay. Sure, $30-$40 extra per day might not break the bank, but some resorts charge much, much more than that. The Waldorf Astoria Punta Cacique, for instance, charges a 12% mandatory daily fee. On rates that tend to hover around $1,250, that's an extra $150 per day! Luckily, Hilton Honors and World of Hyatt waive resort fees on award stays, so you might want to consider those programs first if you're going to redeem points for a hotel on your trip. Related: The 13 best all-inclusive resorts in Costa Rica for beach visits or hiking trips Save on luxury stays with premium card credits There are plenty of very high-end hotels to stay in Costa Rica, and Guanacaste in particular. If you are considering resorts on the costlier side of the budget spectrum, it could be worth taking a look at the cards in your wallet and whether they open up possibilities for booking (and saving) through the issuer's hotel booking portal. For instance, folks with either the American Express Platinum Card® or The Business Platinum Card® from American Express, you can book American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts properties and get up to $300 back in statement credits semiannually for up to a total of $600 per year on prepaid Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection bookings (of two nights or more for the latter) through American Express Travel. Not only that, but by booking through FHR, you also receive benefits like availability-based upgrades, complimentary daily breakfast for two and a $100 credit to use for on-property charges like meals or spa treatments, so you can end up saving even more. That can come in handy at a hotel like Nekajui, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve, where room rates are already high and redeeming Marriott points can come at exorbitant levels. Similarly, if you have the Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees) or the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (see rates and fees) and book a hotel that is part of The Edit by Chase Travel℠, such as the longstanding favorite Four Seasons Resort Peninsula Papagayo, Costa Rica, you are eligible for two statement credits of up to $250 each (for a total of $500) this calendar year to put toward stays of two nights or more. During your stay, you are also eligible for availability-based upgrades, complimentary daily breakfast and a $100 on-property credit. Related: Our favorite American Express Fine Hotels + Resorts around the world Use points toward activities While we often suggest redeeming points for flights and hotel nights to get the most value, don't forget that you can use certain types of points and miles for activities, in addition to travel. For example, you can redeem your Capital One miles from a card like the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card or the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card at a rate of one cent apiece for experiences like a kayak and snorkeling trip around Culebra Bay near Papagayo, or a full-day volcano zipline, horseback ride and whitewater tubing experience in the nearby mountains. If you have a card that earns Chase Ultimate Rewards points, like the Chase Sapphire Reserve or the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees), you can also redeem them at one cent apiece for activities like a catamaran sailing and snorkeling tour, or a horseback ride along Conchal Beach. Are these the highest-value redemptions? No. But if they help you create a memorable experience for yourself and your loved ones during your trip — and save you money — then, why not? Rental car documentation in Costa Rica If you want to cover some ground during your time in Costa Rica, you might consider renting a car. Especially because doing so might be cheaper than paying for your hotel's airport shuttle, and once you get to your accommodations, many resorts provide free parking. However, car rentals in Costa Rica work a little differently than in the U.S., and many other countries, for that matter. That's because you must — no getting out of it — purchase third-party liability insurance from the Instituto Nacional de Seguros, which covers damage and injuries to third parties, but does not cover you or your vehicle. It costs around $10-$20 per day. Then, unlike pretty much anywhere else you rent, just using a credit card to pay for your rental that provides primary or secondary insurance is not enough, either. Some agencies will still require you to purchase their own collision damage and liability insurance, so call ahead to see if you need to factor that in. If you do find an agency that will allow you to rely on your own credit card insurance (Alamo and Avis should let you do so), then you will still need to obtain a formal letter from your credit card stating that your rental will be covered by their insurance. A call to your card's customer service phone number should suffice, then they will email you a letter that you can print and take with you. It's a rigmarole, but worth saving hundreds of dollars over the course of even a short rental. Related: Credit card rental car insurance: Best cards and how it works Bottom line Costa Rica is truly one of the world's most versatile destinations, with something for everyone, whether it's a relaxing beach vacation, a laidback surf trip, an adrenaline-inducing adventure in the jungle or a wildlife-filled rainforest experience. There are also plenty of ways your points and miles can help you save on a trip there, so bookmark this page and come back to it for ideas. And, if you have more questions or tips of your own, feel free to share those in the comments! Frequently asked questions Many of Costa Rica’s major resorts are located along the country’s Pacific coast. The area around Guanacaste, which is served by Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport (LIR), in particular, has plenty of all-inclusive and luxury resorts including the Andaz Peninsula Papagayo Resort, Costa Rica, by Hyatt and the new Waldorf Astoria Costa Rica Punta Cacique. You can also venture up into the national parks of the north and south for a more jungly trip where adventure and wildlife are the main attractions. The best time to visit Costa Rica is from December through April, with the most temperate, sunniest months being January through March. For fewer crowds, consider a visit during the “green season” of May through November, when temperatures can be higher and there is typically a chance of rain. The number of miles you need to fly to Costa Rica depends on which airline you take and which miles you redeem, as well as the time of year since some mileage program require more miles during peak travel times. That said, you can find flights on some airlines, like American, by redeeming as few as 7,500 miles each way. You can find flights to Costa Rica on all the major U.S. airlines including Alaska Airlines, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, Southwest and United. The cost of a trip to Costa Rica depends on when you visit, how long your trip is and where you want to stay. The country has options for travelers ranging from budget flights and accommodations to luxury resorts and rainforest lodges that can cost well over $1,000 a night. Luckily, many hotels in the country are accessible using credit card rewards and hotel points.

item.title: How to get more out of every all-inclusive vacation with IHG One Rewards
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.84
How to get more out of every all-inclusive vacation with IHG One Rewards All-inclusive vacations can simplify trip planning, and IHG Hotels & Resorts makes it easy to discover, compare and book a growing range of participating all-inclusive resorts across destinations worldwide. Booking through IHG can add even more value to the experience. With IHG One Rewards, members can earn and redeem points at participating all-inclusive properties. That means a beach vacation can help fund a future trip or reduce your out-of-pocket cost if you redeem IHG points for your stay. After all, one of the biggest appeals of an all-inclusive vacation is knowing that many of your meals, drinks and activities are included in your stay. But by booking a participating all-inclusive stay through IHG, you may also be able to earn points, work toward elite status and enjoy select IHG One Rewards benefits during your stay. Here's what to know about getting more out of an all-inclusive vacation with IHG One Rewards. IHG has a growing all-inclusive portfolio IHG Hotels & Resorts has expanded its all-inclusive portfolio to give travelers more ways to discover and book resort experiences across a range of brands, destinations and stay types, all through the hotel loyalty program you already know and trust. Iberostar Beachfront Resorts are a key part of IHG's all-inclusive offering, with participating resorts in beach destinations across Mexico, the Caribbean, Europe and Africa. For example, if you're planning an all-inclusive trip to Mexico, you might look at Iberostar Selection Riviera Cancún or JOIA Paraíso by Iberostar. If the Caribbean is calling, Iberostar Selection Bávaro Suites in the Dominican Republic may be worth considering. And if you're thinking about Europe, Iberostar Jardín del Sol Suites in Mallorca might be a good fit. But IHG's all-inclusive options go beyond Iberostar Beachfront Resorts. For example, Holiday Inn Club Vacations Grand Residences All-Inclusive and Holiday Inn Club Vacations The Royal Sands All-Inclusive are notable options in Mexico. And if you're interested in an all-inclusive vacation without leaving the U.S., the voco Sandpiper All-Inclusive Resort in Florida is worth considering. Of course, the best all-inclusive resort for your trip depends on who you are traveling with and what you want from your vacation. Some resorts are better suited for families who want pools, activities and kids clubs. Meanwhile, other resorts are more appealing to couples, friends and multigenerational groups that want to package their stay, dining and activities together. That's one reason it can be useful to start your search on IHG's website or app. You can look for participating all-inclusive resorts by destination and compare options. Plus, booking through IHG ensures your IHG One Rewards number is attached to your reservation. Earn IHG points on all-inclusive stays One of the best reasons to book an all-inclusive stay through IHG is that you can earn IHG points. IHG members earn 10 points per dollar spent on qualifying stays at participating IHG hotels and resorts, including Iberostar Beachfront Resorts and Holiday Inn Club Vacations resorts. Plus, travelers with IHG elite status can earn even more through status bonuses as follows: | IHG elite status tier | Base points on qualifying stays | Status bonus on qualifying stays | Total points earned on qualifying stays | |---|---|---|---| | Member | 10 points per dollar spent | None | 10 points per dollar spent | | Silver Elite | 10 points per dollar spent | 20% | 12 points per dollar spent | | Gold Elite | 10 points per dollar spent | 40% | 14 points per dollar spent | | Platinum Elite | 10 points per dollar spent | 60% | 16 points per dollar spent | | Diamond Elite | 10 points per dollar spent | 100% | 20 points per dollar spent | Earning points can be especially valuable on an all-inclusive stay. Since these stays often cost more than a typical hotel night, a qualifying all-inclusive resort booking could earn you a significant number of IHG points. To earn IHG points on your all-inclusive stay, book through an eligible method such as the IHG website or app and confirm your IHG One Rewards number is attached to your reservation. This is important, as your stay may not qualify for points or IHG One Rewards benefits if you book through another source (including most online travel agencies). Redeem IHG points for all-inclusive stays You can also redeem IHG points for reward nights at all-inclusive properties that participate in the IHG One Rewards program. To redeem IHG points for an all-inclusive stay — including those at Iberostar Beachfront Resorts — go to IHG's website or app, log in to your account and search for your destination, dates and number of guests. Be sure to set your rate preference to "Reward Nights." From there, you can compare properties. On the results page, you'll see the starting nightly award rate and some flags that let you know if the property is all-inclusive or adults only. If you click a specific property, you can see the available room types. Note that some room types may carry a higher nightly award rate. Be sure to click "Reward Nights + All Inclusive" for the room type and rate you select to confirm what's included in the rate. It's important to enter the correct number of guests, including children, when searching for your all-inclusive vacation, as IHG adjusts reward-night pricing based on factors such as guest count and dining plan. For example, a two-night stay at Iberostar Selection Cancun in Mexico might cost 90,000 points per night for two adults but 135,000 points per night for two adults and two children. And at some resorts, such as Iberostar Waves Cristina in Spain, you can choose from breakfast-only, half-board and full all-inclusive award rates, each priced accordingly. If you have an eligible IHG One Rewards credit card, you may be able to get even more value from your points at participating IHG properties. The fourth Reward Night is free when you redeem points for any stay of four or more nights. You'll automatically see the discounted award rates at participating properties if you're logged into your account, have an eligible card and search for a reward stay of four nights or longer. Plus, eligible Cardmembers have an annual Free Night that can be enhanced with points to access hotels above the 40,000-point redemption threshold. Get IHG elite-night credits and benefits on all-inclusive stays Qualifying all-inclusive stays can also help IHG One Rewards members work toward elite status and milestone rewards. Plus, IHG One Rewards members can enjoy select benefits during qualifying all-inclusive stays at participating IHG hotels and resorts and participating Iberostar Beachfront Resorts. Even if you don't have elite status with IHG, you can access member rates, Wi-Fi access and 2 p.m. late checkout, subject to availability at participating hotels. IHG Platinum Elite and Diamond Elite members may be eligible for benefits such as early check-in, room upgrades and a welcome amenity at check-in, subject to availability. And if you have an annual lounge membership that you earned through the milestone rewards program, you can use the Star Prestige facilities when available at participating Iberostar Beachfront Resort properties. All these benefits can be especially useful at a resort. A late checkout can give you a few more hours at the pool before an evening flight, while an early check-in can make a morning arrival less awkward. And a room upgrade can make a special trip feel even more spectacular. Just keep in mind that many elite benefits are subject to availability and may vary by brand, hotel and stay type. Bottom line All-inclusive vacations are appealing because they can make travel simpler, but booking an all-inclusive stay through IHG can add another layer of value. Through IHG Hotels and Resorts, travelers can discover, compare and book all-inclusive resorts in a wide range of vacation destinations. And IHG One Rewards members can earn points on qualifying paid stays, redeem points for all-inclusive stays and enjoy member or elite benefits along the way. Whether you're planning a family beach trip, a couples getaway, a friends trip or a multigenerational vacation, it's worth checking IHG's all-inclusive options before you book.

item.title: Frontier plans first South America service, adds 3 former Spirit routes
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.76
Frontier plans first South America service, adds 3 former Spirit routes Frontier Airlines is getting ready to fly to South America for the first time. The Denver-based budget airline on Thursday announced nonstop service to three cities in Colombia. The trio of routes from Orlando International Airport (MCO) will mark the first time Frontier has sent its planes to the continent. It will also be a clear move to pick up routes abandoned by former rival Spirit Airlines, which had a significant presence in Colombia prior to its collapse earlier this year. Among the routes: nonstop service to the Colombian capital city of Bogota, along with new flights to Medellin and Cartagena. Read more: Spirit is gone. Can other budget airlines survive? "We believe there is strong, unmet demand for low-cost travel between Orlando and Colombia, and we look forward to offering affordable flight options between these two magnificent destinations," Tyri Squyres, Frontier's vice president of public and consumer affairs, said in a statement announcing the news. Read more: Frontier wants to be an airline you want to fly. Will first class and new perks do the trick? Frontier's 3 new Colombia routes Here's the full rundown of the new international service Frontier announced: | Route | Launch date | Frequency | |---|---|---| | Orlando to Jose Maria Cordova International Airport (MDE) in Medellin | Dec. 10 | Daily | | Orlando to El Dorado International Airport (BOG) in Bogota | Dec. 14 | Six times per week at the start; daily after March 6, 2027 | | Orlando to Rafael Nunez International Airport (CTG) in Cartagena | Dec. 19 | Weekly | Picking up where Spirit left off All three of those new Frontier flights were routes once served by Spirit. The now-defunct budget airline had been America's top ultra-low-cost carrier in Colombia and in South America. So, Spirit's collapse left a clear void for consumers looking to fly to the region on a budget airline. TPG's Summer Hull: An ode to Spirit Airlines — Yeah, they were all yellow It's worth watching to see whether Frontier makes further moves to acquire former Spirit routes in Latin America. Frontier executives have said the airline would take a more measured approach in picking up service abandoned by its former competitor. At the same time, the airline isn't done adding former Spirit routes to the mix — even though it has been several months since its big yellow planes were grounded. "There are opportunities to pick off markets that they've obviously exited, now, over the coming year or two," Frontier CEO James Dempsey told me in July. Worth noting The reveal of Frontier's first-ever service to South America comes days after the airline confirmed it was fully exiting America's largest market. The carrier plans to bid farewell to New York City's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) next month. Related reading:

item.title: This tiny airline lets you skip TSA and fly between small airports for less
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.64
This tiny airline lets you skip TSA and fly between small airports for less I had never before been to an airport where I could arrive 20 minutes before my flight, park for free, walk straight into the terminal and board a nine-seat plane without passing through the typical commercial airport security process. But that's exactly what happened when I flew SeaPort Airlines between Spokane, Washington, and Seattle this summer. What is SeaPort? "Please don't tell anyone about this," fellow passenger Ken Batali pleaded, moments after we disembarked a SeaPort Airlines Pilatus PC-12 turboprop plane, grabbed our bags off the cart and walked through a silent terminal to an empty curb. Along with five other passengers — more people than usual, according to our pilot — we had flown on one of SeaPort's fairly new scheduled flights between Felts Field (SFF) airport in Spokane, Washington, and King County International Airport - Boeing Field (BFI), just 5 miles south of downtown Seattle. Instead of flying from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Spokane International Airport (GEG), SeaPort Airlines operates between smaller general aviation airports (which primarily serve private, corporate, charter and other non-major-airline flights); these airports are often much closer to city centers than their larger, commercial counterparts. So, no one had to show up more than 20 minutes before the Spokane-Seattle flight, pay for parking or pass through Transportation Security Administration-style security screening. There was no limit on liquids, and each passenger could bring up to 50 pounds of baggage, including a small pet in a carrier, for free. Batali, who lives about 30 miles north of Seattle, has been flying to Spokane regularly for work. He loves that the SeaPort flights from small airports save him time and hassle when compared to typical commercial flights. How do the prices compare? Batali said he noticed that trying to book a flight weeks in advance on SeaPort usually costs more than booking in advance on either Alaska Airlines or Delta Air Lines (which fly larger planes between the larger airports, SEA and GEG). When we compared commercial versus SeaPort prices, there was about a $50 difference. However, it's the last-minute bookings — a reality of business travel — where Seaport has made Batali's life much easier. "Booking last minute, as I usually do, I can always get a seat, and the ticket price is the same as last minute on Alaska," he said. If word about SeaPort gets out, he's worried it will be more difficult (and more expensive) to make a last-minute reservation on a nine-seat aircraft. And word does seem to be getting out. On our flight, a three-member finance team from a major Spokane company was testing the time and cost benefit of SeaPort's approximately one-hour, Spokane-to-Seattle flight between the two general aviation airports. "The ticket price was pretty much the same, we all had time to have dinner at home, we got free parking, and we'll have lower Uber fees in Seattle because we land closer to downtown," one team member told me. SeaPort Airlines — a Juneau, Alaska-based carrier — began offering scheduled flights between Seattle's Boeing Field and Spokane's Felts Field in March 2026. Flights between Boeing Field and the general aviation provider next to Portland International Airport (PDX) began in May 2025. (A previous incarnation of SeaPort served that route between 2008 and 2016). And this summer, SeaPort offered seasonal service to the general aviation terminal in Redmond, Oregon, near Redmond Municipal Airport (RDM). What was it like to fly SeaPort? In August, I became curious about this tiny airline whose tagline is: "It's about time." So, I took scheduled flights between all four Pacific Northwest cities that SeaPort Airlines serves. Out of habit, I showed up an hour before each flight, which I discovered was far too early since there's no metal detector, formal identification check or other security screening. All bags get weighed, but otherwise, the preflight experience consisted of the pilot and co-pilot greeting passengers in the waiting area, checking names against a list, walking the group out to the plane and loading the bags into a netted area at the rear of the plane. Walking the few steps from the terminal to the plane for the first flight, I stopped and took a step back. Not just because I wanted to snap a photo of the airplane, but because I realized it's been a very long time since I've flown in a small plane — and this Pilatus PC-12 turboprop plane looked very small. I followed my very calm-looking fellow passengers onto the plane and took a seat by the exit door. While not fancy, there was a definite private-jet feeling. The pilot swiveled around from the cockpit to give the safety briefing before takeoff. Like Batali and the finance team from the Spokane company that requested anonymity, my fellow passengers on each flight were mostly business travelers. On my flight from Redmond through Portland and home to Seattle, I met first-time passenger Brian Hayvaz. Hayvaz is the vice president of operations for Aircare International, a Tacoma, Washington-based company that provides emergency training for the crews that staff business and private jets. The SeaPort Airlines flight had popped up in his regular commercial flight search, and he'd booked a seat right away. "I assumed SeaPort was going to be too expensive, but the pricing was competitive. It's easy and convenient," Hayvaz said. "I'd fly this airline to other destinations if I could." In addition to company executives, Andy Kline, SeaPort Airlines' marketing manager, said the passenger makeup is proving a bit surprising. "We get electricians, roofers, project managers and contractors," Kline said. "It's a lot of people who need to get to job sites in other cities and a lot of people who charge by the hour." It's certainly a different, more convenient and often less expensive way to travel regionally. No security screening? The "no TSA-style security screening" aspect of SeaPort Airlines' service is, for some, one of the more appealing and intriguing aspects of the flight experience. Airline staff watches for hazardous materials and issues, such as passengers who may be unfit for travel, Kline said. He also added that relaxed security screening is allowed because the airline is a Part 135 carrier under Federal Aviation Administration regulations, which govern scheduled service carriers operating planes carrying nine or fewer passengers, with some exceptions. But as Hansford Smith, vice president of risk management at Silver Air Private Jets, noted: "The absence of a traditional checkpoint does not mean there is no security screening." There are a variety of reasons why TSA-type screening may or may not apply to passengers on flights operated by other Part 135 operators offering scheduled service, such as Cape Air, JSX, Boutique Air, Tradewind Aviation, Mokulele Airlines and Kenmore Airlines. "In many, if not most, instances, it is a case-by-case determination by the TSA as to what the required security protocols will be," Mark A. Dombroff, partner and aviation attorney at Fox Rothschild LLP, said. He notes that the determining factors may range from the airports involved and whether passengers board or deplane through the sterile or secure areas of the airport, to the maximum certificated weight and seating capacity of the aircraft.

item.title: American and Hyatt are winding down their enhanced loyalty partnership
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.49
American and Hyatt are winding down their enhanced loyalty partnership American AAdvantage and World of Hyatt launched a partnership in 2019. My favorite part of this partnership was reciprocal earnings: Hyatt elite members could earn 1 bonus point per $1 spent on qualifying American Airlines flights, and American elite members could earn 1 bonus mile per $1 spent on qualifying Hyatt stays. Unfortunately, the programs ended reciprocal earnings on Dec. 31, 2024. And now, they've announced plans to end their enhanced loyalty partnership. American and Hyatt are ending their enhanced partnership Press releases from both American AAdvantage and World of Hyatt on Sept. 9 state the programs "have mutually decided to not continue our enhanced relationship." However, both programs say they are "committed to preserving the benefits members can earn through the current earning year in each program (including providing the standard time to select an award after it has been earned)." Specifically, American AAdvantage and World of Hyatt members will see "no interruption in earning, selecting and redeeming their eligible benefits" for "the remainder of each program's current earning year." What happens to current American-Hyatt benefits Nov. 15 will be the last day to link your AAdvantage and World of Hyatt accounts. But if your accounts are linked by Nov. 15, AAdvantage members can continue earning World of Hyatt awards through Loyalty Point Rewards through Feb. 28, 2027, and World of Hyatt members can continue earning AAdvantage awards through Milestone Rewards through Dec. 31, 2026. As a reminder, American's Loyalty Point Rewards program offers members World of Hyatt benefits at select milestones reached within an elite-qualifying year. At some milestones, you'll get perks automatically, while at other milestones, you'll get one or two choices of perks. - 100,000 Loyalty Points: Get World of Hyatt Discoverist status - 175,000 and 250,000 Loyalty Points: Choose World of Hyatt Explorist status - 400,000, 550,000 and 750,000 Loyalty Points: Choose a World of Hyatt Category 1-4 free night award - 1,000,000, 3,000,000 and 5,000,000 Loyalty Points: Choose a World of Hyatt Category 1-7 free night award I wouldn't, and haven't, chosen any of these perks as Loyalty Point Rewards since there are more valuable options. As such, I'm not particularly sad to see these options removed as of March 1, 2027. However, if you reach a Loyalty Point Rewards tier on or before Feb. 28, 2027, you'll still get the standard amount of time to select your reward and then enjoy or redeem it. American currently gives members until March 31, 2027, to select 2026 Loyalty Point Rewards. If you select Hyatt free night awards, they'll expire 180 days from the date they are issued in your World of Hyatt account (be sure to check the expiration date once the free night award is in your account). Meanwhile, the Hyatt Milestone Rewards program lets members choose American Airlines perks at select milestones: - 20 qualifying nights or 35,000 base points and 30 qualifying nights or 50,000 base points: Choose 2 Preferred seat coupons on American Airlines - 40 qualifying nights or 65,000 base points and 50 qualifying nights or 80,000 base points: Choose 2 Main Cabin Extra seat coupons on American Airlines - 70, 80 and 90 qualifying nights: Choose AAdvantage Gold status - 100, 110, 120, 130, 140 and 150 qualifying nights: Choose AAdvantage Platinum status If you reach one of these Milestone Rewards tiers on or before Dec. 31, 2026, you'll still have the standard amount of time to select your rewards and enjoy or redeem them. Seat coupons typically expire 365 days from when they were issued to your AAdvantage account, while AAdvantage status selected as a milestone reward expires on March 31 of the following full year. So if you select an AAdvantage status as a milestone reward on Dec. 1, 2026, your status will be valid through March 31, 2028. We'll also likely see the end of the ability to redeem American miles for Hyatt free-night awards and redeem Hyatt points for AAdvantage Status for a Day. But perhaps the most painful part of this partnership ending for many members will be the end of the status fast tracks for members of both programs. Bottom line American and Hyatt's partnership has already become less valuable since reciprocal earnings ended at the end of 2024, and I won't personally miss most of the current cross-program reward choices. However, I'm sad to see the status fast-track benefits disappear, as they could offer significant value to eligible members of both programs. If your AAdvantage and World of Hyatt accounts aren't already linked, it's worth doing so by Nov. 15. That will let you continue earning the current cross-program rewards through the end of each program's earning year. And even after the enhanced partnership ends, AAdvantage members will still be able to choose to earn 500 miles instead of World of Hyatt points on eligible Hyatt stays.

item.title: Have a travel problem? Here's how to write an effective complaint letter
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.43
Have a travel problem? Here's how to write an effective complaint letter Last December, Scott Tallal redeemed 68,500 American Airlines AAdvantage miles for a business-class ticket from Harrisburg International Airport (MDT) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) via Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD). Unfortunately, when he arrived at the airport for his flight, he learned that it had been canceled. Helpful agents rerouted him, but in the process, they downgraded him to economy. No worries, they told him. American Airlines would refund the difference in miles between the two classes since it was an involuntary downgrade. Six months later, despite numerous calls and emails to American Airlines customer service, Scott's points were still missing. In his last written correspondence with the airline, an agent informed him that his complaint had been extensively reviewed. According to her, American Airlines did not owe him a refund in miles or cash, and the airline considered his complaint closed. That's when Scott sent his request for help to TPG. A gaggle of gripes After I spoke to him and reviewed his paper trail, I had good news: American Airlines did owe him the refund he had been expecting. The Department of Transportation requires it, in fact. But it took me a while to untangle. So what went wrong? Scott had made one of the most common mistakes travelers make when writing a complaint: overcomplicating things. In an effort to convey the full extent of his inconvenience, Scott had submitted a laundry list of grievances. He included a lengthy narrative about previous flights, other cancellations, partner airline experiences, delays and other extraneous information. That turned what should have been a straightforward request into a complicated maze that customer service agents could not follow. In fact, when I first reviewed Scott's complaint, even I had difficulty determining what had happened and what he was asking American Airlines to do. Not surprisingly, when customer service agents — or even a consumer advocate — cannot easily identify the problem, there is little chance of a positive outcome. If you cannot pinpoint the issue, you cannot offer a solution. After I delivered his complaint to my executive contact at American Airlines in a concise, easy-to-understand format, though, Scott quickly received his miles. I review hundreds of consumer complaints each month. Many involve legitimate grievances that customer service agents and even company executives have rejected. In many of these cases, the complaint should have been approved. But the traveler made one or more common — and mostly correctable — mistakes when presenting their request. Here are the top reasons valid complaints fail and how to give yourself the best chance of finding a resolution to your problem. Make sure you're sending your complaint to the right company Even the best travel complaint letter can succeed only if a traveler delivers it to the correct entity. Unfortunately, that isn't as easy as it sounds in 2026. Recently, I received a request for help from Shane McCormick, who thought he had paid Costco Travel $6,000 for two cabins aboard Royal Caribbean's Ovation of the Seas. He was angry about the company's inability to provide what it had promised at the quoted price. Instead of two cabins, his family had been assigned just one when his itinerary came through. So what had happened? When I reviewed his paper trail, a surprising detail emerged. McCormick had not actually been corresponding with Costco Travel. Google search results had misdirected him to a scam call center posing as Costco Travel. All of McCormick's emailed complaints had been sent to the fraudsters, who had very little interest in correcting his mistaken belief — or fixing his problem. Those bad actors were only interested in spending the $6,000 they had convinced him to send them. For several years now, scammers have been flooding the internet with fake customer service centers posing as major airlines and cruise lines. And those human agents are always available and eager to receive your complaint and "help" you fix the problem. Before calling a number or emailing a grievance, it is crucial to make sure you have the company's correct contact information. Never rely on search results to find it. Instead, visit the official website of the business you are trying to reach. Check the URL in your browser to confirm. Downloading the company's app is also another reliable way to find real contact information for a cruise line, airline or hotel. If you need help locating customer service contacts or consumer-facing executives to escalate a problem beyond the frontline, my advocacy organization, Consumer Rescue, maintains a free directory that I continually update. Keep your complaint concise One of the best ways to give your complaint letter a fair chance of succeeding is to keep it concise. Earlier this month, I received a request for help from a United Airlines customer whose EU 261 claim was rejected. He sent me an eight-page missive that he had already submitted to the airline. It read like a court presentation, complete with labeled exhibits and complicated legal jargon. This traveler was surprised that his manifesto had not produced the outcome he had hoped for. He shared his suspicion that no one at United Airlines had actually read his magnum opus. I agreed. Travelers should always keep in mind that the company representative receiving the letter is likely reviewing dozens of complaints every day. You want that person to be able to scan your message and quickly figure out what happened and how to help. You can do that by keeping your complaint brief and factual. Start with the problem. End with the desired resolution. Be realistic about what you ask for. Never send a complaint that extends beyond one page. If the company needs more information, it will ask. Don't "bury the lede" in your complaint "Don't bury the lede" is a foundational rule of good journalism, and the same concept applies when writing a grievance. An effective travel complaint catches the customer service agent's attention and immediately conveys the reason for the letter. I know from my case files, however, that travelers often compose complaints that begin long before getting to the actual problem. They hide the pressing issue hundreds — and sometimes thousands — of words into the narrative. That's a mistake. Most customer service agents likely will not ever reach that far in an individual complaint. Even worse, AI programs are now reviewing and responding to many emailed grievances. These systems often limit how much text they will process. If your critical information is not near the top, the bot may never even consider it. Remember, your goal is to make the problem simple to understand and instantly clear. An easy-to-read, bullet-point list showing what happened and the resolution you are requesting often works best. If you use AI, don't forget common sense and fact-checking Increasingly, consumers are leaning on AI programs to help them compose complaint letters and the results are mixed. These programs can help travelers create professional-looking complaint letters free of typos and grammatical errors. However, AI is also known to invent laws and regulations and encourage travelers to escalate minor grievances into catastrophic, and sometimes sinister, events. In the worst cases, AI creates problems where none exist. Celebrity Cruises customer Cherie Johnson turned to AI after she and her husband were denied boarding a transatlantic cruise aboard Celebrity Equinox. The couple arrived in Lisbon, Portugal, ready to begin their much-anticipated vacation. Instead, the crew told them they needed Brazilian eVisas to board. That was something they did not have. Even before Equinox sailed away without them, Cherie began asking AI who was to blame and whether they really needed those visas. Google Gemini instantly agreed with her suspicion that they did not need visas. According to the AI bot, Celebrity had made a grave error by preventing the couple from boarding. It cited "Brazilian Decree 86715/1981," which Gemini claimed allowed cruise passengers to use the ship as a visa-free transit zone as long as they remained onboard while docked in Brazil. The AI agent also told Cherie that Celebrity was legally required to inform passengers of all documentation requirements before the cruise. But it was all an AI hallucination. Cruise ships are not visa-free immigration zones, and there is no Brazilian decree that makes them so. Cherie sent the AI-created "proof" to Celebrity Cruises' legal department and accused the crew of wrongfully denying her boarding and keeping her money. She included an itemized chart of all the things she expected the cruise line to reimburse her for beyond the cost of the cruise. The grand total exceeded $16,000. Celebrity was not swayed by the confident accusations in Cherie's letter. Despite the AI's certainty that the cruise line had made a mistake refusing to let the couple board the ship, it was wrong and Celebrity knew it. As a result nearly all her letters were simply ignored. By the time Cherie sent me a request for help she had been unsuccessfully trying to convince Celebrity for four months that it owed her $16,000. She hoped I could shine a light on what had happened and succeed in proving the cruise line's mistake. The task of telling her the truth and hopefully ending her futile battle fell to me. AI had misled her by citing an outdated legal doctrine that didn't apply to her situation. The cruise line had not made a mistake in her case. Travelers are responsible for having the documents required for their international flights and cruises. This is written into the terms and conditions of every cruise line and airline that I know of. To ensure you don't end up in the unpleasant situation this couple did, visit the State Department's website. There, you can verify what you need for entry to all countries on your itinerary. Before asking AI to help with your travel complaint, make sure you understand its limitations. These programs can confidently provide false information — especially if your questions suggest the answer you want to hear. Always independently verify the "facts" AI provides. And never sign your name to a complaint letter until you have thoroughly researched every claim it contains. Don't file a credit card dispute before appealing to the company first The Fair Credit Billing Act (FCBA) allows consumers to dispute credit card charges involving billing errors or unauthorized transactions. But a chargeback should not be your opening move. I see consumers misuse this important protection every day — sometimes with devastating consequences. First, ask the company with which you have an issue to try to resolve your problem. Follow its complaint process and give it a reasonable opportunity to investigate. Do not simultaneously file a complaint with the company and a dispute with your credit card issuer. Once a chargeback is underway, the company will typically allow that process to play out instead of continuing to negotiate with you. If you lose the dispute, the company will have very little motivation to reopen your case — even if your original complaint was legitimate. By then, you may also have weakened your chances of getting help from a consumer advocate. The proper order of events is simple: Exhaust your options with the company first. Consider a credit card dispute only after those efforts fail and only if your claim qualifies under the FCBA. Don't insult the company or declare "I'll never be your customer again" Telling a company you're done with it and will never give them business again is counterproductive. Think about it: If you've written off the company, why shouldn't it write you off too? Your complaint letter should be cordial, clearly explain the facts and propose a reasonable resolution. Yet so many complaint letters I receive begin with some version of: "I will never use your services again. Now give me the goodwill gesture I'm asking for." Surely, once the emotion is removed from the situation, most travelers can see the problem with that approach. In nearly every case, the traveler feels mistreated by a company they have been loyal to. They do not really want to never be its customer again. They want to be heard and have their problem handled properly. However, by telling a company that you will never patronize it again, you disincentivize it from helping you. Before sending this type of letter, take a breath and think about what you really want. Maybe even close your browser for the night. In the morning, start again and explain what the company can do to keep you as a valued customer. Do not threaten legal action In the age of AI, this is becoming increasingly important to underscore. AI seems to love escalating minor problems into legal battles. But consumers should understand that once they send a legal threat to an airline, cruise line or other travel provider, they had better be prepared to follow through. The problem is that ordinary travelers are being encouraged to make legal threats without any factual basis. As a professional mediator and TPG's ombudsman, I always begin by attempting a cordial resolution. Most legitimate travel complaints can be resolved with a friendly overture to the company backed by clear facts. But if you open your complaint with a threat to sue or announce that you have involved a lawyer, your letter will likely be forwarded directly to the company's legal department. At that point, frontline customer service may no longer be willing or authorized to help you. I have seen consumers threaten legal action over disputes involving as little as $25. Companies recognize these empty threats for what they are, and those complaints often land in a virtual garbage can. If you genuinely want the company's help, leave the legal threats out of your complaint. Make your complaint clear A concise complaint is not necessarily a clear one. Make sure your message explains what went wrong, when it happened and what you are asking the company to do about it. Include your confirmation or reservation number and any evidence that directly supports your claim, such as a receipt, cancellation notice, or written promise from a company representative. Leave out unrelated documents and details that make the problem harder to follow. Before sending your complaint, ask someone unfamiliar with the situation to read it. If that person can't quickly explain what went wrong and what you want the company to do, the customer service agent probably won't be able to either. Over at Consumer Rescue, I have published a free resource page that includes a template for an effective complaint letter along with a variety of sample letters. The bottom line Writing an effective complaint letter doesn't have to be difficult if you keep a few things in mind. The letters that receive the most favorable response follow the three C's. They are: - Cordial - Concise - Clear But don't forget one more essential ingredient: a reasonable proposed resolution. Travelers often weaken legitimate complaints by asking for far more than the situation warrants. Asking a company to correct its mistake or reimburse a documented loss is reasonable. Demanding a full refund, substantial additional compensation and a pile of loyalty points for a relatively minor problem probably is not. The goal of a complaint is to make you whole — not to provide a windfall. Customer service agents are much more likely to help when they can quickly understand what happened, why you believe the company is responsible and what you are asking to be made right. Leave out the insults, legal threats, lengthy backstory and anything else that distracts from your central problem. You may not receive exactly the outcome you want. But keeping your complaint cordial, concise and clear — and ending with a fair proposed resolution — gives it the best chance of reaching someone who can, and wants to, help. If you have a problem with a cruise line, airline, car rental company, vacation rental or credit card company, send your request for free help to ombudsman@thepointsguy.com. I'll be happy to try to help or offer advice that may allow you to resolve the problem on your own.

item.title: 7 ways I'd redeem the 125,000-mile bonus on the Citi / AAdvantage Executive card
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.37
7 ways I'd redeem the 125,000-mile bonus on the Citi / AAdvantage Executive card Editor's Note American Airlines AAdvantage miles offer excellent value, particularly for lie-flat business-class seats and the occasional first-class flight. With the welcome bonus on the Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® (see rates and fees), you have enough miles to chase some genuinely premium redemptions. Right now, there's a limited-time, best-ever bonus: Earn 125,000 bonus miles after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first five months from account opening. Based on TPG's September 2026 valuations, this bonus alone is worth $1,813. But here's a sweetener: Combine that 125,000-mile bonus with the miles you'll earn on the $15,000 minimum spending requirement (at least 1 mile per dollar), and you're looking at a minimum of 140,000 AAdvantage miles to redeem. The AAdvantage program has both a fixed award chart for most partners and dynamic pricing (which can fluctuate based on demand) for American Airlines and Fiji Airways flights. In this guide, I focus primarily on fixed-price redemptions with partner airlines, as they offer predictable value (though you'll also find some American Airlines and Fiji Airways options). I've used over a million AAdvantage miles to fly to places like Brazil, Hong Kong and Jordan, so here are my top seven picks for redemptions that deliver real value. Business class to Europe Transatlantic business class is one of the most prized redemptions for those with points and miles. You have solid options for American's own Flagship cabin and on partner carriers, each with distinct advantages. American Airlines I flew American's newest business-class seat between Chicago's O'Hare International Airport (ORD) and London's Heathrow Airport (LHR) last summer, and while I don't think it's a world-leading product, it's definitely a step above the older seat. The sliding privacy door is ideal for sleeping on the red-eye flight to Europe. This redemption is priced dynamically. The cheapest I found from ORD to LHR over the next year was 73,500 miles (plus $5.60 in taxes and fees), with a more common price of 97,000 to 100,000 miles. Finnair and Iberia Finnair operates nonstop to Helsinki Airport (HEL) — ideally placed for Nordic exploration and connections throughout Europe — from: - Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) - Miami International Airport (MIA) - New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) - ORD - Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) The carrier's Airbus A350 business-class cabin is comfortable, with excellent food and friendly service. Both Finnair and Iberia offer fixed-price redemptions at 57,500 miles one-way (plus $5.60 in taxes and fees), and you can connect throughout Europe on the same award without burning extra Avios (just pay the applicable taxes). I'm based in Madrid (Iberia's hub) and can confirm it offers strong availability and solid access across the U.S. Avoid British Airways Here's where British Airways stands apart from American Airlines, Finnair and Iberia: It adds fuel surcharges onto award redemptions. An ORD-to-LHR flight on American costs $5.60. Fly the same route on British Airways, and you're looking at $734. That's a huge gap. Qsuite to the Middle East and beyond I've flown Qatar Airways' Qsuite several times, and I'm flying it again at the end of the year to Australia to visit family. This product set the gold standard for business-class design. If traveling with a companion, you can convert two adjacent suites into a double bed. You can fly from most major U.S. airports to Doha's Hamad International Airport (DOH) for 70,000 miles (plus $15 in taxes and fees). Connections to the Middle East, Egypt, India or the Maldives cost no additional miles (just taxes), and onward flights to Africa add 5,000 miles. Award availability for these flights can be tight, so use a tool like Thrifty Traveler or Seats.aero for alerts. Qatar Airways delivers excellent service and food, with Starlink high-speed Wi-Fi on most long-haul flights. Flights from U.S. airports to DOH take 13 to 17 hours, so you can make that time genuinely productive. First class to Asia Cathay Pacific and Japan Airlines are both high-quality Oneworld partners that offer access to first-class travel across the Pacific. AAdvantage gives you access to two distinct products, each with its own appeal. Fly to Tokyo's Haneda Airport (HND) on Japan Airlines for 80,000 miles one-way (plus $5.60 in taxes and fees) in its latest Airbus A350 first class, which operates from DFW, JFK and Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). The airline excels in food and service and features embedded seat speakers for a more immersive experience. This is one of the next redemptions I'm eyeing. Or, you can fly Cathay Pacific first class one-way to Hong Kong International Airport (HKG) for 110,000 miles (plus $5.60 in taxes and fees), with business-class connections throughout Asia included (taxes only). The onboard product feels dated, but you'll get excellent food and access to the newly renovated The Wing, First lounge at HKG, which features private shower suites, fine dining and spa services. Business class to the South Pacific Australia and New Zealand are far away, so premium cabins make sense. Qantas to Australia and New Zealand Flying Qantas, Australia's flag carrier, Down Under costs 80,000 miles one-way in business class (plus $28 in taxes and fees). The airline flies from several U.S. airports to Australia's Sydney Airport (SYD), Melbourne Airport (MEL) and Brisbane Airport (BNE) and also operates from JFK to Auckland Airport (AKL) in New Zealand. I'll be honest: In my experience, it's an average product in terms of customer service, food and the seat itself. But beggars can't be choosers when flying premium cabins across the Pacific. Business-class awards on transpacific flights are among the most coveted redemptions available, so book either 11 months before departure (when the AAdvantage calendar opens) or within a month before departure (when remaining seats are released). Fiji Airways Fiji Airways has dynamic pricing starting at 80,000 miles one-way (plus $5.60 in taxes and fees) to Fiji's Nadi International Airport (NAN). The airline operates from DFW, LAX and San Francisco International Airport (SFO), and Fiji has become an increasingly popular stop on longer South Pacific itineraries. Fiji Airways is known for its warm service and child-friendly environment. Business class to Morocco Royal Air Maroc has reliable award availability for lie-flat business-class seats from JFK, LAX, MIA and Dulles International Airport (IAD) near Washington, D.C., to Mohammed V International Airport (CMN) in Casablanca, Morocco. The product isn't luxurious, but it offers good value at 57,500 miles (plus $5.60 in taxes and fees). You can connect onward through Morocco for no additional miles (taxes only) or catch the high-speed rail to Marrakech in about three hours. More broadly, the airline operates extensive service across Southern and Western Europe, so Casablanca serves as a good connecting hub even if Morocco isn't your destination. Short-haul domestic flights in economy Not every trip calls for premium cabins. Cash fares for domestic flights have increased significantly, so redeeming AAdvantage miles and paying as little as $5.60 in taxes and fees can offer good value. Short-haul economy flights, such as those from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) to DFW, start at just 5,000 miles. Use economy awards strategically on routes where other airlines don't compete effectively. Select flights from airports outside the US The best miles value sometimes comes from redemptions booked outside the U.S., especially if you're already traveling internationally and can position yourself at the right hub. - Australia to Southeast Asia: I'm flying from SYD to Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) in the Philippines in January, with the eight-hour Qantas business-class flight costing me only 40,000 miles (plus $80 in taxes and fees). - Etihad Airways first class between Europe and the Middle East: I've flown this product once before, and you can take a shower in the sky. A sweet spot is flying from its hub at Abu Dhabi's Zayed International Airport (AUH) to Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) or LHR for 62,500 miles (plus $37 in taxes and fees). If you can find award availability, it's one of the most aspirational redemptions in the world. - Gol Airlines within South America: Using cash for domestic flights within Brazil can be expensive. But you can redeem AAdvantage miles on Gol Airlines flights within Brazil (except Manaus) for 7,000 miles one-way (plus $7 in taxes and fees) and from Brazil to Argentina for 10,000 miles (plus $13 in taxes and fees). It's one of the region's best-value redemption options. Bottom line The 125,000-mile welcome bonus on the Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Legend Mastercard is substantial, although the $15,000 spending requirement won't make sense for everyone. If you can meet it without spending more than you normally would, you'll end up with at least 140,000 AAdvantage miles. That's enough for two one-way business-class awards to Europe, a round-trip Qsuite itinerary to the Maldives or a one-way first-class flight to Asia (assuming you can find availability). For me, AAdvantage miles remain most valuable for these fixed-price partner awards, particularly when the taxes and fees are low (as is the case for all of the recommendations in this guide). To learn more, read our full review of the Citi / AAdvantage Executive card. Apply here: Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Legend Mastercard

item.title: We visited the New 7 Wonders of the World on 1 ticket — here's how
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.36
